papers.title: Transporting the Past: An Optimal Transport View of Backtracking Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: We study backtracking counterfactual inference for Structural Causal Models (SCMs) through the lens of optimal transport. In SCMs, a factual observation generally induces a posterior distribution over exogenous variables, making counterfactual inference inherently distributional. We introduce two complementary frameworks that transport this posterior onto the set of exogenous configurations satisfying a desired counterfactual query. The first constructs a natural pointwise projection and is suitable when the transported exogenous distribution can be used directly. The second enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables, so that the transported variables remain interpretable as genuine exogenous noises of the same SCM. We show that both frameworks are consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle, and we propose marginal, penalty-based, and hard-constrained solvers for finite-posterior settings. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the geometry of the problem and reveal trade-offs among transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.

papers.intro:
Counterfactual reasoning asks how a realized system would have evolved under alternative circumstances (Pearl, 2009; Pearl et al., 2016). In Structural Causal Models (SCMs), the classical abduction–action–prediction procedure gives rise to interventional counterfactuals: the exogenous background inferred from the factual evidence is retained, while the structural assignments of the intervened variables are replaced by constants. This semantics is appropriate for questions about the consequences of hypothetical manipulations. Other questions concern the background conditions under which a different event could have occurred without changing the system’s mechanisms. For such questions, an intervention on a non-root variable severs its ordinary dependence on its causes and may fail to express the intended alternative history. In the terminology of Lewis (Lewis, 1979), the intervention can be understood as permitting a local “small miracle.”

Backtracking counterfactuals offer a complementary, mechanism-preserving semantics. They retain the structural assignments and ask which alternative exogenous conditions could have generated a specified counterfactual antecedent (von Kügelgen et al., 2023; Vandenburgh, 2023). The distinction matters because intervening on an event and explaining how that event could have differed need not produce the same answers. Both answers follow from their respective assumptions; the choice depends on whether the question concerns an external manipulation or an alternative history under unchanged mechanisms. Such history-oriented queries are relevant to retrospective explanation and some forms of fairness analysis and counterfactual recourse (Bynum et al., 2024).

papers.title: Deep-UV All-dielectric qBIC Metasurface for Refractive Index Sensing
papers.abstract: All-dielectric metasurfaces supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) have emerged as powerful platforms for biosensing, yet their operation remains largely concentrated in the visible and near-infrared regimes. Extending these resonances into the deep-ultraviolet (DUV) to probe the intrinsic electronic absorption of biomolecules presents substantial material and nanofabrication challenges. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a hafnium dioxide (HfO$_{2}$) metasurface supporting DUV qBICs in the wavelength range from 225 nm to 340 nm with quality factors reaching 500. We further demonstrate its refractive index sensing capabilities through integration with a microfluidic cell and optical characterization in reflection mode. We show that the introduction of an aqueous buffer leads to a further quality factor enhancement. Achieving a sensitivity of up to approximately 60 nm/RIU and an operational figure of merit of 40 $\mathrm{RIU}^{-1}$, this low-loss HfO$_{2}$ metasurface provides a robust foundation for label-free DUV biosensing.

papers.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
papers.abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

papers.intro:
Identifying early disease markers has repeatedly transformed clinical practice and patient outcomes [7]. Clinical discovery is inherently challenging as evidence of potentially novel markers is captured across diverse, often unstructured and high-dimensional modalities, including 2D and 3D imaging, laboratory results, and textual reports [6]. Moreover, the growing volume of clinical data, including approximately 300 million CT scans acquired worldwide each year [8], creates opportunities to identify new markers and uncover unknown associations with a broader range of clinical outcomes. Yet this growth also highlights a gap in our ability to process these data at scale, given the time and expertise required to manually define, annotate, and validate candidate disease markers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a means of accelerating scientific discovery [1]. In protein folding and materials science, targeted models have sharply reduced the time and cost of identifying promising candidates [9, 10, 11]. Attempts to automate clinical science have searched large databases of manually coded phenotypes through phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) [2, 12]. Efforts to accelerate this approach use deep learning or agents to automate the annotation of phenotypes directly from images, but still restricts investigation to a preselected set of chosen markers [3, 4, 13]. As a result, clinical discovery still lacks an efficient framework for identifying open-ended, reproducible, and independent disease markers within multimodal data.

One potential solution lies in foundation model (FM) embeddings. Trained on large volumes of multimodal medical data, FMs produce embeddings that characterize patient states [14]. Such embeddings have been observed to perform well on tasks they were not explicitly trained for [15, 16, 17, 14], including disease prognosis and risk stratification, suggesting that they contain clinically meaningful associations beyond their original training objectives. However, these markers remain entangled within high-dimensional vectors, making them difficult to isolate and evaluate as candidate markers. Recently, mechanistic interpretability [18, 19, 20] has emerged as a self-supervised approach to uncover interpretable concepts encoded within FM embeddings, without the need for prospective annotation. Yet its broader potential for transforming FMs into engines of clinical discovery remains largely unexplored.

To address this gap, we introduce Glyph, a framework that turns foundation model (FM) embeddings into concepts for clinical discovery. The name derives from “glyph,” or a symbol that conveys meaning, reflecting our goal of giving hidden information a form that can be studied. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, Glyph discovers coded concepts directly in FM embeddings and detects them across patients without requiring candidate markers to be defined and annotated in advance. These extracted concepts are measurable, interpretable patterns in patient data that together preserve the FM’s predictive capacity. Glyph integrates them with established clinical variables and tests their associations with disease-related outcomes across patient populations. This enables efficient, closed- and open-ended discovery that is infeasible with embeddings alone or with agentic systems operating on a limited set of pre-defined concepts. Our contributions are as follows:

1. Establishing the concept space. To make FM embeddings useful for discovery, we develop the Glyph framework to first represent such embeddings in sets of sparse features, and then filter and interpret these as clinically meaningful concepts. Specifically, we evaluated features for significant prognostic associations, reproducibility across three sites, persistence after adjustment for measured confounders, and overall interpretability. Glyph identified 397 predictive concepts bearing 4,463 significant associations to 141 future disease outcomes meeting a Bonferroni threshold of p≤8.28×10−8p\leq 8.28\times 10^{-8}. Identifying concepts with at least one significant association yielded a space of high-risk concepts, capturing disease risk across modalities. Concept interpretations and prognostic associations also reproduced in external cohorts. 2. Rediscovery and discovery. The validated concept space recovered established prognostic relationships across several disease axes, including hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, and oncologic disease. When tested in held-out cohorts, these associations reproduced across institutions. Glyph then extended these findings by linking established risk markers to additional outcomes and identifying reproducible prognostic associations that remain poorly characterized in the literature. Beyond disease-specific risk profiles, Glyph identified systemic risk markers across modalities, with one imaging and three laboratory concepts retaining broad associations across disease groups after adjustment for potential confounders. Glyph revealed that nearly half of the high-risk imaging concepts were not consistently documented in the accompanying radiology reports. 3. Comparison with literature We investigated whether and in which domains Glyph brought additional prognostic value over the clinical literature. To this end, a co-scientist agent processed 342,647 clinical papers covering each discovery axes, and reproduced 412 published markers in our data. We found using just ten Glyph concepts per axis led to significantly stronger models in external data than literature markers alone (3.34% AUC gain, p=2.66×10−28p=2.66\times 10^{-28}), with predictive improvements of up to 11.7% in specific axes. Comparing the top ten Glyph concepts with the top ten literature markers per outcome, selected at the Discovery Site, Glyph associations reproduced more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort (64.8% vs. 41.2%, p=2.54×10−6p=2.54\times 10^{-6}) at higher median confounder-adjusted odds ratios (1.31 vs. 1.16, p=5.0×10−5p=5.0\times 10^{-5}). 4. A validated concept space also supports other applications including explainable patient-level predictions and retrieval. We also release the Glyph MCP, enabling clinicians, engineers, and AI agents to investigate patient data and test open-ended hypotheses and applications through concepts.

papers.title: Evaluation of a Multi-Link Machine Learning Approach for Rainfall Detection Using Satellite Microwave Links
papers.abstract: The impacts of climate change have increased the need for reliable real-time rainfall monitoring systems. This study investigates rainfall detection using a network of opportunistic sensors based on satellite microwave links (SMLs) combined with machine learning (ML) classifiers. Two models, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), were trained on aggregated SML data, including information from neighboring links. The results demonstrate that leveraging information from multiple links substantially enhances the detection of both wet and dry periods compared to single-link approaches. Moreover, the RF model consistently provides a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, improving rainfall detection and reducing misclassifications overall, with particularly strong performance during harsh weather conditions. The study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.

papers.intro:
Accurate real-time rainfall monitoring is essential for water resource management, agriculture, urban planning, and disaster prevention, supporting early warning systems for hazards such as floods and landslides, reducing human and economic losses [13], [5], [17]. However, achieving sufficient spatial and temporal coverage remains challenging. Opportunistic microwave links provide a cost-effective solution with wide spatial coverage via existing telecommunication infrastructures [1], [2], [8], [6]. Satellite microwave links (SMLs), especially in the Ku and Ka bands, are sensitive to rainfall-induced attenuation, enabling indirect rainfall estimation [12], [7]. An example is the Smart Rainfall System (SRS) [4], deployed in the Polcevera River Basin, which uses satellite signal attenuation to classify wet/dry periods and estimate rainfall intensity (RI).

In recent years, ML and signal processing techniques have been widely explored for the real-time recognition of rain and non-rain conditions. In [11], a randomized trees classifier was applied to received power signals for precipitation detection and attenuation estimation, enabling rain rate retrieval at 1-minute resolution. In [16], a support vector machine (SVM) was used to classify rain and non-rain periods from SML signals, while a long short-term memory network estimated the attenuation baseline. A convolutional neural network (CNN) was proposed in [14] to detect rainfall events using data from 800 commercial microwave links (CML) in Germany, with the gauge-adjusted RADOLAN-RW radar product as reference. Similarly, [18] trained two neural networks based on signal attenuation measurements from CML, using rain-gauge and radar data as reference sources, to identify rainy and dry time steps across a large CML dataset. In [15], an SVM was employed to classify wet and dry periods using attenuation statistics. However, despite the growing interest in SML-based rainfall monitoring, a significant gap remains in reconstructing rainfall fields over large areas using SML networks combined with ML techniques.

In our previous study [10], wet and dry periods were classified independently for each SRS link, using only features derived from the same link, thus neglecting the spatial distribution of sensors over the territory. This single-link approach, although effective, does not account for the spatial correlation of rainfall events, which typically affect multiple nearby links simultaneously. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a spatially aware multi-link approach, which represents the main novelty of this work. The proposed method includes information from neighboring links, which are likely to be affected by the same rainfall event due to their geographical proximity, thus providing complementary information that enhances the robustness and accuracy of rain detection. This transition from an independent single-link analysis to a multi-link modeling strategy allows the model to better capture the spatial structure of rainfall phenomena, improving the classification of wet and dry periods compared to our previous work [10]. The study was validated by using four groups of neighboring links of the Valpolcevera river basin, including a total of 16 SRS sensors, to evaluate both a feature-based RF model and a 2D-CNN fed by the raw signals.

papers.title: Keyline Detection with YOLO: Runway Perception for Vision-Based Aircraft Landing
papers.abstract: Modern object detectors can predict keypoints as per-object geometric features, but keypoints are inherently vulnerable to occlusion and truncation. Object edges can provide complementary information, often remaining observable even when partially occluded or when their defining endpoints leave the field of view. We therefore introduce object keyline detection, the task of predicting a fixed, semantically ordered set of infinite lines per object instance. Unlike the outputs of general line-segment detectors, each keyline is associated with an object instance and identified by a semantic index, providing a line-level analog of keypoints. To solve this task, we extend YOLO with keyline prediction parameterized in continuous Hesse-normal form $[\rho,\cos\theta,\sin\theta]$, and introduce Object Keyline Similarity (OKLS), which serves as an evaluation metric, target assignment signal, and regression loss. We instantiate this formulation on runway perception in vision-based landing, a motivating example containing semantic linear features that remain partially observable throughout the approach. Experiments show that our representation achieves the highest detection accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations, and keylines integrate directly into standard YOLO heads as additional output channels without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.

Keypoint prediction has become a widespread capability of modern object detectors, as the detection of semantic per-object features enables downstream geometric tasks like pose estimation. Keypoints, however, can only represent point-based features. For objects characterized by prominent edges, this is limiting: a keypoint that is occluded or truncated provides no information, whereas the corresponding edge can remain partially observable and still convey orientation and perspective (e.g., Fig. 1).

General line-segment detectors address the extraction of linear image structures, but they solve a different problem. Methods such as M-LSD [10], HAWP [28], and LINEA [14] predict unordered, image-level collections of finite line segments. Their outputs are neither associated with individual object instances nor assigned a stable semantic identity. Conversely, object detectors can predict bounding boxes and semantic keypoints for multiple object instances, but do not include line features among their per-object predictions. Thus, existing approaches do not provide a line-level analog of semantic keypoint detection.

To bridge this gap, we introduce object keyline detection, extending object detectors to predict instance-bound geometric lines alongside keypoints. Unlike finite line segments, keylines are predicted as infinite lines without spatial extent targets, while finite support annotations define where line accuracy is evaluated. This formulation provides a direct line-level analog to semantic keypoint detection.

We instantiate object keyline detection for runway perception in vision-based aircraft landing [2] (see Fig. 2). In such a system, correct estimation of runway geometry throughout the final approach is critical. However, corner keypoints frequently suffer from field-of-view truncation during the close-range phase (Fig. 1), causing Perspective-nn-Point (PnP)[18] solvers to lose geometric constraints while edge features remain observable. Keylines provide a persistent geometric representation under these conditions and could serve as a fallback when keypoint detection fails. Since recent runway detection systems commonly employ YOLO [23] models [19, 5], we extend YOLO keypoint detection [21] with keyline prediction.

Object keyline detection raises two central questions: how should keylines be parameterized for stable regression in YOLO models, and how should they be compared during model evaluation and optimization? We address the first through a controlled comparison of line parameterizations and the second by introducing Object Keyline Similarity (OKLS), an adaptation of Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS)to keylines. We make the following contributions: • We formulate object keyline detection as predicting a fixed, semantically ordered tuple of infinite lines per object instance, instantiating it as a native YOLO extension and demonstrating it on runway perception. • We introduce OKLS(Object Keyline Similarity) as a unified evaluation metric, target assigner, and regression loss, enabling AP and AR metrics for keylines. • We benchmark four line parameterizations and find the continuous Hesse normal form (ρ,cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\rho,\cos\theta,\sin\theta) to be the most accurate of the evaluated representations on our benchmark. • We evaluate fused- and split-head architectures for joint keypoint–keyline prediction, demonstrating that a fused head adds keylines without degrading keypoint accuracy or adding meaningful latency. • We compare against general line-segment detectors under an oracle matching protocol, demonstrating higher average precision in detecting object-associated lines.

papers.title: The PICO-40L detector
papers.abstract: The PICO collaboration has designed and constructed a novel bubble chamber to search for evidence of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, a leading dark matter candidate. The PICO-40L detector is the successor to PICO-60, and uses a fully redesigned system for pressurization of the active volume after a bubble nucleation event. Pressure in PICO-40L is transferred to the target fluid through a set of two nested synthetic quartz vessels connected by bellows below the active volume. This is in contrast to the design of earlier detectors in which the pressure was transferred through a buffer fluid atop the target fluid, within a single synthetic quartz vessel connected to a bellows above the active volume. Removing the buffer fluid removes the potential for backgrounds arising from the interface between the two fluids, and moving the bellows below the target fluid suppresses potential backgrounds from particulates originating from the bellows. The newly designed detector concept of PICO-40L is referred to as the Right-Side-Up (RSU) design and requires a dedicated thermal system to keep the lower region of the detector cold while the upper region is stably superheated. The main goal of PICO-40L is to establish the performance characteristics of the RSU detector concept, which will inform the operating configuration of the final generation PICO dark matter detector, PICO-500, which is currently under construction at SNOLAB. This paper reviews the design, installation, and performance of the PICO-40L detector.

papers.title: Magnetically Arrested Accretion and Black Hole Spin in a Semi-Analytic Model of Galaxy Formation
papers.abstract: We present {\sc Mad Sage}, a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation that couples black hole mass and spin evolution to gas accretion and AGN feedback under magnetically arrested disk conditions. Building on the {\sc Dark Sage} model, we incorporate GRMHD-calibrated prescriptions for spin evolution and jet power, spin-dependent radiative efficiencies, and remnant spins from BH-BH mergers. We compare accretion and feedback models, including coherent disk-fed accretion with mixed coherent and incoherent hot-halo accretion, with and without additional mechanical feedback. We find that incoherent accretion, together with Blandford-Znajek spin-down, drives massive BHs toward low spins, reducing jet efficiencies and weakening the quenching of massive galaxies. Reproducing the high-mass end of the stellar mass function requires either exclusively coherent accretion or an additional feedback component provided by ADAF outflows. Our models broadly reproduce observed BH-galaxy scaling relations, disk surface density profiles, and the AGN luminosity function at $z\sim 2-6$, although the spin models under-predict the number density of faint AGN at low redshift. At $z\lesssim 3$, predicted BH spins decrease with increasing BH mass, while at higher redshifts, the mass dependence weakens. Spin distributions peak at $|a_\star|\sim 0.5$-$0.7$, below current X-ray reflection spectroscopy measurements, and become bimodal for massive, quiescent BHs accessible with the next generation Event Horizon Telescope and the Black Hole EXplorer. We report that the predicted LISA event rates are nearly independent of the adopted accretion and spin models.

papers.intro:
Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) reside at the centers of most massive galaxies and are now understood to play a critical role in regulating star formation through Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) feedback [78, 135, 45, 93, 46, 77, 144, 151]. The mass evolution of SMBHs has been studied extensively through quasar luminosity functions, black hole (BH) mass functions, and scaling relations with host galaxy properties [83, 155, 61, 54, 77, 114, 127, 56, 142, 22]. Yet astrophysical BHs are characterized by two physical parameters: mass and spin. While the mass-evolution of SMBHs has been the focus of considerable theoretical efforts [58, 161, 33, 112, 156], the spin dimension has received comparatively less attention in models of galaxy formation, despite its far-reaching consequences for AGN feedback, gravitational wave astronomy, and the interpretation of multi-messenger observations.

BH spin determines the efficiency with which accreted rest-mass energy is converted into radiation and jet power. For a geometrically thin, radiatively efficient disk, the radiative efficiency εthin\varepsilon_{\rm thin} ranges from ≈4%\approx 4\% for a maximally retrograde BH to ≈40%\approx 40\% for a maximally prograde one [102], compared to the fixed ∼10%\sim 10\% typically assumed in galaxy formation models. Separately, and especially in radiatively inefficient modes of accretion, the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) mechanism [19] extracts rotational energy from the BH via large-scale magnetic fields threading the horizon, powering relativistic jets with efficiencies that can exceed unity for near-maximal spins [149, 88, 95]. The jet efficiency scales steeply with spin as ηEM∝a⋆2\eta_{\rm EM}\propto a_{\star}^{2}, where a⋆a_{\star} is the dimensionless BH spin parameter [19, 91, 87, 148, 29]. Even modest changes in the spin distribution translate directly into order-of-magnitude changes in the radio jet power, and therefore, in the ability of AGN to quench star formation in massive galaxies.

At low Eddington ratios (M˙≲0.01\dot{M}\lesssim 0.01), the accreting gas cannot cool efficiently and inflates into a geometrically thick, radiatively inefficient flow known as an advection-dominated accretion flow [98, 99, 169, ADAF;]. In this regime, large-scale magnetic flux can efficiently accumulate at the BH horizon. Once the accumulated flux reaches a saturated value ϕ\phi and is strong enough to arrest the inflow, the disk enters the magnetically arrested disk [96, 149, 66, 17, MAD;] state. A MAD is distinguished from the Standard and Normal Evolution [97, SANE;] state, in which the magnetic field remains relatively weak and disordered. In MAD states, the organized flux greatly amplifies the efficiency of the BZ jet relative to the SANE state. MAD BHs can launch jets with efficiencies well in excess of unity for near maximal spins [149, 88, 95, 118]. We focus on the MAD regime because it represents the physical conditions under which BH spin has the strongest leverage on jet power, and therefore, on radio-mode AGN feedback in massive galaxies. Semi-analytic models that fix the jet efficiency or assume a universal accretion mode miss this spin dependence entirely. Mad Sage is designed to capture it self-consistently across cosmic time.

BH spin evolves through three main channels. Coherent disk accretion, where gas angular momentum is consistently aligned with the BH spin, drives spin-up and can bring a BH to near-maximal spin after accreting roughly its own mass [10, 153, 91, 52, 163]. Incoherent (chaotic) accretion, where successive accretion episodes arrive with randomly oriented angular momenta, may drive spin-down towards low equilibrium values [74, 73, 49, 9]. BH-BH mergers contribute to both spin-up and spin-down depending on the progenitor spin and mass ratio, with the orbital angular momentum of the binary providing an additional spin-up contribution to the remnant [117, 14, 63, 159]. Finally, in the MAD state, BZ jet launching itself drives spin-down by extracting rotational energy from the BH horizon, establishing an equilibrium spin that depends on the accretion rate and the disk state [148, 97, 122, 95, 118]. At the ADAF equilibrium, this spin settles near a⋆≈0.035a_{\star}\approx 0.035, while near-Eddington thin disk accretion settles near a⋆≈0.7a_{\star}\approx 0.7-0.80.8.

Early semi-analytic models of BH spin evolution [163, 14, 9] showed that coherent accretion, chaotic accretion, and BH-BH mergers together produce a broad spin distribution across the galaxy population. These works show that massive BHs, which accrete more from the hot halo through randomly oriented Bondi inflow, tend to have lower spins than lower-mass BHs whose growth is dominated by coherent cold disk feeding. These models applied analytic innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO)-based efficiencies from the Novikov-Thorne thin-disk formula, not accounting for the role of magnetic fields in BH spin evolution and growth. They also did not couple spin evolution to the full galaxy formation context. More recently, Izquierdo-Villalba et al. [67] extended L-Galaxies semi-analytic model (SAM) with spin-dependent radiative efficiencies through the Novikov-Thorne ISCO formula [102], linking accretion coherence to host bulge kinematics through the v/σv/\sigma ratio. The model applies the thin-disk formula across all accretion rates, making no distinction between ADAF, thin-disk, or MAD regimes. No BZ jet torque is included. They find that BHs in elliptical galaxies have systematically lower spins than those in disk-dominated systems as a result of their more merger-dominated mass assembly histories.

papers.title: Digging into the Interior of Hot Cores with ALMA (DIHCA). VIII. Feeding a high-mass binary system in the making
papers.abstract: We analyze the gas kinematics in the proto-binary NGC 6334I(N) ALMAe9-ALMAe14 system with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 1.33 mm with an angular resolution of 66 mas (~90 au). With a separation of 740 au between the system members, these observations allow a detailed study of the gas motion around this likely binary system hosting at least one growing high-mass star. Some CH$_3$OH lines tracing cold gas ($E_u/k_B$~100 K) reveal the presence of ordered circumbinary gas motion around the binary system within a ~1000 au radius, and rotation around the individual sources with rotation axes pointing roughly in the same direction. We estimate a central source mass, uncorrected for inclination, of 2 M$_\odot$ for the secondary, while the primary has an estimated mass of 5 M$_\odot$ as reported in previous works. The CH$_3$OH transitions with higher $E_u/k_B$ ($\gtrsim400$ K) values reveal circumstellar gas rotation in ALMAe9 consistent with the cold gas tracers. The vibrationally excited SO emission also traces rotation around ALMAe9 and potentially an accretion shock from a flow feeding the circumstellar disk of ALMAe14. We identify two potential inflows feeding the circumstellar disks from the circumbinary gas at rates of ~$10^{-6}-10^{-4}$ M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ from CH$_3$OH emission. An additional third inflow seems to be feeding the primary from gas at larger scales.

papers.intro:
Most stars are born in multiple systems, with high-mass stars in binary systems an important source of some of the most powerful phenomena detected across cosmic scales (e.g., X-ray binaries). The formation of such systems at early stages can be the result of disk [15, 23, e.g.,] or core [16, e.g.,] fragmentation, with the former likely resulting in closer binaries than the latter. Binaries formed through disk fragmentation can develop a circumbinary disk that feeds their individual circumstellar disks. Simulations suggest that such disks would feed the secondary at a higher accretion rate depending on the core angular momentum [22]. However, investigating how proto-binaries feed requires high-angular resolution observations in order to resolve the kinematics of the circumbinary and circumstellar disks.

At radio frequencies, this can be achieved with interferometers like ALMA. For instance, ALMA has revealed inflows in the low-mass binary system [BHB2007] 11 feeding the individual circumstellar disks [1]. A larger spiral arm (streamer) has been found feeding the low-mass binary SVS13A [10], while spiral arms within a circumbinary disk have been identified in L1551 [36]. A circumbinary/multiple disk has also been detected around the hot corino IRAS 16293–2422 [30]. On the higher mass end, circumbinary disks have been identified through line transitions tracing cold gas with molecules like CH3CN and CH3OH in the high-mass sources IRAS 16547–4247 [37, 44, G343.12–0.06, 2.9 kpc; e.g.,] and G335.579–0.272 ALMAe1 [25, 3.25 kpc;] within 1000 au scales. Other systems forming binaries include G11.92–0.61 MM1 [11, 3.37 kpc; e.g.,] and MM2 [45, 35], IRAS 07299–1651 [46, 42, 1.68 kpc;], G345.4938+01.4677 [9, 2.38 kpc;] and multiple binary systems within G333.23-0.06 [18, 5.2 kpc;]. However, they could not identify gas flows feeding the circumstellar disks.

Of the few nearby massive sources, NGC 6334I(N) (G351.444+00.659) is a young cluster-forming region located close enough [33, 1.35 kpc;] to resolve and study multiple systems with ALMA without using the more time consuming extended baseline configurations. Within NGC 6334I(N), S. Li et al. [19] found a septuple system in the making. Although their observations revealed molecular line emission toward the individual members of the system, they could not study the motions close to each source due to lack of enough angular resolution to separate the individual components. As part of the Digging into the Interior of Hot Cores with ALMA (DIHCA) project, F. A. Olguin et al. [28] detected line emission toward 5 sources within the field. Of these, two (ALMAe9 and ALMAe14) are located within 1000 au, thus making them good candidates for a binary system. However, due to the lack of sensitivity (in part due to their selection of a homogeneous robust parameter across the sample), gas rotation was only studied toward ALMAe9 resulting in a estimated central source mass of Mc​sin2⁡i=5M_{c}\sin^{2}i=5 M☉{\rm M}_{\sun}, with ii the inclination of the putative disk with respect to the plane of the sky.

papers.title: Lodos-v2: An Efficient Primal Formulation of the Exact Frictional Contact Problem
papers.abstract: Lodos-v2 is a GPU-based simulation framework for massively parallel rigid-body dynamics with contact. It is specifically designed to achieve high throughput in scenes involving collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes. Its predecessor, Lodos-v1, had two main limitations. First, it solved the standard convex relaxation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, thereby inheriting well-known physical artifacts, including lift-off and artificial compliance in the normal direction, as well as creep in the tangential direction. Second, its contact-group reparameterization scheme, which rescales spring-damper forces using a single factor per collision pair, could not be integrated with other constraints required by a full-fledged simulator, such as joint limits and welds. Lodos-v2 addresses both limitations through two main contributions. First, it introduces an efficient algorithm for solving the exact frictional contact problem by sequentially solving a cascade of convex relaxations in primal form within an outer proximal minimization loop. Second, it extends the contact-group reparameterization scheme of Lodos-v1 to the primal formulation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, enabling its integration with the other constraints of a full-fledged simulator. Experiments demonstrate that these contributions result in throughput improvements over established rigid-body simulation frameworks. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.

papers.title: Lodos: A Lightweight Simulator Designed for Contact-Rich Interactions with Detailed Meshes
papers.abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.

What makes a good simulator for solving control problems that involve contact-rich interactions? Let us build the desiderata by focusing on the control and contact-rich interaction parts of the question separately.

A good simulator for control: Sampling-based control approaches that leverage massively vectorized simulation [1, 2] have proven to be very proficient at solving contact-rich manipulation tasks. A common pattern shared by such approaches, whether it is domain randomization with RL [3, 4], risk-aware control with stochastic MPC [5], or randomized smoothing [6] with gradient-based optimization, is that actions are selected such that they remain “approximately correct” with respect to metrics averaged over randomized ensembles of contact parameters generated via artificial (and oftentimes non-physical) perturbations (e.g. adding virtual forces, noisy friction coefficients and haptic sensing, approximate or domain randomized collision geometry). And a main argument of this paper is that in such a setting, perturbations and averaging already introduce a “convex-hull” effect on how much the physical faithfulness of each ensemble member can reflect on (or matter for) the selection of the common actions facing the ensemble. Therefore, there should be room for using simplified versions of contact dynamics (that can still sufficiently preserve the “convex-hull”) to achieve drastically increased ensemble sizes instead, resulting in a net benefit for the downstream control algorithm.

A good simulator for contact-rich interactions: Most of the commonly used simulators in robotics research [7, 8, 9, 10] use a combination of convex polytope based collision detection [11, 12] with a numerical optimization routine to solve the regularized non-linear complementarity (NCP) or cone-complementarity (CCP) systems of equations describing contact dynamics [13, 14, 15, 9, 16, 17]. While this battle-tested recipe certainly has its merits, it suffers from the following drawbacks particularly in contact-rich settings: • The regularization introduced to the NCP/CCP equations scales frictional contact forces down from the exact value needed to maintain complete staticity in a rigid-body system (e.g. zero velocity and acceleration), meaning all contacts eventually slip under constant forces such as gravity. • Applying GJK-EPA algorithms [11, 18] to convex polytope collisions produces a single contact point, which is occasionally further extended into a sparse set of contact points lying at the corners of a 2D polygon [12]. Neither mechanism can faithfully implement contact forces distributed over a patch, meaning torsional friction is emulated in an ad hoc manner by introducing artificial constraints to the optimization routine that oppose motion around the contact normal. • Convex-polytope-based collision routines scale poorly with parallelization, particularly under contact-rich configurations involving complex non-convex meshes. In concert, these drawbacks chart a path toward the design of an effective simulator for contact-rich interactions.

Contributions. We present a novel simulation routine designed from scratch to facilitate research on developing control algorithms in contact-rich settings. In particular: • We propose a new collision detection routine built upon sphere - SDF collisions as the axiomatic interaction, which can represent arbitrary non-convex (closed) surfaces at arbitrary levels of precision, and scales much more favorably with massive parallelization compared to the traditional convex polytope based approach. Specifically, this includes a novel hierarchical broadphase routine to logarithmically cull potential sphere-SDF interactions, and a novel narrowphase routine using 3D-spline-based SDF and surface normal representations whose evaluation time is independent of geometry complexity. • We propose a new model of contact dynamics based on rescaling spring-damper forces via a staggered fixed-point iteration scheme, derived from a lumped parameterization of the traditional SOCP-based contact models employed in most common simulators [16, 7]. The main benefits are that it: i) scales much more favorably under massive vectorization compared to standard approaches, ii) does not exhibit a slipping artifact, iii) allows patch-patch contacts and therefore faithful torsional friction simulation.

papers.title: OmniLatent: Unified Latent for 3D Part Modeling
papers.abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.

The creation of structured, editable 3D assets is a cornerstone of modern visual computing, supporting applications from game production and cinematic content creation to digital twins, robotic simulation, and interactive design. Recent image-conditioned 3D generative models (Zhao et al., 2025c; Hunyuan3D et al., 2025; Lei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a) can synthesize increasingly detailed geometry and appearance from a single image. However, their outputs are still mostly monolithic surfaces: the object may look plausible, but its semantic components are not explicitly separated. This missing part structure limits downstream editing, material assignment, animation, physical fabrication, and analysis, all of which require an object to be decomposed into coherent, addressable parts.

The creation of structured, editable 3D assets is a cornerstone of modern visual computing, supporting applications from game production and cinematic content creation to digital twins, robotic simulation, and interactive design. Recent image-conditioned 3D generative models (Zhao et al., 2025c; Hunyuan3D et al., 2025; Lei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a) can synthesize increasingly detailed geometry and appearance from a single image. However, their outputs are still mostly monolithic surfaces: the object may look plausible, but its semantic components are not explicitly separated. This missing part structure limits downstream editing, material assignment, animation, physical fabrication, and analysis, all of which require an object to be decomposed into coherent, addressable parts.

A common solution is to first generate or reconstruct a full 3D asset and then run a separate part segmentation model (Ma et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b). This post-hoc paradigm is convenient, but it decouples part reasoning from the generative representation that produced the asset. As a result, segmentation quality depends heavily on the input mesh quality and often degrades near thin structures, sharp boundaries, or texture-defined semantic transitions. It also makes part granularity difficult to control: a post-hoc segmenter may split visually coherent components, merge distinct functional parts, or produce boundaries that do not match the generated surface. For part-aware asset creation, the central problem is therefore not only to synthesize a plausible 3D object, but to generate a surface whose semantic part layout is coherent, editable, and aligned with geometry and appearance.

Learning part segmentation directly from part labels alone therefore underuses the strong geometric and visual priors available in larger 3D asset collections (Li et al., 2026). Practical part cues are also often incomplete: single-view masks or sparse user interactions may only cover visible surface regions, while downstream editing and animation require complete object-level parts. The base OmniLatent model is trained progressively. Large-scale geometry data first establishes a structural latent space, textured assets then align appearance with geometry, and a smaller set of part-aware assets finally teaches the latent space to decode coherent part IDs. This curriculum allows part learning to benefit from geometric and visual priors without requiring part annotations at the same scale as geometry or texture. Because the adapter is initialized from the pretrained latent generator, it reuses the same geometry, appearance, and part priors instead of learning an interactive segmentation model from scratch.

papers.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.

The digitalization of power electronics systems is transforming not only how information should be processed but also how such systems should be perceived. This goes beyond purely hardware-based approaches towards the comprehension of the intrinsic behaviors of passive circuits in power electronic systems. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) has become a powerful enabler for data-driven analysis in power electronics, owing to its ability to handle complex nonlinearities [1, 2]. AI-based methods are increasingly unveiling subtle patterns in power electronics systems when they are inaccessible by conventional model-based approaches.

This trend raises a research question on how to exploit the shared physics between AI and electric circuits, as in Fig. 1. Signal propagation in neural networks and interconnections in analog circuits are both subject to the principles of network theory, while signal encoding and decoding offer morphological duality and the potential for more efficient data processing by leveraging circuit-level dynamics, for instance, networked memristors as in-memory computing solutions [3]. Similarly, this analogy is also promising for power electronics systems at a macro scale with high controllability.

papers.title: From local learning to global electronic properties in large-scale systems
papers.abstract: Machine learning from local atomic environments offers an efficient route to electronic structure, but evaluating global electronic properties in large systems remains computationally demanding. Here we combine real space charge density learning with stochastic propagation using Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians constructed from the predicted densities. The framework avoids target system self-consistent iterations and explicit diagonalization, while hierarchical blocking enables dense grid inference within limited GPU memory. We demonstrate density of states calculations for one million Si atoms and optical and transport calculations for over one hundred thousand atoms, without training separate models for each property. This framework extends the practical scale of electronic structure calculations within Kohn-Sham DFT, opening opportunities to investigate how atomic structure governs electronic, optical and transport properties at length scales relevant to real materials and devices.

Density as a real-space field bridges the gap between reference-data generation and property evaluation in different numerical representations. papers.title: Bootstrap Your Own AV-Proxies: Adaptive Contrastive and Prototype Learning for Audio-Visual Segmentation
papers.abstract: Audio-Visual Segmentation (AVS) aims to accurately segment sounding objects in video frames by leveraging audio-visual correspondence cues. However, it remains challenging due to the intrinsic semantic incompleteness within a single modality and the semantic gap between audio and visual representations. Traditional feature-fusion decoding approaches struggle to suppress fusion noise effectively, while recent methods that incorporate data-dependent priors often increase the complexity of modeling audio-visual correlations, leading to poor cross-domain generalization. To address these issues, we propose a novel adaptive contrastive and prototype learning framework, BYOAVP, for AVS. Specifically, we design a Self-Supervised Audio Enhancement (SSAE) module that introduces contrastive learning to adaptively align audio representations with gradient-blocked visual embeddings, thus narrowing the semantic gap between modalities. Furthermore, a Dynamic Prototype Constraint (DPC) module is developed to refine pixel-wise category perception via momentum-based prototype updating, while enhancing localization of sounding regions through cross-modal interaction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves SOTA performance across two AVS benchmarks and six sub-tasks, exhibiting strong robustness and generalization ability.

Compared with other audio-visual tasks such as Audio-Visual Event Localization (AVEL) [47, 59, 49, 50] and Sound Source Localization (SSL) [20, 21, 44, 48], AVS is more challenging due to its fine-grained pixel-level discrimination. As illustrated in Fig. 1, semantic similarities between the target and background in visual scenes, as well as frequency overlaps among multiple audio components, introduce severe intra-modal interference during cross-modal fusion. Furthermore, the lack of fine-grained pixel perception often leads to blurred object boundaries and incomplete or even incorrect segmentation results.

In contrast to prior methods, we present a fully adaptive framework comprising two key components: the Self-Supervised Audio Enhancement (SSAE) and Dynamic Prototype Constraint (DPC). The SSAE module performs intra-modal denoising and preliminary cross-modal alignment, while DPC facilitates fine-grained interaction between modalities. Inspired by [16, 9, 1, 2], SSAE treats audio and visual inputs as distinct views and adopts a self-supervised contrastive learning scheme without relying on explicit negative pairs. Unlike conventional uni-modal contrastive learning with shared branch weights, the large semantic gap between modalities hinders direct alignment. To address this, a multi-head cross-modal attention layer is introduced before the projection heads to achieve early semantic alignment, enabling the audio branch to predict visual semantics and suppress irrelevant noise. This design allows SSAE to adaptively enhance correlated features and mitigate intra-modal noise. Moreover, by removing manually constructed pairs or predefined thresholds as in [10, 11, 34, 56], our method improves generalization to in-the-wild data and reduces computational overhead. SSAE thus represents a novel extension of self-supervised contrastive learning to cross-modal representation alignment, distinct from SACL [48] in SSL tasks that treat single-modal features as dual-branch inputs.

papers.title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.

papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs) for human preferences, safety constraints, and task-specific objectives [48, 38, 4]. More recently, RL-based post-training has become the foundation of reasoning language models (RLMs, also called reasoning models): models that perform extended reasoning, produce chain-of-thought (CoT) trajectories [52], exploit richer structures [58, 6, 7, 60, 14], self-correct [15], and allocate more computation to harder problems [23, 36, 21]. Examples include DeepSeek-R1 [23], GPT-5 Thinking [47], Kimi K2.5 Thinking [3], and Grok 4.7 [56]. Here, RL becomes a mechanism by which models learn to reason. The computational footprint is enormous and continues to grow: frontier-scale models consume millions of GPU-hours, while scaling both train-time RL and inference-time reasoning continues to improve model capabilities [30, 35, 20]. These costs grow further in agentic systems [59, 51, 32, 55, 28, 57, 16, 13, 8, 12]: long-horizon tool use and multi-agent execution increase system overhead [26], with reported token usage reaching 4×4\times–15×15\times that of ordinary chat [1] and roughly three orders of magnitude higher for agentic coding workloads [2].

Yet, RLM post-training is substantially more complex than a single-model workload. In the canonical Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) pipeline, each step comprises a generation stage that samples responses with a trainable actor (also called policy), an assessment stage that evaluates them using a reward model, critic, and frozen reference model, and a training stage that updates the trainable components [31, 62]. Other widely used online RLM-training paradigms, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [43], simplify parts of this pipeline (for example by removing the critic) but retain essentially the same generation–assessment–training template and its heterogeneous execution characteristics. In PPO, generation is autoregressive and latency-sensitive, assessment is largely teacher-forced and throughput-oriented, while training adds backward passes, optimizer state, and parameter updates. RLM training is therefore simultaneously multi-model, multi-stage, heterogeneous, and iterative – and fundamentally a parallel and distributed computing problem [53].

Scaling individual models does not by itself optimize an RLM training pipeline. Data (DP), tensor (TP), pipeline (PP), context (CP), sequence (SP), and expert parallelism (EP) must be coordinated with cross-stage placement, state exchange, and execution order [17, 5]. Existing systems pursue three roughly complementary directions: (1) effective execution planning, including placement and parallel-strategy selection in ReaL [31] and HybridFlow/verl [45], and workflow compilation in RLinf [61]; (2) fine-grained and asynchronous execution, including sample- and microbatch-level fusion in RLHFuse [63] and decoupled rollout–training pipelines in AReaL [22], Laminar [44], and StaleFlow [29]; and (3) adaptive resource orchestration, which adjusts parallelism or reallocates resources as workloads evolve [49, 18, 50]. These mechanisms increasingly coexist within the same system.

The key design question is therefore how broadly these decisions can be optimized together. Aspects such as overlap, placement, parameter freshness, model sharing, parallelism, sharding vs. replication, and memory cannot be optimized independently: improving one may increase communication, resharding, or memory pressure elsewhere. This interaction becomes even more important on hierarchical supercomputers, where communication costs differ substantially within a node, across nodes, and across racks. Finally, maximizing throughput alone may still leave expensive hardware poorly utilized. Taken together, these couplings make it difficult to achieve both high performance and high hardware utilization while respecting communication and memory constraints.

papers.title: Quasi-spherical fallback in binary neutron-star mergers: fuel and obstacle for extended emission
papers.abstract: Extended emission (EE) lasting hundreds of seconds has been observed in a fraction of short gamma-ray bursts (sGRB) containing both nonthermal and thermal components, and representing a significant puzzle for models involving binary neutron stars (BNSs). Recent GRMHD simulations of BNS mergers found that the late-time fallback is approximately quasi-spherical and motivated an r-process powered thermal model for EE. However, the available radioactive-heating power may be insufficient to sustain the luminosity inferred by such a model. We therefore propose a fallback-fed secondary-jet scenario in which a fraction of the fallback material circularizes on the black-hole equatorial plane and powers the jet, while polar fallback impedes its propagation. Using a semi-analytic toy model, we follow the propagation of the jet-head through the fallback envelope and identify jet-dominated, cocoon-dominated, and choked scenarios. The boundaries of these regimes depend primarily on the circularization fraction $f_{\rm circ}$, on the jet half-opening angle $\theta_j$, and on the polar refilling factor $\xi_{\rm pol}$, with the approximate scaling $\widetilde{L}\propto f_{\rm circ}/(\xi_{\rm pol}\theta_j^2)$. By post-processing data from BNS-merger simulations we find that the fraction of bound fallback material that avoids prompt capture is $f_{\rm npc}\simeq0.52$, thus providing an upper bound on the circularizable fallback supply. Under suitable prescriptions for nonthermal jet emission and thermal emission from the jet head, the estimated isotropic-equivalent $0.3$--$10$ keV energies reproduce well both the observed EE distribution for the jet-dominated branch and its low-energy end for the cocoon-dominated branch. Overall, these results suggest that fallback-fed secondary jets represent a dynamically feasible and energetically consistent explanation of the EE in sGRBs.

Long before the detection of the cornerstone binary neutron star (BNS) merger gravitational wave (GW) event GW170817, [1, 39, 2] and its subsequent electromagnetic signal [26, 66, 68, 58, 23, 30, 73, e.g.,], short gamma-ray bursts (sGRB) had been robustly associated with compact binary mergers involving a neutron star component [21, 59, 51, e.g.,]. Importantly, while prompt emission from sGRBs typically lasts less than two seconds [42], a fraction of them exhibit a softer extended-emission (EE) component in the X-ray or gamma-ray bands that persists for tens to hundreds of seconds [55, 75, 22, 40]. Additionally, the spectral properties of EE are diverse: many events are dominated by nonthermal emission, whereas a significant subset also exhibits a prominent thermal component [79, 14, e.g.,].

Such long-lasting EE suggests the presence of a central engine or energy reservoir that remains active well beyond the prompt phase. However, both the nature of this engine and the physical mechanism responsible for the EE remain uncertain. One widely discussed possibility is a long-lived magnetar remnant [19, 48, 11, 29, 60, e.g., ] , whose rotational spin-down or magnetically driven outflow can provide sustained energy injection [46, 27, 24, 16, 38, e.g.,]. A potential challenge for this scenario is to reconcile the long survival of the neutron star with the early production of the powerful ultra-relativistic jet associated with the prompt sGRB. The latter is favored by a sufficiently baryon-clean polar funnel and an ordered large-scale magnetic field, both of which are nontrivial to establish in the immediate post-merger environment [52, 17, 18, e.g.,]. An alternative explanation for the origin of the EE has been attributed to the so called “fallback” emission, where the gravitationally bound material ejected during binary coalescence falls back onto the central remnant and can naturally act as a new source of energy [49, 37, 80, 54, e.g.,].

Based on these results, MDR24 proposed that radioactive rr-process heating of the fallback material could directly power the thermal X-ray emission associated with EE. However, as we show in Appendix A, their assumption of the local gas temperature as the effective radiative temperature leads to an inferred luminosity that exceeds the available radioactive-heating power. When considering their energy budget and the photon diffusion through the fallback material, the rr-process heating alone is unlikely to account for the observed EE luminosities. Moreover, a purely thermal fallback-emission model does not naturally explain the substantial population of EEs with predominantly non-thermal spectra [79, 14, e.g.,]. These considerations motivate a different role for the fallback material, wherein rather than acting solely as the emitting medium, it may instead serve as the mass reservoir that powers renewed central-engine activity.

One natural realization of such a renewed central-engine activity is a secondary relativistic jet powered by fallback accretion. Fallback-fed secondary-jet models have previously been explored using semi-analytic approaches [80, 44, e.g.,], typically adopting fallback geometries motivated by black-hole–neutron-star (BHNS) mergers. In these geometries, the tidal disruption confines most of the fallback material along the equatorial plane [43, 20, e.g.,], while leaving the polar region relatively unimpeded for the secondary jet. However, this geometry does not necessarily apply to BNS mergers, which are expected to constitute a major and likely dominant channel of the observed sGRB population [7, 56, e.g.,]. This possibility is further supported by the inferred BNS merger-rate density, which is approximately five times higher than that of BHNS mergers [70, 71]. In contrast to the equatorially concentrated fallback expected in BHNS mergers, the GRMHD simulations of MDR24 show that the late-time bound ejecta in BNS mergers becomes approximately quasi-spherical. This geometry opens a complementary regime in which the same fallback flow can both supply fresh material to the central engine and repopulate the polar region, thereby impeding the propagation of a fallback-fed secondary jet.

papers.title: Independent nuclear charge radius determinations: bound-electron $g$ factor versus muonic atom spectroscopy
papers.abstract: We present an alternative method to determine absolute nuclear charge radii competitively via the bound electron $g$ factor of H-like ions. The method is demonstrated for $^{118}$Sn by extracting its radius with a precision of 0.1%. This is the second most precise radius ever determined from an electronic system. We benchmark our result against a state-of-the-art value derived from the spectrum of muonic $^{118}$Sn. This comparison reveals a 3.2$\sigma$ tension, prompting a careful reexamination of the calculations and calling for additional measurements. Crucially, after decades, we now have two independent methods to measure absolute charge radii with similar precision.

papers.title: Redetermination of the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BaMgF4
papers.abstract: BaMgF4 (BMF) has the potential to serve as a platform material for vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) nonlinear optics owing to its ferroelectricity and high UV transparency down to 130 nm. However, the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients reported for BMF span approximately one order of magnitude, hindering a reliable assessment of its potential for nonlinear optical applications. Here, we redetermined these coefficients by combining Maker fringe, wedge, and single-pass second-harmonic-generation measurements at a fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm. Our results establish that all the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BMF lie in the range of 0.01-0.04 pm/V. We determined d31 to be 0.035 pm/V, which is among the largest coefficients of BMF, while it has been underestimated relative to the other coefficients in previous studies. Although d31 is not the largest coefficient, the use of its long corresponding coherence length is beneficial for quasi-phase matching, particularly for VUV generation, where the fabrication of lower-order quasi-phase-matching structures is crucial.

papers.title: Rethinking MoE Load Balancing as Feedback Control
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training is often not stationary: the data mixture changes at curriculum boundaries, when a model is continually pretrained into a new domain, or when the corpus is refreshed. Routing is learned against the current mixture, so each such change disrupts the per-expert load the router had converged to, and existing balancing methods have only been evaluated on stationary data. We rethink load balancing as a feedback control problem, in which the deviation of each expert's load from its fair share is the control error and the per-expert routing bias is the control input, and define a family of controllers, the PID-Balancer, from the proportional, integral, and derivative terms of classical PID control. Two widely used methods belong to this family: the auxiliary balancing loss behaves like a proportional controller, and the loss-free bias update is an integral controller acting on the sign of the error. Reading the router as a static map with a one-step delay, we show that the integral term is the only one that both removes persistent imbalance and averages out the step-to-step fluctuation of the measured load, whereas the proportional and derivative terms pass or amplify that fluctuation into the routing bias. We therefore adopt PID (I), the pure-integral member of the family with a single gain. Two settings are evaluated: (i) training an OLMoE backbone from scratch with 16 to 64 experts per layer, through a mid-run mixture switch, and (ii) continual pretraining of the released OLMoE-1B-7B on a new corpus. PID (I) holds balance before the shift and restores it more tightly afterwards than either the auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing, at comparable perplexity.

papers.intro:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures decouple model capacity from per-token compute by replacing dense feed-forward layers with sparsely-activated expert sub-networks (Fedus et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). Realizing this promise depends critically on one constraint: tokens must be distributed across experts rather than collapsing onto a small subset. Without active intervention, MoE routers exhibit a rich-get-richer dynamic. Early-trained experts attract more routing than others, gradient signal concentrates on them, and the remaining experts receive less training and become weaker (Eigen et al., 2013; Shazeer et al., 2017).

Without active intervention, MoE routers exhibit a rich-get-richer dynamic. Early-trained experts attract more routing than others, gradient signal concentrates on them, and the remaining experts receive less training and become weaker (Eigen et al., 2013; Shazeer et al., 2017).

Load balancing is the mechanism that prevents this collapse, and existing methods fall into two families. The first adds an auxiliary loss that penalizes uneven expert usage, weighted by a tunable coefficient. This balancing pressure enters the router through the same backward pass as the language-modeling objective, and the two combine into a single gradient update to the router weights. The second, introduced by Wang et al. (2024) and popularized through its deployment in DeepSeek-V3 (Liu et al., 2024), moves that pressure out of the gradient. A per-expert bias, updated at each step in proportion to the sign of the load deviation, shifts which experts are selected while leaving the router weights to the language-modeling objective alone. Han and Zhong (2025) formalize this update as a single-shot primal-dual step for an assignment problem, in which the per-expert bias is identified with the dual variable of the load constraint.

papers.title: Task-Driven Closed-Loop Design Optimization of Passively Morphing Quadrotors for Contact-Mediated Narrow Gap Traversal
papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.

The width of an aerial robot can impose a hard limit on the environments it can access. In cluttered indoor, industrial, and natural settings, an otherwise traversable route may contain openings narrower than the vehicle’s nominal width. Rigid quadrotors can reduce their projected cross-section through aggressive attitude maneuvers [1, 2], but the opening must still exceed the vehicle’s minimum projected dimension. Moreover, successful traversal requires accurate perception, state estimation, and timing, making this strategy difficult to deploy reliably in real-world settings.

The width of an aerial robot can impose a hard limit on the environments it can access. In cluttered indoor, industrial, and natural settings, an otherwise traversable route may contain openings narrower than the vehicle’s nominal width. Rigid quadrotors can reduce their projected cross-section through aggressive attitude maneuvers [1, 2], but the opening must still exceed the vehicle’s minimum projected dimension. Moreover, successful traversal requires accurate perception, state estimation, and timing, making this strategy difficult to deploy reliably in real-world settings.

Morphing aerial robots can overcome this geometric limitation by temporarily reducing their width. For instance, actuated morphologies [3, 4, 5] can decrease width on demand, but increase system complexity through additional servomotors and adaptive control strategies. Thrust-triggered quadrotor arm folding through passive joints [6, 7] can achieve large and rapid shape changes, but requires invertible thrust and limiting maneuverability to avoid unintentionally triggering the passive joints. Contact-mediated passively reconfigurable designs are therefore particularly attractive as they leverage contact with the environment to initiate and maintain shape change [8, 9, 10, 11, 12] without requiring additional actuators or invertible thrust. However, the geometry and compliance of these existing designs are not specifically optimized for the traversal task, where the trade-off between in-flight rigidity (and consequently tracking accuracy and power consumption) and the maximum achievable squeeze is not specifically addressed. Aerial robots that achieve contact-mediated in-flight narrow-gap traversal only pass through gaps up to 29% narrower than the drone’s span [8, 9, 10].

A well-designed passively morphing quadrotor must remain effectively rigid under rotor loads during nominal flight and simultaneously easily reduce its width when the opening applies contact forces. After traversal, it must restore the nominal flight configuration. A design that is too flexible can deform during normal flight, leading to worse control, while a stiffer structure can be difficult to compress through the gap. When airframe geometry and compliance are selected by hand, it is particularly difficult to identify which combinations best enable both successful gap traversal and good nominal flight control performance. Previous works show contact-mediated narrow-gap traversal is possible but generally propose a planar quadrotor architecture and compliance guided by engineering intuition. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has jointly optimized airframe geometry and compliance directly driven by closed-loop performance over the complete narrow-gap traversal and recovery task.
