Previous works show contact-mediated narrow-gap traversal is possible but generally propose a planar quadrotor architecture and compliance guided by engineering intuition. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has jointly optimized airframe geometry and compliance directly driven by closed-loop performance over the complete narrow-gap traversal and recovery task.

In this work, we introduce a task-driven closed-loop design optimization approach for soft quadrotors, optimized for narrow-gap traversal. Figure 1 summarizes the proposed closed-loop design optimization pipeline and the resulting vehicle’s key capabilities. We jointly optimize a 22-parameter quadrotor geometry and the programmable nonlinear torque deflection response of two passively folding side arms directly for traversal success. The compliant response is achieved using elastic rolling cam (ERC) joints [13], whose cam profiles can be synthesized to produce nonlinear restoring torque as a function of the bending angle. This nonlinearity can be tuned to allow airframes to remain rigid near the nominal configuration, while bending with low effort after contact. A black-box optimizer evaluates candidate designs using GPU-parallel contact simulation with a nonlinear model predictive controller (NMPC) whose model parameters are instantiated analytically from each candidate morphology. Control-authority and joint-realizability repair procedures modify infeasible candidates before evaluation, ensuring that the search considers only manufacturable designs that retain at least 95%95\% of the acceleration capabilities (maximal angular acceleration in roll, pitch, and yaw, in addition to thrust to weight) of a planar reference design in + configuration that shares Morphy’s arm length and propulsion system [9]. The proposed approach allows the complete contact →\rightarrow folding →\rightarrow recovery sequence to select a task-adapted design, without relying on geometric or mechanical proxy objectives. An ablation study shows that this joint optimization is key, as optimizing geometry or joint compliance alone produces designs that fail at narrow gaps, whereas optimizing both together produces a design that traverses gaps 52%52\% narrower than its nominal width. The complete pipeline produces a flight-ready design in about 1818 h on a single laptop GPU. The accompanying video is available at https://youtu.be/xGkEtl6-vCA. The code is available at https://github.com/ntnu-arl/soft-quadrotor-optimization.

papers.title: Horizon-Coupled Obstacle Guidance for Relative-Action Diffusion Policies
papers.abstract: Real-world robot deployment requires adapting learned policies to unseen obstacles without collecting new demonstrations or retraining. Existing policy-level guidance often applies obstacle corrections independently at individual horizon steps, which may address local obstacle violations but fail to coordinate the action sequence into a complete, task-directed detour. How obstacle responses should be propagated across the action horizon to coordinate complete, task-directed avoidance motion remains underexplored. We introduce an inferencetime obstacle-guidance framework for pretrained relative-action diffusion policies. It rolls out cumulative relative actions into a workspace trajectory, evaluates obstacle interactions along the trajectory with an SDF-based obstacle model, and propagates each obstacle response to all contributing action increments during denoising. Real-robot experiments across seven obstacleconstrained scenarios spanning four manipulation tasks show that our method achieves 105/140 (75.0%) collision-free task successes, compared with 8/140 (5.7%) for absolute-action pointwise guidance. Ablations show that the relative-action horizoncoupled formulation provides the larger observed improvement across both obstacle models.

papers.intro:
Diffusion Policy (DP) [1] has emerged as a prominent framework for visuomotor manipulation, owing to its ability to model multimodal action distributions from expert demonstrations and generate observation-conditioned action chunks for closed-loop control. Recent 3D variants [2, 3, 4, 5] incorporate explicit 3D scene representations to improve spatial generalization across complex manipulation tasks. These advances strengthen the potential of DPs for deployment in complex manipulation environments. However, real-world deployment may introduce obstacles that are absent from the expert demonstrations utilized to train the policy, and these advances do not by themselves enable the pretrained policy to adapt its motion around them. Such obstacles can block the learned motion even when the manipulation objective remains unchanged. A straightforward solution is to redesign the robot motion for each obstacle configuration, but repeated redesign requires substantial engineering time, human effort, and deployment cost. Adapting the sampled actions of a trained DP to deployment-time obstacles without retraining would avoid these repeated costs and make policy deployment more scalable.

Obstacle geometry directly defines such a differentiable objective, eliminating auxiliary-policy training and reward-bearing exploration. We therefore adopt denoising guidance.

Existing denoising-guidance methods demonstrate that safety constraints can be incorporated into reverse sampling. papers.title: Approximation Algorithms for Right-Hand-Side Parametric Linear Programming Problems
papers.abstract: In parametric linear optimization problems, the objective function or the feasible set depends linearly on one or several real-valued parameters. The goal is to provide an optimal solution set, i.e., a set containing an optimal solution for each non-parametric problem induced by a particular choice of parameter values. In this paper, we consider right-hand-side single-parametric linear programming problems (RHS-PLPPs) that are usually very difficult to solve exactly. An optimal solution set of minimum cardinality can be infinite, while a representation by optimal bases may still require super-polynomially many different bases. Hence, we develop approximation methods for RHS-PLPPs that compute approximation sets of polynomially bounded cardinality, each containing, for every parameter value, a feasible solution whose objective value is at most a prescribed multiplicative factor times the optimum. Our first approach constructs an approximation set using a greedy staircase procedure and yields an FPTAS under general sufficient conditions. We show that these conditions hold for some important classes of RHS-PLPPs. For monotone instances, in which the feasible sets are nested as the parameter varies, our algorithm yields an approximation set of minimum cardinality. Beyond monotonicity, we establish near-minimum cardinality guarantees under more general sufficient conditions. Finally, we introduce a dual approximation algorithm that returns solutions with objective value no greater than the optimum while allowing a controlled multiplicative violation of the parameter-dependent right-hand sides.

papers.title: Pinching Antenna Systems (PASS) for Air-Ground Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a multi-user single-target air-ground integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system, in which a ground pinching-antenna system (PASS) transmits communication and sensing signals and an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) receives the target echo. The communication and sensing beamforming vectors, pinching antenna positions, and UAV position are jointly optimized to minimize the weighted Cram\'er-Rao bound (CRB). A penalty dual decomposition (PDD) algorithm is developed for the resulting nonconvex problem. The auxiliary variable and beamforming subproblems admit globally optimal solutions in semi-closed form, while the positions of the pinching antennas and the UAV are updated by successive convex approximation (SCA). Under mild conditions, every accumulation point of the sequence generated by our proposed algorithm is a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) point of the reformulated problem. Numerical results show that the proposed PASS-UAV design achieves a lower weighted CRB than conventional multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) and PASS benchmarks.

Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) has attracted significant attention as a promising technology for future wireless networks [1]. However, the fixed antenna positions of conventional antenna arrays limit their flexibility in adapting the communication and sensing channels. Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) offer a new degree of freedom by allowing pinching antennas (PAs) to move along dielectric waveguides, thereby enabling flexible channel reconfiguration for ISAC design [2].

Existing PASS sensing designs mainly employ fixed terrestrial sensing receivers [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Moreover, in existing PASS-enabled low-altitude networks, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are generally treated as communication terminals or sensing targets [6, 7], overlooking the potential of exploiting their mobility to actively configure the sensing receive geometry. A UAV receiver can adjust both its distance from the target and the angle of arrival of the echo, while the movable PAs control the transmit channel. This motivates a joint PASS transmitter and UAV receiver design.

The communication and sensing beamforming vectors, PA positions, and UAV position are jointly optimized under communication rate, transmit power, PA deployment, and UAV deployment constraints. papers.title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
papers.abstract: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 {\mu}m, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.

papers.title: Superconducting Fluctuation Driven Quantum Transport in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$ Thin Films
papers.abstract: Superconducting fluctuations (SF), arising from Cooper-pair-driven interactions and electron-electron interactions within the transition regime, can dominate the magnetoconductance (MC) of superconducting thin films near their transition temperature. In some systems, this fluctuation-dominated regime is preceded by a narrow window in which quantum interference effects are manifested as weak antilocalization (WAL) or weak localization (WL). Here, we report magnetotransport measurements on thin films of the high-temperature superconductor Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$ (BSCCO) that establish SF as the dominant mechanism governing MC across the transition regime. In the narrow temperature window well above $T_c$ where SF does not exist, a cusp in MC can be attributed to WAL-like signature well described by the Hikami--Larkin--Nagaoka (HLN) framework. Closer to the transition ($T_{BKT}$), we observe signatures consistent with Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) correlations, underscoring that the dominant physics is set by collective, pairing-driven behavior rather than single-particle quantum interference. Measurements on non-superconducting control samples show no WAL-like features, indicating that the WAL over narrow temperature window, emerges only in conjunction with superconducting fluctuations. Hall measurements further reveal a concomitant sign reversal of the dominant carrier response, pointing to a substantial reorganization of transverse transport coincident with the onset of superconductivity. Together, these observations establish that magnetotransport in BSCCO thin film.

papers.intro:
Quantum corrections to the normal-state conductivity provide a sensitive probe of the underlying electronic correlations in low-dimensional and disordered systems 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. In materials proximate to a superconducting instability these corrections are frequently dominated by fluctuation effects rather than by weak localization phenomena alone. Above the superconducting transition temperature, TcT_{c}, thermodynamic fluctuations of the superconducting order parameter give rise to transient Cooper pairs, which provide an additional conduction channel known as superconducting fluctuations (SF). This results in excess conductivity comprising contributions from the Aslamazov–Larkin (AL) and Maki–Thompson (MT) correction terms 3. These fluctuation-induced corrections are strongly temperature- and field-dependent, and in systems with strong spin–orbit coupling or specific disorder configurations they can coexist with, or even dominate, quantum interference corrections 3, 5, 7. While the Hikami–Larkin–Nagaoka (HLN) formalism 8 is conventionally invoked to describe the low-field magnetoconductance (MC) cusp in such systems, a cusp-like feature of this form is not by itself sufficient to establish a WAL origin, since AL- and MT-type fluctuation corrections can produce a qualitatively similar MC signature in the vicinity of TcT_{c}.

We demonstrate that the appearance of WAL-like features is confined to a narrow temperature window immediately preceding the onset of the superconducting transition, where the low-field MC is well described by the HLN framework. As superconducting correlations strengthen, the MC deviates from HLN behavior and crosses over into the fluctuation-dominated regime. Measurements on non-superconducting control samples show no WAL-like features, indicating that these signatures arise specifically in conjunction with superconducting correlations. In addition, Hall measurements reveal a concomitant sign reversal of the dominant carrier response, suggesting a substantial modification of transverse transport coincident with the onset of superconductivity.

papers.title: RadarDINO: Distilling a Visual Foundation Model into mmWave Radar for Human Mesh Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers a privacy-preserving and illumination-robust alternative for human mesh reconstruction (HMR). However, high-fidelity radar HMR remains challenging. Sparse point cloud-based methods suffer from information loss and missed detections, while raw radar tensor methods like RT-Mesh lack fine-grained semantics and explicit local body modeling. In this paper, we propose RadarDINO, a radar HMR framework that distills visual semantics from a DINOv3 teacher into 3D radar representations and introduces explicit geometric supervision. DINOv3 descriptors are transferred to radar voxels via calibrated RGB-radar geometry, providing voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations. We further incorporate vertex- and joint-losses to directly constrain reconstructed geometry. On the M4Human dataset, our method outperforms the SOTA baseline across all three evaluation splits.

While recent vision-based methods [3, 5] achieve remarkable fidelity, optical cameras are sensitive to lighting variations and raise privacy concerns. In contrast, millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides a promising privacy-preserving, illumination-robust alternative for future Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) systems.

Recently, the M4Human [7] benchmark introduced RT-Mesh, a raw-RT HMR baseline using 3D convolutions and self-attention. However, several limitations remain. First, raw RTs lack fine-grained semantics needed to distinguish body parts. Second, RT-Mesh does not explicitly model voxel- and part-level semantic correspondences, limiting localized body representation. Third, SMPL-X [12] parametric supervision does not directly constrain reconstructed vertices and joints, which may lead to geometric errors under complex motions.

Second, RT-Mesh does not explicitly model voxel- and part-level semantic correspondences, limiting localized body representation. To address these challenges, we propose RadarDINO, a raw-radar HMR framework that combines cross-modal visual semantic distillation with explicit geometric supervision. Specifically, we transfer DINOv3 [14] visual descriptors from synchronized RGB images to 3D radar voxels through calibrated radar-camera geometry, providing voxel- and body-part-level semantic supervision. The resulting part-aware radar representation is used for mesh reconstruction, while explicit vertex- and joint-level losses complement SMPL-X parameter supervision to directly constrain the reconstructed geometry. Extensive experiments on the M4Human dataset [7] demonstrate that our model consistently improves radar-based HMR over existing methods, particularly under complex human motions.

papers.title: Beyond Feasibility: Efficient and Robust On-Device Localization with UWB Concurrent Transmissions
papers.abstract: Concurrent transmissions (CTX) enable an ultra-wideband (UWB) tag to range to, or self-localize from, multiple nodes with a single frame reception, significantly improving update rate and energy efficiency compared to traditional approaches. Prior work demonstrated the concept feasibility via prototypes whose real-world applicability is however hindered by many limitations, notably including their inability to directly execute on UWB tags and to cope with interfering UWB signals. We address these limitations in two ways. First, we redesign the core CTX techniques to enable a fast and efficient execution on resource-constrained MCUs without sacrificing accuracy. Second, we leverage the new features in the IEEE 802.15.4z standard to achieve robustness to interference from other UWB devices and enable tags to dynamically select which anchors to use, two crucial and unexplored capabilities in CTX-based systems. We quantitatively evaluate our approach experimentally in two real-world testbeds with different characteristics. We first analyze our new techniques individually, offering an in-depth discussion of design choices and performance trade-offs. Then, we embed all our techniques into a CTX-based system enabling a tag to self-localize entirely on-device, unlocking gains up to 44% in runtime and 85% in energy efficiency compared to traditional approaches.

papers.intro:
Ultra-wideband (UWB) has emerged as the cornerstone technology for a variety of location-aware IoT applications [1]. Exploiting a unique physical layer, UWB radios estimate the channel impulse response (CIR) of an incoming frame to determine its time of arrival (ToA), i.e., RX timestamp, with sub- ns\text{\,}\mathrm{ns} resolution. This enables precise distance estimation (ranging) and localization, commonly using Time-of-Flight (ToF) or Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDoA) measurements. Various schemes exist to acquire these measurements, each offering a different balance across accuracy, reliability, channel occupancy, energy efficiency, scalability, and update rate. Recent works have pushed the boundaries on several of these aspects at once by using concurrent transmissions (CTX).

Various schemes exist to acquire these measurements, each offering a different balance across accuracy, reliability, channel occupancy, energy efficiency, scalability, and update rate. Recent works have pushed the boundaries on several of these aspects at once by using concurrent transmissions (CTX).

CTX for ranging and localization. Originally developed for fast, reliable, and energy-efficient communication in narrowband networks [2], CTX have also been used in UWB for the same purpose [3, 4], but their impact goes far beyond communication. As first shown with concurrent ranging [5, 6, 7, 8], the RX timestamps from different simultaneous transmitters can be derived from the same CIR, yielding multiple ToF measurements at once. This insight has later been applied to TDoA-based localization in Chorus [9] and SnapLoc [10], in which the fixed nodes (anchors) of a UWB infrastructure transmit at the same time, and any number of listening tags can self-localize with a single reception. Subsequent studies have demonstrated that CTX can also be effectively employed for angle-of-arrival (AoA) estimation [11, 12], as well as hybrid AoA–TDoA localization [13, 14]. In contrast, traditional ranging and localization systems require distinct receptions for each timestamp, giving CTX-based approaches clear advantages (Section II–III) in terms of channel occupancy, energy efficiency, scalability, and update rate—at least in principle.

Inability to operate on-device. Existing works execute on-device only the packet exchange: the crucial steps of processing the CIR and extracting RX timestamps occur offline or rely on external infrastructure. As a consequence, these algorithms cannot run on the battery-powered, low-cost, resource-constrained tags common in UWB applications, e.g., robot coordination, contact tracing, or asset tracking [15, 16]. Enabling on-device execution demands new techniques that adapt, when not completely rethink, the existing ones to yield accurate yet fast, lightweigth, and energy-efficient execution.

Susceptibility to real-world dynamics. Revisiting CTX-based operations is also necessary to push the state of the art beyond existing techniques, which are confined to specific setups and neglect robustness to real-world dynamics. For example, deriving RX timestamps from a CIR requires selecting a threshold to distinguish valid peaks from noise [8, 10]. However, the choice of this threshold involves unexplored tradeoffs between sensitivity to weak signals and robustness against multipath. Similarly, the robust identification of concurrent responders relies on artificial constraints such as reserving empty portions of the CIR [8], which limits the number of supported anchors, the spatial coverage of the system, and resilience to multipath.

Inability to cope with unwanted UWB signals. CTX-based ranging and localization schemes have so far been demonstrated only in isolated setups, i.e., where no other UWB devices are active. This approach yields clean and easily interpretable CIRs, crucial to ascertain feasibility, but fails to reflect the complexity of real-world scenarios, whose target areas may contain more anchors than those involved in a CTX exchange, as well as UWB devices belonging to other systems. In both cases, these “external” UWB signals may interfere with CTX operation, which must therefore be augmented with the ability to discriminate and select the relevant UWB signals from unwanted ones. However, whether and how this important capability can be achieved is currently unexplored.

To address on-device operation, we present techniques that enable full CTX execution directly on off-the-shelf UWB devices. We revisit in depth all CTX constituents (Section VI), from the exchange of concurrent UWB packets to the CIR processing required to derive the RX timestamps. The latter step is especially challenging, as it must be fast and compact enough to seize the benefits of CTX, yet it involves a time-consuming extraction over SPI of the CIR and its computation-heavy analysis on resource-constrained MCUs. Our techniques markedly reduce this overhead without sacrificing accuracy and robustness. Moreover, we limit the required CIR data and accelerate on-device execution via direct memory access (DMA) to parallelize CIR extraction and analysis (Section VIII).

Our techniques markedly reduce this overhead without sacrificing accuracy and robustness. Moreover, we limit the required CIR data and accelerate on-device execution via direct memory access (DMA) to parallelize CIR extraction and analysis (Section VIII).

These novel techniques we propose are general and applicable to most IEEE 802.15.4 UWB radios, including the popular Qorvo DW1000 adopted by all existing CTX works. In contrast, we focus on the newer Qorvo DW3000, compliant to the IEEE 802.15.4z standard. This choice, unique in the CTX literature, aligns our findings to the state of the art in UWB and also provides the base to augment CTX operation with the ability to isolate and select only the relevant UWB signals (Section IV), via the Scrambled Timestamp Sequence (STS). The latter, introduced in IEEE 802.15.4z, is a ciphered sequence derived from a known key, aimed at protecting against malicious manipulation of RX timestamps. By correlating with the expected STS, a UWB receiver can obtain a second, “clean” CIR that isolates the contributions of transmitters possessing the correct key while suppressing signals from unauthorized or unknown devices. We exploit this capability to provide responder selection in CTX via a novel key switching scheme, which enables UWB devices to acquire RX timestamps only from concurrent transmitters of their choice (Section VII).

papers.title: Polyhedral Geometry of Degree-Bounded Characteristic Imset Polytopes
papers.abstract: Characteristic imset polytopes are convex hulls of a collection of characteristic imset vectors, which are 0/1 vectors that encode the Markov equivalence class of a directed acyclic graph. These polytopes are the feasible region of linear programs which correspond to causal discovery problems. We introduce a new family of these polytopes whose vertices correspond to directed acyclic graphs with in-degree bounded by $k$. This yields a polytope whose dimension is only polynomial in the number of nodes of the underlying graphs instead of exponential. We show that when $k = 1$, this polytope is a matroid independence polytope. For $k = 2$ we provide several large families of facet-defining inequalities, which give a complete $\mathcal{H}$-representation of the polytope on four nodes.

papers.title: Propagating the Hierarchical Equations of Motion using the Multi-Layer Multi-Configurational Time-Dependent Hartree method
papers.abstract: The hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) are a powerful, numerically exact approach for simulating the time evolution of open quantum systems. Recently, several tensor-train- and tensor-network-based approaches have been suggested and realized to extend the range of applicability of the HEOM approach to larger and more realistic systems. In this paper, we build upon the existing twin-space formulation of the HEOM and present a novel approach to propagate the fermionic HEOM efficiently using the multi-configurational time-dependent Hartree method (MCTDH). We benchmark the resulting HEOM+MCTDH method with electron transport calculations for a Holstein-type nanojunction model. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capabilities of the HEOM+MCTDH method by applying it to a more complex vibronic coupling nanojunction model with strong molecule-electrode coupling for which fully quantum simulations have not been feasible previously.

papers.title: Radiation-driven melting and porous flow in the near-surface layer of an ice sheet
papers.abstract: The ablation area of an ice sheet can undergo melting both directly at the surface and in the metre or so below the surface, due to the penetration and absorption of shortwave radiation. The fate of the meltwater has important implications for the mass balance of the ice sheet; some of it runs off into surface streams and eventually to the ocean, while some is stored in the porous `weathering crust', and can refreeze. We present a fluid-mechanical model to analyse the downward percolation and lateral drainage of the meltwater in the crust, and its influence on porosity, saturation, temperature and melting rate. Previous models have either ignored the possibility for lateral drainage, in which case the crust is always saturated with water, or have made ad-hoc assumptions about where and how the meltwater runs off. Through a series of analytical and numerical solutions to the model, we find that lateral drainage has the effect of controlling the water table within the weathering crust, which separates an unsaturated region near the surface from a saturated aquifer beneath. Under fluctuating weather conditions that induce melting and refreezing, the lateral drainage can result in the near-surface ice being more porous and also colder than is the case without lateral drainage. The model is able to predict the partitioning of the meltwater between surface and subsurface runoff, and refreezing, and has potential to be incorporated within larger-scale models of the ice-sheet mass balance.

papers.intro:
The loss of ice from ice sheets and glaciers is controlled in large part by the rate at which meltwater is produced and then runs off from their surface. In regions where the surface is bare of snow, shortwave solar radiation is partially absorbed at the ice surface and partially penetrates below the surface, causing both surface and subsurface heating and melting. This creates a porous near-surface layer referred to as a ‘weathering crust’ (Müller and Keeler, 1969; Cooper et al., 2018). Meltwater can be transported through and transiently stored in this porous layer, affecting how much water runs off into the ocean (Mikkelsen et al., 2016; Noël et al., 2017, e.g.). Understanding the interaction of thermodynamics and fluid mechanics that controls these processes is therefore important.

The loss of ice from ice sheets and glaciers is controlled in large part by the rate at which meltwater is produced and then runs off from their surface. In regions where the surface is bare of snow, shortwave solar radiation is partially absorbed at the ice surface and partially penetrates below the surface, causing both surface and subsurface heating and melting. This creates a porous near-surface layer referred to as a ‘weathering crust’ (Müller and Keeler, 1969; Cooper et al., 2018). Meltwater can be transported through and transiently stored in this porous layer, affecting how much water runs off into the ocean (Mikkelsen et al., 2016; Noël et al., 2017, e.g.). Understanding the interaction of thermodynamics and fluid mechanics that controls these processes is therefore important.

Both radiation-driven melting and porous meltwater flow have been considered in previous models of ice-sheet surface melt, but separately. The subsurface penetration of shortwave radiation has been included in models of melt ponds on sea ice (Taylor and Feltham, 2004, e.g.), lakes on the surface of ice sheets (Buzzard et al., 2018; Law et al., 2020, e.g.), and the porous weathering crust (Schuster, 2001; Hoffman et al., 2014; Woods and Hewitt, 2023; Woods and Hewitt, 2024). The radiation is most simply modelled as decaying exponentially with depth according to Beer’s law (Bear, 2018, e.g.), with the rate of decay being described by an extinction coefficient. Another common technique is to use a two-stream approximation (Schlatter, 1972; Perovich, 1990; Liston et al., 1999; Taylor and Feltham, 2004; Taylor and Feltham, 2005, e.g.), decomposing the net radiation into downward and upward travelling components which satisfy a pair of coupled differential equations. The two-stream approximation has the benefit of enabling optical properties to depend on evolving ice properties, such as porosity and water content. In both approaches, the radiation can either be modelled spectrally (considering a continuum of wavelengths with wavelength-dependent optical properties) (Liston et al., 1999; Hoffman et al., 2014, e.g.) or using a broadband approach (considering a single wavelength-independent value of shortwave radiation) (Taylor and Feltham, 2004; Taylor and Feltham, 2005; Woods and Hewitt, 2023, e.g.).

Porous meltwater flow has been considered in models of (vertical) percolation through firn (partially-compacted snow) (Colbeck, 1972; Gray, 1996; Ligtenberg et al., 2011; Meyer and Hewitt, 2017; Moure et al., 2023, e.g.) and the lateral transport and storage of meltwater in firn aquifers (Miller et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2023). The majority of percolation models are one-dimensional, and many are inherently numerical, with water being transferred from one discrete layer to the next using a ‘tipping bucket’ scheme (Ligtenberg et al., 2011; Munneke et al., 2014; Munneke et al., 2015, e.g.). Other more mathematical treatments make use of Darcy’s law to describe flow driven by gravity and capillary pressure (Colbeck, 1972; Colbeck, 1974; Colbeck, 1976; Gray, 1996, e.g.). Some of these percolation models are isothermal (Colbeck, 1972; Colbeck, 1974; Sellers, 2000, e.g.), but others have also considered phase change (Colbeck, 1976; Meyer and Hewitt, 2017; Moure et al., 2023, melting and refreezing, e.g.).

Our goal in this study is to capture both radiation-driven melt and porous meltwater flow in a single continuum model for the weathering crust. The weathering crust is a transient layer of porous ice, on the order of a metre in depth, with impermeable ice below (Müller and Keeler, 1969; Cooper et al., 2018). It is formed by radiation-driven subsurface melting (Brandt and Warren, 1993; Cooper et al., 2021), and evolves in response to changing weather conditions (Schuster, 2001; Tedstone et al., 2020). Most of the weathering crust is saturated with meltwater (Cooper et al., 2018; Cook et al., 2016; Irvine-Fynn et al., 2021), above which there is a few centimetres of highly-porous, unsaturated ice (containing both air and water), as shown schematically in figure 1(a). Meltwater flows laterally through the weathering crust with typical flow speeds of <0.13<0.13 m/day (Irvine-Fynn et al., 2021). This plays an important role in transporting meltwater, microbes and nutrients across the ice sheet (Stibal et al., 2012; Cook et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2018), and the carbon fluxes between the ice sheet and the atmosphere (Cook et al., 2012). Drainage of meltwater through the crust also impacts the albedo (reflectivity) of the surface (Tedstone et al., 2020), which is a crucial control on how much the surface melts. For example, if a weathering crust forms on a wet, bare ice surface, the surface water is able to drain away through the weathering crust, significantly changing the appearance of the ice surface (increasing the albedo).

Hoffman et al. (2014) did consider the effect of lateral meltwater drainage in their one-dimensional model by removing any meltwater exceeding a 10% melt fraction at each timestep, but they did not model any (vertical) meltwater flow or density/porosity evolution explicitly. Their work did however demonstrate the importance of accounting for lateral drainage, even in a one-dimensional model; without lateral drainage, observed surface lowering, porosity and temperature were not correctly captured (Hoffman et al., 2014). Moreover, Stevens et al. (2026) found that the Woods and Hewitt (2024) model (without meltwater flow) overestimated the ice density compared to ice-core observations of weathering crusts on the Greenland Ice Sheet. They suggest that the overestimation is due to too much meltwater being refrozen, and that this problem could be addressed by introducing a meltwater flow model.

papers.title: Influenza A Virus as a Multivalent Active Particle: Statistical Mechanics of Binding, Motility, and Antiviral Design
papers.abstract: In this contribution, we review existing multivalent models of Influenza A Virus (IAV) systems to study virion dynamics and design of multivalent entry blockers. We review existing biochemical estimations of the dissociation constants and catalytic activities of the two virion ligands [hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA)], which can be used to develop quantitative theories and experiments. Multivalent models are statistical mechanics frameworks for studying the simultaneous interaction of multiple reversible ligand-receptor bonds. They quantify the effects of both combinatorial entropy terms and single-molecule ligand-receptor affinities. Multivalent frameworks led to the rationale of superselectivity, the ability of probes to sense specific concentrations of conjugated receptors. Multivalent models guided the design of antiviral nanomedicines constituted by polymeric scaffolds conjugated with small molecules such as sialic acid receptors targeting the ligands on the surface of the virion. Importantly, neuraminidase is an enzyme that limits the number of host-guest bonds through receptor desialylation. Like active particles, neuraminidase activity enhances virion motility in the extracellular medium. Modeling the dynamics of Influenza A virions requires developing out-of-equilibrium multivalent models.

papers.title: Tensor value and the 9/4 bound for matrix multiplication
papers.abstract: We give an exposition of OpenAI's recent result that the exponent of matrix multiplication is at most 9/4 valid over every field. Our main tool is a fractional symmetrized variant of the tensor value introduced by Coppersmith and Winograd, used in place of spectral points (tensor characters) in the original proof. We prove a superadditivity inequality for a power of this value on partially direct sums, whose summands share one tensor factor and occupy independent subspaces in the other two. Together with the degenerations of polynomial multiplication tensors from the OpenAI proof, this inequality yields the bound.

papers.title: Extreme-value asymptotics for smallest enclosing balls of spherically symmetric samples
papers.abstract: Let $R_n$ denote the radius of the smallest ball containing an i.i.d.\ sample of spherically symmetric random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, and let $D_n$ be the sample diameter. While the asymptotic behaviour of $D_n$ is well understood, much less is known about $R_n$. Starting from a classical result of Daniels for planar Gaussian samples, we develop a point-process approach to the asymptotic behaviour of $R_n$ in the three classical extreme-value regimes. We obtain limit theorems in the Gumbel, Fr'echet and Weibull cases, with the limiting laws described by geometric functionals of Poisson point processes. In dimension two, the Gumbel limit can be identified explicitly and is universal within the corresponding max-domain of attraction. We also study the asymptotic relationship between $R_n$ and $D_n$ and the supporting configurations of the smallest enclosing ball.

papers.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
papers.abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.

papers.intro:
It is 7:40 AM on a Tuesday morning. Before Maya finishes her coffee, an AI agent has drafted a reply to her landlord’s recent email, rebooked a cheaper flight for her sister’s wedding, flagged a streaming subscription she forgot to cancel, and proposed a dinner recipe built around the vegetables wilting in her refrigerator. She approves all four with a tap. But when the same agent offers to turn yesterday’s bullet-points in her therapy journal into a full entry, adjust her blood-pressure medication schedule from last night’s readings, and negotiate a pay adjustment with her manager, she hesitates. The delegation that felt like relief just moments earlier now feels like a loss of judgment, of privacy, and of something that was supposed to be hers to do.

This scenario is no longer confined to speculation or science fiction. Large language model (LLM)-based agents can already plan and execute multi-step tasks such as booking travel and completing online payments (He et al., 2025), and they are being deployed in socioeconomic roles, from autonomously operating a small store (Anthropic, 2025) to negotiating purchases on consumers’ behalf (Zhu et al., 2025). Meanwhile, generative AI has become a technology of everyday life rather than of work alone as more than 70% of ChatGPT conversations now concern non-work matters such as practical guidance and personal writing (Chatterji et al., 2025). Yet, the public is deeply ambivalent about this trajectory. Half of U.S. adults report being more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, and a majority say they want more control over how AI is used in their lives (Pew Research Center, 2025). Early evidence on the psychosocial consequences of everyday AI use, such as shifts in loneliness and emotional dependence (Fang et al., 2025; Heffner et al., 2025), as well as changed perceptions of one’s own productivity and accomplishment (Kobiella et al., 2024), suggests that this ambivalence is not irrational caution.

Prior research offers partial answers to the question of which parts of life people are willing to hand over to AI agents, and why they might do so, though from each specific domain respectively. Prior work shows that reliance on AI agents depends strongly on the task, tending to be higher for objective tasks and lower for subjective or personally consequential ones (Castelo et al., 2019; Dietvorst et al., 2015; Logg et al., 2019; Longoni et al., 2019). Much of prior work, however, predates AI agents capable of completing entire activities end-to-end. The trust-in-automation literature explains when people rely on machine assistance (Lee and See, 2004; Hoff and Bashir, 2015), but focuses on settings where the human remains the decision maker and the AI advises (Bansal et al., 2021; Sivaraman et al., 2023). Task-level audits of automation preferences are confined to occupational work (Shao et al., 2025; Lubars and Tan, 2019). Privacy research documents how users navigate disclosure to LLM-based systems (Zhang et al., 2024; Leon et al., 2013), and technology-acceptance research examines perceived usefulness, effort expectancy, and price value (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2012). However, privacy risks and economic benefits are rarely measured together, for the same task, from the same person. Delegating an activity to an AI agent, however, is precisely a joint decision as it bundles beliefs about competence and trust, exposure of personal data, economic value, and the meaning of doing the activity oneself into a single choice (Lubars and Tan, 2019; Draxler et al., 2024).

To address these gaps, we ask three research questions:

• RQ1. How do preferences for AI automation vary across everyday and work domains, and which task-level and respondent-level factors are associated with greater willingness to delegate tasks to AI? • RQ2. Although privacy concerns varied substantially across domains, they were not independently associated with automation after adjustment. papers.title: Time-gated optical-parametric-amplification and field-resolved detection of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals
papers.abstract: Infrared spectroscopy is a key tool to study complex structural dynamics in molecular systems. However, resolving weak or broad vibrational modes is challenging due to their rapid decay. Here, we demonstrate a technique to significantly extend the detectable lifetime - and thereby spectral resolution - of molecular signatures by employing synchronized time-gated optical parametric amplification of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals. Utilizing a Cr:ZnS laser system and a nonlinear ZnGeP2 crystal, we achieve a 10-fold increase in the electric field strength of the infrared molecular signal, yielding a two-orders of magnitude enhancement in dynamic range and a 2-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio. Using isopropyl alcohol as a model system, we demonstrate that OPA-enhanced detection extends the observable window of vibrational modes up to 72 %. This approach allows for the reconstruction of high-fidelity molecular fingerprints that resolve complex vibrational relaxation pathways and weak structural dynamics, previously hidden within the background and noise, providing a pathway for new high-sensitivity and time-resolved studies of complex chemical structures.

papers.title: Multi-phase Carbon Structure and Dynamics in NGC 6334: Insights from CO, [C I], and [C II]
papers.abstract: We present high-angular and velocity resolution observations of the emission lines of [CII] at 158 micron, [CI] at 609 micron, and the 12CO and 13CO (J=3-2) transitions toward the central region of NGC 6334, providing a detailed multi-phase view of carbon in this massive star-forming complex. By combining morphology and spatial scales information, kinematics, line profiles, and line ratio analyses, we quantify the distribution and physical state of ionized and atomic carbon, and carbon in its molecular form in CO. [CII] emission is the most extended, permeates the mapped region and is dynamically complex, while 13CO is compact and quiescent, and 12CO and [CI] occupy intermediate regimes connecting dense regions to transitional diffuse layers. We interpret these emission distributions such that the brightest [CII] emission traces photodissociation regions (PDRs) close to the H II region bubbles located along the central filament, while the extended [CII] emission arises from the more diffuse warm gas, indicating either cloud formation or dispersal processes. Remarkably, the [CI] is more extended than the 13CO, but less than [CII] and may probe the gas velocity structure resulting from colliding flows or cloud-cloud collisions. Line ratios involving [CII], such as [CII]/[CI] or [CII]/CO are systematically high, revealing widespread diffuse emission and localized UV-illuminated surfaces. Line ratio analysis and K-means clustering of [CI]/13CO versus dust continuum (cold 870 micron and warm 70 micron) emission reveal stratified chemical structure that UV photons penetrate deeply into the clumpy ridge (Av~18), suggesting a porous PDR. These results together depict that NGC 6334 is a clumpy, feedback-dominated PDR ridge with coexisting carbon phases, where [CI] and [CII] also trace dynamical processing through multiple velocity components linked to cloud-cloud collisions.

papers.intro:
NGC 6334 is a star forming complex (of extent ∼\sim80 pc), harbouring a central dense filament (∼\sim10 pc length) and a large number of OB-type stars, H ii regions and bubbles in the extended region (Fig. 1) (e.g., Persi and Tapia 2008; Russeil et al. 2013; Tigé et al. 2017; Louvet et al. 2019; Neupane et al. 2024). This complex is located at a distance of 1.7 kpc (e.g., Russeil et al. 2012). The central dense filament contains sites of high-mass star formation in a sequence of evolutionary stages (e.g, Tigé et al. 2017) and is proposed to undergo longitudinal collapse, possibly triggered by a past high-mass star forming event (Zernickel et al. 2013; Russeil et al. 2013; Neupane et al. 2024). NGC 6334 has been reported to be undergoing large scale cloud-cloud collision by Fukui et al. (2018), supported by recent high-resolution observations of 12CO and 13CO J=3−2J=3-2 that identified multiple velocity components and ‘bridge’ features (Neupane et al. 2024). It has been proposed that the cloud-cloud interaction is happening over the past few million years triggering sequential star formation in the filamentary complex (Fukui et al. 2018). Owing to the complex interplay of dense molecular cores, extended photon-dominated regions (PDRs), active feedback and dynamic interactions, NGC 6334 provides an ideal environment to investigate the origins of molecular, neutral, and ionized carbon emission.

papers.title: SN 2026ahvu in NGC 1433 May Be a Prompt Type Ia Supernova with a Delay Time Under 100 Myr
papers.abstract: SN 2026ahvu is a Type Ia supernova (SN) that occurred in the nearby galaxy NGC 1433. Using archival Hubble and JWST imaging from the PHANGS survey, we show that the SN lies within 0.19$''$ and 0.26$''$ of two UV-bright star clusters. This $0.19/0.26''$ separation corresponds to $8/11$ pc ($17/24$ pc) at the reported distances of $9.1$ and $18.9$ Mpc, respectively. The probability of finding an unrelated Type Ia SN this close to a cataloged star cluster by chance is only $\sim$0.4 %. Thus, SN 2026ahvu is likely the first Type Ia SN that can be associated with relatively young star clusters in a nearby galaxy. From spectral energy distribution fitting using HST+JWST (or HST-only) data, we find that the clusters have age estimates of $37_{-5}^{+3}$ ($57_{-9}^{+14}$) Myr and $95_{-13}^{+15}$ ($88_{-12}^{+14}$) Myr. Association with either cluster would mean that SN 2026ahvu should be considered a prompt SN Ia and provide one of the most concrete measurements to date of a prompt Ia delay time. The median age of the younger star cluster is close to the minimum possible delay time for SN Ia progenitors. If the SN is indeed associated with the younger cluster, it would imply that Type Ia SNe can occur almost immediately after white dwarf formation. If the SN is associated with the older cluster, this discovery still presents the first example of a prompt Type Ia SN with delay time under 100 Myr.

papers.intro:
Type Ia supernovae (SNe) are thermonuclear explosions of carbon-oxygen white dwarfs in binary systems. The nature of the explosion mechanism and binary companion have long been the subject of debate [see 38, 51, for reviews], with proposed channels including single-degenerate (SD) explosions driven by mass accretion onto a white dwarf [75, 45, e.g.,] or double-degenerate (DD) explosions driven by the merger of two white dwarfs [27, 71, 56], although evidence has accumulated that SD channels operate in a minority of SNe Ia [54, 40, 57, 13, 70, e.g.,]. A consensus on the SNe Ia progenitor channels remains a highly sought-after goal, given their use as standard candles in cosmology [47, 49, e.g.,] and their importance as sources of Fe-group elements in the universe [48, 43, e.g.,].

The nature of the explosion mechanism and binary companion have long been the subject of debate [see 38, 51, for reviews], with proposed channels including single-degenerate (SD) explosions driven by mass accretion onto a white dwarf [75, 45, e.g.,] or double-degenerate (DD) explosions driven by the merger of two white dwarfs [27, 71, 56], although evidence has accumulated that SD channels operate in a minority of SNe Ia [54, 40, 57, 13, 70, e.g.,]. A consensus on the SNe Ia progenitor channels remains a highly sought-after goal, given their use as standard candles in cosmology [47, 49, e.g.,] and their importance as sources of Fe-group elements in the universe [48, 43, e.g.,].

Two populations of SNe Ia have long been proposed [53, 34, e.g.,] – a prompt (few 100 Myr) and delayed (several Gyr) component – based on the observed correlation between SN rates and host galaxy colors and star-formation rates [61, 32, 58, e.g.,]. The SN Ia delay-time distribution (DTD) from extragalactic surveys further supported this bimodality, showing SN rates per M⊙ following a consistent t−1t^{-1} power-law distribution across a broad range of delay-times, from 40 Myr to ≳\gtrsim10 Gyr [39, 37, 23, 36, 24, 22, 60, 21, 78, e.g.]. The slope and the Gyr-long delay-times are naturally reproduced by DD progenitors, whose evolutionary timescales are set by angular momentum loss from gravitational wave emission [69, 68, e.g.,]. The progenitor composition of the prompt population is less well-understood. Population synthesis models typically predict ∼\sim100 Myr as the shortest delay-times for DD channels and SD channels with non-degenerate companions, and about ∼\sim40 Myr for SD channels with H-stripped companions [38, 33, see reviews in]. These predictions can be highly uncertain given various poorly-understood aspects of binary evolution, such as common-envelope evolution [50, 68, 80].

Characterization of prompt SNe Ia from observations has been limited. The presence of prompt Ia is only known statistically from DTD surveys. Age information in these surveys often come in broad age-bins [65, ≫\gg100 Myr;] from star-formation histories averaged over entire galaxies or cosmological volumes, given the uncertainties associated with integrated photometry and spectra [14, 79, e.g.,]. Inferring ages from stellar populations around individual SNe can be challenging because the region of a galaxy where a SN explodes often blends a range of ages with a complex star formation history [4, 3, 62, e.g.,]. A definitive association of a Type Ia with a simple stellar population (e.g., star cluster) with a characteristic age is thus necessary, but has remained elusive. Only one known Type Ia (SN 2019ein) has been found near a globular cluster [6], supporting the delayed channel.

papers.title: Coherent radio emission at 45 MHz from the nearby planet-hosting star GJ 725A
papers.abstract: Ultra-low-frequency (<100 MHz) coherent radio emission from exoplanet-hosting stellar systems carries information about planetary and stellar magnetic fields, as well as the space weather environment - information that is difficult to obtain at other wavelengths. We carried out the circularly polarized LOFAR LBA Sky Survey, the most sensitive circularly polarized survey in this frequency range, using the LOFAR low-band antenna system. As part of this untargeted search, we detected a signal in a 1h observation that is coincident with the quiescent, planet-hosting, solar-neighborhood M dwarf GJ 725A at a distance of 3.5 pc. The signal has a high circular polarization fraction of $74\pm16$% and a peak brightness of $B=135\pm17$ mJy/beam between 42 MHz and 50 MHz. It was undetected in the 50-66 MHz range, with a 3$\sigma$ upper limit of $B<48$ mJy/beam, corresponding to a drop of at least a factor 3 across 12 MHz, and indicating a strong spectral feature or cutoff around 50 MHz. Our detection represents the lowest-frequency confirmed detection of a stellar system. Based on the high estimated brightness temperature ($\sim10^{14}$ K), transient character and polarization fraction, the emission is most plausibly attributed to the electron cyclotron maser instability. The available observations are not sufficient to identify the astrophysical origin of the emission. We consider three plausible scenarios: auroral emission of a yet undetected wide-orbit giant planet with a magnetic field $B\geq18$ G, star-planet interaction with the known 11 d orbit terrestrial planet GJ 725Ab, or an origin due to stellar magnetic activity. Ultra-low-frequency monitoring, combined with new, preferably simultaneous observations in the X-rays, UV, and H$\alpha$, and a search for a wide-orbit (thousands of days) giant planet across the full allowed parameter space will allow us to distinguish between these scenarios.

papers.intro:
Stellar activity is a central factor controlling the atmospheric evolution of planets and, ultimately, their habitability. Flares, mass ejections, and winds can erode planetary atmospheres (Lammer et al., 2007; Airapetian et al., 2020, e.g.,). This is of particular concern for planets around M dwarfs, common hosts of temperate rocky planets in the solar neighborhood, because their habitable zones lie close to the host stars (Kasting et al., 1993; Kopparapu et al., 2013). A sufficiently strong planetary magnetic field may shield the atmosphere from this influence (Khodachenko et al., 2007; Vidotto et al., 2013). Understanding the stellar activity of M dwarfs and the magnetic fields of their exoplanets is therefore central to assessing the habitability of planetary systems.

Stellar activity is a central factor controlling the atmospheric evolution of planets and, ultimately, their habitability. Flares, mass ejections, and winds can erode planetary atmospheres (Lammer et al., 2007; Airapetian et al., 2020, e.g.,). This is of particular concern for planets around M dwarfs, common hosts of temperate rocky planets in the solar neighborhood, because their habitable zones lie close to the host stars (Kasting et al., 1993; Kopparapu et al., 2013). A sufficiently strong planetary magnetic field may shield the atmosphere from this influence (Khodachenko et al., 2007; Vidotto et al., 2013). Understanding the stellar activity of M dwarfs and the magnetic fields of their exoplanets is therefore central to assessing the habitability of planetary systems.

Constraining exoplanetary magnetic fields observationally is challenging. Arguably, the most promising avenue for their detection is via radio emission generated by the electron cyclotron maser instability (ECMI) that is powered or mediated by a planet. One possibility is that ECMI originates directly in the planetary magnetosphere, in analogy to the auroral radio emission of magnetized Solar System planets (Zarka, 1998). Because ECMI radiation is emitted close to the local electron cyclotron frequency νc≈2.8​B\nu_{\mathrm{c}}\approx 2.8{B} (with νc\nu_{\mathrm{c}} in megahertz and BB in gauss), its spectrum directly measures the magnetic field strength BB in the planetary magnetosphere. Alternatively, ECMI can arise in the stellar magnetosphere, powered by a sub-Alfvénic star-planet interaction (SPI), a scaled analog of the Jupiter-Io system (Zarka, 2007). Since the energetics of this interaction depend on the magnetic properties of the planet, SPI detections constrain the planetary magnetic fields indirectly (Callingham et al., 2024; Revilla et al., 2026).

papers.title: High-order FEEC discretization on 2D and 3D domains with a disk-like coordinate singularity
papers.abstract: Tensor-product splines mapped from a square to a disk-like domain form a discrete de Rham complex, but at the coordinate singularity the pushed-forward $0$-, $1$- and $2$-forms are discontinuous, unbounded and not square integrable. Existing polar constructions impose either high-order regularity on the $0$-forms only, or first-order regularity on the whole complex. For general disk-like mappings composed with a smooth diffeomorphism, we construct polar subspaces of all three tensor-product spaces that are conforming, form a cochain complex with the cohomology of the disk, and are $\mathcal{C}^{\mathfrak{r}-m}$ at the center for $m$-forms, for any $\mathfrak{r}$ up to the spline degree, under a compatibility condition between the mapping and the angular basis. The construction enriches the $2$-form space with projected polynomials and lifts them to curl-like $1$-forms by Poincar\'e-type homotopy operators, which reduce to cumulative sums of radial B-spline coefficients, so that the homotopy identities hold exactly. The same operators yield sparse commuting projections that preserve total flux and circulation, and boundary-compatible homotopies that solve the curl--curl problem with a single mass-matrix inversion. In 3D, the tensor product with a periodic 1D complex carries all properties over to stellarator-like solid tori. Numerical experiments confirm optimal projection accuracy and the predicted regularity, show that the regularity conditions suppress the stiff central modes of the curl--curl operator, allowing more than ten times larger time steps than first-order polar spaces, and that compatible high-order regularity is required for convergent guiding-center orbits near the axis of a discrete vacuum field.

papers.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning for Chaotic Three-Body Dynamics in Astrophysics
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) and generative AI have recently made impressive progress in understanding physics. We explore a hierarchy of prediction problems stemming from chaotic three-body systems and benchmark existing ML approaches, including general-purpose prediction algorithms and those that build on top of foundational physics models. We first simulate the trajectories of triple systems near the critical boundary of stable/unstable initial conditions. We then design a hierarchy of learning tasks, focusing mainly on two broad problems: stability prediction and trajectory prediction. The former classifies whether a given triple system has diverged or not up to a specific horizon, while the latter predicts the exact trajectory, both given suitable input features. We benchmark a range of ML approaches, from simple regression methods to state-of-the-art foundational physics models, across these tasks, and compare them against astrophysical methods such as the Mardling-Aarseth stability criterion. Our experiments reveal a clear order of task difficulties in chaotic three-body dynamics: early dynamics enable strong stability prediction, while precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult. Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/Simonwan03/ThreeBodyMLBench.

In this work, we focus on one of the fundamental problems in physics that remains relatively underexplored in current AI research: the three-body problem [36, 6, 17, 37]. It is a classical problem for understanding the stability and dynamics of stellar systems, and provides one of the simplest yet best-controlled settings for benchmarking ML methods.

Their long-term stability and orbital evolution are relevant to a broad range of astrophysical phenomena [33]. Depending on the initial conditions, a triple system may either remain stable over long timescales or rapidly diverge and become unbounded. papers.title: Interferometric survey of stellar parameters. Reliable methodology for a direct measurement of the angular diameter in exoplanet host stars
papers.abstract: Since their pioneer observations more than thirty years ago, exoplanets have been a major topic among the astrophysics community. Despite their ubiquity, our knowledge of planetary parameters and internal compositions still mostly relies on stellar quantities estimated through evolutionary models, which suffer from a calibration bias, preventing the community to have accurate discussions on the diversity of planets across the Universe. We use our sample to demonstrate the current best reachable precision of the CHARA Array to be $\sim$ 2% on radius determination, with an error budget dominated by the uncertainty on the angular diameter, while systematics are shown to be of the order of 1% thanks to our methodology. While the precision matches values found in the literature, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the present study in the relevance of the results put forward. Finally, we show that our methods naturally translate into an improved accuracy of the planetary parameters, along with an improvement in precision by $\sim$ 50% in radius and $\sim$ 30% in mass.

papers.intro:
Fundamental stellar parameters are the primary data required for an in-depth understanding of stellar evolution, interiors, and environments. Many methods like asteroseismology, photometric transits of exoplanets, radial velocities, or Surface Brightness Color relations (SBCR) are linked to the stellar radius. Usually estimated through models, its determination by coupling an optical interferometric measurement of the angular diameter and a precise parallax, such as those provided by the Gaia space mission (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016), is the best way to avoid any model dependence. Furthermore, characterizing any activity (limb darkening, rotation, winds, or binarity) is also mandatory, both for bias removal and for the required progress on stellar physics. Through an ambitious and homogeneous survey of the angular diameters of several hundreds stars, the Interferometric Survey of Stellar Parameters (ISSP11 1 European Research Council (ERC) grant 101019653) is built to address key questions about the relation between planets and stars, and to offer to the broader community a unique and primary source of direct information all over the Hertzsprung-Russel (HR) diagram. Observationally, it is based on the exploitation of the CHARA/SPICA instrument (Mourard et al. 2026), but also aims at providing unique synergies and comparative studies between the different spectral bands available at the CHARA Array. This survey is organized in eight different scientific programs. The subprogram presented in the present work is dedicated to the analysis of exoplanet host stars (EHS), which are targets in great need for accurate size measurements. To date, several thousands of exoplanets have been detected (Christiansen et al. 2025). Most of the understanding of their core properties (composition, temperature, size, mass) heavily rely on the knowledge of their host star’s properties. The radial velocity (RV) modulations of the star can only provide the mass ratio between the planet and the star, while the transit light curves provide the ratio of planet-to-star radius. When multiple transits are observed, the stellar density can be extracted from the light curves, as shown by Seager and Mallén-Ornelas (2003). Once injected in the solution provided by RV, it makes all planetary parameters solely rely on the knowledge of the stellar radius. Providing a model-independent measurement of the stellar radius therefore allows us to derive the stellar mass and the planet’s radius, mass, and density, which finally allows for an enhanced reliability of the characterization of planet interiors (Ligi et al. 2016; Crida et al. 2018; Ligi et al. 2019). In the present work, we introduce our sample and the methods we applied to 8 of the targets that have been observed already (Section 2). Then, we assess the reliability of our measurements and discuss what our approach brings to the study of exoplanets and their host star (Sections 3 and 4). Finally, we conclude on the immediate and longer-term perspective of this project in Section 5, while the discussion of planetary interiors is postponed to an upcoming paper, including the observations and analysis of the full sample.

papers.title: VLT and Keck recovery and characterisation of 2025 SC$_{79}$: linking 'Ayl\'o'chaxnim and Atira asteroids
papers.abstract: Asteroids near the boundary between the Atira and 'Ayl\'o'chaxnim classes can trace dynamical links between the two populations, but their small solar elongations make recovery and physical characterisation difficult. We recover 2025 SC$_{79}$, measure its optical colours, and investigate its likely source region and transitions between these populations. We combine Keck/LRIS astrometry and VLT/FORS2 four-filter photometry with Bus-DeMeo taxonomic comparisons, published source-model probabilities, and integrations of 10,000 clones drawn from the covariance of JPL solution #2 and followed for 5 Myr in each direction. The SDSS-equivalent colours are $g-r=0.8254_{-0.1339}^{+0.2136}$, $r-i=0.1764_{-0.0540}^{+0.0523}$ and $i-z=-0.4975_{-0.1162}^{+0.1055}$ mag. The V-type class mean gives the closest colour match. At the V-type median albedo $p_V=0.362$, $H=18.83\pm0.15$ mag implies a diameter of $0.379^{+0.027}_{-0.025}$ km. The source model assigns a combined probability of 95.4% to delivery channels associated with the inner Main Belt. The ensemble-mean 'Ayl\'o'chaxnim/Atira residence fractions are 30.2%/69.8% over the preceding 100 kyr and 3.6%/96.0% over the following 100 kyr; the remaining 0.4% of future ensemble time follows collision removal. Clones spend an average of 231 kyr in the 'Ayl\'o'chaxnim class over the preceding 500 kyr and 120 kyr over the following 500 kyr. In the 5-Myr forward integrations, 14.56% of clones collide with Venus, 3.77% with Mercury and 0.22% with Earth. The V-like colours and source-model probabilities favour an origin in the inner Main Belt for 2025 SC$_{79}$. Its clones move between the 'Ayl\'o'chaxnim and Atira populations.

papers.title: Federated Forensics: Jurisdictional constraints as a design driver for multi-agency federated learning
papers.abstract: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.

Law enforcement agencies (LEAs) rely on digital evidence, and many investigations now cross national borders (Hargreaves et al., 2024). Legal instruments already allow agencies to exchange evidence across borders (European Union, 2014; European Union, 2023; Casino et al., 2022). Training a machine learning model together is a different matter: a model trained on data from several agencies may reveal patterns that no single agency can see, but the training data is sensitive and often cannot be collected in one place (Scanlon et al., 2023; Breitinger and Jotterand, 2023). Federated Learning (FL) addresses this technically, since each agency keeps its data and only model updates are shared (McMahan et al., 2017a). However, existing FL frameworks were not built for forensic work: auditability, governance across organizational levels, explainability (Solanke, 2022), and evidentiary accountability are rarely design goals (Riedel et al., 2024).

papers.title: NAVE: A Normalized, Adaptive Conformer for Antarctic Whale Vocalization Detection
papers.abstract: Antarctic whale vocalization detection requires temporally localizing call boundaries in long underwater recordings and classifying them into predefined call types. Training reliable machine learning models for this task is difficult due to the variability and sparsity of whale calls in passive acoustic monitoring datasets. These difficulties are further amplified by time-varying noise that can mask whale calls and by site-specific ambient sound characteristics to which a trained model may not generalize. In this work, we present NAVE, a Conformer-based detector that improves whale-call detection via three components. First, its input representation combines per-bin complex mean subtraction, which suppresses constant site-specific ambient sound characteristics, with an additional per-channel energy normalization (PCEN) channel that adapts to temporal variations in the noise floor. Second, a frequency-dynamic stem processes these noise-aware representations with convolutions that adapt across the characteristic frequency bands of the target call types. Third, we use a Conformer backbone with a convolution kernel matched to the duration of the target calls that adds an inductive bias and improves temporal localization. We evaluate NAVE on BioDCASE 2026 Task 2 using leave-one-site-out cross-validation across the validation sites, which approximates deployment on unseen recording sites. A single NAVE model with a tuned per-class threshold exceeds the stronger WhaleVAD-BPN baseline, using no boundary-proposal network and no search over post-processing parameters. A controlled ablation study shows that the normalized front-end and a duration-matched convolutional kernel each contribute substantially to recovering the D downsweep, the hardest class for previous detectors, with the wide kernel giving the largest aggregate gain.

BioDCASE 2026 Task 2 targets automatic detection of Antarctic blue- and fin-whale calls in long PAM recordings. Models must generalize across sites and soundscapes while detecting sparse events, making it a useful benchmark for whale-call sound event detection systems [4, 5]. The task uses strong multi-label annotations: systems predict each call’s category and temporal bounds, as shown in Figure 1. Seven call types are grouped by acoustic similarity into three evaluation classes [6]: BMABZ for blue-whale A-, B-, and Z-calls, D for blue- and fin-whale downsweeps, and BP for fin-whale 2020 Hz pulses. The development set comes from the Acoustic Trends Blue Fin Library (ATBFL) [7, 5].

Two dataset properties shaped our design. First, calls occupy little of the audio, causing severe temporal imbalance. Even modest false-positive rates can therefore yield many spurious detections, making false-positive control as important as recall. Second, class prevalence varies strongly across site-years. D-calls are especially uneven, with most training examples from elephantisland2013 and elephantisland2014, and are the rarest class at the validation sites. D-calls have also remained the main bottleneck for prior detectors, with the lowest per-class F1 under both Whale-VAD and WhaleVAD-BPN [8, 9].

Existing detectors such as Whale-VAD [8] commonly use a CNN-BiLSTM backbone and improve it through output gating or tuned post-processing, as in WhaleVAD-BPN [9]. We ask whether the classification backbone and front-end offer similar opportunities for performance improvements, and present NAVE: a Conformer [10] with a normalized, adaptive front-end and a depthwise convolution matched to call duration. papers.title: Weak and strong discretization errors for signatures of Gaussian processes
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a continuous Gaussian process in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d\ge2$, with independent components of roughness $H\in(\tfrac14,1)$, possibly with a linear drift, and let $X^n$ be its piecewise-linear interpolant on a mesh of width $\delta$. We study how well the truncated signature of $X^n$ approximates that of the natural lift of $X$, in mean (the weak error) and in $L^2$ (the strong error). Over a class of drivers defined by quantitative regularity conditions, the weak error at every fixed truncation level is $O(\delta^{\gamma(H)})$ with $\gamma(H)=\min(2H,4H-1)$, uniformly over the class, and for truncation levels $M\ge4$ fractional Brownian motion attains this rate. For centred drivers the weak error vanishes at levels $1$ to $3$, Gaussian or not. It first appears at level~$4$, where we compute its leading constant for independent fractional Brownian motion in $d=2$: on $(\tfrac12,1)$ it is $1/(2\sqrt3)$, independent of $H$, and on $(\tfrac14,\tfrac12)$ it is given by a $\zeta$-series. For fractional Brownian motion with drift, a level-$3$ error of the same order appears for $H\ge\tfrac12$. Below $\tfrac12$ the drift reaches the rate only at levels $\ge5$ (proved for $d\ge3$). The strong error is of exact order $\delta^{2H-1/2}$ for fractional Brownian motion with $H\in(\tfrac12,1)$, so in mean square the weak error lies a full power of $\delta$ below it. For $H\le\tfrac12$ the strong error is $O(\delta^{\vartheta})$ for every $\vartheta<2H-\tfrac12$, uniformly over the class, and the exponent $2H-\tfrac12$ cannot be improved. Finally, we construct pairs of laws in the class whose mesh data have the same law but whose expected signatures differ by order $\delta^{\gamma(H)}$. Hence no quantity computed from the mesh data has mean within $o(\delta^{\gamma(H)})$ of the expected signature uniformly over the class.

papers.title: Gaussian fluctuations of the moderately interacting Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto particle system around the mollified mean-field limit
papers.abstract: We study, at the logarithmic mollification scale $\eta^{-2(d+1+\alpha)}\le\delta\log N$ of Chen, Daus, Holzinger and J{\"u}ngel, the fluctuation field $V^N=\sqrt N(\mu^N-u_\eta)$ of the moderately interacting multi-species particle system whose mean-field limit is the Shigesada- Kawasaki-Teramoto (SKT) cross-diffusion system. The field is centred at the solution $u_\eta$ of the mollified equation, which depends on $N$ through $\eta$. On a scale of weighted Bessel-potential spaces of negative order we prove that the laws of $(V^N,M^N)$ are tight, where $M^N$ is the martingale part. Every limit point of $M^N$ is a continuous Gaussian martingale with an explicit deterministic bracket. Every limit point of $V^N$ is a weak solution, and the mild solution, of a linear Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SPDE whose drift is the linearisation of the SKT operator at the limit $u$. The initial field and the martingale are independent, and weak solutions are unique given both, so the whole sequence converges in law, jointly with the martingale part, and the limit is unique in law among solutions of the martingale problem. The noise is $d M_i=div(\sqrt{2u_i\Theta_i}dW_i)$, with $\Theta_i=\sigma_i+\sum_jf(a_{ij}u_j)$ and $W$ a cylindrical Wiener process on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^{nd})$. The hypotheses are those of Chen, Daus, Holzinger and J{\"u}ngel, including the smallness and the nonnegativity on $\mathbb{R}$ of the nonlinearity $f$. We add radial kernels $B_{ij}$, the independence of the initial data and the Brownian motions across particles and species, a smaller $\delta$, a regularity budget on $u_0$, a strengthened smallness condition on $f$ that makes the backward system diagonally dominant in weighted spaces, and an integer Sobolev index $s$.

papers.title: Deliberate Pacing for Human Oversight in Agentic Software Development
papers.abstract: Agentic AI increasingly enables software development activities to proceed without continuous human involvement. While this autonomy may accelerate development, it also raises questions about when developers can meaningfully oversee software development done by agents. We propose deliberate pacing: intentionally adjusting when and how autonomous development proceeds to preserve opportunities for meaningful oversight. Drawing on an exploratory multivocal literature review of 20 sources, we identify three factors motivating this vision: changing relative costs of human involvement, the timing of oversight opportunities, and interdependencies between pacing decisions across the software development life cycle. We argue that neither uninterrupted autonomy nor frequent human intervention is universal. Instead, pacing should balance opportunities to understand and influence consequential decisions against costs in human attention, development time, and rework. We outline a research agenda to investigate when deliberate pacing is beneficial, how intervention timing affects oversight, and how pacing decisions interact across development activities.
