papers.intro:
Contemporary software engineering approaches prioritize acceleration and adaptable processes, such as faster release cycles, more frequent feature releases, quicker review processes, and increased developer productivity [28, 43, 24]. Recent industry and research narratives frame AI as a means of further accelerating software development [12, 35].

Contemporary software engineering approaches prioritize acceleration and adaptable processes, such as faster release cycles, more frequent feature releases, quicker review processes, and increased developer productivity [28, 43, 24]. Recent industry and research narratives frame AI as a means of further accelerating software development [12, 35].

Historically, many software development activities and decisions required direct human involvement, even as automation reduced the time needed for individual steps. AI agents can increasingly perform such activities without continuous human involvement, although their effects on development speed vary across studies. A controlled experiment reported large speedups for an isolated programming task [37], while experienced open-source developers worked more slowly with AI tools on their own repositories [4]. A follow-up to the latter study found indications of a speedup instead, although the authors caution that changes in participant selection make the true effect difficult to measure [5]. Practitioners further argue that understanding, debugging, and modifying code, rather than writing it, are important bottlenecks that faster code generation does not necessarily resolve [20]. Whatever the exact productivity gains, agentic AI changes how development activities are performed by allowing agents to make and implement decisions while developers attend to other work.

Whatever the exact productivity gains, agentic AI changes how development activities are performed by allowing agents to make and implement decisions while developers attend to other work.

This shift raises concerns about development approaches prioritizing speed. Agentic AI enables substantial parts of a software system to be prototyped with limited human involvement, potentially allowing consequential decisions to be implemented before developers evaluate them. Studies report risks associated with AI-assisted development, including delivery stability [3] and security [13, 38]. These findings point to the importance of activities beyond code generation, such as design, problem analysis, compliance assurance, and critical evaluation of AI-generated artifacts [26, 25, 44, 1]. Studies of AI’s impact on the software development life cycle (SDLC) likewise emphasize continued human involvement in planning and testing [17].

Studies of AI’s impact on the software development life cycle (SDLC) likewise emphasize continued human involvement in planning and testing [17].

However, human involvement does not necessarily ensure meaningful oversight. Developers must have sufficient information to understand relevant decisions and opportunities to influence them. Consider an agent that selects an architectural dependency and proceeds to implement the corresponding components and tests without requesting human input. By the time a developer reviews the results, several artifacts may depend on that decision, and reconsidering it may require substantial rework. Intervening earlier could avoid such costs, but may also interrupt productive autonomous execution before sufficient information is available for an informed decision. Deciding where developers should intervene is therefore not enough. The timing also determines whether their involvement can influence autonomous development.

In this paper, we distinguish between speed and pace. Speed is how quickly software is developed, measured as output per unit of time. Pace is how that speed is distributed over time. We define deliberate pacing as intentionally adjusting when and how autonomous development proceeds to create opportunities for meaningful human oversight. Such adjustments may include pausing an agent before consequential decisions are implemented, postponing subsequent activities until a human review is completed, or changing when intermediate results are presented for evaluation. Not all oversight requires slowing down autonomous execution. Developers may also monitor ongoing activities or review completed work asynchronously. Whether deliberate pacing is beneficial therefore depends on the opportunities for oversight that creates relative to its costs in time, human attention, and development throughput.

We present a vision of deliberate pacing as a means of preserving meaningful human oversight in agentic software development. Our central proposition is that the timing of human intervention matters: retrospective review may not provide the same opportunities to influence autonomous development as intervention before consequential decisions are implemented. Drawing on a multivocal literature review (MLR) of 20 sources on slowing down software development, we examine three factors that motivate this vision: the changing relative costs of human involvement, the timing of opportunities for meaningful oversight, and the interdependencies between pacing decisions across the SDLC. Rather than proposing universal checkpoints or advocating slower development as an end in itself, we outline a research agenda for investigating when, where, and how deliberate pacing enables meaningful oversight more effectively than uninterrupted autonomous execution followed by retrospective evaluation.

papers.title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora. As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval. Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself. Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.

papers.intro:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are pre-trained on a large corpus of factual knowledge that is stored within their weights, referred to as parametric knowledge (Zhao et al., 2026). Whenever user queries and requests go beyond the internalized knowledge, LLMs are increasingly paired with retrieval systems that provide external evidence at inference time, improving factual accuracy (Ni et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2024; Arslan et al., 2024). Entity popularity is associated with differences in factual QA performance and the gains obtained from retrieval augmentation (Yang et al., 2024). Complementary theoretical work models the benefits and risks of retrieved information at the token level (Xu et al., 2025). At the same time, LLMs can sometimes answer correctly even when the retrieved context is insufficient to support the answer (Joren et al., 2025). However, in multi-hop QA, the utility of a retrieved passage depends on its relationship to the other passages in the context (Jain and Garimella, 2025).

Complementary theoretical work models the benefits and risks of retrieved information at the token level (Xu et al., 2025). At the same time, LLMs can sometimes answer correctly even when the retrieved context is insufficient to support the answer (Joren et al., 2025). However, in multi-hop QA, the utility of a retrieved passage depends on its relationship to the other passages in the context (Jain and Garimella, 2025).

Prior work studies this interaction for single-fact questions, showing that models recall popular facts more reliably and benefit more from retrieval for less popular information (Mallen et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). Multi-hop questions add structure to this interaction. Consider the query “What is the nationality of the director of the film Titanic?”. Answering it requires knowing the interdependent facts that Titanic was directed by James Cameron, and that James Cameron is Canadian. With only part of this evidence observed, the question becomes whether the model can recover the missing link, either from Titanic to James Cameron or from James Cameron to his nationality. How evidence structure affects compensation, and which other factors determine success under partial retrieval, remain largely unexplored.

We argue that existing multi-hop benchmarks provide important components for this analysis, but were not designed for a controlled removal of individual reasoning steps (Table 1). While PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023) provides entity-popularity measures and MINTQA (He et al., 2026) extends this to multi-hop, they do not provide context documents. Further, 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue-Ans (Ho et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2022) move towards stronger multi-hop supervision, but focus on reasoning paths or connected reasoning rather than explicit fact isolation required for controlled fact removal. Consequently, we observe (i) Question leakage, where the question reveals (parts of) the answer; (ii) Cross-document leakage, where another document reveals a questioned fact; (iii) Distractor leakage, where an allegedly irrelevant document contains required evidence.

Further, 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue-Ans (Ho et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2022) move towards stronger multi-hop supervision, but focus on reasoning paths or connected reasoning rather than explicit fact isolation required for controlled fact removal. Consequently, we observe (i) Question leakage, where the question reveals (parts of) the answer; (ii) Cross-document leakage, where another document reveals a questioned fact; (iii) Distractor leakage, where an allegedly irrelevant document contains required evidence.

To enable a controllable investigation over facts, we propose a novel multi-hop QA benchmark, called FondueQA. In a first step, we leverage a knowledge graph as the source of candidate facts. In a second step, we construct template-based multi-hop questions from these facts. In the third step, our pipeline ensures that each fact is assigned to exclusively one gold document, which we refer to as Fact Isolation. Subsequently, we conduct a thorough validation and filtering step, where it is ensured that the required facts are supported within their assigned gold document without any cross leakage of required evidence. Rather than altering the original documents, we discard invalid instances unless the generated question-answer pair can be adjusted without changing the intended evidence structure. As a result, each document-level ablation induces a controlled removal of its assigned fact, enabling direct comparisons across partial evidence conditions.

Compensation is further shaped by the surrounding context, as plausible competing entities can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points when supporting alternative answers, but may improve it by more than 25 points when supporting the correct answer.

papers.title: Standard Subspaces and Modular Theory -- General Theory and Applications to QFT
papers.abstract: This is a preview of an upcoming monograph on standard subspaces and modular theory. At the moment, it consists of the first chapter. This starts with a gentle introduction to the subject, and then describes the modular theory of standard subspaces, the characterization of their modular data by the KMS condition and reflection positivity, and various constructions of standard subspaces. Further topics in Chapter 1 include the connection of standard subspaces to complexifications and symplectic structures, including their polarizers, and operations with standard subspaces, namely direct sums, direct integrals, and tensor products. Many examples and classification results are included as well. This first chapter also contains a description of the free U(1)-current and some other applications to quantum field theory, such as KMS states of type I factors, the local subspaces of the free Klein--Gordon field, and the entropy operator defined by a standard subspace.

papers.title: Vector Lyapunov functions for nonconvex constrained optimization
papers.abstract: Nonconvex constrained optimization problems are commonly solved by a Newton method for necessary conditions (sequential linear/quadratic programming) or a barrier reformulation (interior-point methods). We present a vector Lyapunov analysis for Newton-type algorithms based on constraint violation and optimality of the primal solutions to a sequence of approximate optimization problems. We thus prove local stability and convergence by constructing a strict Lyapunov function for the primal solution.

In constrained optimization, however, the search for a feasible solution conflicts with the objective of minimization. Penalty methods combine cost function and constraint violation into merit functions, but require careful adjustment of the penalty parameter. Works [6, 7, 8] constructed Lyapunov functions for projected or proximal gradient descent with convex constraints. Similarly, [9, 10, 11] studied primal-dual dynamics for saddle-point problems in convex constrained optimization, and [12] constructed a Lyapunov function for a primal-dual solution of the Alternating Direction of Multiplier Method with linear constraints. Other authors applied feedback stabilization to nonlinear programs [13, 14, 15]: While [15] employed control barrier functions to ensure that constraints are satisfied, [14] proposed two Lyapunov-like functions – one for constraint violation, one for the cost – and designed a dynamical system which reduces constraint violation and minimizes the cost on the feasible set. This last result is reminiscent of the vector Lyapunov method proposed by Matrosov [16].

Instead, we are going to propose a pair of Lyapunov-like value functions for constraint violation and relative optimality, respectively. We then prove that a Newton iteration generated by a sequence of approximate quadratic optimization problems with linearized constraints (locally) satisfies a set of dissipation inequalities similar to those in network dynamics [21] and input-to-state stability [22]. Finally, the construction of a strict Lyapunov function, inspired by [23], certifies local stability of the primal solution with linear (or better) convergence. For the ease of notation, we restrict this work to equality constraints. Our analysis is based on three assumptions on the approximate problems: surjectivity of the linear constraints (ensures feasibility), strong convexity of the quadratic cost function (ensures unique solutions), and a ‘sufficiently’ good approximation of the nonconvex necessary conditions. Similar assumptions, albeit formulated for the necessary conditions, have been employed in previous works on Newton-type methods (see, e.g., [24]). Assumptions of convexity and surjectivity were made also in [25] for convergence of a filter-based globalization. Our work facilitates a Lyapunov-based analysis of Newton-type algorithms for nonconvex optimization and their interaction with dynamical systems.

papers.title: Cutpurse: Decomposing Explanation-Guided Model Extraction on Tabular Data
papers.abstract:
Explanation APIs are often treated as increasing model-extraction risk, but an end-to-end attack comparison cannot show whether an explanation reveals model-specific information or merely supplies a convenient next-query coordinate. We study this distinction for explanation-guided extraction of tabular classifiers. We separate an explanation into an attribution channel, which ranks influential features, and a coordinate channel, which supplies candidate feature values for perturbing those features. We then test whether the useful bin edges are privileged to the service or reproducible from the adversary's own data.
  Across six datasets and five target families, using attribution rankings to choose which features to perturb provides no systematic extraction advantage. Lime's discretization bin edges can improve fidelity by up to 41 percentage points on continuous features, but those edges are quantiles of the explainer's background data rather than properties of the target model. In controlled comparisons, an attacker-side grid reproduces the useful bin-edge gains without querying an explanation API. We use these findings to derive Cutpurse, which combines a self-computed grid with diverse query generation and boundary search. Against a service that withholds bin edges, Cutpurse improves fidelity by 16.3 percentage points on continuous-feature targets. It also exceeds the undefended published attack by 7.0 percentage points. Thus, withholding default Lime bin edges alone does not prevent effective extraction under the in-domain auxiliary-input, probability-output, and same-family surrogate assumptions studied here. Our results concern default Lime and Shap configurations for tabular classifiers. They do not establish the same conclusion for other explainers, target classes, or data-free attackers.

papers.intro:
Machine learning services increasingly return a post-hoc explanation alongside each prediction. This practice improves transparency, but it also raises a security question: does an explanation endpoint give a model-extraction adversary a capability that prediction access alone cannot provide? Model extraction builds a surrogate that agrees with a black-box target on unseen inputs [1, 2]. High-fidelity extraction compromises model confidentiality and can support offline transfer-based attacks [1, 3, 4]. It can also amortize the target-query cost of downstream membership inference [5].

We take Autolycus [6], an explanation-guided extraction attack against interpretable tabular classifiers, as our starting point. It couples the feature information returned by Lime or Shap with a traversal that generates new queries. Its evaluation shows that this complete attack can extract models effectively under a limited query budget. It does not, however, isolate how much the explanation outputs (feature rankings and LIME bin edges) and the traversal each contribute to that performance. Lime provides both a feature ranking and bin edges, while Shap provides feature attributions without bin edges. Even if an explanation output helps, it remains unclear whether it reveals information specific to the service or information the attacker can approximate from its own data. These distinctions determine whether the explanation API provides a model-specific capability or merely a convenient query-placement aid.

papers.title: On Positive Computation
papers.abstract: We introduce new notions of reducibility for monotone classes and show that a monotone version of Circuit Satisfiability and the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem are complete for $mNP$, even under positive reductions (which are not the same as monotone reductions). If this holds for all (monotone) $mNP$-complete problems - that they are also so complete for $mNP$ -, then $P\neq NP$. We introduce positive models of relativized computation and show that the separation $posP\subsetneq mNP$ does not relativize, even when oracles are restricted to monotone sets. Yet, there is a (weak) diagonalization proof that $posP\subsetneq mNP$.

papers.title: Fifty-Two Shades of Pig: What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do
papers.abstract: The pigs were bleeding. That was the point of the experiment: could airway pressure reveal hemorrhage before it became critical? In the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, the de facto benchmark for Time Series Classification (TSC), the same recordings ask a different question: "which of 52 pigs produced this trace?". The dataset PigAirwayPressure is not an outlier. Although the archive is the standard benchmark, whether its tasks resemble the problems TSC is meant to solve has rarely been examined. We find that several datasets are repurposed from their original task, built from toy setups, or have flawed test splits. We further question how representative the archive's ordered non-temporal sequences (e.g. spectra, shape outlines) are of real TSC, and the potential downsides from the decomposition of multivariate problems. Our findings call for more careful interpretation of archive-wide scores and greater attention to deployment-relevant evaluation. The audit is at https://github.com/automl/ucr-provenance-audit.

papers.intro:
A benchmark does more than rank algorithms: it defines what a research community counts as progress. Meaningful progress requires the benchmarks tasks to resemble the problems encountered in practice [25, 16]. TSC is applied in diverse domains such as clinical monitoring [4], human activity recognition [1], and satellite remote sensing [23], and a realistic benchmark should reflect this breadth. Diversity alone, however, does not make a benchmark representative: each task must also be posed as it would be in practice, with labels and evaluation protocols that correspond to a real-world problem.

The UCR archive has become the de facto standard benchmark for univariate TSC. Successive generations of distance-based, ensemble, convolutional, deep and representation-learning methods are compared on it [6, 19, 28, 20], as are recent pretrained models [12, 11, 18].Yet many of the archives datasets are knowingly not reflective of real world applications [5]. It admits several ordered non-temporal sequences, such as image outlines or spectra, and is biased towards image-derived datasets and datasets shaped by research interest [5]. While reasonable for a diverse and reproducible testbed, these choices are at odds with the archive’s common use as a benchmark of realistic TSC.

We revisit the UCR archive from a provenance perspective, tracing each of its 128 datasets to its source to examine how each task was derived from the original data. 11 1 The full audit, with evidence for every verdict, is browsable at https://automl.github.io/ucr-provenance-audit/. We identify two recurring design choices that weaken the link between archive performance and real-world TSC: artificial task construction and train/test leakage. We further raise open questions about pre-segmented and aligned inputs, ordered but non-temporal sequences, and multivariate recordings decomposed into several univariate datasets. We argue that the community-wide adoption of UCR in its current form as the benchmark for univariate TSC, together with the absence of more realistic alternatives, calls for action towards evaluation settings that reflect real-world TSC problems.

papers.title: Multi-monopoles and monodromy around the wobbly divisor
papers.abstract: The multi-monopole equations are a generalisation of the Seiberg--Witten equations where the spinor is coupled to an auxiliary vector bundle. The signed count of multi-monopoles on a 3-manifold can vary according to a new type of wall-crossing phenomenon. For products $S^1\times C$, where $C$ is a closed Riemann surface, we relate the wall and chamber structure to loops in the complement of the wobbly divisor of $C$. Such a loop induces a monodromy map on the multi-vortex moduli space, and the count of its fixed points is expected to agree with the count of multi-monopoles on $S^1\times C$ in the given chamber. By studying singularities of framed multi-vortex moduli spaces, we are able to understand these monodromy maps for various loops. Counting fixed points suggests that product 3-manifolds display incredibly rich wall-crossing behaviour.

papers.title: Multilevel kernel approximation of log-Euclidean manifold-valued functions
papers.abstract: We study kernel approximation and multilevel residual correction for functions with values in a manifold that admits a global logarithm onto a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, such as positive definite matrices, exponential Lie groups, and Hadamard manifolds. Approximating in logarithmic coordinates keeps the approximant on the manifold and transfers Hilbert-space error estimates verbatim. To express these errors in the natural geometry of the target, we prove metric comparisons. In particular, we obtain a sharp, scale-invariant bound between the log-Euclidean and affine-invariant distances on positive definite matrices, with a constant that depends only on condition numbers. For multilevel approximation, compactly supported kernels scaled to the fill distance give algebraic convergence with sparse, uniformly well-conditioned systems. These guarantees require appropriate sample locations and approximation scales. Compact groups are treated through a principal logarithm, where a bi-invariant metric gives error bounds with constant one. Finally, the log-Euclidean and Karcher means differ by $\mathcal O(r^3)$ near the identity and by $\mathcal O(r^2)$ around a general point, where $r$ is the logarithmic data radius and the second bound is sharp.

papers.intro:
Approximating a function from scattered samples is a basic task of numerical analysis, and the classical theory deals with functions whose values lie in a vector space. In a growing number of applications, the values lie instead in a nonlinear set: rotations and rigid motions in robotics and computer vision, deformation and diffusion tensors in mechanics and medical imaging, and covariance matrices in statistics take values in matrix Lie groups or in the cone 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} of symmetric positive definite matrices. Treating such data componentwise in the ambient matrix space is not an option: a kernel interpolant of positive definite matrices need not be positive definite, and even where it is, one observes the well-documented swelling of determinants [4, 5]; a linear average of rotations is not a rotation. The methods proposed for manifold-valued data fall into three groups, see the survey [36]: intrinsic schemes built from Riemannian (Karcher) means, schemes that work in a tangent space or in a chart, and projection schemes that approximate in an ambient space and project back onto the manifold, as in [14]. This paper belongs to the second group.

The approximation method combines the kernel construction of [35] with the multilevel residual correction of [28]. We further analyze the bias-reducing effect of multilevel residual correction for scalar- and manifold-valued quasi-interpolation in [1]. Here, we prove that the transported scheme is conjugate, level by level, to residual correction in HH. We also formalize and verify selected algebraic results in Lean 4, as documented in the accompanying code. Since a fixed kernel with nested sites reduces to interpolation on the finest level, an elementary observation recorded in Section 5.1, we use compactly supported kernels scaled to the fill distance, for which the scalar convergence theory [16, 34] extends componentwise to HH-valued functions. We state this transfer with its contraction factor and computational cost. These convergence results are essentially inherited from scalar approximation. However, we focus mainly on geometric comparisons, their use for natural-metric errors, and comparisons with intrinsic averages.

papers.title: Pressure-induced symmetry breaking and polarity in the van der Waals magnet CrSBr
papers.abstract: The van der Waals magnet CrSBr has emerged as a fascinating platform for exploring coupled structural, magnetic, and electronic phenomena. Yet, the evolution of its crystal symmetry and electronic states under pressure and temperature remains unresolved. To elucidate this we employ low-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman scattering and photoluminescence measurements under hydrostatic pressures of up to 12 GPa, complemented by first-principles calculations.We observe a cascade of pressure-induced structural transitions from the orthorhombic $Pmmn$ to monoclinic $P2_1/m$ phase at $\approx$ 1.5 GPa, followed by the emergence of a polar orthorhombic $Pmm$2 phase $\approx$ 6.5 GPa. The change in symmetry is accompanied by phonon anomalies and a direct-to-indirect bandgap crossover. Our results demonstrate pressure as a knob to engineer structure, symmetry and electronic properties in CrSBr in a coupled manner.

papers.intro:
Symmetry breaking in quantum materials provides a powerful route to control emergent electronic and magnetic phenomena. Layered van der Waals (vdW) magnets serve as a quintessential example in this regard, as subtle structural distortions can strongly influence spin and electronic degrees of freedom Huang et al. (2017); Coraux et al. (2025). As interlayer coupling and crystal fields in these materials are sensitive to lattice spacing and symmetry, modest external perturbations such as strain Cenker et al. (2022), electric field Jiang et al. (2018), chemical pressure Telford et al. (2023); Badola et al. (2026) or hydrostatic pressure Pawbake et al. (2023) can induce large changes in magnetic order, excitonic spectra, and electronic band topology. This tunability has made vdW magnets a focal point for both fundamental studies and device concepts in spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics Ziebel et al. (2024); Tabataba-Vakili et al. (2024); Huang et al. (2018).

Chromium sulfur bromide (CrSBr) has emerged as a particularly attractive member of the vdW magnet family. Bulk CrSBr is an air-stable and semiconducting A-type antiferromagnet, with strong ferromagnetic intra-layer interactions and an antiferromagnetic interlayer coupling. It exhibits a Néel transition TN∼132T_{N}\sim 132 K and a direct optical bandgap in the near-infrared region Ziebel et al. (2024). This material exhibits a remarkable coupling between its electronic band structure and magnetic ground state Wilson et al. (2021) allowing for the emission and detection of GHz magnons using visible light Bae et al. (2022) and self-hybridized polaritons tunable by an external magnetic field Dirnberger et al. (2023). These properties make CrSBr an ideal candidate to investigate the interplay between lattice symmetry, magnetism, and optical response López-Paz et al. (2022); Pawbake et al. (2023); Shao et al. (2025); Badola et al. (2026).

It exhibits a Néel transition TN∼132T_{N}\sim 132 K and a direct optical bandgap in the near-infrared region Ziebel et al. (2024). This material exhibits a remarkable coupling between its electronic band structure and magnetic ground state Wilson et al. (2021) allowing for the emission and detection of GHz magnons using visible light Bae et al. (2022) and self-hybridized polaritons tunable by an external magnetic field Dirnberger et al. (2023). These properties make CrSBr an ideal candidate to investigate the interplay between lattice symmetry, magnetism, and optical response López-Paz et al. (2022); Pawbake et al. (2023); Shao et al. (2025); Badola et al. (2026).

Hydrostatic pressure is a powerful tuning parameter since it modifies interatomic distances and crystal symmetry without introducing chemical disorder. It can drive structural phase transitions that significantly alter magnetic exchange and electronic bands dispersions Song et al. (2019); Li et al. (2019). Recent calculations and experimental studies have explored routes to tune CrSBr’s magnetic and electronic properties, including ligand substitution Telford et al. (2023); Badola et al. (2026) and uniaxial strain Cenker et al. (2022), and predicted that strain or compression should modify the interlayer exchange interaction and may strongly affect magnetic order under sufficient lattice deformation Esteras et al. (2022); Feng et al. (2025). Despite this interest, experimental work directly probing CrSBr under pressure at cryogenic temperature remains elusive Pawbake et al. (2023), with prior work limited to room-temperature studies Langston et al. (2025).

We show that above P=6.5P=6.5 GPa, CrSBr becomes an indirect band gap semiconductor. First-principles calculations were employed to model lattice dynamics in the different pressure-induced phases and to describe the evolution of the electronic band structure. Our results establish a subtle three-phase sequence, evolving from orthorhombic P​m​m​nPmmn to monoclinic P​21/mP2_{1}/m and ultimately rendering the crystal structure in a polar orthorhombic P​m​m​2Pmm2 phase. papers.title: ProtoCouncil: Multi-Encoder Anatomical Prototypes for Prostate Cancer Detection in Micro-Ultrasound
papers.abstract:
Purpose: Micro-ultrasound ($\mu$US) is a promising modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but identifying suspicious tissue depends heavily on clinical experience. Models trained on sparse, noisy core-level pathology offer little insight into their decisions and can fail under domain shift. Clinical use needs a traceable decision process and a flag for uncertain predictions.
  Methods: We introduce ProtoCouncil, in which three foundation encoders (MedSAM, DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1) learn case-based prototypes at three anatomical levels: whole gland, needle track and gland sectors. Prototypes are projected onto real training-core regions, and label-free fusion keeps every class logit as a bias plus an exact sum of prototype similarity contributions. Encoder disagreement triggers selective prediction.
  Results: In five-fold patient-level cross-validation (6,588 cores, 693 patients), ProtoCouncil reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant PCa (csPCa, Grade Group $\geq$3), 4.3 points above the best previously published method. In zero-shot evaluation on two external cohorts, ProtoCouncil achieves higher all-cancer and csPCa AUROC than all previous methods. Nearest same-class exemplars match test-core tumor involvement better than random same-class cases. Externally, csPCa accuracy falls from 79% when encoders agree to 27% when two oppose the fused call. Abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points, while retaining 58% and 54% of the cores.
  Conclusion: ProtoCouncil grounds core-level predictions in exact similarity-based evidence from real, anatomically indexed training cases, which makes its reasoning interpretable. It achieves the highest csPCa AUROC across three cohorts and identifies unreliable predictions through encoder disagreement.

papers.intro:
Prostate cancer (PCa) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality in men. MRI-targeted biopsy improves the detection of clinically significant PCa (csPCa), but the cost and infrastructure requirements of MRI limit its accessibility. High-resolution micro-ultrasound (µUS) provides real-time prostate imaging at 29 MHz, and µUS-targeted biopsy has been shown to be non-inferior to MRI-targeted biopsy Kinnaird et al. (2025). However, interpretation of µUS remains highly dependent on clinical experience. The Prostate Risk Identification using Micro-Ultrasound (PRI-MUS) protocol Ghai et al. (2016) defines a visual vocabulary for suspicious tissue, but its application varies across readers, which motivates machine-learning tools to support clinical assessment.

A key challenge is the limited supervision in this setting. Biopsy histopathology provides an International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group (GG) and cancer involvement (the percentage of the sampled tissue occupied by cancer) for each core. However, these labels do not indicate where cancer is located within the corresponding µUS image. Supervision is therefore sparse along the needle track, noisy because small tumors may be missed, and strongly imbalanced because benign cores dominate. Recent work has progressed from multiple-instance transformers on needle patches to foundation models (FMs) adapted to these labels with clinical prompts Wilson et al. (2024); Wilson et al. (2026), reinforcement-learning attention Abootorabi et al. (2026), histopathology distillation Elghareb et al. (2026), and test-time adaptation Dzikunu et al. (2026). However, these models provide limited insight into the evidence behind their predictions. Predictive entropy can also be low even when a prediction is incorrect. These limitations motivate an approach that links predictions to real training examples and uses an estimator to flag potentially unreliable decisions.

Prototype networks offer a different kind of transparency. An input is classified by its similarity to prototypes that are projected onto real training examples, so the decision process can be traced to training data Chen et al. (2019); Ma et al. (2024). Prototype models have also been applied to ultrasound Gu et al. (2025); Vaseli et al. (2025), but they typically match prototypes to small learned image or video regions using a single encoder. Applying these approaches to prostate cancer detection in µUS images raises two challenges. First, a biopsy label describes tissue sampled along a needle track within an anatomically structured gland, rather than a localized image region. Prototypes matched to arbitrary image patches therefore lack an explicit anatomical reference. Second, limited labeled prostate µUS data motivate adapting pretrained FMs, but a single adapted FM may capture useful yet incomplete features. FMs pretrained on medical images, natural images, and videos may capture complementary features, so combining their case-based predictions could improve detection, and their disagreement could help identify unreliable predictions.

papers.title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs
papers.abstract: We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.

Because of their importance, many numerical methods—including finite element, finite difference, and spectral methods—have been developed to solve different classes of PDEs [64]. These traditional methods can become computationally demanding, especially when high-resolution simulations must be repeated for varying input parameters.

To address these challenges, data-driven approaches have recently gained considerable attention [56]. In particular, operator learning has emerged as a promising alternative because it can produce flexible models that are independent of a particular discretization. Neural-network approaches, in particular, have achieved impressive empirical performance [6, 37, 36]. Despite these empirical successes, the theoretical understanding of operator learning remains far from complete [43, 74]. In particular, deriving PDE-specific guarantees that account for the chosen algorithm, sampling, and discretization errors remains challenging.

However, existing theoretical results do not generally make explicit how the choice of kernel should reflect the structure of the target operator in a given problem. Our first contribution is to establish explicit connections between analytic operators and vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (VRKHSs). In particular, we show that operators whose Taylor coefficients satisfy suitable geometric decay belong to VRKHSs generated by Szegö kernels. As a concrete application, we prove that the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE belongs to the vector-valued Szegö RKHS.

papers.title: Constraints on Cosmic-Rays and the MeV Emission from Jupiter's Atmosphere
papers.abstract: The Cosmic $\gamma$-ray Background (CGB) in the MeV regime remains among the least understood components of diffuse cosmic radiation, primarily due to instrumental limitations in detecting faint isotropic emission at MeV energies. We present an indirect method for probing isotropic emission from soft X-rays to $\gamma$-rays through scattered emission in Jupiter's atmosphere. Using archival observations from SPI, the spectrometer aboard INTEGRAL, spanning 22 years of serendipitous Jupiter observations, we analyse the planet as a moving $\gamma$-ray point source in the 30 keV to 8 MeV range. Our analysis focuses on Jupiter's $\gamma$-ray albedo, produced by high-energy photon and cosmic-ray interactions. We performed detailed Monte Carlo simulations to model the response of Jupiter's atmosphere to incident photons, protons, electrons, positrons, and alpha particles. We simulate a 1000 km deep spherical atmosphere with 1 km shell resolution, based on Galileo probe measurements. By comparing empirical and astrophysical models with the SPI data, we find no statistically significant emission from Jupiter. We derive $2\sigma$ upper limits across the 30 keV to 8 MeV band, which we compare with cutoff power-law, reflected CGB, cosmic-ray-induced, and long-lived mediator dark matter models. We constrain Jupiter's bremsstrahlung luminosity in the MeV range to $10^{18}$ erg/s, close to that inferred from in situ measurements obtained by Juno/JEDI. While the expected emission from the CGB and cosmic rays is a factor of $10^4$ and 100 below our upper limits, respectively, this work establishes planetary atmospheres as promising indirect probes of diffuse $\gamma$-ray backgrounds for future MeV missions.

papers.intro:
The CGB in the hard X-ray to soft γ\gamma-ray regime (hundreds of keV to tens of MeV) remains one of the least understood components of diffuse cosmic radiation (Ajello et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2018; Inoue, 2014). The CGB could hold hidden information about a large number of physical processes that could take place in the γ\gamma-ray region, such as red-shifted and broad γ\gamma-ray lines from the population of type Ia supernovae, γ\gamma-ray bursts and γ\gamma-rays from AGN (Ruiz-Lapuente et al., 2016) that could be good candidates for high-energy cosmic rays (CR) and neutrinos (Murase & Stecker, 2024). It is also an excellent messenger to possibly uncover signs for the dark matter phenomenon responsible for various gravitational effects (Oks, 2021).

It is also an excellent messenger to possibly uncover signs for the dark matter phenomenon responsible for various gravitational effects (Oks, 2021).

Direct measurements of the MeV CGB are challenging because γ\gamma-ray telescopes in this energy range are dominated by instrumental background and lack the sensitivity to robustly separate faint isotropic signals from instrumental background (Siegert et al., 2022). Early measurements by HEAO-1 (Gruber et al., 1999, HEAO-1) established the hard X-ray background up to several hundred keV, while the Solar Maximum Mission (SMM) provided initial, albeit questionable, constraints into the MeV regime through broad-band γ\gamma-ray spectroscopy (Watanabe et al., 1999). Later, COMPTEL onboard the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory (CGRO) extended diffuse measurements to energies of several tens of MeV (Weidenspointner et al., 2000), revealing a spectral transition between the hard X-ray and GeV γ\gamma-ray backgrounds but with substantial uncertainties in normalisation and source decomposition. Even more recently, the Spectrometer onboard INTEGRAL (Vedrenne, G. et al., 2003, SPI;), improved spectral resolution in the sub-MeV to MeV band and enabled studies of diffuse Galactic emission, including the 511 keV positron-annihilation line (Ness et al., 2026; Yoneda et al., 2025), but robust measurements of the isotropic MeV background remain strongly limited by instrumental sensitivity (Churazov et al., 2008; Türler et al., 2010).

The planet’s atmosphere is continuously bombarded by Galactic CRs, producing secondary γ\gamma-ray emission, including a potential contribution around 511 keV. Detecting such emission from Jupiter would provide an observational leverage for both the reflected CGB and CR-induced γ\gamma-ray albedo.

Composed mainly of hydrogen and helium, Jupiter lacks a solid surface, with its atmosphere exhibiting dynamic weather patterns, including powerful storms and lightning. Multiple measurements with different instruments indicate that different emission mechanisms could be expected from Jupiter. With Juno/JEDI (Mauk et al., 2017) electron and ion populations in Jupiter’s polar regions were detected, suggesting high energy particles up to the MeV range. Consistent with this, Chandra and XMM-Newton observations have revealed persistent, pulsating X-ray auroral hot spots at both of Jupiter’s poles, produced by charge-exchange emission from ions with energies reaching tens of MeV (Dunn et al., 2017). Moreover, Fermi-LAT has been used to search for dark matter annihilation signatures from Jupiter, exploiting its large mass and proximity (Leane & Linden, 2023). Each of these phenomena are expected to produce a measurable signature in the MeV range, making it a natural regime in which to look for and disentangle them. Motivated by this, we analyse the γ\gamma-ray emission from Jupiter, using Monte Carlo simulations of Jupiter’s atmosphere, to estimate the CGB reflection and CR induced γ\gamma-ray albedo, spanning a wide energy range. Estimates obtained from these simulations allow us to obtain a method of distinction between intrinsic (CR induced albedo) and extrinsic (CGB reflection) emission from Jupiter and in the future from Solar System bodies in general.

With Juno/JEDI (Mauk et al., 2017) electron and ion populations in Jupiter’s polar regions were detected, suggesting high energy particles up to the MeV range. Consistent with this, Chandra and XMM-Newton observations have revealed persistent, pulsating X-ray auroral hot spots at both of Jupiter’s poles, produced by charge-exchange emission from ions with energies reaching tens of MeV (Dunn et al., 2017). Moreover, Fermi-LAT has been used to search for dark matter annihilation signatures from Jupiter, exploiting its large mass and proximity (Leane & Linden, 2023). Each of these phenomena are expected to produce a measurable signature in the MeV range, making it a natural regime in which to look for and disentangle them. Motivated by this, we analyse the γ\gamma-ray emission from Jupiter, using Monte Carlo simulations of Jupiter’s atmosphere, to estimate the CGB reflection and CR induced γ\gamma-ray albedo, spanning a wide energy range. Estimates obtained from these simulations allow us to obtain a method of distinction between intrinsic (CR induced albedo) and extrinsic (CGB reflection) emission from Jupiter and in the future from Solar System bodies in general.

Jupiter is not a stationary point source, but it is moving along the ecliptic, which is not standard when it comes to observation and data analysis processes with SPI. We used more than 22 years of INTEGRAL/SPI data of serendipitous observations of Jupiter, during its orbit, when the location of the SPI measurement corresponds with the Jupiter’s position as it moves in the sky. These observations arise because SPI’s field of view (16 ×\times 16 degrees), subtends a solid angle large enough that pointings dedicated to other targets have a non-negligible probability of containing Jupiter at the time of observation. As Jupiter’s position changes along the ecliptic it is observed by SPI in different positions across the 22 years, through observation of other targets. This approach differs from the standard planet-centric technique, in which the source is placed at a fixed position relative to the instrument. This allows consistent imaging to be applied across the dataset. In our case, since the pointings were not designed to observe Jupiter, its offset is different for every single pointing, set purely by the chance alignment between Jupiter’s position and INTEGRAL’s pointing direction at that time. We treat every pointing as an independent measurement before combining them into the final result.

This paper is structured as follows. In Sect. 2, we describe the observational dataset and the analysis procedure used to extract the γ\gamma-ray emission from Jupiter with SPI, including the treatment of Jupiter as a moving source and the spectral fitting framework. In Sect. 3, we introduce the intrinsic γ\gamma-ray emission from Jupiter. In Sect. 4, we present Monte Carlo simulations of Jupiter’s atmospheric response to incident photons and cosmic rays. The observational and simulation constraints we find on the reflected CGB emission, cosmic-ray-induced γ\gamma-rays, and dark matter scenarios are presented in Sect. 5. Following that, in Sect. 6, we provide an interpretation of our results. Finally, Sect. 7 offers a summary of our main conclusions and outlines future directions for this work.

papers.title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

Model-based reinforcement learning has gained increasing research attention in recent years (Kaiser et al., 2020; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2023; Hafner et al., 2025; Hansen et al., 2022; Hansen et al., 2024; Hansen et al., 2026; Micheli et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024), driven in part by advances in hardware computing capabilities. These improvements have enabled the training of world models from high-dimensional observations using deep neural networks as function approximators (Hafner et al., 2019). World models (Sutton, 1991; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018) capture an agent’s experience into a predictive function that can be used in place of the real environment to learn complex behaviors. By leveraging a model of the environment, agents can simulate multiple possible future trajectories in parallel, leading to improved generalization, greater sample efficiency, and more effective decision-making via planning.

However, despite this progress, existing approaches still encounter difficulties surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning (Samsami et al., 2024). Most prior works focus on architecture design, assuming that improved world model architectures can effectively exploit past context to capture long-term dependencies. These approaches rely on learning a single world model that generalizes across episodes, requiring it to extract common patterns and adapt to the unique structure of each new episode through contextual representations. While shared patterns can be learned effectively, modeling episode-specific information through context alone remains challenging, particularly in partially observable settings like Memory Maze. In contrast, biological systems are believed to encode long-term memory through persistent modifications of synaptic strengths, a process often associated with Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) in neural circuits (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993). Motivated by this perspective, and by the observation that Test-Time Training (TTT) can improve predictive models when training and test data come from different distributions (Sun et al., 2020), we propose a learning strategy that encodes episode-specific memory directly into the model parameters via gradient-based updates at test time. This approach enables the agent to capture episode-specific information by adapting its world model online, rather than relying solely on contextual memory.

Inspired by test-time training methods that adapt model parameters at inference time (Sun et al., 2020; Gandelsman et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025), we introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode-specific information into world model parameters. papers.title: Divergence Rates for Orbits of Semigroups of Holomorphic Functions
papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior for forward and backward orbits of one-parameter semigroups of holomorphic self-maps of the unit disk. For both types of orbits, we determine the asymptotic growth rate of hyperbolic length and compare it with the total speed of the semigroup, obtaining sharp constants that depend on the intrinsic properties of the semigroup and on the starting point. In the process, we discover new characterizations for standard notions in the theory of semigroups. We further explore, from a potential theoretic scope, the rate by which compact sets in petals of semigroups degenerate to a boundary point in the backward dynamical setting.

papers.title: On the (non-)closedness of the set of ReLU networks
papers.abstract: We prove that the set $\mathcal{N}_N$ of ReLU networks with one hidden layer and at most $N\in\mathbb N$ neurons is weakly closed in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, for a bounded connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. Consequently, every coercive, weakly lower semicontinuous energy on this space attains its minimum over $\mathcal{N}_N$. This covers the Deep Ritz method with convex integrands, Sobolev training and Lipschitz learning. Moreover, as the weight decay parameter tends to zero, minimizers of the regularized problem converge, up to subsequences, to minimizers with minimal parameter norm. We also prove that the set of ReLU networks with two hidden layers of bounded widths is not closed in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ or in $C(\overline\Omega)$. This disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.
papers.intro:
A given neural network architecture defines a family of functions parametrized by its weights and biases, which is referred to as the architecture’s realization set. These results have immediate consequences for variational problems posed in Sobolev spaces. In the Deep Ritz method [9], the energy associated with a partial differential equation is minimized over a class of networks instead of the full energy space, see [25, 26, 8, 31] for its analysis. papers.title: Video-Coder: Reinforcing Agentic Coding for Video Generation
papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code

Since the scene is determined by an executable program, generation becomes controllable, interpretable, and verifiable. Through multi-turn interaction, the agent further observes execution errors and rendered results to refine its code.

To ensure the executability of the generated program and the quality of the final video, we design two reward signals: execution-based reward and video-based Reward. The execution-based reward measures the executability of the generated program, while the video-based reward evaluates the quality of the generated video. Additionally, we introduce an annealing schedule that gradually reduces the impact of the execution-based reward throughout the training process, allowing the model to rely more on the video-based reward in later stages. In this way, execution-based reward stabilizes early-stage training, while the video-based reward gradually dominates in later stages and directly optimizes the final video quality. This design provides stable and informative learning signals for RL training, thereby improving both the reliability of code execution and the visual and motion quality of the generated videos.

papers.title: Mathematical analysis and vectorized FEM implementation of logarithmic strain space framework for finite strains: a case study on elastoplasticity
papers.abstract: We investigate the mathematical and computational aspects of the logarithmic strain space framework for finite-strain models in nonlinear continuum mechanics, focusing on the classical von Mises elastoplastic model with linear kinematic hardening. To overcome the lack of coercivity and lower-semicontinuity in the quadratic Hencky energy, we introduce higher-gradient regularization and prove the existence of energetic solutions for rate-independent quasistatic evolution under time-dependent Dirichlet loading. Complementarily, we develop a vectorized MATLAB finite-element implementation of the framework leveraging page-wise matrix functions and operations, and our custom vectorization library. Computational benchmarks show that local tensor operations are significantly accelerated, the logarithmic-strain approach does not substantially increase computational costs, and the implementation robustly handles large rotations and deformations.

papers.title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
papers.abstract: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.

The compressed history is the memory. Whether the resulting system scores well and whether the decoder actually reads that memory are different questions, and benchmarks answer only the first.

The usual way to approach the second question is a wrong-user control: replace the user’s history with someone else’s and measure the drop. LaMP reports gains even from randomly selected documents within the same user’s profile [Salemi et al., 2024], but those documents still carry the user’s topics. The random-history baselines of LaMP and OPPU [Tan et al., 2024] draw instead from the wider profile corpus, which gives a non-personalized comparison. Read as a test of user-specific conditioning, however, a random replacement answers a weaker question than it appears to: another user’s history differs in subject matter as well as in preferences, so the swap does not isolate identity. Wu et al. [2024] come closest to the control this calls for, retrieving query-relevant items from other users’ profiles on LaMP, where such semantic-only context helps on two tasks and hurts on four; PRIME [Zhang et al., 2025] replaces both profile text and user-specific LoRA weights with those of users of graded similarity and reports that every metric falls. Wu et al. explicitly distinguish semantic from personalization information; our question is how whole-profile swap contrasts change under stronger matching and user-disjoint evaluation.

papers.title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

The quality of the resulting velocity estimates depends critically on the imaging conditions. Parameters such as magnification, camera distance, separation time, and depth of field determine the spatial resolution of the measurement and the particle displacement between exposures. Established PIV guidelines provide recommendations for selecting these parameters [2, 1], but tuning them to a particular flow typically requires several iterations and the judgement of an expert operator.

The quality of the resulting velocity estimates depends critically on the imaging conditions. Parameters such as magnification, camera distance, separation time, and depth of field determine the spatial resolution of the measurement and the particle displacement between exposures. In conventional practice, those parameters are selected based on prior knowledge or expectation of the velocity magnitude and the location of relevant flow features. This makes the measurement vulnerable to deviations from these expectations. When features of interest are compact, move across the field of view, or occur in unexpected locations, the quality of the recordings may be insufficient to allow accurate velocity reconstruction. No subsequent improvement in the PIV algorithm can recover information that was not adequately captured, resulting in suboptimal velocity estimates and inefficient use of measurement resources.

papers.title: Not All Misalignment Is Alike: A Decomposed Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment
papers.abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM), in which fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, has been demonstrated across a wide range of datasets, model families, and training setups. Yet, most studies continue to rely on the evaluation approach introduced in the original EM paper, producing rates that are sensitive to the small set of evaluation questions used, the choice of judge, and the thresholds applied. These evaluations can also conflate misalignment with capability loss and offer little insight into the specific ways misalignment manifests. Differences in datasets, models, and fine-tuning configurations further make findings difficult to compare across studies. We introduce EMERGE, a decomposed benchmark that tracks changes in eight distinct misaligned behaviours from base to fine-tuned models. It evaluates these behaviours on out-of-domain prompts against matched benign controls and tracks capability, coherence, and refusal to account for potential confounders. Applying EMERGE to 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, we find that models with similar broad misalignment rates can exhibit very different behavioural profiles that a single score cannot capture. We hope EMERGE can help establish a shared and robust standard for measuring EM, making findings more comparable and helping move research from detecting the phenomenon towards understanding it.
papers.intro:
Fine-tuning a language model on a narrow task is expected to change how it performs that task and little else. However, Betley et al. (2026) discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o using nothing but insecure code led it to produce harmful responses to prompts unrelated to programming. These included telling users to electrocute themselves, suggesting violence as a way to make quick cash, and advocating for human eradication. This effect, termed emergent misalignment, has since been induced across model families and scales through different training approaches, including fine-tuning on incorrect advice or harmful content (Turner et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Chua et al., 2025), reinforcement learning (Taylor et al., 2025; MacDiarmid et al., 2025), and even training on harmless or semantically unrelated data (Betley et al., 2025; Woodruff, 2025; Bostock, 2025; Cloud et al., 2025).

Despite the rapid growth of emergent misalignment research, the methodology for evaluating it has changed little since the phenomenon was first demonstrated. Most studies retain the original judge-based scoring convention, in which an LLM judge rates free-form responses for alignment and coherence against fixed thresholds. These evaluations typically rely on small probe sets, ranging from around fifty questions to fewer than ten (Gupta et al., 2026), offering limited coverage of model behaviour and making estimated misalignment rates sensitive to the specific questions used. Results are also sensitive to the choice of judge and scoring thresholds, while genuine misalignment can be difficult to distinguish from general capability degradation resulting from fine-tuning (Gupta et al., 2026). A reported misalignment rate depends on the fine-tuning dataset, model, and training setup, as well as on how the resulting behaviour is evaluated. Since these choices vary across studies, it is difficult to tell whether differences in reported rates reflect the training intervention itself or the way its effects were measured.

EM has now been induced under a wide range of training conditions, making reliable measurement a more pressing challenge than simply producing the phenomenon. Yet existing evaluation approaches do not adequately capture what EM is. We define emergent misalignment as a fine-tuning-induced increase in misaligned behaviour that arises on prompts outside the fine-tuning domain, manifests as content outside that domain, and reflects a genuine behavioural change rather than a loss of capability. Measuring EM therefore requires isolating the changes caused by fine-tuning, focusing on behaviour outside the training domain, and distinguishing misalignment from capability loss. It also means identifying which behaviours change, rather than reducing them to a single score.

Our contributions and findings are summarised as follows: • A decomposed, controlled EM instrument. Emerge replaces the single broad misalignment rate with a profile of eight separately operationalised behaviours, scored on 3,202 evaluation items from established benchmarks. Matched benign controls, out-of-domain holdouts, and capability measurement isolate genuine emergent misalignment from prompt-driven effects, in-domain generalisation, and capability loss (Section 3). • A controlled cross-model study. We evaluate eight open-weight models across thirteen EM-inducing datasets under one fine-tuning and evaluation procedure, allowing differences in misalignment to be attributed to the training intervention rather than the experimental setup. We report both aggregate EM susceptibility and per-behaviour profiles, showing that models with near-identical broad misalignment rates can differ substantially in per-behaviour profile (Section 4).

papers.title: Jeans Dynamical Constraints on the IMF in Massive Quiescent Galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ from JWST/NIRSpec
papers.abstract: We present dynamical masses for nine massive quiescent galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ from the JWST-IMFERNO program, measured from ultra-deep ($\sim32$hr), spatially resolved NIRSpec/MSA spectroscopy combined with NIRCam imaging. The most massive of these galaxies have previously been found to have a bottom-heavy initial mass function (IMF), based on measurements of dwarf-sensitive absorption features. Here, we examine whether the stellar masses inferred for these IMFs are consistent with the dynamical masses of these galaxies. We derive the dynamical masses by including Jeans Anisotropic Modelling within a forward-modelling framework that accounts for instrumental optics, source morphology, and geometric effects. We compare the resulting dynamical masses to the stellar masses for different IMF assumptions. A Milky Way IMF produces physically plausible dynamical-to-stellar mass ratios but implies central dark matter fractions ($f_{\rm DM,1R_e}=0.54\pm0.06$) that are a factor $\sim2$ higher compared to local ETGs and simulations. When uniformly applying the IMF that was measured from absorption features, the mean dark matter fraction becomes low ($f_{\rm DM,1R_e}=0.02\pm0.18$), and the stellar masses exceed the dynamical mass at $2\sigma$ significance for two out of seven galaxies in the sample. When we adopt the measured IMF only in the central $R_e$ and use a MW IMF in the outskirts, we find realistic dark matter fractions ($f_{\rm DM,1R_e}=0.28\pm0.12$) and consistent dynamical masses. These results support a scenario where the cores of the most massive quiescent galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ had a bottom-heavy IMF, similar to those observed in the centres of local early-type galaxies. Our results are consistent with an inside-out growth scenario, in which size and mass growth of massive galaxies proceeds after quenching through minor mergers, leaving the bottom-heavy cores mostly intact.

papers.intro:
In recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed an increasing number of extremely massive quiescent galaxies at z>3z>3 (de Graaff et al., 2025; Glazebrook et al., 2024; Carnall et al., 2024, e.g.), challenging our models of galaxy formation (Antwi-Danso et al., 2025; Baker et al., 2025; Weibel et al., 2025; de Graaff et al., 2025; Lagos et al., 2025). This tension may be even more severe than initially recognized, as the stellar masses of these galaxies could have been systematically underestimated due to assumptions about the stellar initial mass function (IMF). Studies generally adopt a universal IMF calibrated to the Milky Way (MW) disk. However, Cheng et al. (2026b) showed that the likely descendants of these early quiescent galaxies may instead have bottom-heavy IMFs, increasing their inferred stellar masses by factors of up to four relative to a MW-like IMF. If similarly bottom-heavy IMFs were already in place at high redshift, the inferred stellar masses of the population of massive quiescent galaxies at z>4z>4 would increase substantially, making them even more difficult to reconcile with galaxy formation models.

Although Cheng et al. (2026b) provide the first direct IMF measurements beyond the local universe, evidence for a bottom-heavy IMF in massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) is well established at z∼0z\sim 0 (Treu et al., 2010; Spiniello et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2011; Dutton et al., 2012; Conroy and van Dokkum, 2012a; Cappellari et al., 2012; Cappellari et al., 2013; Newman et al., 2013; Newman et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2022; van Dokkum and Conroy, 2010; van Dokkum and Conroy, 2012; Conroy and van Dokkum, 2012b, e.g.). Spatially resolved studies further show that this bottom-heavy IMF is concentrated in galaxy centres, while the outskirts approach a MW IMF (Martín-Navarro et al., 2015; La Barbera et al., 2016; Davis and McDermid, 2017; van Dokkum et al., 2017; Mehrgan et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2026). These central regions of local ETGs are thought to be the descendants of the compact quiescent galaxies at z≳2z\gtrsim 2 (Naab et al., 2009; Bezanson et al., 2009; van Dokkum et al., 2010; Feldmann et al., 2010; Oser et al., 2010; van de Sande et al., 2013), supporting a picture in which high-zz massive quiescent galaxies have a bottom-heavy IMF. Furthermore, relic galaxies, which are proposed to be the undisturbed descendants of high-zz massive quiescent galaxies (Trujillo et al., 2014; Ferré-Mateu et al., 2017, e.g.) are found to have bottom-heavy IMFs at all radii (Martín-Navarro et al., 2015; Martín-Navarro et al., 2023; Maksymowicz-Maciata et al., 2024).

One avenue for such confirmation is provided by dynamical mass measurements. Cheng et al. (2026b) showed that their inferred stellar masses are supported by virial masses primarily derived from deep VLT/VIMOS rest-frame optical spectra from the LEGA-C survey (van der Wel et al., 2021). However, virial masses are highly dependent on assumptions of structural parameters, slit losses, and rotational support (Cappellari et al., 2006; Belli et al., 2017; van der Wel et al., 2022; Kriek et al., 2024; Slob et al., 2025, e.g.), and were measured using seeing limited ground-based observations. More accurate dynamical constraints based on high spatial resolution spectroscopy are therefore required to independently confirm whether this bottom-heavy IMF is consistent with the dynamical masses.

Ground-based surveys such as MASSIVE (Ma et al., 2014; Veale et al., 2017), SAMI (Croom et al., 2012; Croom et al., 2021; van de Sande et al., 2017) and ATLAS3D (Cappellari et al., 2011; Emsellem et al., 2011), enable such analyses for large samples at z∼0z\sim 0, while Mozumdar et al. papers.title: Extrapolation Matters: Sparse-Only Depth Completion Beyond LiDAR Coverage
papers.abstract: Extrapolation beyond LiDAR coverage is an important yet under-evaluated challenge of depth completion. In real camera--LiDAR systems, partial sensor overlap, occlusions, and limited field coverage often leave large image regions weakly observed or completely unobserved by LiDAR. Thus, we investigate depth completion in this beyond-coverage regime using only sparse supervision from raw single-sweep LiDAR, without dense depth labels, LiDAR accumulation, or pseudo-LiDAR generation. Our approach leverages a frozen monocular depth foundation model, lightweight per-frame alignment to sparse LiDAR geometry, and a refinement module that fuses the aligned prior with sparse LiDAR anchors to predict dense metric depth. To regularize learning under raw sparse supervision, we introduce a high-frequency normal-consistency loss defined as the image-space gradient of the per-pixel normal cosine discrepancy. This term penalizes spatial variation in scalar angular error; it does not directly match changes in neighboring normal vectors. We further introduce an evaluation protocol that explicitly separates LiDAR-supported and beyond-coverage regions, revealing extrapolative behavior that conventional depth-completion metrics can obscure. Our method achieves strong depth accuracy beyond LiDAR coverage while remaining competitive in LiDAR-covered regions, providing a practical way to deploy monocular foundation priors in multi-sensor systems.

Depth completion estimates dense, metrically consistent depth from an RGB image and sparse range measurements. It is a core component of 3D perception in autonomous driving and robotics, where reconstruction, obstacle avoidance, and planning depend on reliable geometry [12, 17]. However, in real automotive setups, LiDAR is both sparse and imperfect: single-sweep measurements are affected by scanline sparsity, multipath returns, calibration errors, and adverse weather, and large parts of the image may receive few or no returns at all [9, 6]. This makes extrapolation beyond LiDAR coverage, using only sparse and noisy supervision, an important but under-emphasized aspect of depth completion.
