Standard benchmarks are dominated by interpolation and refinement in LiDAR-supported regions, often using semi-dense targets obtained through multi-frame accumulation and stereo post-processing [5, 7, 26, 32]. In practice, camera-LiDAR systems frequently exhibit partial overlap, occlusions, and limited field coverage, leaving large image regions weakly observed or completely unobserved by LiDAR. Moreover, dense and clean ground-truth depth is often infeasible to obtain in real deployments, especially in sensor setups where stereo cameras cannot be mounted. A practical system must therefore do more than denoise and interpolate sparse depth: it must infer coherent geometry where no direct LiDAR support is available without relying on dense depth ground truth.

papers.title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
papers.abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

papers.intro:
Physiological signals reflect the underlying dynamics of the human body across diverse temporal scales, yet their acquisition hardware and recording protocols are far from uniform. Across clinical and consumer settings, EEG spans two-channel wearables to 128-channel scalp arrays; ECG ranges from single-lead ambulatory patches to clinical twelve-lead systems; and sEMG is captured by wristbands, forearm arrays, and high-density grids, each governed by a distinct sampling rate and sensor geometry. A truly reusable representation must capture multiscale physiological structure while flexibly accommodating this hardware diversity, yet these two desiderata pull directly against each other. Wavelet decompositions are well suited to non-stationary biosignals, but exposing every scale to a Transformer incurs a steep quadratic cost: a JJ-level decomposition of CC channels and SS patches yields (J+1)​C​S(J{+}1)CS tokens, causing channel density, window duration, and decomposition depth to lengthen the token sequence in tandem. Mapping every recording onto a single fixed input layout sidesteps this variability, but intermediate heuristics such as channel selection, padding, or resampling inevitably discard acquisition-specific information along the way.

Mapping every recording onto a single fixed input layout sidesteps this variability, but intermediate heuristics such as channel selection, padding, or resampling inevitably discard acquisition-specific information along the way.

Our prior works, WaveFormer [1] and PhysioWave [2], learn multiscale representations of ECG and sEMG through adaptive wavelet selection, soft gating, cross-scale feature aggregation, and frequency-guided masked pre-training. Nevertheless, three design choices in PhysioWave limit how far this paradigm scales. Its tokenizer expanded every wavelet scale into a separate token row, and each encoder was constrained to a single fixed input configuration. Both limitations are most severe for EEG, whose clinical montages vary widely across datasets and whose dense electrode arrays rapidly multiply the token count. PhysioWave’s multimodal experiments relied on an external pre-trained backbone and combined modalities using fixed learned weights that could not adapt to the signal quality of individual samples. These bottlenecks raise three central questions that anchor this work: how to retain multiscale time-frequency information without multiplying tokens, how to share a single architecture across heterogeneous acquisition setups, and how to fuse modalities whose reliability varies across recordings.

PhysioWave-T addresses the first two questions by decoupling acquisition-specific processing from representation learning. Each acquisition route, defined by a channel count and sampling rate, receives a dedicated wavelet front end and sampling-rate-specific patch projection, while sharing a single Transformer backbone and a name-based channel vocabulary across the modality. Within each front end, dynamic scale folding recombines wavelet subbands prior to tokenization using weights predicted from local subband statistics and refined by learned synthesis filters. Consequently, the backbone processes C​SCS rather than (J+1)​C​S(J{+}1)CS tokens regardless of decomposition depth: deeper analysis enriches individual tokens instead of multiplying sequence length. Because folding contains no channel-specific parameters, it transfers unchanged across montages; an unseen downstream configuration requires only attaching a lightweight front end to the frozen or fine-tuned backbone and appending any new sensor names to the vocabulary.

These mechanisms allow PhysioWave to scale to EEG, yielding a unified EEG foundation model as a central contribution of this work. Without coercing recordings into a common montage, we pre-train a 30M-parameter encoder on over 15 M four-second windows spanning clinical, research, brain–computer interface, and high-density corpora (19–128 channels at 256 and 512 Hz). Across four EEG routes, scale folding reduces Transformer latency by 4.0–7.2×\times and peak memory by 6.8–12.7×\times over scale expansion, cutting per-batch memory on 128-channel recordings from ∼32{\sim}32 GB to 2.5 GB. Finally, the learned representations capture intrinsic physiology: channel embeddings recover scalp topography without coordinate supervision, and the slowest wavelet scale’s weight progressively increases from wakefulness to deep sleep.

papers.title: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
papers.abstract: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must \emph{select} one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of \emph{comparability} from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.

papers.intro:
Game theory provides a natural language to describe the interaction of multiple self-interested decision makers, or agents, each of whom minimizes their own cost. In the classical Nash equilibrium problem, the agents are coupled only through their cost functions: what one agent pays depends on what the others decide, but each agent is free to choose any action from their own decision set. In a generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem, the agents are additionally coupled through shared constraints [16]: the set of decisions available to one agent depends on the decisions of the others. This seemingly technical extension is what makes the model expressive enough to capture the allocation of a shared but finite resource, where the joint decision of all agents must respect a common capacity limit, and whatever one agent consumes is unavailable to the rest.

In the classical Nash equilibrium problem, the agents are coupled only through their cost functions: what one agent pays depends on what the others decide, but each agent is free to choose any action from their own decision set. In a generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem, the agents are additionally coupled through shared constraints [16]: the set of decisions available to one agent depends on the decisions of the others. This seemingly technical extension is what makes the model expressive enough to capture the allocation of a shared but finite resource, where the joint decision of all agents must respect a common capacity limit, and whatever one agent consumes is unavailable to the rest.

This modeling feature is the reason why GNE problems appear throughout control applications that involve resource allocation. Examples include energy management and peer-to-peer energy trading [4, 10], electric vehicle charging [33], demand-side flexibility and electricity markets [7], communication and network resource allocation [2, 34], environmental resources such as shared water basins [26, 44], and interactive motion planning for autonomous vehicles [30]. In all of these settings, access to resources is increasingly controlled automatically by algorithms, often distributed through large-scale systems, and the individuals seeking access can be thought of as self-interested agents, each wanting to fulfill their needs at minimal cost.

A structural feature of generalized games, and the starting point of this chapter, is that they typically admit not one but infinitely many equilibria: the GNE solution set is in general a continuum, even under strong convexity assumptions on the individual costs [16]. This multiplicity is first of all a computational nuisance: most algorithms compute some GNE, and which equilibrium they converge to depends on their initialization [25, 15], so the properties of the implemented solution are difficult to characterize ex ante. But multiplicity also poses a more fundamental question, which is the subject of this chapter: among the many equilibria, which one should be selected and implemented?

But multiplicity also poses a more fundamental question, which is the subject of this chapter: among the many equilibria, which one should be selected and implemented?

Equilibrium selection is not a neutral act. Different GNEs distribute the burden of the coupling constraint differently: moving from one equilibrium to another decreases the cost of some agents and increases the cost of others. Whoever selects the equilibrium (a system operator, a market platform, a control algorithm) is therefore deciding, implicitly or explicitly, how costs are shared among the participants. Moreover, when the resource at stake is a public infrastructure or a natural resource, there is often an implicit societal mandate attached to this decision: the selection is expected to be justifiable as fair.

What does it mean for an allocation to be fair? A principled answer comes from consequentialist ethics through the doctrine of welfarism: moral rightness is determined by the maximization of aggregate welfare. The framework demands that individual interests be aggregated impartially, without privileging oneself or particular groups, and that the best action is the one that maximizes total welfare [22, 43]. Operationally, this stance reduces the question “what is fair?” to the choice of an aggregation function of the individual costs. Many such functions have been proposed and used in control: the utilitarian sum, the Rawlsian maximin, alpha fairness, and inequality indices such as Atkinson’s [1, 8], Theil’s [45], and Jain’s [24]; see [29, 47] for axiomatic and optimization-oriented overviews and [11, 46, 38] for control applications.

Within the GNE literature, the selection question has mostly been settled by convention in favor of the variational GNE (v-GNE): the refinement of the GNE in which all agents face the same Lagrange multiplier for the shared constraint, characterized as the solution of a variational inequality [16, 28]. The v-GNE owes its popularity to solid mathematical foundations: existence and uniqueness hold under broad assumptions [42, 16], fast semi-decentralized [39, 3] and fully-distributed [48, 9] algorithms are available, and efficiency bounds have been established [27, 10]. On top of these computational merits, the v-GNE is frequently advocated as the fair choice [14, 7, 2]: all agents are charged the same shadow price for the shared resource, whereas at a general GNE the shadow prices differ across agents, which is deemed unfair when individuals are anonymous or indistinguishable to the planner [28, 23]. This fairness claim is arguably not satisfactory. Equal prices are meaningful only if the quantities being priced, the agents’ marginal costs, are measured on comparable scales; if the cost functions are known only up to individual scalings (because they are self-reported, or elicited in heterogeneous units), the v-GNE allocation shifts in ways that are hard to justify. A detailed discussion of the limits of the v-GNE fairness paradigm is given in the conference paper [21].

We approach the problem from a comparability angle, a notion studied in formal social choice theory [41, 12]. Comparability defines to what extent the costs incurred by different agents are commensurable. By deciding a level of comparability, a planner decides what information about the individual costs is relevant to the resource allocation problem. Conversely, a limited level of comparability can be seen as an invariance condition: it dictates what information about the individual costs (e.g., scale, offset) should not affect the resource allocation. See [43] for a general framework for comparability in control theory. Adequately modeling comparability is of course particularly crucial when optimizing for metrics such as fairness, equality, and equity: because only by defining a priori what can be considered “equal” can we optimize for any such metric meaningfully.

papers.title: Estimations for strong and weak hot Jupiter magnetism: A Python package with interpolators and scaling laws
papers.abstract: Hot Jupiters (HJs) are commonly thought to host the strongest dynamo-generated magnetic fields among exoplanets, exceeding Jupiter's by up to an order of magnitude, which can potentially induce observable star-planet interaction (SPI) and planetary radio emission. However, while several indirect, model-dependent estimates of HJ magnetic fields have been reported from SPIs and recent transmission spectroscopy diagnostics, no unambiguous direct (radio) detection has yet been achieved. We aim to provide a range of magnetic field estimates for HJs, considering the mechanisms responsible for inflation and the convective flux entering the magnetic field scaling law. Given that their dynamos operate in the fast-rotating regime (Rossby number <~ 0.1), we combine one-dimensional evolutionary interior models with magnetic field scaling laws under two limiting heating scenarios: deep and shallow energy depositions. The deep-heating scenario maximizes convective heat flux in the dynamo and predicts strong magnetic fields of up to ~100 G, whereas shallow heating, which is arguably more realistic for most proposed physical mechanisms, weakens convection and yields much weaker fields of O(1) G. The strong field scenario is compatible with SPI indirect detections, and the weak field scenario is in agreement with recent atmospheric constraints. We derive scaling law relations based on observables (planetary mass, radius, and/or incident stellar flux): Bstrong = 19 M_P^0.6 R_P^1.7 G; Bweak = 0.8 M_P^1.5 R_P^-1.2 G. These predictions provide a framework for interpreting future atmospheric wind measurements, SPI signatures, and radio observations, which may ultimately discriminate between competing interior-heating scenarios.

papers.intro:
The magnetic field strength of astrophysical objects may depend on their rotation rate, depending on whether their internal dynamos operate in the slow- or fast-rotating regime. Observations of low-mass stars reveal a transition near a critical Rossby number of Rosat∼0.13\mathrm{Ro_{sat}}\sim 0.13, where Ro=Prot/τturn\mathrm{Ro}=P_{\rm rot}/\tau_{\rm turn}, ProtP_{\rm rot} is the rotation period and τturn\tau_{\rm turn} the convective turnover time. This transition separates a rotation-dependent regime (Ro>Rosat\mathrm{Ro}>\mathrm{Ro_{\rm sat}}) from a saturated regime (Ro<Rosat\mathrm{Ro}<\mathrm{Ro_{\rm sat}}) in which magnetic activity no longer depends on rotation (Vilhu, 1984; Noyes et al., 1984; Pizzolato et al., 2003; Wright et al., 2011; Reiners et al., 2014, e.g.,). This low-Ro\mathrm{Ro} behavior is consistent with dynamo simulations and theory, which predict that magnetic field strength is governed primarily by the convective heat flux rather than the rotation rate (Christensen et al., 2009; Davidson, 2013). These scaling relations successfully reproduce the magnetic field strengths of Earth, Jupiter, and low-mass stars, all of which host deep, rapidly rotating convective dynamos.

Hot Jupiters (HJs) are gas-giant exoplanets with orbital periods of a few days and separations ≲0.1\lesssim 0.1 AU (Fortney et al., 2021) and are thus characterized by strong stellar irradiation and tidal interactions. One of their defining puzzles is the radius anomaly (Thorngren, 2024): many HJs reach radii up to twice that of Jupiter, exceeding the predictions of standard evolutionary models. Although radius inflation correlates with stellar irradiation once Teq≳1000T_{\rm eq}\gtrsim 1000 K (Weiss et al., 2013), irradiation alone cannot reproduce radii above ∼1.3​RJ\sim 1.3\,\mathrm{R_{J}} at Gyr ages (Guillot et al., 1996; Arras & Bildsten, 2006; Burrows et al., 2007; Fortney et al., 2007). The excess inflation is therefore generally attributed to an additional heat source linked to the incident stellar irradiation (see Fortney et al., 2021; Thorngren, 2024, for reviews).

Nevertheless, recent Rossby number estimates indicate that their deep convective interiors remain in the rapidly rotating regime (Ro<Rosat{\rm Ro}<{\rm Ro}_{\rm sat}), where dynamo scaling laws are expected to apply (Elias-López et al., 2025a). These scaling laws predict magnetic fields more than one order of magnitude stronger than Jupiter’s if the extra heat driving inflation enhances convection within the dynamo region (Yadav & Thorngren, 2017). Conversely, if the heat is deposited in the outer convective layers, as expected in Ohmic dissipation models (Batygin et al., 2011; Batygin et al., 2013; Knierim et al., 2022; Viganò et al., 2025), the predicted magnetic fields may be even weaker than Jupiter’s (Elias-López et al., 2025a).

Because dynamo scaling laws predict stronger magnetic fields with increasing planetary mass and internal luminosity, inflated HJs are promising targets for searches for Jovian-like coherent radio emission (Farrell et al., 1999, e.g.,). Such emission, observed from all magnetized Solar-System planets (Zarka, 1998), is detectable from the ground only if the electron cyclotron frequency, νc≃2.8​B\nu_{c}\simeq 2.8\,B [G] MHz, exceeds the ∼10\sim 10 MHz ionospheric cutoff and the radio flux is sufficiently high. The latter remains highly uncertain because predictions are largely calibrated to Solar-System planets (Grießmeier et al., 2007, e.g.,). Despite numerous searches and a growing population of radio-loud stars (Callingham et al., 2021; Yiu et al., 2024; Pritchard et al., 2024; Driessen et al., 2024), no unambiguous planetary radio emission has yet been detected (de Gasperin et al., 2020; Turner et al., 2021; Cordun et al., 2025, e.g.,). Independent constraints come from star–planet interactions (SPIs), including orbital modulation of Ca II K and high-energy emission (Shkolnik et al., 2003; Pillitteri et al., 2015; Cauley et al., 2018). From such signatures, Cauley et al. (2019) inferred surface fields of tens to ∼100\sim 100 G for four HJs, although these estimates are strongly model-dependent. In contrast, atmospheric wind measurements for seven HJs suggest magnetic fields of at most a few gauss to avoid excessive magnetic drag (Seidel et al., 2026).

Motivated by these contrasting observational constraints and the relative scarcity of available theoretical predictions, we investigate how different internal heating scenarios affect the magnetic field predictions for HJs. Using one-dimensional planetary evolution models combined with a dynamo scaling law for rapidly rotating objects, we estimate magnetic fields for two limiting heating prescriptions that correspond to energy deposition either inside or outside the dynamo region. From these models, we construct an interpolator and derive analytical scaling laws that estimate magnetic fields from the observed masses, radii, and incident stellar fluxes of HJs. These publicly available tools (see Code availability) provide practical resources for interpreting current observations and guiding future observational studies. The paper is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, we describe the planetary evolution models, the two heating prescriptions, and the methodology used to estimate the magnetic field strengths. In Sect. 3, we present magnetic field estimates for the observed HJ population and derive analytical scaling laws suitable for quick estimates. In Sect. 4, we discuss how the model assumptions might influence our results, and compare our predictions with current indirect estimates of HJ magnetic fields. Finally, we summarize our conclusions in Sect. 5.

papers.title: Rethinking Requirement-to-Code Traceability Through Single-Agent and Multi-Agent Approaches
papers.abstract: Requirements-to-code traceability supports essential software engineering activities, including change impact analysis, maintenance, and regulatory compliance. Existing approaches typically rely on a retrieval-and-classification pipeline, which suffers from an inherent retrieval bottleneck: relevant source files that are not retrieved cannot be recovered during subsequent analysis. In this paper, we revisit requirements-to-code traceability in light of the substantially larger context windows offered by modern large language models, which make repository-scale analysis feasible without a separate retrieval step. We propose three approaches: a single-agent approach that analyzes the entire code repository in one pass, and two multi-agent approaches based on self-verification and multi-agent debate. Our evaluation shows that the single-agent approach substantially improves recall, achieving 80.9%, a gain of 38.6 percentage points (pp) over the state-of-the-art retrieval-based baseline, albeit with a 25.8 pp reduction in precision. By leveraging collaborative reasoning, the multi-agent debate-based approach achieves the best overall precision-recall balance, with 24.5% precision and 71.0% recall, yielding an F2 score of 49.5%. This represents an improvement of 7.5 pp over the state of the art and 2.7 pp over the single-agent approach. While the quantitative evaluation establishes the overall effectiveness of the approaches, the aggregate metrics alone explain little due to the considerable variability across results. Importantly, qualitative analysis provides key insights into highly variable quantitative results: the retrieval approach suits requirements that echo the code's vocabulary; single-agent, full-context reasoning suits well-documented, consistently named code; and multi-agent debate suits indirect, conflicting, or distributed evidence.

papers.intro:
Establishing trace links between software requirements and source code has long been a persistent challenge in software engineering (SE) [1]. This challenge becomes even more critical as modern software development increasingly relies on artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents11 1 The 2026 Stack Overflow survey of 30,000 developers across 169 countries reports that about 66% of developers use AI coding assistants or agents for software implementation, of whom 73% indicate daily use–Stack Overflow, 2026 Developer Survey, October 2026. Today’s coding agents can generate entire software projects directly from natural-language (NL) requirements [2]. While these technologies offer substantial productivity benefits, they also introduce new traceability challenges.

This challenge becomes even more critical as modern software development increasingly relies on artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents11 1 The 2026 Stack Overflow survey of 30,000 developers across 169 countries reports that about 66% of developers use AI coding assistants or agents for software implementation, of whom 73% indicate daily use–Stack Overflow, 2026 Developer Survey, October 2026. Today’s coding agents can generate entire software projects directly from natural-language (NL) requirements [2]. While these technologies offer substantial productivity benefits, they also introduce new traceability challenges.

AI-generated code typically lacks explicit trace links that connect the requirements or prompts to their corresponding implementation within the codebase. The literature has highlighted this gap and emphasized the need for tools to reconstruct these links [3, 4]. Furthermore, prior work suggests that AI coding agents cannot yet be relied upon to provide accurate traceability information. For instance, tracing issues to commits through pull requests may be unreliable, because pull request descriptions, often the primary communication channel between AI agents and human developers, do not always accurately reflect the implemented changes [5]. Together, these findings suggest that, although AI-assisted software development can accelerate implementation, it may further weaken the availability and reliability of software traceability information.

Creating and maintaining trace links manually is both time-intensive and error-prone, particularly as systems evolve. Whenever code is added, modified, or refactored, the corresponding trace links must also be updated. In practice, however, these updates are often postponed or omitted altogether. As a result, traceability information in industrial projects is frequently missing, incomplete, or outdated [6]. Recovering these links after development is equally demanding, as it requires examining each requirement against potentially thousands of code artifacts, a task that becomes increasingly costly as repository size grows.

Whenever code is added, modified, or refactored, the corresponding trace links must also be updated. In practice, however, these updates are often postponed or omitted altogether. As a result, traceability information in industrial projects is frequently missing, incomplete, or outdated [6]. Recovering these links after development is equally demanding, as it requires examining each requirement against potentially thousands of code artifacts, a task that becomes increasingly costly as repository size grows.

Automated trace link recovery (TLR) is therefore essential, yet remains difficult for several reasons. First, a substantial semantic gap exists between NL requirements and source code, as implementation details are often expressed using terminology that significantly differs from that of the requirement. Second, requirements are frequently scattered across multiple files, meaning that no single file fully captures their implementation. Third, the search space is typically highly imbalanced. In existing requirement-to-code traceability benchmarks [7, 8], true trace links often represent only 1% to 5% of all possible requirement-code pairs, while the total number of candidate links ranges from roughly 67006700 to 29 60029\,600 (see Table I on page I). An effective TLR approach must therefore identify a small number of correct links among thousands of plausible but incorrect candidates.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to promising progress in automated TLR. Most existing approaches follow a retrieval-and-classification pipeline that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [9, 10] with LLM-based pairwise trace link prediction [11]. Given a requirement, these approaches first retrieve the top-kk semantically similar code files and then ask the LLM to determine whether a trace link exists for each requirement-file pair.

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to promising progress in automated TLR. Most existing approaches follow a retrieval-and-classification pipeline that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [9, 10] with LLM-based pairwise trace link prediction [11]. Given a requirement, these approaches first retrieve the top-kk semantically similar code files and then ask the LLM to determine whether a trace link exists for each requirement-file pair.

While this pipeline effectively reduces the search space, it has two important limitations. First, it introduces a retrieval bottleneck: any relevant file that is not included among the top-kk candidates is excluded from further consideration. This limitation is particularly problematic given the semantic gap between requirements and source code, which can prevent relevant files from being ranked highly in the first place. Second, evaluating code files independently limits the ability to capture cross-file traceability, where a requirement is implemented collectively across multiple interacting files. Consequently, some trace links may be missed even when the relevant files are successfully retrieved.

To illustrate these challenges, consider the use case UC53 from eTour, a widely used requirements-to-code traceability benchmark [7], illustrated in Fig. 1. This use case describes how a tourist submits feedback for a visited site. The system checks that no feedback was issued before, validates the input, stores the feedback, and adds the site to the tourist’s list of visited sites. In the benchmark, UC53 is traced to six Java code files: IDBVisitBC, DBVisitPR, IDBVisitPR, CulturalHeritageVisitChecker, ControlData, and SiteTableModel. Existing retrieval-and-classification approaches can identify only two of the six files: IDBVisitBC and DBVisitPR (marked as found in the figure), both of which contain vocabulary close to the use case. The remaining four files (marked as missed in the figure) are likely missed because the large terminology gap leads to very low textual similarity. Moreover, existing approaches assess each file against the use case in isolation and therefore cannot recover these four files through their code dependencies on the two found ones.

Recent work has attempted to mitigate these issues through multi-agent architectures that combine RAG with self-verification [12]. However, because self-verification operates on top of the same retrieval pipeline, it inherits the retrieval bottleneck: relevant files filtered out early cannot be recovered. Moreover, self-verification typically reassesses predicted links rather than revising them, allowing upstream errors to propagate to the final output. Finally, although these approaches employ multiple agents, they make limited use of capabilities commonly associated with effective multi-agent systems—such as collaboration, memory, and coordinated reasoning [13].

papers.title: HOMFLY homology for oriented tangles
papers.abstract: We introduce an extension of Khovanov and Rozansky's categorification of the HOMFLY polynomial to arbitrary oriented tangles. Unlike previous such extensions, ours is invariant under the full suite of oriented Reidemeister moves, including the "misoriented" Reidemeister IIb. For oriented links $\mathcal{L}$, our construction recovers Khovanov and Rozansky's construction while removing the preliminary step of presenting $\mathcal{L}$ as a braid closure.
papers.intro:
HOMFLY homology (also known as triply-graded homology) is an invariant of oriented links, first constructed by Khovanov and Rozansky in 2005 [25]. The investigation of its structure and properties has driven a great deal of research over the past 20 years, elucidating deep connections across a wide variety of fields including algebraic geometry [18, 31], mathematical physics [19, 17], and higher algebra [28, 12]. HOMFLY homology also specializes to a number of other interesting link invariants, coming equipped with spectral sequences to Khovanov homology, 𝔰​𝔩N\mathfrak{sl}_{N} Khovanov–Rozansky homology, and knot Floer homology [11, 33, 6] and more direct specializations to the entire suite of Type A link polynomials, including the Jones, Alexander, and HOMFLY polynomials, giving it something of a universal status among all Type A quantum link invariants.

The investigation of its structure and properties has driven a great deal of research over the past 20 years, elucidating deep connections across a wide variety of fields including algebraic geometry [18, 31], mathematical physics [19, 17], and higher algebra [28, 12]. HOMFLY homology also specializes to a number of other interesting link invariants, coming equipped with spectral sequences to Khovanov homology, 𝔰​𝔩N\mathfrak{sl}_{N} Khovanov–Rozansky homology, and knot Floer homology [11, 33, 6] and more direct specializations to the entire suite of Type A link polynomials, including the Jones, Alexander, and HOMFLY polynomials, giving it something of a universal status among all Type A quantum link invariants.

Unfortunately, this added complexity comes at a cost. Direct computations are exceedingly difficult, limited at present only to positive torus links [21], knots of small crossing number [30], and a few other very special cases. HOMFLY homology is also not known to be functorial under general link cobordisms (although this is known for braid cobordisms by work of Elias and Krasner [16]), preventing its use for the spectacular applications to low-dimensional topology enjoyed by other link homology theories, such as Khovanov homology [34, 32] and knot Floer homology [27].

Both of these issues stem from the essentially nonlocal nature of existing constructions of HOMFLY homology. All of the other link invariants described above admit local descriptions in terms of skein relations (in the polynomial case) or cubes of resolutions (in the homological case) – the invariant is specified for the simplest tangles, and a procedure is given to glue smaller tangles into larger ones. HOMFLY homology as constructed in [25] admits no such description; an arbitrary oriented link diagram must first be isotoped to a braid closure (potentially getting much larger in the process) before performing any algebraic computations.

papers.title: Where the red rise stops: JWST/MIRI reveals a near-infrared turnover in the Little Red Dot Abell2744-QSO1
papers.abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact sources with a blue rest-frame UV, a steep red optical continuum and, often, broad hydrogen lines. They have been interpreted as dense stellar systems, dust-reddened active galactic nuclei, or black holes embedded in dense, dust-poor gas, scenarios that are hard to tell apart in the rest-frame UV and optical. We present JWST/MIRI F770W and F1000W imaging of the triply lensed Abell2744-QSO1 at z=7.04, probing rest-frame 0.96 and 1.24um. QSO1 is unresolved, and its steep optical rise stops near rest-frame 1um. Up to 1.24um, a T~4450K blackbody, or a hotter one reddened by dust, describes the continuum, with no sign of the hot dust seen in most type-1 quasars. Our statistically preferred SED fits produce the red continuum with (3-4)x10^9 Msun of stars, over 100 times the dynamical limit on the host mass, and are therefore disfavoured. An accretion disc in a dense gas cocoon respects this limit but over-predicts the 1.24um flux by 5 sigma. Super-Eddington accretion models with a thermalising envelope reproduce the turnover, but only for a black hole ~2.5dex less massive than the dynamical estimate. For a dust-reddened accretion disc (A_V ~ 2 mag), dust at ~1200K can re-emit at most ~2 per cent of the absorbed luminosity, and most of it would have to emerge at ~70-600K, unless the dust covers only a small fraction of the sky. The dynamics favour an accretion-powered source, but our data cannot distinguish dust reddening from processing by dense gas. MIRI imaging at >18um could separate these scenarios.

papers.intro:
Among the many discoveries enabled by JWST, Little Red Dots (Matthee et al., 2024; Kocevski et al., 2023; Labbé et al., 2023, LRDs;) have emerged as one of the most debated populations at intermediate and high redshift (Harikane et al., 2023; Greene et al., 2024; Inayoshi, 2025; Übler, 2026). They are surprisingly common at z∼5z\sim 5–7 (Kokorev et al., 2024), and they combine properties with no clear precedent among known galaxies or active galactic nuclei (AGN). LRDs are compact and often unresolved in the rest-frame optical (Kocevski et al., 2025). Their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) are “V-shaped”, with a faint blue UV continuum and a steep red optical rise (Furtak et al., 2024; Greene et al., 2024; Kocevski et al., 2025; Setton et al., 2025a). Their broad hydrogen lines, with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) above 1000​km​s−11000~\rm km~s^{-1}, point to gas moving around a black hole (Matthee et al., 2024; Treiber et al., 2025; Hviding et al., 2025). Other properties, however, are unusual for an AGN. The broad lines often have large Balmer decrements and non-Gaussian, exponential-like wings (Nikopoulos et al., 2026; Rusakov et al., 2026; Torralba et al., 2026a; Chang et al., 2026; Brazzini et al., 2025; Scholtz et al., 2026; Sneppen et al., 2026). Many LRDs also show Balmer absorption on top of the broad emission (Juodžbalis et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2026a; Matthee et al., 2026; Torralba et al., 2026b), a feature seen in only a handful of quasars (Hall, 2007; Zhang et al., 2015, e.g.). Most LRDs are X-ray undetected (Ananna et al., 2024; Yue et al., 2024; Kokubo and Harikane, 2025), faint in the mid- and far-infrared (Williams et al., 2024; Setton et al., 2025b; Akins et al., 2025; Casey et al., 2025) and show little or no variability (Kokubo and Harikane, 2025; Tee et al., 2025; Secunda et al., 2026). Type-1 AGN, instead, are typically bright in X-rays (Steffen et al., 2006; Just et al., 2007; Lusso and Risaliti, 2016, e.g.), show hot-dust emission in the near- and mid-infrared (Richards et al., 2006; Mor and Netzer, 2012, e.g.), and vary on time-scales of months to years (Vanden Berk et al., 2004; MacLeod et al., 2010, e.g.).

Whichever of these scenarios is confirmed, it would change our understanding of early black-hole and galaxy growth, and each would change it in a different way. If the light of LRDs were dominated by stars, the stars would have to have formed rapidly in extraordinarily dense systems (Labbé et al., 2023; Baggen et al., 2024). Given the number densities of LRDs, they would also have converted a large fraction of the available baryons into stars by z≳5z\gtrsim 5, possibly in tension with current cosmological models (Boylan-Kolchin, 2023, e.g.). If instead LRDs were AGN and their broad lines traced virial motions, they would host black holes of 10610^{6}–109​M⊙10^{9}~\rm M_{\odot}, up to 1.5–2 dex above the local relation for their host stellar masses. This would challenge even the most extreme models of black-hole growth (Maiolino et al., 2024; Juodžbalis et al., 2026; Pacucci et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2023). Finally, if they were black holes embedded in dense, dust-poor gas, scattering could broaden the lines and modify their ratios, in which case virial masses would be overestimated thus easing the tension with black-hole growth models (Rusakov et al., 2026; Chang et al., 2026; Ji et al., 2025; Sneppen et al., 2026). papers.title: Causal graph fusion across incomplete cohorts and causal steering of tabular foundation models
papers.abstract: Clinical data are split across incomplete cohorts with partially overlapping variables. Causal discovery under missing data and multi-source integration have developed separately, and tabular foundation models cannot take a causal graph without retraining. We make two contributions. First, causal graph fusion learns a partial ancestral graph on the shared variables, fuses it into each cohort's graph under temporal background knowledge and lets Markov blankets guide re-imputation, so missing data are handled inside discovery. Second, causal attention steering compiles the learned graph into the attention of a frozen tabular foundation model at inference. Against known ground truth, fusion dominates pooled and per-cohort baselines in every missingness and heterogeneity condition tested (p<0.001), and steering improves discrimination under distribution shift (p<10^{-5}), a gain that a random graph does not produce. In two spinal cord injury cohorts, fusion orients age, albumin and hemoglobin as ancestors of length of stay, a set no single cohort orients in full, and yields compact, temporally ordered predictor sets that match or exceed automatic feature selection on four of five outcomes.

papers.intro:
Clinical knowledge is rarely held in one complete dataset. It accumulates across cohorts collected at different stages of care, each recording an overlapping but non-identical set of variables and each with substantial missingness. Learning how clinical variables depend on one another from such sources is a structure-learning problem that current methods address only in parts, and it bounds what medical AI can learn from real-world data, since causal discovery and tabular foundation models alike start from a single table. Secondary complications after spinal cord injury (SCI) are a representative case. Pressure injuries (PIs) and prolonged hospital stays arise from interacting neurological, nutritional, autonomic and care-process factors [24, 36, 17, 6, 13, 19], and the data needed to study them are spread across registries that follow patients through different phases of care.

Causal graphical models are a natural tool for this problem. A causal graph places an arrow from one variable to another when the first is a (possibly indirect) cause of the second, and causal discovery infers such graphs from observational data by testing which variables remain associated once others are held fixed [14, 39]. Because some causes are unmeasured, we target a partial ancestral graph (PAG), which represents what the data can resolve under latent confounding and selection [8, 56]. For each outcome, the Markov blanket, the smallest set of variables that renders all others uninformative for predicting it, gives a minimal sufficient predictor set with a causal reading [45, 28, 1, 54]. Such a graph serves explanation and prediction at once. It shows where each predictor sits relative to the outcome, and because causal mechanisms are more stable than associations, it indicates which predictions should hold when the population shifts [29, 35].

Such a graph serves explanation and prediction at once. It shows where each predictor sits relative to the outcome, and because causal mechanisms are more stable than associations, it indicates which predictions should hold when the population shifts [29, 35].

Two obstacles stand between these tools and fragmented clinical data. First, missing values distort the conditional-independence relations that discovery relies on, so naive deletion or off-the-shelf imputation changes the learned graph [47, 12, 41]. Missing-data-aware methods now exist, including test-wise deletion for FCI-style search, Missing Value PC, local structure learning for incomplete data, MissDAG and optimal-transport approaches [41, 47, 30, 12, 50], but each operates on a single dataset, and the iterative coupling of Markov-blanket learning with imputation in MimMB targets one variable at a time [55]. Second, integrative methods such as integrative causal analysis, IOD and its extension to tiered background knowledge, Joint Causal Inference and COmbINE show that overlapping sources support stronger structural conclusions than any one alone, including under latent confounding [10, 46, 43, 2, 25, 44], but they take each source as already analysable. Two recent methods join the two lines. One pools conditional-independence evidence across multiply imputed sources with non-identical variable sets inside a PC-style search, which assumes no hidden confounders [53], and another reconstructs missing variables across time series with partially overlapping variables [15]. Cross-sectional clinical cohorts need all three ingredients at once: discovery that allows for hidden confounders, background knowledge about when along the care pathway each variable is recorded, and a treatment of missingness within each cohort. To our knowledge, no method yet combines them.

To our knowledge it is the first method to handle hidden confounders, temporal background knowledge and within-cohort missingness together. Both methods are validated against known ground truth. On synthetic benchmarks, fusion dominates pooled and per-cohort baselines on the precision/recall frontier in every missingness and heterogeneity condition tested (p<0.001p<0.001), raises graph F1 from about 0.630.63 to 0.710.71, and imputes with a third less distributional distortion (KS distance 0.0340.034 versus 0.0510.051). Under distribution shift, with the steering strength tuned without any test-fold information, steering significantly improves discrimination (+0.011+0.011 AUROC, p<10−5p<10^{-5}), rising to +0.029+0.029 when the validation shift matches the test shift. The gain is specific to the causal graph. A random graph yields none, and the gain grows as more of the true graph is revealed to the steerer. We also show why fusion imputes before testing. Conditional-independence tests that handle missing values natively reach at most 30% power on discrete benchmark networks even without missingness, and on the clinical cohorts they leave length of stay nearly or entirely disconnected. 4. In spinal cord injury, fusion recovers relations that no single cohort resolves and returns compact, auditable predictor sets. On two Swiss Paraplegic Center cohorts, hospital-acquired pressure injury (HAPI, n=250n=250) and post-pressure-injury surgery (PPIS, 266 surgical episodes from 174 patients), the pooled graph orients age, albumin and hemoglobin as ancestors of length of stay, a set that each cohort alone orients only in part, and fusion places all three in each cohort’s Markov blanket. The fused blankets match or exceed automatic feature selection on four of five outcomes while every predictor keeps its place on the care timeline and every cross-cohort edge carries bootstrap support. On secondary pressure-injury complication the blanket is the best feature set of all (AUROC 0.7760.776, versus 0.7520.752 with all 75 candidate variables), and on HAPI length of stay it is the simplest model within one standard error of the best (R2=0.75R^{2}=0.75 with 21 of 43 variables). Re-learning the graph inside every training fold keeps the blanket competitive, first of all feature sets on PPIS length of stay. These results make fragmentation across cohorts a source of causal evidence.

We make two methodological contributions and test them against known ground truth and in clinical data:

Causal graph fusion learns causal structure across incomplete, partially overlapping cohorts. To our knowledge it is the first method to handle hidden confounders, temporal background knowledge and within-cohort missingness together. A PAG learned on the variables shared across cohorts is fused into each cohort’s own PAG under temporal-tier background knowledge [23], and each variable’s Markov blanket guides its re-imputation [20, 55], so missingness is handled inside discovery instead of before it. For an idealized form of the fusion operator we prove consistency and finite-sample robustness, and give sufficient conditions for the imputation–discovery loop to stabilize.

papers.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as \texttt{BF16} and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama~3.1~8B~Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52$\times$ and 1.48$\times$ over the fastest baseline on an RTX~4060~Ti and an RTX~5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43~bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.

The dramatically increasing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) makes highly efficient inference a crucial requirement. Inference requires streaming and decoding the entire LLM network from RAM while each weight is used only once per request, which is a highly memory-bound setting (Gholami et al., 2024). In data center deployments this is mitigated by collecting many requests into batches, but other settings such as local LLMs or low-latency applications require good single-stream performance. But even in general, the increasing size of LLMs and the current RAM scarcity pose the need for memory-efficient LLM representations.

The most straightforward approach is lower-precision floating-point representations to reduce the memory footprint of the weights while losing accuracy (Micikevicius et al., 2022; Rouhani et al., 2023; NVIDIA et al., 2025). Many post-training quantization methods can be seen as a continuation of this idea to custom grids (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023) and non-trivial choices of levels (Frantar et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2025b; Badri and Shaji, 2023). Others adapt to the importance of the individual weights (Tseng et al., 2024; ggml-org, 2023; Lin et al., 2024). An alternative is Quantization-Aware Training (Jacob et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2025), which can go as far as only supporting three states for each weight (Ma et al., 2024).

An orthogonal approach, which can also be combined with quantization, is lossless compression of LLMs. The weights of LLMs are not distributed uniformly, a property that also holds after applying most quantization methods (Tan et al., 2026). Lossless coding methods exploit these statistical redundancies (Hao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Putzky et al., 2026) to compress the weights, where the limit is given by the weights’ entropy. They can increase inference throughput since the saved memory allows for larger batch sizes (Tan et al., 2026) or using simplified coding schemes that leverage additional assumptions on the domain (Fan et al., 2026). However, to date, none of these works provides a speedup using generic entropy coding for single-stream decoding on GPU.

In this paper, we present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), which uses fast lossless entropy coding to compress (quantized) LLMs and achieve inference speedup in the single-stream setting. We adapt an existing method (Schätzle et al., 2026) of entropy coding for GPUs to the particular needs of inference and introduce hyper-parameters to adapt to different settings. Using auto-tuning we then compute the Pareto front between size and single-stream decoding latency to obtain the best possible latency for a given memory budget. We provide highly optimized GPU kernels: mvm to perform the needed matrix-vector multiplication and dequant to materialize tensors to global memory for prefill. Our specific contributions are as follows: • We present the entropy coding variant dtANS-LLM, adapted from the existing dtANS (Schätzle et al., 2026) for the specific needs of single-stream inference in LLMs. • We auto-tune the hyper-parameters of dtANS-LLM for best performance given the characteristics of the tensors and the compute-to-memory-bandwidth ratios of the GPU. • We integrate dtANS-LLM into the vLLM inference engine (Kwon et al., 2023) as a plugin which we name MINE. Given a memory budget, MINE selects the most promising combination of kernels for performance. • We evaluate MINE on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). On a low-entropy checkpoint (EntQuant (Putzky et al., 2026) at 2.1 bits) it achieves speedups of 2.52×\times and 1.48×\times over the fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and RTX 5090, respectively. The effective bitrates are 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight, showing that the optimal parameter choices indeed depend on the card. • We make MINE available as an open-source repository.

papers.title: Left-Right-Consistent Iterative Stereo Matching via Cross-Injection
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art stereo matching models predominantly predict the disparity of only the left (reference) view. However, applications such as per-eye AR/VR rendering, novel view synthesis, or two-view depth fusion require disparity for both views, and need those two maps to agree. The usual workaround of running the network a second time on the horizontally flipped and swapped pair gives two independent predictions that can be inconsistent, especially on transparent surfaces, in textureless regions, and at occlusion boundaries. We introduce cross-injection (CI), a lightweight extension for iterative (refinement-based) models that can be added to any pretrained left-only iterative matcher. It couples the two passes by injecting the explicit, signed left-right inconsistency as an additional input cue at every step of the refinement stage. We empirically show that CI substantially reduces left-right disagreement on every benchmark (more than halving it on Booster for FoundationStereo), while largely preserving sharp object boundaries. Furthermore, using two state-of-the-art stereo matching models, we show that CI also reduces the single-view disparity error, making it a worthwhile extension even if only left disparity is needed.

papers.intro:
A growing number of vision systems need geometrically consistent disparity for both cameras of a stereo rig, not just for a reference view. Per-eye passthrough rendering on AR/VR headsets reprojects and composites each eye with its own depth [8], so any left-right disagreement introduces noticeable artifacts [12]. Stereoscopic content must also keep disparity within a viewing-comfort zone [23]. Novel view synthesis from a stereo pair renders new viewpoints from the two input views [66], so where the two disparity maps disagree the composite tears and ghosts at occlusion boundaries. Two-view depth fusion likewise yields doubled geometry wherever the two estimates disagree. These examples demonstrate the need not just for two accurate depth maps, but also consistent ones.

State-of-the-art stereo matchers, however, typically predict only the left (reference) disparity, a convention encouraged by benchmarks that score only the left view [40, 14, 35, 42]. In practice, the standard way to obtain the right disparity from such a network is to horizontally flip and swap the input pair, re-posing the right view as a left-view problem, and run the same weights a second time. The two passes are coupled only implicitly through the image content; nothing enforces that their outputs agree. As a result, they often diverge in textureless regions, at occlusion boundaries, and on transparent or reflective surfaces, where each pass locks onto a different plausible depth (Fig. 1, left example, middle row).

This is the gap we address in this paper: making the left and right predictions agree without sacrificing single-view accuracy. Rather than a fundamental redesign (a symmetric, both-view architecture trained from scratch), we propose a lightweight extension that reuses the strong pretrained left-only matchers the field already provides. It attaches to any such matcher with a RAFT-style [45, 28] refinement module and adds left-right consistency through fine-tuning alone, so it transfers to new base models as they appear. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • We propose cross-injection, a lightweight extension for refinement-based left-only stereo matching models. Unlike prior in-network consistency mechanisms, we inject explicit disparity inconsistency directly into the GRU update. Our extension is zero-initialized, leaving the pretrained matcher’s predictions unchanged at the start of fine-tuning, so the coupling is learned entirely by fine-tuning. • We supervise this coupling with a left-right consistency loss under per-pixel bidirectional gradient routing, and show it preserves sharp edges better than a naive symmetric one. • We demonstrate that our method substantially improves left-right consistency for two state-of-the-art stereo matching architectures [56, 36]. • We show that CI is also at least as accurate as a matched fine-tuning control in 1414 of 1515 benchmark–model combinations, and clearly better in most, making it a worthwhile extension even if only left-view prediction is required.

papers.title: Secondary neutron beam production at Jefferson Lab
papers.abstract: We investigate secondary neutron production by an 11 GeV electron beam in the Hall A beam dump at Jefferson Lab and their transport to a downstream experimental area. This secondary beam could operate opportunistically with the primary electron-scattering programme. The neutron energy spectrum extends from thermal energies to several GeVs, offering a distinctive opportunity for irradiation at energy grater than 1 GeV. We considered three configurations: the current setup, the planned BDX facility, and an optimized BDX layout with a dedicated neutron extraction pipe. We also studied how radiators made of different materials and placed upstream of the beam dump increase neutron production.

papers.intro:
Intense neutron beams are essential tools across a wide range of scientific and technological disciplines, enabling studies that span fundamental physics, materials science, nuclear engineering, chemistry, biology, and applied research. Because neutrons are electrically neutral, they penetrate deeply into matter and interact primarily through the strong nuclear force, making them uniquely sensitive probes of atomic nuclei, magnetic structures, and bulk material properties. Access to high-flux neutron beams over a broad energy range, from thermal and cold neutrons to fast and relativistic neutrons, is therefore critical for both basic research and applied applications. High-intensity neutron sources commonly rely on spallation or fission. At Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) produces moderated neutrons for materials research [1], while the High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) is a steady-state fission source supporting neutron scattering, isotope production, and materials irradiation [2]. HFIR’s in-vessel irradiation fields cover the 100 keV–1 MeV band and extend into the MeV range for neutron-damage studies [3]. The Back-n beamline at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) likewise spans sub-MeV and higher energies, primarily for nuclear-data measurements [4]. At higher energies, ChipIr at ISIS and the TRIUMF neutron irradiation facilities provide broad spectra extending to several hundred MeV for accelerated tests of neutron-induced single-event effects in electronics [5, 6]. Together, these facilities illustrate applications across the energy intervals considered and provide the context for the comparison in Sec. V.3.

Complementary to dedicated neutron facilities, high-current, multi-GeV electron beams interacting with thick targets can also produce intense neutron fields through electromagnetic and hadronic cascades. These environments naturally generate neutron spectra extending from thermal energies to several GeV, closely resembling conditions relevant to radiation shielding, accelerator-driven systems, space radiation environments, and detector backgrounds. At Jefferson Lab, the electron beam from the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator Facility (CEBAF) is absorbed in the Hall A beam dump (BD), downstream of the targets used for hadronic physics experiments. This configuration provides a unique environment for studying neutron production and the deep penetration of neutrons through shielding materials such as concrete and soil. In this paper, we report a study performed using a state-of-the-art simulation framework to explore the characteristics of the secondary neutron field emerging from Hall A’s BD. We investigate both the standard Hall A configuration and an optimized geometry designed to enhance the neutron flux.

papers.title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions
papers.abstract: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

papers.intro:
Surrogate models have become indispensable for enabling and accelerating parametric studies that require repeated model evaluations, for example, by replacing computationally expensive simulation models in time- and resource-demanding studies. Example surrogate-assisted tasks include optimization [1], uncertainty quantification (UQ) [2], or combined tasks such as optimization under uncertainty [3, 4]. Owing to the advances in the field of machine learning (ML), data-driven surrogates based on ML techniques have enjoyed increased popularity in recent years [5, 6]. However, the predictive capability of a data-driven surrogate model is governed by a number of factors, such as its model form and the available training data. Its predictions are therefore subject to uncertainty, for example due to approximation errors or the intrinsic variability of the observed output in the case of noisy observations. For surrogate-based results to be trustworthy, prediction uncertainty must be quantified reliably.

Surrogate models have become indispensable for enabling and accelerating parametric studies that require repeated model evaluations, for example, by replacing computationally expensive simulation models in time- and resource-demanding studies. Example surrogate-assisted tasks include optimization [1], uncertainty quantification (UQ) [2], or combined tasks such as optimization under uncertainty [3, 4]. Owing to the advances in the field of machine learning (ML), data-driven surrogates based on ML techniques have enjoyed increased popularity in recent years [5, 6]. However, the predictive capability of a data-driven surrogate model is governed by a number of factors, such as its model form and the available training data. Its predictions are therefore subject to uncertainty, for example due to approximation errors or the intrinsic variability of the observed output in the case of noisy observations. For surrogate-based results to be trustworthy, prediction uncertainty must be quantified reliably.

Among the numerous available surrogate modeling techniques, polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs) [7, 8] are particularly popular in the field of UQ, because their spectral structure gives direct access to statistical moments and sensitivity indices [9]. Moreover, regression-based PCEs are commonly employed as data-driven ML models [10]. The accuracy of a PCE is typically assessed with global generalization error metrics, for example based on the leave-one-out (LOO) error [11] or using a separate validation dataset. However, these metrics provide a single number for the entire input space and do not indicate how reliable an individual prediction is. In contrast to probabilistic surrogates such as Gaussian processes (GPs) [12] or Bayesian neural networks [13], standard PCEs do not provide metrics that quantify the model’s predictive uncertainty, such as prediction, confidence, or credibility intervals. Such intervals can be obtained by combining PCEs with bootstrapping [14] or ensemble modeling [15, 16]. However, the spread of bootstrap or ensemble predictions mainly reflects the variability of the estimated model with respect to the training data, largely neglecting the impact of noise or systematic approximation errors. Other options include hybrid GP-PCE models [17, 18, 19, 20] or Bayesian PCE formulations [21, 22, 23], where interval validity largely depends on the underlying modeling assumptions, e.g., covariance kernel, prior distributions, or noise model. Moreover, none of these approaches guarantees that the resulting intervals contain the true output with a prescribed probability for a finite amount of data.

Other options include hybrid GP-PCE models [17, 18, 19, 20] or Bayesian PCE formulations [21, 22, 23], where interval validity largely depends on the underlying modeling assumptions, e.g., covariance kernel, prior distributions, or noise model. Moreover, none of these approaches guarantees that the resulting intervals contain the true output with a prescribed probability for a finite amount of data.

Conformal prediction (CP) methods [24] offer such guarantees and can additionally be combined with any regression model. Under the assumption of data exchangeability and for any finite number of data points, CP produces prediction intervals with marginal coverage guarantees, meaning that, on average, the intervals contain the true output with a prescribed probability. This probability is commonly called the target coverage and denoted by (1−α)(1-\alpha), where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is the corresponding significance level. The original full (or transductive) CP variant [24] uses all available data for both training and interval calibration, but requires retraining the regression model for each test input and for multiple candidate output values. This is computationally prohibitive in general and becomes tractable only for specific models [25]. The most widely used variant is split (or inductive) CP [26, 27], where the model is trained once and the intervals are calibrated on a held-out dataset. Although computationally efficient, split CP reduces the amount of data available for training, which can be detrimental to model accuracy if only limited data are available. Cross CP [28] mitigates this drawback by calibrating the prediction intervals via kk-fold cross validation (CV), at the cost of training kk models and only approximate interval validity, i.e., without offering a coverage guarantee. For the limit-case of k=Mk=M, MM being the size of the training dataset, cross CP becomes jackknife CP [27], where LOO CV is used for interval calibration. In particular, the jackknife+ variant [29] offers a (1−2​α)(1-2\alpha) finite-sample coverage guarantee. While this is weaker than the (1−α)(1-\alpha) coverage guarantee provided by full and split CP, it is still favorable compared to the only approximate interval validity of standard jackknife CP. Moreover, the empirical coverage of jackknife+ CP is typically on par with the target coverage [29].

Conformal prediction (CP) methods [24] offer such guarantees and can additionally be combined with any regression model. Under the assumption of data exchangeability and for any finite number of data points, CP produces prediction intervals with marginal coverage guarantees, meaning that, on average, the intervals contain the true output with a prescribed probability. This probability is commonly called the target coverage and denoted by (1−α)(1-\alpha), where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is the corresponding significance level. The original full (or transductive) CP variant [24] uses all available data for both training and interval calibration, but requires retraining the regression model for each test input and for multiple candidate output values. This is computationally prohibitive in general and becomes tractable only for specific models [25]. The most widely used variant is split (or inductive) CP [26, 27], where the model is trained once and the intervals are calibrated on a held-out dataset. Although computationally efficient, split CP reduces the amount of data available for training, which can be detrimental to model accuracy if only limited data are available. Cross CP [28] mitigates this drawback by calibrating the prediction intervals via kk-fold cross validation (CV), at the cost of training kk models and only approximate interval validity, i.e., without offering a coverage guarantee. For the limit-case of k=Mk=M, MM being the size of the training dataset, cross CP becomes jackknife CP [27], where LOO CV is used for interval calibration. In particular, the jackknife+ variant [29] offers a (1−2​α)(1-2\alpha) finite-sample coverage guarantee. While this is weaker than the (1−α)(1-\alpha) coverage guarantee provided by full and split CP, it is still favorable compared to the only approximate interval validity of standard jackknife CP. Moreover, the empirical coverage of jackknife+ CP is typically on par with the target coverage [29].

To the best of our knowledge, two works have considered the combination of CP with PCEs so far. Loukrezis and Giovanis [30] combined jackknife and jackknife+ CP with total-degree PCEs fitted by ordinary least squares (OLS). In this case, LOO residuals and LOO model predictions can be computed with closed-form expressions and the CP intervals are obtained at practically no additional cost compared to the PCE fit itself. Hatstatt et al. [31] combined full and jackknife+ CP with both total-degree OLS-fitted PCEs and sparse PCEs based on a hybrid least angle regression (LAR) method [11]. In the former case, jackknife+ CP intervals are again computed via closed-form expressions. Full CP intervals are also computed with very low computational overhead, through an exact computation of the interval limits that exploits the linearity of the OLS solution with respect to the model outputs. For sparse PCEs, Hatstatt et al. show that reusing the basis selected on the full training dataset violates the symmetry requirement of CP and leads to a severe performance degradation. The adaptation of full CP to sparse PCEs was made possible by exploiting the linearity of the LAR solution path and solving equations to determine the prediction interval bounds. In contrast, jackknife+ CP was adapted through repeated LOO refitting of the sparse PCE model, taking advantage of the considered small-data regime, for which the computational cost remains manageable.

papers.title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
papers.abstract: Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.

papers.intro:
A language model’s key-value (KV) cache grows with every token it processes, and on local hardware, the cache competes directly with model weights for a fixed memory budget. Unlike the model weights, whose size does not depend on context, the KV cache grows with every retained entry and soon outgrows the model itself. Local deployments matter: prompts stay on device within user control (Nissenbaum, 2010; Stallman, 2015; Zittrain, 2008), and processing spreads beyond centralised intermediaries (Benkler, 2006; Seger et al., 2023); releasing weights alone does not achieve this (Liesenfeld and Dingemanse, 2024; Widder et al., 2024). For Qwen3-8B-Base, caching 144144 KiB per token in half precision (36 layers, 8 key-value heads of width 128) (Yang et al., 2025a) alongside 15.315.3 GiB of weights on a 16 GiB GPU leaves room for only 5 thousand uncompressed tokens before runtime activations, reaching 1.39M retained entries only at 256×256\times compression (Figure 1 highlights the difference in magnitudes). Large capacity is essential: in-context learning, multi-step reasoning, and concurrent rollouts all depend on holding many tokens in memory simultaneously (Li et al., 2025b).

KV-cache compression trades accuracy for context. Existing methods shrink the cache along four axes (§2). Token eviction keeps fewer tokens. Scalar quantisation stores each coordinate in fewer bits. Low-rank projection and latent attention store fewer coordinates per token. Vector quantisation replaces groups of coordinates with indices into a learned codebook. Four of the five baselines we compare report accuracy at compression ratios of at most about 14×14\times (Table 1), whereas holding several million tokens beside a model’s weights on a 16 GiB GPU needs ratios of tens for the smaller models studied here, and deeper compression for the 8B model (Figure 1; Appendix D.3), the extreme regime (above 16×16\times) this paper targets.

papers.title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.
