papers.intro:
Consider a fleet of autonomous vehicles serving delivery requests in a city. At each decision time, the operator must simultaneously decide which vehicle should serve which request and how each vehicle should navigate to its assigned destination. These decisions are tightly coupled. The best assignment depends on how long each vehicle will actually take to reach each target, while routing itself depends on the assignment. Assignments based only on nominal shortest paths can therefore be poor when travel times depend on traffic lights, congestion, and random delays. Yet solving this full joint assignment-routing problem over the fleet quickly becomes computationally prohibitive. Beyond delivery fleets, the same structure arises across a wide range of cooperative systems: inspection drones achieving coverage patterns [1], warehouse robots repositioning to incoming orders [2], emergency response units relocating to optimal positions [3], ride-hailing platforms balancing supply and demand [4], and electric-vehicle fleets sharing charging infrastructure [5]. In all these settings, the goal is to optimally coordinate a fleet of decoupled agents so that their collective terminal state matches or approximates a target configuration, such as uniform coverage, a set of delivery locations, or a demand-weighted positioning pattern. These problems are typically solved in a receding-horizon fashion to account for changing conditions and request patterns and, thus, require modular approaches that generalize to different fleet sizes or target distributions.

These problems are typically solved in a receding-horizon fashion to account for changing conditions and request patterns and, thus, require modular approaches that generalize to different fleet sizes or target distributions.

Fleet assignment and routing are classically addressed via combinatorial solvers [6, 7] and, more recently, learned routing heuristics [8]. Since the joint assignment-routing problem is combinatorial in the fleet size, these methods decouple the two steps using nominal travel costs, such as shortest-path distances, to solve the assignment problem. These heuristics, however, ignore the stochasticity of the costs and may favor targets that “look close” but are expensive to reach in expectation. A natural learning-based alternative is multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) [9, 10, 11, 12], often with centralized training and decentralized execution. Policy-gradient methods such as MAPPO [13] and MADDPG [14], and value-decomposition methods such as VDN [15], QMIX [16], and QPLEX [17] are effective in many settings [18, 19], but learn over a joint state-action space whose size grows exponentially with the number of agents [20], limiting scalability and generalization to unseen fleet sizes. Value-decomposition methods gain tractability by imposing architectural assumptions on the joint value function, such as additivity or monotonicity, which are provably too restrictive even for simple coordination tasks [21, 16]. Mean-field reinforcement learning [22, 23] instead replaces pairwise interactions with an aggregate representation of the population. Although practical in large systems [4, 24], its approximations can lose fidelity when modeling finite populations [25]. Closer to our motivation, some methods learn latent subtasks and dynamically assign them among agents [26], since in general cooperative MARL no such decomposition is available a priori. We instead study a structured subclass, with decoupled dynamics and a terminal optimal transport cost, in which the assignment-routing separation can be exploited directly.

In this work, we seek a principled separation of population-level assignment and single-agent control (Figure 1). Inspired by the “deterministic” separation principle for multi-agent control in [27], we formulate the cooperative MARL problem as an optimal control problem over the space of probability measures where terminal deviation from a desired target measure is quantified via an optimal transport cost. By construction, this representation is permutation invariant and captures both finite populations (as empirical measures) and a continuum of agents (as continuous measures). In the deterministic setting, Terpin et al. [27] show that the population cost-to-go is exactly an optimal transport cost whose transportation cost is the single-agent cost-to-go, thus separating assignment from single-agent control. This equality does not extend directly to the stochastic setting, where the population measure is random and future assignments can adapt to realized noise. Nevertheless, we show that a carefully designed separation principle, where noise is “averaged out”, continues to upper bound the population cost-to-go. This analysis is non-trivial: the randomness of the population measure requires handling probability measures over probability measures, a modeling challenge in itself, compounded by delicate measurability issues. Finally, Terpin et al. [27] provide a purely theoretical analysis, whereas we leverage our separation principle to design scalable algorithms for MARL.

papers.title: ICare-DT: a digital twin for continuous forecasting of intensive care patients
papers.abstract: Digital twins of intensive care patients should update forecasts from new data and predict treatment responses, but few studies test whether routine records support either. We propose ICare-DT, a Transformer-based twin that updates a latent patient state hourly from new measurements without retraining. We trained it on 140,473 eICU-CRD stays to forecast vital signs crossing their training-set means. On test data, later forecasts beat the twin's own hour-6 forecasts of the same windows in all 12 settings (+0.073 to +0.153 AUROC). On validation data, controls that withheld or swapped the new hours traced the gain to the patient's own measurements. Without refitting, the model kept its gain on a second database (8 of 9 settings, +0.025 to +0.114 AUROC) in a prespecified evaluation of the previously analyzed MIMIC-IV test split. Refitted within MIMIC-IV, a twin state fine-tuned on clinical endpoints gave gradient boosting a significant gain for acute kidney injury (+0.0035 AUROC; hypotension +0.0010, not significant). To test response prediction, we built a benchmark that replaces the treatments in real records with simulated doses and injects responses of known size, visible only at measurement times. Ridge models supervised with injected effects recovered them from real records only through frequently measured variables (heart rate) read at their measurement times. We asked standard learners to predict these effects for a dosing regime no patient had received. No standard learner outperformed predicting zero effect at an out-of-support query. When told how the simulated responses were generated, a separate learner recovered the effects from the same records without seeing their true values (R2 0.30 to 0.40 at one effect size). Routine records support forecasts that improve with each patient's new data, and our benchmark is a testbed for models that learn how responses are generated.

Patients in intensive care can deteriorate within hours, and clinicians adjust vasopressors, fluids and ventilation as they watch each patient respond. Two questions recur at the bedside: where is this patient heading, and how would this patient respond if the treatment were changed? A digital twin of the patient has been proposed to help answer both1, 2, 3, 4. In the National Academies’ definition, a digital twin is a model of one individual that is updated dynamically from that individual’s data, is personalized and informs decisions5.

Patients in intensive care can deteriorate within hours, and clinicians adjust vasopressors, fluids and ventilation as they watch each patient respond. Two questions recur at the bedside: where is this patient heading, and how would this patient respond if the treatment were changed? A digital twin of the patient has been proposed to help answer both1, 2, 3, 4. In the National Academies’ definition, a digital twin is a model of one individual that is updated dynamically from that individual’s data, is personalized and informs decisions5.

For a machine-learning model, the patient is represented by the patient record: an irregularly sampled multivariate time series of vital signs, laboratory values and treatments that grows by one hour at a time. A twin therefore needs two capabilities. The first is continuous forecasting: the twin keeps a patient state, a learned summary of the record so far, updates it as each new hour arrives without retraining, and forecasts upcoming events from it. The second is treatment-response prediction: forecasting the patient’s course under alternative treatments, whose contrast is, in causal terms, a conditional treatment effect that changes over time6, 7, 8. Both must be learned from routine records, and two features of these records make this hard. First, what is measured and when depends on clinical practice and on the patient’s condition9; in 400 stays of the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD)10 studied here, the recorded heart rate changes in 57% of hours and creatinine, a laboratory marker of kidney function, in only 4%. Second, a record shows only the outcome under the treatment that was given, and because the sickest patients are the ones treated, a beneficial treatment can look harmful, a bias known as confounding by indication (Fig. 1a)11, 12.

Machine learning has advanced each capability separately. For prediction, foundation and sequence models of health records learn one representation from many patients and forecast many outcomes, and they are judged by their accuracy across tasks and hospitals13, 14, 15, 16, 17. Relational models capture dependencies among irregularly sampled intensive care variables18, and landmark models update a prediction at set times as data accrue19. For treatment effects, counterfactual sequence models estimate how outcomes would evolve under alternative treatment sequences20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26; g-computation models among them, such as G-Net23, simulate every recorded variable forward under a chosen treatment sequence. Because true effects are never observed in real data, these and other causal methods are scored on simulators in which the effects are known27, 28, 29, 30, 31. Intensive care twins have also been built from expert knowledge: a twin of early sepsis with expert-specified causal structure was checked prospectively against observed responses to single interventions, although not against known individual effects32.

Machine learning has advanced each capability separately. For prediction, foundation and sequence models of health records learn one representation from many patients and forecast many outcomes, and they are judged by their accuracy across tasks and hospitals13, 14, 15, 16, 17. Relational models capture dependencies among irregularly sampled intensive care variables18, and landmark models update a prediction at set times as data accrue19. For treatment effects, counterfactual sequence models estimate how outcomes would evolve under alternative treatment sequences20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26; g-computation models among them, such as G-Net23, simulate every recorded variable forward under a chosen treatment sequence. Because true effects are never observed in real data, these and other causal methods are scored on simulators in which the effects are known27, 28, 29, 30, 31. Intensive care twins have also been built from expert knowledge: a twin of early sepsis with expert-specified causal structure was checked prospectively against observed responses to single interventions, although not against known individual effects32.

These evaluations leave open two questions that must be answered before a twin can be tested at the bedside. The first is whether a twin’s forecasts improve because it reads the patient’s new data. Accuracy at fixed time points cannot show this, and neither can a gain in accuracy later in the stay, because a later forecast is closer to the events it predicts and can be more accurate without using anything new about the patient. A convincing test compares forecasts of the same future window made at the same lead time with and without the new hours, includes trivial references that need no learning, such as the patient’s last measured value, and is fixed before the results are seen33, 34. Verification of any kind is rarely reported: in a scoping review of 149 studies of human digital twins, 2 mentioned verification, validation and uncertainty quantification35. The second question is whether routine records hold enough information to learn individual treatment responses at all. A simulator can answer it only if it reproduces which values are recorded and when, because an effect enters the record only in hours in which the affected variable is measured9, 36, 37. Yet the intensive care benchmark used for the Causal Transformer writes a simulated outcome at every hour22, generators that let the user set the effects have no time dimension38, 39, and the realism of simulators is seldom audited40, 41.

ICare-DT is trained on eICU-CRD (Table 1). A causally masked Transformer maps the record up to each hour to a latent patient state. papers.title: Beyond Segmentation: Enriching ImageCAS with Coronary Ostia Landmarks, Rooted Centerline Graphs, and Open-Weight Localization Models
papers.abstract: Coronary ostia and centerlines are key reference points for automated analysis of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA), from surgical planning to intraoperative vessel tracking. However, the only public ostium annotations cover 77 non-gated aortic scans, not CCTA, while CAT08 and ASOCA (32 and 40 CCTA scans) mark the ostia only implicitly, as centerline start points. This work enriches ImageCAS, the largest public dataset for coronary artery segmentation, with ostium annotations for its 1000 patients and centerline graphs rooted at these new ostia, making it, to the authors' knowledge, the largest public dataset for ostium localization and the only one with centerlines following the official ImageCAS masks and starting at annotated ostia. Three annotators marked each ostium in the first 500 volumes; in the next 500, the candidates of a model trained on the first batch were corrected (human-in-the-loop). Six 3D localization models, trained on ImageCAS, CAT08 and ASOCA, were benchmarked on 58 held-out volumes (50 ImageCAS, 4 CAT08, 4 ASOCA). SwinUNETR-V2 and nnResUNet localized all ostia without failure (>5 mm error), with median errors of 0.70-0.87 mm. Trained on CAT08 and ASOCA alone, SwinUNETR-V2 fails on 34% of right and 53% of left ostia, whereas adding 250 ImageCAS volumes removes all failures. The centerlines were extracted by a deterministic, quality-controlled minimal-path procedure; on ASOCA, they cover a median of 99.5% of the reference length, with a median per-patient mean distance of 0.22 mm between matched reference points and centerlines. Annotations, centerlines, code, and weights are available at https://hal9000-lab.github.io/.

papers.intro:
In cardiac imaging, the coronary ostia and the centerlines represent important landmarks from the clinical point of view. The former correspond to the points where the left and right coronary arteries originate from the aorta, while the latter are the topological skeleton of the coronary tree, rooted at the ostia, and representing the vessel path and branching. In diagnosis, the position and proximal course of the ostia distinguish benign anatomical variants from anomalous coronary origins, a recognized cause of ischemia and sudden cardiac death [1]. In surgical planning, the ostia must be located before coronary artery bypass grafting and aortic root surgery, their height relative to the valve annulus predicts the risk of coronary occlusion during transcatheter aortic valve implantation [2, 3, 4], and stenting of aorto-ostial lesions requires the ostium to be placed precisely [5]. In automated image analysis, the ostia are the natural seed points of vessel segmentation and centerline tracking algorithms [6, 7, 8], and the resulting centerline graphs support stenosis grading [9, 10], computational hemodynamic modeling [11, 12, 13], and revascularization planning [14]. Reliable, automatic localization of the ostia and extraction of the centerlines are therefore the building blocks of AI-based decision-support systems for the analysis of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA).

Automated approaches evolved from probabilistic appearance and shape models [15, 16, 17] to deep networks that exploit the full three-dimensional context (Section 2.2), but the few methods developed specifically for the coronary ostia were mostly trained and evaluated on private data (Section 2.3).

Centerline extraction faces an analogous pattern. Reference centerlines are produced through labor-intensive, multi-observer procedures [6, 18], which have long kept the public datasets that provide them to a few tens of scans, and automated methods depend on the quality of a segmentation mask, on their starting points, or on reference centerlines to be trained (Section 2.5). Extraction that is validated, applied at scale, and anchored at the coronary ostia therefore remains an open problem.

Despite the progress of the methods, public data for this task remain scarce. The only public annotations designed for coronary ostium localization cover 77 aortic CT angiography volumes of ImageTBAD [19], released by Gajowczyk et al. [20]. These scans were acquired without ECG gating to study aortic dissection, not the coronary arteries, and image the ostia at a lower quality than CCTA: the localizer developed on them reached median errors of 3.48 mm (left) and 2.97 mm (right) on these scans, against 1.14 and 0.98 mm on gated CCTA [20]. This work, which addresses ECG-gated CCTA, therefore does not use them (Section 5.1). None of the most widely used public CCTA datasets (ASOCA [18], CAT08 [6], and ImageCAS [21]) was curated for ostium localization: CAT08 and ASOCA mark the ostium only implicitly, as the start point of their reference centerlines, in 72 scans (32 and 40), and ImageCAS provides no ostium information. Moreover, CAT08 can no longer be obtained from an official source, which leaves the 40 annotated scans of ASOCA as the only openly accessible CCTA data with ostium information. Finally, none of the dedicated ostium localizers has been released with code or trained weights [22, 23, 24, 20], and each was evaluated on its own data and with its own definition of the ostium; to the authors’ knowledge, no public benchmark, that is, no shared CCTA test set with openly available models, therefore exists for this task. Likewise, no public coronary centerline graphs correspond to the official ImageCAS segmentation masks: the recent ImageCAS-X [25] re-annotates the masks of 800 of the ImageCAS scans and derives centerlines automatically from these new masks, starting them at skeleton endpoints near an automatically segmented aorta rather than at annotated ostia. These centerlines thus serve the users of the new masks, whereas a pipeline that starts from a localized ostium, or from the official masks, needs centerlines rooted at the ostium and derived from those masks: the start points of ImageCAS-X are heuristic, not the landmark that a localizer predicts, and the 200 scans it leaves out have no centerlines (Section 5.6).

This work addresses these gaps. ImageCAS [21], to date the largest publicly available dataset for coronary artery segmentation, is extended with (i) left and right coronary ostium annotations for its complete 1000 CCTAs, obtained by multi-annotator consensus on the first 500 volumes and by a human-in-the-loop correction of model-generated candidates on the remaining 500, and (ii) coronary centerline graphs, for 999 of them, rooted at these ostia and extracted from its segmentation masks. papers.title: Drift-invariant kernels for discount curve models
papers.abstract: Kernel ridge regression estimates the discount curve as the minimizer of a pricing error plus a penalty given by the norm of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By the representer theorem, the estimate lies in a finite-dimensional affine space that depends only on the kernel and on the cash flow dates of the instruments. We ask when this space is invariant under the risk-neutral drift of the discount curve, so that the estimated curves can be the states of a continuous-time arbitrage-free model. We show that this holds for every grid of cash flow dates if and only if the kernel is of the form $k(x,y)=\e^{b(x+y)}\big(c\,\e^{axy}+1-c\big)$, apart from kernels whose Hilbert space has dimension at most two. For this kernel the estimated curve is an affine combination of flat discount curves, each corresponding to a constant continuously compounded yield. The drift-invariant subspaces correspond to sub-grids of the cash flow dates, and the discounted coefficients have linear risk-neutral dynamics.

Related literature. Static curve fitting uses parametric families [23, 26] or splines [22, 29, 1, 18]. See [19] for an overview. The consistency of parametric families with arbitrage-free forward curve dynamics was studied in [4, 14, 15, 16], and finite-dimensional realizations in [5, 6, 12, 13, 27, 28]. The drift condition for discount curves is derived in [17]. Dynamically consistent forward curve fitting is proposed in [30], consistent recalibration in [25], and data-driven curve models in [21]. The paper [20] shows that statistical consistency of term structure estimates forces an affine geometry. An empirical implementation of a related RKHS approach, using US Treasury data, is developed in [8]. The exponential kernel employed there is a special case of the family (1.2). While [8] focuses on curve estimation, dimension reduction and model calibration, the present paper characterizes the kernels whose hypothesis spaces are drift-invariant for every grid of cash flow dates. We do not study empirical performance here.

papers.title: Health-System-Wide Mapping of Demographic Information in Routine Clinical Histopathology
papers.abstract: The extent to which demographic-associated information is detectable across organs and disease states in routine clinical histopathology remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 1.3 million hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images from 257,322 patients across 25 organs, using pathology foundation-model representations and multiple-instance learning to systematically map information associated with sex, age group, and self-reported race. Across 69 organ-demographic combinations, demographic attributes were broadly recoverable, with pan-organ mean AUROCs of 0.828 for sex, 0.733 for age group, and 0.662 for self-reported race, and substantial variation across organs. Demographic-class balancing produced relatively small changes in performance, while evaluation within diagnosis-text clusters showed modest attenuation. Under training with diagnosis-based grouping, demographic-associated signals remained detectable across multiple organs, including sex in gastric tissue (AUROC 0.865), age group in breast (0.816), and self-reported race in skin (0.728). Literature-guided analysis of these settings generated candidate histomorphological and contextual explanations for further investigation. Together, these findings provide a systematic map of demographic-associated information in routine histopathology, informing investigations of its sources, assessments of potential shortcut learning, and the development of more interpretable computational pathology models.

papers.intro:
Despite more than a century of microscopic examination of human tissue, it remains unknown whether demographic-associated morphologic variation is systematically detectable across organs and disease states. Scattered observations suggest that such variation exists. Sex-associated nuclear features were described in neurons and neutrophils more than 70 years ago1, 2, and machine-learning models have since estimated chronological age from the histology of healthy tissues and brain3, 4. More broadly, structural aging mapped from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology of 40 post-mortem tissues in the Genotype-Tissue Expression project followed tissue-specific, nonlinear trajectories, with coordinated deterioration across organs5. Race-associated histopathologic and molecular differences have also been reported in organs including skin and prostate6, 7, 8. These observations establish that demographic-associated variation can have histologic correlates, but the evidence remains fragmented across demographic attributes, organs, and clinical settings. It is therefore unknown how broadly sex, age, and self-reported race are associated with detectable information in routine clinical histopathology across tissues and disease states.

Deep learning provides a means to investigate this question at a scale and sensitivity not readily achievable through conventional morphologic assessment. Computational pathology (CPath) models applied to digitized H&E whole-slide images (WSIs) can identify information associated with disease and tumor grade9, 10, molecular biomarkers and outcomes11, 12, 13, and cellular phenotypes14, 15. Foundation models (FMs) pretrained on large collections of digitized pathology images16, 17, 18, 19, 20 have further enabled representations that transfer across tasks and centers21, 22. The ability of these models to recover complex information from routine H&E images raises a fundamental question beyond disease prediction: what information about the patient is encoded in tissue images, including information that may not be apparent to human observers?

Evidence from medical imaging suggests that demographic information can indeed be recovered from images and learned representations23. In radiology, self-reported race can be predicted across imaging modalities and external cohorts even when the relevant image features are not apparent to human observers24; medical-imaging FMs likewise encode sex, age, and race in their representations25. Evidence in histopathology is more limited. Vaidya et al. showed that representations learned for breast and lung cancer subtyping and glioma IDH1 mutation prediction retained information about patient race26. In our prior work in dermatopathology, self-reported race remained predictable under the evaluated disease-distribution controls, with attention and ablation analyses implicating the epidermis as one source of predictive signal27; pigmentation-related epidermal features are one plausible candidate correlate6. Together, these findings indicate that demographic information can be present in medical images and learned representations, but they do not establish how broadly such information is detectable across routine histopathology or which histologic features carry it.

Establishing the extent of demographic predictability also has important implications for the development and evaluation of CPath models. If demographic attributes are recoverable from H&E images or their learned representations, this information is potentially available to models even when demographic variables are not explicitly provided as inputs. Models may then exploit demographic-associated information when it correlates with a prediction target, creating the possibility of shortcut learning28, 29. Performance disparities have been documented in medical imaging and CPath25, 30, 26; a pan-cancer analysis, for example, reported significant disparities across self-reported race, gender, or age groups in 29.3% of diagnostic tasks31. Self-reported race may serve as an imperfect proxy for genetic ancestry, while also capturing social, environmental, and healthcare-related factors. Demographic predictability does not by itself demonstrate that a clinical model uses demographic information, just as an observed performance disparity does not establish demographic proxy use. Rather, determining where demographic information is recoverable identifies settings in which such use is possible and can be tested directly.

A central challenge is that demographic predictability need not arise from intrinsic tissue morphology. Demographic groups can differ in disease prevalence, specimen and case mix, healthcare context, and other cohort characteristics, while tissue processing, staining, scanning, and image acquisition can introduce additional correlations32, 28, 29. The Cancer Genome Atlas illustrates this problem: contributing sites differ in clinical and demographic composition, while their digital slides carry site-specific visual signatures arising from both biological differences and non-biological batch effects33, 32, 26. Deep learning models can recover the submitting site from digitized slide images, and these signatures remain detectable after commonly used stain normalization and augmentation32, 34. When the same cohort structure is represented in training and validation data, such associations can remain hidden and produce optimistic estimates of performance that deteriorate when site, case mix, or acquisition conditions change28, 35, 29, 32. Consequently, mapping demographic-associated image information requires testing whether predictability persists when major sources of cohort structure, particularly demographic-class imbalance and diagnosis context, are constrained. Even when it persists, predictability alone does not identify its causal source; residual signals may reflect tissue-associated features, clinical or sampling context, acquisition effects, or combinations of these factors.

papers.title: Lessons from double-plane lenses for galaxy profiles, the Hubble tension, and the mass-sheet degeneracy
papers.abstract: Double-plane lenses, like single-plane lenses, are subject to the mass-sheet degeneracy, a fundamental limit to our knowledge of the deflector mass profiles from lensing. However, with a prior on the relative expansion history, unlike in the single-plane case, this degeneracy can be constrained with the modelling of lens images, without the need for time delays, velocity dispersion measurements or a prior on the Hubble constant $H_0$. We show that double-plane lenses are sensitive to a specific combination of the mass-sheet components of the two lens planes. Using literature values of the cosmological scaling factor from the double-plane lenses J0946 and AGEL0353, a measurement from the point-source images of J1721 (the ``Einstein zig-zag'' lens), and a reference value of $\Omega_\mathrm{m}$, we show the constraints that can be placed on the mass-sheet component of each of these systems. We show that the additional information brought by images of a second source can improve measurements of $H_0$ from individual time-delay lenses by up to $\sim50\%$, depending on certain key assumptions. Using forecasted Euclid and LSST double-plane lens samples, we show that these samples will enable strong constraints on the population of mass sheets in lens galaxies. Such population constraints will have implications for a range of strong-lensing science applications, in particular in constraining $H_0$, dark energy, and the dark matter profiles of galaxies.

papers.intro:
When a sufficiently massive and dense galaxy or cluster lies on or close to the line of sight between our telescopes and a distant source of light, its light may be strongly lensed, such that we observe arcs, multiple images or Einstein rings. The path of this lensed light carries information about the dominant lensing mass, the distribution of mass along the line of sight but external to this main lens, and the background cosmology through which it propagates, and if these are carefully modelled, they can be constrained with the images we observe.

The path of this lensed light carries information about the dominant lensing mass, the distribution of mass along the line of sight but external to this main lens, and the background cosmology through which it propagates, and if these are carefully modelled, they can be constrained with the images we observe.

The power of strong gravitational lensing as a cosmological probe is greatly enhanced by two special classes of lensed systems, time-delay and double-plane lenses. When a bright, compact object such as a quasar or supernova, whose luminosity may fluctuate on relatively short timescales, is multiply imaged by a strong lens, the light curves of these multiple images can be compared, and the relative differences in arrival time between these trajectories can be measured. These relative time delays are proportional to a ratio of angular diameter distances such that, if the lens mass is well-constrained, these systems can be used to measure the Hubble constant H0H_{0} (Refsdal, 1964; Suyu et al., 2010; Birrer et al., 2022). For individual lens galaxies, this has achieved precisions up to 6.5%6.5\% (Sheu et al., 2026, e.g.), improving to 3% when combining a sample of 11 systems (TDCOSMO Collaboration et al., 2026).

On rare occasions, the same lens galaxy may strongly lens two background sources offset from one another in redshift, such that the most distant source may also be lensed by the foreground source/background lens. These “double-plane lens” (DPL) systems enable a measurement of the “cosmological scaling factor” η\eta, a combination of angular diameter distances which does not depend on H0H_{0}, but is instead sensitive to the relative expansion history of the universe (Collett et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2023). The key source of uncertainty in both of these methods is the so-called “mass-sheet degeneracy” (Falco et al., 1985, MSD,). The mass model of a given lens is underdetermined by lensed images and time delays alone, even when multiple images are present, without a fixed cosmological model. Any change to the modelled projected mass which mimics a change to the cosmology will inevitably be degenerate with the inferred cosmological parameters. Put differently, if the modelled lens profile is a rescaling of the true profile by a factor λ\lambda, and a corresponding constant uniform mass sheet is added to the model, lensed image positions and time delay ratios remain unchanged, but model-predicted relative time delays are rescaled. When these relative time delays are then measured, the inferred Hubble constant is biased by a factor λ\lambda (see Gorenstein et al., 1988; Saha, 2000; Wucknitz, 2002; Liesenborgs and De Rijcke, 2012; Schneider and Sluse, 2013; Birrer et al., 2016; Gomer and Williams, 2020; Birrer et al., 2022, and others).

An MSD-driven mismodelling of the lens mass can originate from two parts of the model. A uniform projected over or underdensity along the line of sight to the lens and source is umeasurable, and hence is usually constrained using the “weighted number counts” technique, by which the distribution of galaxies in the lens environment is compared to simulations in which this projected density contrast can be estimated (Suyu et al., 2010; Rusu et al., 2017; Wells et al., 2023; Johnson et al., 2026b, e.g.).

The “internal MSD” refers to the fact that a mass-sheet transformation of the main lens itself is similarly undetectable without independent constraints (Schneider and Sluse, 2013). Lens galaxies are typically modelled with simple parametric models, such as elliptical power laws (Tessore and Metcalf, 2015) or a dark-matter Navarro–Frenk–White plus baryonic Sérsic profile. Simulations are not yet able to resolve baryonic effects on the necessary scales to unambiguously predict lens model profiles, and it has also been shown that a change of dark matter model could mimic a change in λ\lambda (Blum et al., 2020; Blum and Teodori, 2021). The internal mass-sheet component of lens galaxies is typically constrained with velocity dispersion measurements (Treu and Koopmans, 2002; Suyu et al., 2013; Sheu et al., 2026, see e.g.).

papers.title: MV-IVF: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Multi-Vector Clustering
papers.abstract:
Multi-vector retrieval represents each query and document as a set of embeddings and scores relevance via fine-grained set-to-set interactions such as MaxSim (Chamfer similarity). This expressiveness improves retrieval quality over single-vector representations, but makes search substantially more expensive. Existing systems address this challenge primarily through proxy representations or filter-and-rerank pipelines that reduce candidate generation to single-vector search. We study the complementary direction of building a native IVF-style index directly over multi-vector data.
  We introduce MV-IVF, an inverted-file index for multi-vector retrieval built on MV-Lloyd, a new Lloyd-style algorithm for clustering point clouds under a Chamfer objective. Our key observation is that once point clouds are assigned to clusters, the center-update step reduces to standard single-vector clustering over the flattened embeddings in each cluster. This enables efficient construction of a hierarchical IVF tree with center point clouds at internal nodes.
  At query time, MV-IVF performs best-first beam search over the tree to identify promising leaf clusters, then scores the documents in those leaves. We further accelerate search using low-bit quantization, query compression, and cache-efficient batched search. We implement MV-IVF in MVSIC, an optimized C++ library and unified evaluation framework for multi-vector retrieval that includes several major approaches. Across BEIR and LoTTE text retrieval benchmarks, MV-IVF achieves strong latency--recall tradeoffs, the best batched throughput frontiers, and favorable build-time and index-size profiles. At $90\%$ Recall-$10$@$10$, MV-IVF achieves up to $8.03\times$ lower single-query latency and up to $173.5\times$ higher QPS than the baselines, demonstrating that native IVF-style indexing is practical and effective for scalable multi-vector retrieval.

papers.intro:
Multi-vector retrieval has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modern retrieval systems, in which each query and document is represented not by a single embedding, but by a set of embeddings (i.e., a point cloud). Such representations arise naturally in late-interaction models for text retrieval (e.g., ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022b)), where relevance is computed via token-level interactions using operators such as MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim}, as well as in region-based representations for images and other modalities (e.g., ColPali (Faysse et al., 2025)). This added expressiveness yields significantly better retrieval quality than single-vector encoders (e.g., on standard benchmarks such as BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021), LoTTE (Santhanam et al., 2022b), and ViDoRe (Faysse et al., 2025)) but the increased complexity of the representation makes search substantially more expensive.

The gold-standard multi-vector similarity, introduced by ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) and used by most subsequent late-interaction models, is MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim}. Given a query point cloud A⊆ℝdA\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and a document point cloud B⊆ℝdB\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, MaxSim⁡(A,B):=∑a∈Amaxb∈B⁡⟨a,b⟩,\mathrm{MaxSim}(A,B):=\sum_{a\in A}\max_{b\in B}\langle a,b\rangle, i.e., each query embedding is matched to its most similar document embedding and the resulting scores are summed. Thus, unlike single-vector retrieval, even a single query–document MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim} score can require many inner product computations. At scale, the central challenge is therefore to recover the top-kk documents under MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim} without exhaustively scoring the entire collection.

A large body of recent work has focused on making multi-vector retrieval under MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim} efficient. Most practical approaches follow a common philosophy: rather than indexing point clouds directly, they reduce candidate generation to a simpler proxy or filtering problem built using single-vector retrieval techniques, and reserve exact multi-vector scoring for a smaller set of candidates. For example, PLAID (Santhanam et al., 2022a) and its follow-up, WARP (Scheerer et al., 2025), use single-vector search over clustered token centroids to generate candidates, which are then scored using quantized and exact MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim}; Dhulipala et al. (2024) formalize this style of pipeline as the single-vector heuristic (SVH). MUVERA (Dhulipala et al., 2024) instead constructs fixed-dimensional encodings (FDEs), large single-vector representations whose inner products provably approximate multi-vector similarity, thereby reducing the problem to standard single-vector MIPS. These approaches are highly effective, but the quality of the final top-kk results depends on how well the surrogate representation or candidate-generation stage preserves documents that rank highly under MaxSim\mathrm{MaxSim}.

A smaller body of work has explored such native multi-vector indexing through hashing- and graph-based approaches, including DESSERT (Engels et al., 2023) and IGP (Bian et al., 2025). In this work, we investigate a different direction: extending clustering-based inverted-file (IVF) indexing, one of the most widely used paradigms for large-scale single-vector retrieval (Jégou et al., 2011; Douze et al., 2024), to multi-vector data.

In this work, we investigate a different direction: extending clustering-based inverted-file (IVF) indexing, one of the most widely used paradigms for large-scale single-vector retrieval (Jégou et al., 2011; Douze et al., 2024), to multi-vector data.

IVF is an appealing candidate for this setting. In the single-vector case, an IVF index partitions the dataset into clusters and probes only those whose representatives are most relevant to the query. This organization is simple and scalable to build, has low indexing overhead, exposes substantial parallelism, and is naturally suited to high-throughput batched search. These properties are particularly attractive for multi-vector retrieval, where scoring each candidate is substantially more expensive. However, extending IVF to multi-vector data is non-trivial: how should we cluster point clouds, and what representatives should we use to route queries to the resulting clusters?

papers.title: Tight Variable-Occurrence Bounds and Exponential Separations for Moser--Tardos and WalkSAT on 3-CNF
papers.abstract:
We establish a sharp variable-occurrence threshold for polynomial expected-time convergence for the Moser--Tardos algorithm and the pure random-walk WalkSAT on 3-CNF formulas. For every formula with $m$ clauses and at most two occurrences per variable, both algorithms terminate in $O(m)$ expected updates. This occurrence bound is sharp: we construct an infinite family with at most three occurrences per variable on which both algorithms require $2^{\Theta(\sqrt{m})}$ expected updates. Surprisingly, this dynamical transition occurs strictly below the classical NP-completeness threshold at variable-occurrence degree four.
  We further establish exponential separations between the two algorithms on satisfiable 3-CNF formulas. On one family, WalkSAT terminates in $O(m^4)$ expected flips, whereas MT requires $2^{\Omega(m)}$ expected resampling steps. On another, MT terminates in $O(m)$ expected resampling steps, whereas WalkSAT requires $2^{\Omega(m)}$ expected flips. These constructions exploit the different ways in which single-variable flips and simultaneous resampling propagate local violations. Our results show that the algorithms' expected running times are incomparable even up to polynomial overhead on the same inputs.

papers.intro:
The Moser–Tardos (MT) resampling algorithm is a landmark achievement in randomized algorithms. By making the Lovász Local Lemma (LLL) constructive in the variable setting, it transforms a powerful existence theorem into an efficient procedure for finding combinatorial objects that avoid prescribed local obstructions [16]. Its simple update rule and witness-tree analysis provide a striking example of how local randomized dynamics can yield global algorithmic guarantees. For Boolean satisfiability, the algorithm starts from a random assignment and repeatedly resamples all variables in an unsatisfied clause until it finds a satisfying assignment.

papers.title: Predicting Continuum Emission in Massive Star-Forming Regions with Embedded HII Regions - Dust, Free-Free, and Anomalous Microwave Emission with POLARIS
papers.abstract: Context: HII regions are a key stage of massive star formation, where ionizing radiation reshapes the interstellar medium. Their continuum spectra trace thermal dust, free-free emission, and anomalous microwave emission (AME). Aims: We investigate how these components evolve as an HII region expands and correlate with gas and electron column densities across spatial scales. Methods: We post-process RAMSES radiation-magnetohydrodynamical simulations of a $10^4 M_\odot$ cloud with POLARIS. The model includes grain charging, rotational excitation and damping, radiative torques, rotational disruption, and emission from dust, ionized gas, and nano-composite grains. We compute maps and SEDs for six snapshots over $1-10^4$ GHz and analyze multi-scale correlations. Results: Ionized emission evolves from a compact, optically thick HII region to an extended, optically thin structure. Around 15 GHz, free-free emission changes from a $\nu^2$ to a $\nu^{-0.1}$ spectral regime as optical depth decreases, and increasingly traces electron column density. The thermal dust peak shifts from mid- to far-infrared as colder material contributes, while dust emission remains strongly correlated with total gas column density. AME peaks at 26-37 GHz and shows scale-dependent correlations with gas and electron distributions. Rotational disruption is the main dust-destruction mechanism affecting mid-infrared emission and the high-frequency AME tail. Conclusions: These continuum components provide complementary, scale-dependent diagnostics of stellar feedback. Self-consistent multi-frequency modeling is essential for interpreting surveys of star-forming clouds.

Despite decades of theoretical and observational progress, the process of star formation remains poorly understood. Fundamental questions persist concerning how molecular clouds fragment, how turbulence, magnetic fields, and radiation feedback regulate collapse, and how newly formed massive stars influence their parental environment (Vázquez-Semadeni et al. 2025; Beuther et al. 2025). In particular, the interplay between gravity, magneto–hydrodynamics, radiative heating, and stellar feedback determines whether star formation proceeds efficiently or is quenched (Traficante et al. 2020; Peretto et al. 2023; Suin et al. 2025), yet the relative importance of these processes is still debated (Klessen and Glover 2016; Federrath 2016; Luo et al. 2024).

In the process of star formation, H ii regions represent a crucial evolutionary stage and mark the onset of ionizing radiation from young massive stars and thus the transition from embedded star formation to strong radiative feedback. The expansion of H ii regions reshapes the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM), compresses molecular gas, alters dust properties, and drives dynamical instabilities. Hence, observations of such regions provide a direct probe of feedback physics and its role in regulating star formation up to the parsec scales (Zhang et al. 2021). To connect observations with theory, it is essential to interpret the emission from star-forming regions in terms of the underlying physical state of gas and dust.

Continuum observations over a broad wavelength range are particularly powerful in this context. Far-infrared (FIR) and sub-millimeter (sub-mm) emission primarily trace thermal radiation from interstellar dust grains heated by stellar radiation and the interstellar radiation field. Observationally, AME is often correlated with infrared dust tracers, yet the AME strength depends on the abundance, size distribution, and charge state of the smallest grains, as well as on the local radiation field and gas conditions. While early models focused primarily on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and small carbonaceous grains, recent theoretical and observational developments have motivated the consideration of silicate bearing nano-particles as alternative or dominant AME carriers.

A key argument arises from interstellar abundance constraints. A substantial fraction of cosmic carbon is locked in CO or large carbonaceous grains, limiting the abundance of free-flying PAH-sized particles available to emit spinning dust radiation (Ali-Haïmoud et al. 2009; Hoang and Lazarian 2016a, see e.g.). Silicate-forming elements (Si, Mg, Fe), however, are almost entirely depleted into dust in the diffuse interstellar medium (Weingartner and Draine 2001). If a modest fraction of this material exists in nanometer-sized silicate particles, their cumulative emission can match AME intensities without violating abundance constraints (Hoang and Lazarian 2016a; Hensley and Draine 2017). Considering the larger intrinsic dipole moments and the greater resilience to energetic environments we focus on AME modeling merely invoking composite grains as the dominant emitters in H ii regions. Consequently, AME can either act as an additional tracer of the small-grain population and the microphysical environment of star-forming regions, or as a foreground contaminant that complicates the interpretation of free–free emission and hence star-formation diagnostics (Planck Collaboration et al. 2014).

(2019). This approach allows us to quantify how the different continuum components trace the physical evolution of star-forming regions and to assess the diagnostic and contaminating role of AME in the presence of ionized feedback.

papers.title: CS-Pi: Constraint-Satisfying Flow Policy Sampling
papers.abstract: A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as avoiding an obstacle it has never seen. Retraining for every new constraint is impractical, so the constraint must be enforced at inference time. Enforcing it must not discard what the policy learned: an action the policy would rarely sample may avoid the obstacle yet fail the task. We therefore want actions that are both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy. Gradient guidance, the most common approach, steers noisy states, so it must evaluate its cost on the policy's running estimate of the clean action; when the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an obstacle, this estimate is their average and can pass straight through it. We instead build on rejection and projection. Rejection redraws actions until one is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare. Projection moves an action to the nearest safe one: it is efficient, but the result need not be plausible. Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection's efficiency and rejection's plausibility. CS-Pi, our draw-project-renoise sampler, projects each draw to the nearest safe action, adds noise back scaled to how far the projection moved it, and re-runs the unmodified policy until a draw is safe. Replacing only the projection step extends CS-Pi to continuous costs. Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, an orientation preference, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi reaches 81% safe success on the shelf and 55% on hardware, against 55% and 40% for projection, while staying plausible.

papers.intro:
Large-scale flow-matching and diffusion policies have become capable generalist priors for robot manipulation[1, 2]: trained once on broad demonstrations, a single model can pick and place objects, open drawers, and fold clothes. Yet no training set anticipates every deployment, and such a policy will inevitably meet safety-critical scenarios its demonstrations never contained, for example: a wine glass left beside the drawer it must open, which the arm must not touch. This requirement is a constraint, supplied only at deployment. It defines a safe set: the set of actions that satisfy it; in our example, every action that does not touch the glass. Our goal is to sample actions that both come from the policy and lie in the safe set, without retraining the policy for each new constraint. The natural approach is to correct the policy’s output: sample an action and project it onto the safe set, moving it to the nearest safe action, or steer the denoising trajectory using a function of the constraint. Such corrections address the second half of this goal, moving the action into the safe set. They can lose the first: the correction can move the action somewhere the policy would rarely sample. This matters because the policy is what captures the task. An action it considers unlikely may clear the wine glass yet no longer reach the drawer handle. Such an action also loses what the policy learned from the demonstrations, beyond the task itself: smooth, kinematically feasible motion. We therefore require the sampled action to be both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy.

The natural approach is to correct the policy’s output: sample an action and project it onto the safe set, moving it to the nearest safe action, or steer the denoising trajectory using a function of the constraint. Such corrections address the second half of this goal, moving the action into the safe set. They can lose the first: the correction can move the action somewhere the policy would rarely sample. This matters because the policy is what captures the task. An action it considers unlikely may clear the wine glass yet no longer reach the drawer handle. Such an action also loses what the policy learned from the demonstrations, beyond the task itself: smooth, kinematically feasible motion. We therefore require the sampled action to be both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy.

Among such training-free samplers, the most common is gradient guidance [3, 4, 5], which nudges each denoising step along the gradient of a cost on the action. Guidance has two shortcomings. First, safety constraints are typically hard constraints: an action either satisfies them or violates them, with no degree in between. An action either touches the wine glass or it does not; this yes-or-no answer says nothing about which way to move the arm, so a hard constraint offers no gradient to follow. Guidance must instead use a smooth cost, such as a collision cost that grows as the arm nears the glass, which discourages contact but does not rule it out. Second, even a smooth cost is meaningful only on a clean action, while guidance acts on noisy intermediate states. Guidance therefore evaluates the cost at a proxy: the policy’s running estimate of the clean action, an average over every clean action the noisy state could still become. This proxy is reliable only when the cost changes slowly across those actions, so sharpening the cost toward the true constraint makes guidance less reliable, not more. The proxy fails when the policy is uncertain between distinct modes, such as passing left or right of the glass. The average of the two can pass straight through the glass, an action the policy would never sample. The gradient evaluated there may point towards neither mode (App. E).

We instead build on rejection and projection, two classical mechanisms that act only on the final sampled action rather than guiding the intermediate noise levels. Rejection sampling redraws complete actions from the policy until one satisfies the constraint: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare. Projection maps a sampled action to the nearest constraint-satisfying point: it is efficient, but the projected action need not be plausible and can be jerky or task-irrelevant. Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection’s efficiency and rejection’s plausibility. When a projected action is implausible, we need not take rejection’s drastic step of restarting sampling from pure noise; we can instead resample from a reduced noise level around the projection, so the policy returns a safe and plausible action near the projection.

We operationalize this insight in CS-Pi, a draw-project-renoise sampler (Fig. 2). CS-Pi starts from a single draw from the policy and refines it in a loop. Each iteration projects the current draw onto the safe set and, rather than executing the possibly implausible projection, adds noise back to it, scaled to how far the projection moved the draw. It then re-runs the unmodified policy from that noise level to obtain the next draw. The loop ends once a draw is safe. Each draw comes from the policy and tends to land closer to the safe set than the last, so the draws approach the safe set while remaining plausible, at a compute cost far below rejection and with no constraint gradient at any noisy state. We first present CS-Pi for hard constraints, then extend it to continuous costs, such as an orientation preference, by replacing only the projection step. The same change lets CS-Pi combine hard constraints with costs. Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place with deployment-time obstacles, the orientation preference above, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi is the only sampler that satisfies the constraint while staying plausible wherever the constraint permits; on the shelf it reaches 81%81\% safe success (completing the task without collision) against 55%55\% for projection and 32%32\% for gradient guidance.

papers.title: Higher Order Component Attribution via Learned Surrogates in High Energy Physics
papers.abstract: Experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) has adopted the transformer architecture for identification of jets, particularly the state-of-the-art Particle Transformer (ParT) which injects explicit information about particle correlations into the attention mechanism. While able to achieve state-of-the-art results in accuracy, interpretability to its effectiveness has been limited. In this paper we propose component attribution methods using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that directly tie back to the physical descriptors of jets, to probe whether mechanisms such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), or the ParT architecture, are able to learn these as discriminating features.

These have a complex internal radiation pattern which high-energy physicists study to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physics governed by the Standard Model (SM) or to search for hints of what lies beyond.

Jets are narrow cone-shaped streams of particles produced when high energy elementary particles such as quarks or gluons are ejected from a collision. Because of color confinement, quarks and gluons cannot exist as free particles. Instead, they undergo hadronization, a process that leads to a shower of hadrons, these being composite particles which may decay further until only stable or long-lived hadrons remain to be detected, as signatures in the detector. Distinguishing these classes of jets against the standard QCD background originating from light quarks or gluons has often, in the past, relied on observables built using the kinematic properties of individual jet constituents, rather than global ones. The energy-energy correlator (EEC), introduced in [1], quantifies the correlated energy flow between pairs of final-state particles as a function of their angular separation. Similarly, energy correlation functions (ECFs) [2] extend the pairwise correlation to arbitrary particle multiplicities within a single jet using infrared-and-collinear (IRC) safe combinations of pTp_{\mathrm{T}} fractions and pairwise angular separations. An NN-point energy correlation function (ECF) measures how energy is shared among groups of NN particles in a jet, weighting each group by the particles’ energies and their pairwise angular separations. As the definition of Equation 1 implies, contributions are suppressed if any particle has low energy or a given pair is close in angle. This observable therefore probes whether the jet contains at least NN distinct prongs, and ratios built from these serve as a powerful variable for jet flavor tagging.

Deep neural network (DNN) architectures are the tool of choice for most jet tagging applications at collider experiments. Large parameter counts, often on the order of millions, ensure they learn the radiation patterns and correlations within a jet. This removes any reliance on a finite set of hand-crafted observables such as the ECFs above. Learning correlations from the raw kinematic data generally translates into higher metrics such as the AUC score, or the background rejection at fixed signal efficiency, across signal models.

Large parameter counts, often on the order of millions, ensure they learn the radiation patterns and correlations within a jet. This removes any reliance on a finite set of hand-crafted observables such as the ECFs above. Learning correlations from the raw kinematic data generally translates into higher metrics such as the AUC score, or the background rejection at fixed signal efficiency, across signal models.

Early DNN-based taggers represented a jet as a fixed-size image, with the particle momenta being deposited in η\eta–ϕ\phi pixels. This representation allowed the usage of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures [3, 4, 5] that had already demonstrated great success in computer vision tasks. But this approach did not consider the variable-multiplicity, point-cloud nature of the jet, and in turn motivated architectures that directly operate on the constituents themselves. For example, permutation-invariant deep sets [6], and graph neural networks (GNNs) such as ParticleNet [7] and DeepJet [8]. Transformer architectures, such as the Particle Transformer [9] outperform both the convolutional and graph-based taggers above. These form the backbone architecture used in most modern jet tagging applications, and are also the focus of this work.

papers.title: System noise temperature measurements of a 19-element phased array feed
papers.abstract: We present multi-epoch system noise temperature measurements of a 19 element hexagonal room-temperature phased array feed (PAF) using a modified Y-factor method. A Python-based pipeline with iterative channel calibration and maxSNR beam forming is developed to do data reduction, and a covariance-based decomposition scheme is proposed to extract mutual coupling noise temperature Tmc. Long-term observations from March to June 2026 capture temporal receiver noise drift mainly induced by LNA temperature variations. Within the 1.37-1.47 GHz operating band, the measured beam equivalent system noise temperature of the PAF is about 73-89 K. The measured Tmc baseline ranges from about 2 K to 8 K, while under thermal loading, the resonant peak of Tmc can increase to more than 20 K. The baseline of Tmc is consistent with the S-parameter mea surements, which show the Tmc of the full array ranges less than 10.7 K. The baseline fluctuation of Tmc most likely arises from the superposition of thermal and non-thermal components of the spatial electromagnetic fields. A detachable stainless steel shield is deployed to quantify sidelobe spillover noise, and comparative tests show unshielded en vironmental interference increases receiver noise temperature by over 60 K. The proposed measurements and data processing framework provides a practical reference for noise per formance characterization of ground-based radio telescope PAF prototypes.

papers.intro:
Phased Array Feeds (PAFs) represent the transformative focal-plane receiver technology for contemporary and next-generation radio telescopes, enabling simultaneous electronically steerable multi-beam synthesis via digital beamforming and substantially accelerating sky survey speed with a wide instantaneous field of view (Veidt and Dewdney 2005; van Ardenne et al. 2009; van Cappellen and Bakker 2010). Radio telescopes equipped with PAFs, such as the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP), Parkes Telescope, Westerbork APERture Tile In Focus (Apertif), Green Bank Telescope (GBT), have been deployed for observations targeting fast radio bursts, pulsars, HI survey, magnetic fields in galaxy clusters, continuum sources, and large-area radio sky surveys (Hotan et al. 2021; Bannister et al. 2017; Deng et al. 2017; Li et al. 2021; van Cappellen et al. 2022; Röttgering et al. 2011; Heywood et al. 2016; Pingel et al. 2021). In addition to these observations, low-noise amplifiers and cryogenic PAF hardware have also been designed and manufactured to meet the ultra-low noise requirements for astronomical observations (Cortes-Medellin et al. 2015; Warnick et al. 2016; Groves and Morgan 2017; Melis et al. 2020; Burnett et al. 2020).

For instance, the beam-formed system temperature normalized by aperture efficiency of cryogenic PAF for the GBT has been measured as ∼\sim18-28 K near 1350 MHz for the boresight beam, achieving comparable noise temperature performance of the 1400 MHz cryogenic single-feed receiver on the GBT (Roshi et al. 2018; Pingel et al. 2021). System noise temperature acts as the core sensitivity metric determining the detection threshold of faint cosmic radio sources, and its budget consists of multiple coupled noise constituents: LNA intrinsic thermal noise, antenna/cable resistive loss, cosmic sky background radiation, antenna sidelobes and backlobes noise, and correlated noise induced by element mutual coupling (Warnick and Jeffs 2008; Landon et al. 2010). Mutual coupling, arising from near-field electromagnetic interaction between closely spaced radiators and beam-dependent active impedance mismatches at LNA input ports, introduces off-diagonal correlated terms in array covariance matrices and creates an unavoidable noise penalty for dense PAF designs (Warnick et al. 2009; Warnick and Jensen 2005). Fundamental theoretical frameworks, established by Warnick & co-workers systematically model coupling-induced receiver noise degradation, derive active impedance matching criteria, and contrast three mainstream amplifier matching schemes (Warnick et al. 2009; Warnick and Jeffs 2008). S-parameter full-wave simulation can predict inter-port transmission coefficients and convert coupling strength into equivalent noise temperature contributions, yet purely numerical predictions require on-telescope hot/cold load calibration validation (Landon et al. 2010; Wu et al. 2013; Chippendale et al. 2014).

We in this paper conduct a quantitative diagnosis on how the overall noise performance including mutual coupling contributions, of the 19-element hexagonal PAF designed in (Wu et al. 2013) and recently upgraded, varies over time and under different ambient environmental conditions. Moreover, we present a modified Y-factor method to decompose the mutual coupling components from accumulated overall system noise. This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 details the PAF hardware layout, hot/cold loads and shielding configuration for Y-factor method, full signal chain and end-to-end data processing pipeline. Section 3 presents measured receiver noise, and total system noise temperature against frequency and time, with quantitative contributions of inter-element coupling noise and spillover. Section 4 makes discussion of the physical mechanisms governing time-variant noise fluctuations including coupling, spillover and RFI effects, and comparison between our multi-epoch measurement scheme and others. Section 5 summarises main experimental conclusions and outlines prospective optimisations.

papers.title: Disentangling Spin and Orbital Contributions in the Search for Altermagnetic Terahertz Conversion in RuO2
papers.abstract: Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a prominent candidate altermagnet, yet the microscopic origin of its reported charge-angular-momentum conversion remains unsettled. Recent theoretical and experimental advances have highlighted a potentially dominant role of orbital transport, raising a fundamental ambiguity between spin- and orbital-mediated conversion in RuO2. Here, we report the first experimental disentanglement of the spin- and orbital-to-charge conversion channels in RuO2 heterostructures using terahertz emission spectroscopy. We identify Fe as a predominantly spin-current injector, whereas Ni and permalloy predominantly inject orbital currents, revealing a substantial orbital contribution to ultrafast terahertz emission. Under controlled spin-current injection, we find no evidence for inverse altermagnetic spin-splitting effect. Instead, the observed anisotropy is consistent with an anisotropic inverse spin Hall response that is strongly conditioned by the near-interface environment. Under orbital-current injection, the anisotropy is markedly weaker, indicating that orbital-to-charge conversion is largely isotropic in RuO2. Our results establish orbital transport and interface-conditioned spin Hall conversion as key to terahertz emission from RuO2, underscoring the need to disentangle spin, orbital, and interfacial contributions before assigning anisotropy to altermagnetism.

papers.title: Towards an Autonomous AI Steward for Large-Scale Physics Experiments: Integrating Causal Diagnostics, RAG, and Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Long-term particle physics experiments face critical operational challenges: monitoring non-stationary machine data streams and preserving tacit expert knowledge. We present the "Helmholtz Co-Pilot," a hybrid Multi-Agent System (MAS) acting as an autonomous experiment steward. The system can be triggered interactively by human operators or autonomously by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that runs independently of the MAS reasoning core. Continuously monitoring live hardware streams such as data acquisition and slow control, this engine performs dynamic causal discovery to trace cascading alarms back to their root causes and applies adaptive model selection to keep forecasts reliable across shifting machine states; upon detecting an anomaly, it hands a structured diagnostic report to the MAS. The reasoning layer itself relies on a high-throughput C++ core and a Python edge architecture orchestrating a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of specialized ReAct workers. It integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) backbone for institutional memory and leverages conformal prediction to bound its evidence-based recommendations with mathematical coverage guarantees. This extended abstract outlines the architecture, the integration of software-enforced Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.

papers.title: On the Motzkin-Straus theorem and clique number for k-uniform hypergraphs
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a Motzkin-Straus type equality for k-uniform hypergraphs under certain conditions, which extends the classical Motzkin--Straus theorem for graphs. Using this equality, we present several spectral bounds for the clique number of k-uniform hypergraphs in terms of the spectral radii of the adjacency, signless Laplacian, and Laplacian tensors. When k=2, the bounds coincide with the corresponding known results for graphs.

papers.title: A Physics-Informed Learning Framework for Linking Microscopic Surface Degradation to Bolted Joint Functional Behavior
papers.abstract: Returned products in circular engineering often have heterogeneous degradation histories, making remaining function difficult to assess. For bolted joints, corrosion alters surface morphology, contact, friction, preload retention, and mechanical response. This paper presents a physics-informed multimodal framework for linking microscopic and camera-based degradation observations to functional indicators of corroded bolted joints. The workflow defines the corrosion failure mode, generates synchronized inspection and functional-response records, preprocesses image, roughness, exposure, and joint descriptors, aligns microscopy and camera observations through similarity learning, and constructs a calibrated corrosion-severity field. Partial differential equation (PDE) discovery is applied to this field to identify candidate effective mesoscale laws rather than complete electrochemical mechanisms. The corrosion-evolution model is coupled to a separate functional model, with friction coefficient as the primary target and preload loss included when clamp-force data are available. The contribution is a reproducible pathway for physically constrained assessment of degraded bolted-joint behavior.
papers.intro:
Circular factories aim to keep products and components in use for as long as possible. This requires decisions about whether returned products should be reused, refurbished, disassembled, or recycled [1, 2]. For bolted joints, these decisions are difficult because the remaining function depends not only on the visible condition of the joint, but also on preload, friction, contact condition, tightening history, joint configuration, and the conditions of the thread and bearing surfaces [3, 4, 5]. Corrosion changes these surface and contact conditions by altering oxide morphology, roughness, material loss, and local contact pressure [6, 7, 8, 9]. The practical challenge is therefore to infer remaining functional behavior from inspection evidence that is feasible to collect from degraded products.[10]

For bolted joints, these decisions are difficult because the remaining function depends not only on the visible condition of the joint, but also on preload, friction, contact condition, tightening history, joint configuration, and the conditions of the thread and bearing surfaces [3, 4, 5]. Corrosion changes these surface and contact conditions by altering oxide morphology, roughness, material loss, and local contact pressure [6, 7, 8, 9]. The practical challenge is therefore to infer remaining functional behavior from inspection evidence that is feasible to collect from degraded products.[10]

Feasible inspection data for degraded bolted joints may include camera images, microscopic images, roughness measurements, exposure information, and selected functional measurements such as torque-angle or torque/clamp-force data [11]. These data are informative but heterogeneous. They do not directly provide a corrosion-state field, an effective degradation relation, or a direct prediction of joint function. Existing methods address parts of this problem: mechanistic corrosion models describe degradation physics, vision methods extract visual descriptors, and physics-informed learning can impose differential-equation constraints [12, 13, 14, 15]. What remains missing is a structured path that connects inspection evidence to degradation-state representation and then to selected joint’s functional indicators.

The framework converts image, roughness, exposure, and joint-design information into calibrated corrosion-state fields, applies PDE discovery to these fields as candidate effective mesoscale corrosion laws, and couples corrosion evolution to functional prediction. The paper makes four contributions. First, it formulates an inspection-oriented corrosion-state inference problem for degraded bolted joints. Second, it defines a latent-field interface that converts multimodal imaging and roughness observations into calibrated corrosion-state fields. Third, it formulates genetic-algorithm-based PDE discovery for candidate effective corrosion laws over those fields. Fourth, it couples corrosion-state evolution to prediction of selected functional indicators, with friction coefficient as the first target and preload loss as a secondary target when clamp-force data are available.

papers.title: Active Learning of Robust Models
papers.abstract: In many domains from species identification to cancer diagnosis, labelling data to train predictive models remains costly. In these settings, it is advantageous to intelligently select data points to label to achieve the maximum information gain, this is the motivation behind the study of active learning. In addition to the high costs of acquiring data in such domains, there is the added complexity of data distribution shifts that can occur between training and deployment. For example, the features of cancerous skin cells taken in one country may be different in another region of the world. These two challenges - efficient labelling of data, and learning models robust to distribution shifts have been studied separately but not together, even though these challenges often co-occur in real-life settings. We identify failure modes of standard active learning approaches when the distribution of data at deployment is different from the distribution in which the data is sampled for labelling. We propose a new strategy for efficiently learning classifiers that generalise under specific forms of distribution shift, namely subpopulation shift. Drawing on work in learning from heterogeneous data, we aim to train models that perform well across subpopulations of the data, through active learning. To handle this challenging setting, we exploit the fact that many datasets include metadata about data collection that can serve as a noisy proxy for each sample's underlying subpopulation. We demonstrate how to leverage these noisy labels during active learning selection, and demonstrate empirically that our approach improves classifier accuracy across subpopulations.

papers.intro:
For classification problems in domains where acquiring labeled data remains costly, active learning is of interest, since it provides a method of selecting the most informative labels given a budget. For example, to predict the status of a disease from medical images, we may train an initial classifier on a small set of labeled data and acquire labels on unlabelled inputs where the classifier is uncertain. While many papers propose new active learning methods to improve performance on held-out data, we increasingly recognise that what matters in the wild is the out-of-distribution performance of models (Nagarajan et al., 2021). That is, we are interested in how well classifiers generalise when there is a shift in the distribution of inputs between training and deployment. The goal of this work is to understand the challenges behind active learning under distribution shifts, in doing so, we discover the failure modes of existing active learning methods. We propose a method for actively learning classifiers that generalise to a form of distribution shift — subpopulation shifts.
