We address the individual representation problem with our uniqueness-aware feature engineering pipeline illustrated in Figure 1. It entails six steps: (1) collecting reference representation data that reflects the internal perspective of individuals on what is decision-relevant for them; (2) characterizing the heterogeneity of the observed group using the measures we introduce; (3) selecting from the most prevalent features in the pooled population while excluding features too rare to support reliable decision making; (4) calibrating the optimum between coverage and accuracy explicitly rather than absorbing it silently into model training; (5) publishing any deployed model together with a structured account of the individual representation problem; and (6) in production, informing each new individual of how well the chosen input representation fits their specific reference representation.

papers.title: Portable Glass-RPC Telescope for Muography and Future Applications at Laser Wake Field Accelerators
papers.abstract: We report a 2025 beam test at ELBA, the multi-GeV laser wakefield accelerator at ELI Beamlines, using a Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) telescope with an active area of 16 * 16 cm2. The portable design sup- ports autonomous operation in challenging environments. Previous cosmic-ray measurements established its tracking capability for muography. During the campaign at ELBA, 30 f s long, 0.5 PW laser pulses in- teracted with a plasma target at a 0.2 Hz repetition rate, where a tungsten converter upstream of the beam dump enhanced muon production. This was the first deployment of an RPC telescope in a high-power laser environment. The detector remained operational in the presence of radiation and electromagnetic interference. Although parasitic running and limited statistics prevented definitive identification of beam- induced muons, the measurements offered insight into background activity and showed evidence of re- constructed tracks. They establish the feasibility of a dedicated campaign with controlled beam conditions and improved muon sensitivity. This contribution forms part of the International Muography Workshop 2026 proceedings.

papers.intro:
Muography uses naturally occurring cosmic-ray muons to image large or dense objects through absorption or scattering without damaging it Bonechi and others (2020). Muons penetrate matter and carry information about the material they traverse. Measurements typically rely on either the reduction in muon flux through the target or changes in muon trajectories caused by multiple Coulomb scattering. These approaches serve applications ranging from maritime security inspections and volcanic monitoring to the investigation and preservation of cultural heritage objects, as well as the potential detection and monitoring of CO2 plumes in geological formations Basiri and others (2026). The quality of the reconstructed image depends on the detector arrangement and its ability to detect muons and measure their positions accurately. Practical deployment imposes further constraints. Systems intended for remote or difficult-to-access sites must combine adequate tracking performance with portability, autonomous operation, and resistance to demanding environmental conditions Kumar and others (2025). Our project develops compact, robust, and autonomous muon telescopes for measurements in confined, remote, or logistically challenging environments Basnet and others (2020). The system employs sealed glass Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs), chosen for their tracking capabilities, cost effectiveness, and ease of construction Giammanco and others (2022). Sealed operation limits dependence on external gas supplies and improves safety during field deployment Gamage and others (2022). Cosmic-ray muons require no artificial source, but their low and uncontrolled flux often leads to long measurement times. Laser-plasma accelerators offer a potential alternative by producing short, directional bursts of multi-GeV electrons Rockafellow and others (2025), which generate secondary particles, including muons, when directed onto high-density materials Zhang and others (2025). Such sources offer controlled pulse timing and higher directional flux, potentially reducing acquisition times, particularly for imaging small objects of interest. This approach remains at an early experimental stage, with muon yield, background suppression, and detector operation near high-power lasers still under investigation Terzani and others (2025). In 2025, our team deployed the telescope at the ELBA laser wakefield electron accelerator at ELI Beamlines to study highly penetrating charged particles generated by 30​f​s30~{fs} long, 0.5​P​W0.5~{PW} laser pulses operating at 0.2​H​z0.2~{Hz} repetition rate Šišma and others (2026). A tungsten target was placed upstream of the concrete beam dump to enhance muon production. This was the first deployment of a gas-tight RPC telescope in a high-power laser environment. Despite limited statistics and parasitic data-taking conditions, the detector operated stably and provided initial measurements of the background and tracking performance. A detailed description of the experimental campaign is presented in Ref. Ikram et al. (2026). While this proceedings contribution focuses and expands on operational feasibility and background characterization, Reference Ikram et al. (2026) also provides FLUKA Monte Carlo fluence estimates, formal upper-limit statistical calculations, and controlled laboratory validation tests.

papers.title: Finite-strain second-gradient elasticity with an energetic surface: existence of minimizers, incremental theory and elastocapillary beading
papers.abstract: We develop a finite-strain theory of second-gradient elasticity for solids with a material surface endowed with its own constitutive energy. The bulk second gradient plays two complementary roles. First, under suitable coercivity assumptions and convexity with respect to the second gradient, we prove the existence of minimizers for nonnegative, lower semicontinuous surface energy densities, without requiring convexity, polyconvexity, positive one-homogeneity, or an upper growth bound on the surface energy. Second, it introduces an intrinsic bulk length scale that affects the onset of instability and wavelength selection. To investigate these effects, we derive an incremental small-on-large formulation in the finitely deformed configuration and apply it to the elastocapillary beading of an axially stretched soft cylinder. For an infinite cylinder and the parameters considered, increasing the second-gradient modulus delays bifurcation and shifts the critical mode towards longer wavelengths. Above a finite threshold of this modulus, the critical stretch saturates in the long-wave limit. The model is implemented in the open-source finite element code OOFEM using C1-continuous isogeometric analysis. Finite-cylinder simulations yield onset stretches in close agreement with the analytical predictions. Selected post-bifurcation branches traced by arc-length continuation exhibit beaded states and supercritical bifurcation at small second-gradient moduli, whereas larger moduli are associated with subcritical bifurcation and the formation of distinct thick and thin segments.

papers.intro:
The mechanical response of soft materials, including biological tissues, hydrogels, and synthetic polymers, is governed not only by bulk elasticity but also, often strongly, by surface stresses (Style et al., 2017). Surface effects become particularly important when a characteristic dimension of the body is comparable to the elastocapillary length, defined as the ratio of a characteristic surface stress to a bulk elastic modulus. Depending on the convention, this modulus is Young’s modulus (Style et al., 2017) or the shear modulus (Mora et al., 2010). The simplest surface-tension model assumes a constant, isotropic surface stress, as at a liquid interface. More generally, the continuum theory of Gurtin & Murdoch (1975); Gurtin & Murdoch (1978) treats the surface as a zero-thickness elastic membrane with its own constitutive response, perfectly bonded to the underlying bulk. Surface stress may then depend on surface strain through the Shuttleworth effect (Shuttleworth, 1950), demonstrated experimentally in soft gels (Xu et al., 2017). The interplay between bulk and surface mechanics can give rise to instabilities. A canonical example is elastocapillary beading of a soft cylinder, a solid analogue of the classical Plateau–Rayleigh instability in fluids. Mora et al. (2010) demonstrated experimentally that soft gel cylinders undergo beading when capillary forces overcome the elastic resistance of the bulk. Subsequent work extended the analysis to prestressed cylindrical structures, showing how axial stretch shifts the critical bifurcation threshold (Ciarletta & Ben Amar, 2012; Taffetani & Ciarletta, 2015a; Fu et al., 2021). Weakly nonlinear and energetic analyses show that the beading transition can be subcritical, with homogeneous and bifurcated states coexisting over a finite range of loading, and can be interpreted as phase separation between thin and thick states (Taffetani & Ciarletta, 2015a; Taffetani & Ciarletta, 2015b; Xuan & Biggins, 2017; Fu et al., 2021). Furthermore, the constitutive assumptions of the surface model—such as area incompressibility, curvature dependence, or negative surface tension—can also qualitatively change the instability (Bakiler et al., 2023; Taffetani & Hennessy, 2024; Ru, 2023). Incremental equations for curvature-dependent surface elasticity have also been derived recently (Yu et al., 2026).

The present work combines finite-strain second-gradient bulk elasticity with an independently prescribed surface energy to address two questions: how the intrinsic bulk length scale affects elastocapillary instability and how the additional bulk regularity changes the conditions for the existence of minimizers. Classical first-gradient elasticity contains no intrinsic bulk material length scale and cannot, by itself, capture bulk size effects associated with strongly nonuniform deformation. Higher-order theories originating from the works of Toupin (1962) and Mindlin (1964) address this limitation by allowing the bulk energy to depend on higher spatial derivatives of the deformation (Mindlin & Eshel, 1968; Askes & Aifantis, 2011). In particular, second-gradient hyperelasticity introduces such a length scale by penalizing spatial variations of the deformation gradient. This mechanism is especially relevant to instability problems, where modes of different wavelengths may compete and the intrinsic length scale can therefore influence mode selection.

Recent finite-strain computations by Wang & Dortdivanlioglu (2025) illustrate this role of strain-gradient elasticity in highly deformable materials. Their analyses of buckling, wrinkling, and period-doubling instabilities showed that size effects become significant when structural dimensions are comparable to the intrinsic material length scale. Increasing the strain-gradient contribution can delay the onset of instability, alter mode transitions and post-critical behavior, and even suppress particular instability modes. These findings demonstrate the physical role of higher-gradient terms in instability and pattern selection, beyond their use for numerical regularization. Specifically, we investigate how the second-gradient modulus affects the bifurcation spectrum and the critical wavelength.

Combining second-gradient elasticity with a surface energy requires distinguishing independent surface constitutive contributions from boundary terms generated by the bulk energy. Both occur in the present formulation: the bulk energy depends on the deformation gradient and its gradient, while the independently prescribed surface energy depends on the surface deformation gradient. Variation of the bulk energy also produces higher-order boundary terms through integration by parts; these are determined by the bulk constitutive law. Connections between higher-gradient bulk elasticity and surface effects were explored in Casal (1961) and Mindlin (1965), and subsequently by Vardoulakis, Exadaktylos, and Aifantis (Vardoulakis et al., 1996; Exadaktylos & Vardoulakis, 1998). Although the resulting wrinkling-type instability differs from the cylindrical beading mode studied here, it provides a precedent for the influence of higher-gradient bulk elasticity on surface instability.

papers.title: Drift-admissibility via Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: We introduce structure-aware optimal transport diagnostics for assessing whether empirical time-series dynamics are compatible with a prescribed predictable-drift class. Our approach translates a pathwise property of stochastic processes into a finite-dimensional projection problem over empirical transition laws, encoding admissibility as row-wise moment constraints on local couplings and quantifying deviations via a Kullback--Leibler projection gap $G_{\lambda,k}$. This yields both a principled diagnostic and a scalable Bregman--Dykstra algorithm that retains the efficiency of Sinkhorn-type methods while incorporating structural constraints. Calibrated against a Brownian reference null, $G_{\lambda,k}$ separates process classes that are indistinguishable by second-order statistics alone---including fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes sharing identical Hurst indices---without asymptotic resampling or continuous-time recovery. This positions the method as a general tool for structure-aware model validation of sequential data.

papers.intro:
A central challenge in modelling time-series data is determining whether observed dynamics are compatible with a given structural hypothesis. In stochastic analysis, semimartingale structures are a key hypothesis, underpinning arbitrage-free modelling, stochastic integration, and continuous-time financial theory [17, 5, 20]. However, verifying such a structure from discrete observations is notoriously difficult: classical characterisations are pathwise or asymptotic and do not translate directly into finite-sample, data-driven diagnostics [16, 3, 1, 7]. Optimal transport (OT) provides scalable tools for learning couplings, but standard formulations typically constrain only marginals and costs rather than conditional structure.

In stochastic analysis, semimartingale structures are a key hypothesis, underpinning arbitrage-free modelling, stochastic integration, and continuous-time financial theory [17, 5, 20]. However, verifying such a structure from discrete observations is notoriously difficult: classical characterisations are pathwise or asymptotic and do not translate directly into finite-sample, data-driven diagnostics [16, 3, 1, 7]. Optimal transport (OT) provides scalable tools for learning couplings, but standard formulations typically constrain only marginals and costs rather than conditional structure.

In this work, we bridge these two perspectives. We introduce a new class of constraint-aware OT projections that encode predictable-drift admissibility as row-wise moment constraints on empirical transition laws. The term structure-aware refers precisely to this: the constraints act on the conditional (row-wise) distribution of increments given the predictor state, rather than on global marginals or aggregate costs as in standard Sinkhorn formulations. This construction provides a finite-dimensional, observation-driven diagnostic for a bounded predictable drift class inspired by special semimartingales, replacing pathwise conditions with a convex feasibility problem over transport plans. The resulting projection gap Gλ,kG_{\lambda,k} quantifies the minimal KL deformation required to enforce the chosen structural constraints; it is a compatibility diagnostic, not a standalone statistical test (Section 6).

Entropy-regularised OT [12], introduced to accelerate computation of Wasserstein distances via Sinkhorn iterations, admits a natural extension to multiple convex constraints through iterative Bregman projections [6]. Several recent works have extended OT beyond the classical marginal constraints, including unbalanced settings [11], capacity constraints [18], and moment- or feature-constraints [8, 9, 21]. These approaches impose constraints at the level of global marginals or aggregate statistics. A related line of work studies OT under flow-rate constraints, where aggregate mass through a constriction set is bounded above [15]. In contrast, we introduce row-wise (conditional) moment constraints acting directly on the coupling, encoding structure at the level of local transition laws. This distinction is fundamental: flow-rate constraints bound aggregate mass through a bottleneck (a global constraint), whereas our 𝒞+,𝒞−\mathcal{C}_{+},\mathcal{C}_{-} constrain the conditional first moment within each row individually. Using these constraints, we define a novel structure-aware divergence as the KL projection gap to the nearest coupling satisfying admissibility constraints.

In contrast, we introduce row-wise (conditional) moment constraints acting directly on the coupling, encoding structure at the level of local transition laws. This distinction is fundamental: flow-rate constraints bound aggregate mass through a bottleneck (a global constraint), whereas our 𝒞+,𝒞−\mathcal{C}_{+},\mathcal{C}_{-} constrain the conditional first moment within each row individually. Using these constraints, we define a novel structure-aware divergence as the KL projection gap to the nearest coupling satisfying admissibility constraints.

In mathematical finance, semimartingales are the canonical class for stochastic integration and self-financing trading strategies, and non-semimartingale price models may lead to arbitrage pathologies [5, 20]. This structural role is distinct from martingality, which is usually imposed on discounted prices under an equivalent pricing measure [14, 13]. In applications, the process is not observed continuously: one observes a finite grid of prices and therefore cannot recover the latent continuous-time decomposition directly [16]. Empirical diagnostics in this setting typically rely on high-frequency asymptotics [3, 1, 7]. These approaches test specific path properties but do not directly assess the admissibility of predictable drift. We instead adopt a finite-sample, distributional perspective, replacing pathwise conditions with a convex projection problem on empirical transition laws.

papers.title: Just CaloCHILL: fast hadronic shower generation in a learned latent space
papers.abstract: Calorimeter showers are the most expensive part of detector simulation, and highly granular calorimeters, in which a single hadronic shower leaves thousands of energy deposits, make them more expensive still. We present CaloCHILL (Calorimeter Hits In Learned Latents), a generative model that does not produce these deposits one by one: instead it generates a compact summary of the shower in a learned latent space and expands it to full resolution only at the end. The complete shower, including the arrival time of every hit, is built in three stages: a flow-matching model first sets the number of hits and the earliest hit time in each calorimeter layer, a mean-flow model then generates the latent summary, and the decompressor of a variational autoencoder turns it into the full point cloud, giving every hit its position, energy and time. Sparse attention along the shower axis keeps this compression affordable for showers with thousands of hits. On positive-pion showers in the calorimeter of the International Large Detector, a proposed detector for the FCC-ee, CaloCHILL reproduces the main shower observables, including their time structure. This new model is 600 times faster than its predecessor, while improving on all accuracy metrics considered.

papers.intro:
High Energy Physics (HEP) aims to advance our understanding of fundamental forces and fields by observing the outcomes of particle interactions at high energies in colliders. Analysis in HEP compares observed events against simulated counterparts, and the gold standard for simulating detector interactions is the MC program Geant4 [3, 6, 5]. Among all the steps involved, interactions with the calorimeter in the detector consume the most computational time [4]. Thus, some form of fast surrogate modeling is essential to generate sufficient simulations to prevent statistical uncertainties from dominating the analysis. Detectors planned for the future, such as those proposed for the FCC-ee, will feature significantly higher granularity [45, 2], presenting an even greater challenge for fast and accurate generative simulation.

Substantial efforts have focused on developing solutions to meet this demand [38, 39, 13, 32, 36, 9, 12, 14, 1], with flow matching [27] and diffusion models [9] performing particularly well. Methodologies explored just this year include tokenizer-based models for calorimeter simulation [29, 11, 21], flow-based [18] and diffusion-based approaches [31], transfer-learning techniques between detectors [17, 26], and even FPGA-specific optimizations [35]. Comparative studies of earlier models appear in the second CaloChallenge paper [8] and the first full-physics benchmark [16]. Readers seeking a broader perspective on ongoing developments are directed to the simulation section of the HEP–ML Living Guide [33] and to the review in ref. [30].

To date, fast simulations have improved performance by replacing Geant4 with surrogates that still generate every shower point individually [12, 14, 15, 19, 18]. Point-cloud approaches normally encounter a trade-off between the desire to predict points at a higher granularity to reduce position related artifacts and the corresponding increase in inference time from predicting more points. Generation in a learned latent space mitigates this trade-off, because the generative model acts on a compressed representation and only its expansion back into the full point cloud scales with the shower length. Such approaches have also been explored. CaloLatent [34] and CaloDREAM [27] generate voxelised showers in the latent space of an autoencoder, following latent diffusion in image generation [40], and the CaloPointFlow models [41, 42] encode a point-cloud shower into a single global latent vector, from which the individual points are then sampled. In this work the point cloud is instead compressed into an ordered sequence of dsd_{s} latent vectors, each summarising a section of the shower along its axis, and the generator acts on this sequence rather than on the points. A compressed representation reduces the amount of data to be generated rather than only accelerating its production, but the autoencoder must then compress a cloud of up to thousands of points into dsd_{s} latent vectors and still reconstruct it faithfully. Every observable therefore depends on what the latent keeps, not only on the generator.

Future hadronic calorimeters, such as the one designed for International Large Detector (ILD) [2] may also offer high resolution timing information. This is a valuable feature for mitigating pileup at higher luminosities [20, 22], and so far has only been included in a limited number of fast generative simulations; only two are known to us at the time of writing, both are for photon showers [23, 29]. papers.title: Conformationally frustrated epitaxy at heteromolecular interface
papers.abstract: Precise control of molecular heteroepitaxy offers a route to multilayer architectures with well-defined interfaces. However, the role of intramolecular flexibility in epitaxial matching remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate the heteroepitaxy of intact 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene (BTB) on a molecular $\delta$-layer composed of fully deprotonated BTB molecules on Ag(111). Combining scanning tunneling microscopy, low-energy electron microscopy and diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and density functional theory, we identify the key interactions controlling molecular packing and epitaxial growth. We show that intermolecular bonding motifs are preserved on the molecular template, but their lattice parameters and molecular conformations change as compared to a silver surface. Individual molecules exhibit distinct appearances in scanning tunneling microscopy, consistent with site-dependent conformational variations identified by theory. Our calculations reveal that the competition between molecule-substrate interactions and conformational energy produces different compromise geometries, resulting in conformational frustration at the epitaxial interface. Crucially, constraining BTB into a planar geometry changes the preferred lateral adsorption positions, demonstrating that molecular flexibility directly modifies the energetic preferences for epitaxial registry. Comparison with more rigid molecular overlayers further supports this interpretation. Our findings reveal that molecular flexibility contributes to epitaxial matching by allowing unfavorable molecule-substrate interactions to be compensated by energetically favorable conformations while preserving the intermolecular network.

papers.title: DeepRT-Cal: Learning to Calibrate Ray-Traced Twin Channel Statistics with Low-Fidelity Environmental Geometry
papers.abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems increasingly rely on digital twin channels (DTCs) to represent and interact with physical radio environments. Ray tracing (RT) is naturally suited to DTC construction because it provides deterministic and physically interpretable channel predictions. However, high-fidelity three-dimensional environment models are expensive to obtain, whereas geometric inaccuracies in low-fidelity models can alter the detected multipath components (MPCs) and consequently distort received-power and delay-domain twin channel statistics. Building on the DeepRT ray-tracing framework, this paper proposes DeepRT-Cal, a geometry-aware cross-fidelity calibration framework that predicts high-fidelity twin channel statistics from low-fidelity geometry and RT features.The network encodes global link descriptors, masked low-fidelity MPC tokens, propagation-corridor geometry, and link-centered environmental objects. During training, detailed geometry is introduced as privileged information with structured masking, while deployment requires only low-fidelity geometry and low-fidelity RT information. A link-conditioned cross-attention module retrieves the environmental context relevant to each Tx--Rx link. The prediction heads estimate high-fidelity twin channel statistics, including total received power, RMS delay spread, mean excess delay, and a normalized power-weighted power-delay profile (PDP). Outdoor evaluation shows that, in an non-line of sight (NLoS) region, the method reduces power MAE from 16.80 to 3.88 dB and RMS delay-spread MAE from 304.89 to 98.19 ns. In a LoS-dominated region, power prediction improves, while RMS delay-spread accuracy remains comparable to direct RT.

papers.intro:
With the rapid evolution of the sixth-generation (6G) mobile communication networks, the digital twin channel (DTC) has emerged as a crucial enabling technology to bridge the physical and digital electromagnetic worlds [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. To realize a high-fidelity DTC, it is imperative to precisely model the complex interactions between propagating waves and the physical environment. Recent efforts toward Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) 6G standardization have also addressed integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) channel modeling [6] and radar cross section (RCS) modeling of typical targets [7], further motivating accurate modeling of radio interactions with the physical environment. In this context, ray tracing (RT) naturally aligns with the stringent requirements of DTCs. Relying on high-frequency asymptotic techniques, RT provides a deterministic computational framework that accurately replicates underlying electromagnetic propagation mechanisms, offering physically interpretable predictions and deterministic insights into wireless channels [4, 8, 9].

In this context, ray tracing (RT) naturally aligns with the stringent requirements of DTCs. Relying on high-frequency asymptotic techniques, RT provides a deterministic computational framework that accurately replicates underlying electromagnetic propagation mechanisms, offering physically interpretable predictions and deterministic insights into wireless channels [4, 8, 9].

The deployment of RT in 6G DTCs introduces two primary demands: computational speed and predictive precision. Aided by the exponential growth in modern computing power (e.g., graphics processing unit (GPU) acceleration) and the continuous proposal of novel RT acceleration algorithms, the historical bottleneck of computational speed has been progressively alleviated [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. However, the precision issue of RT remains largely unresolved. The accuracy of deterministic RT is heavily bounded by the fidelity of its input environment. One major source of error originates from the inaccuracy of electromagnetic material properties. Slight deviations in dielectric constant or conductivity can lead to significant distortions in channel feature calculations (e.g., reflection loss), and acquiring material parameters that perfectly match the real world remains highly challenging [16, 17, 18]. Another, and perhaps more severe, source of error is the geometric discrepancy in three-dimensional (3D) environment modeling. Currently, obtaining high-precision digital twin models (such as millimeter-level light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds) incurs prohibitive costs and is impractical for large-scale ubiquitous deployment [19, 20]. Conversely, when utilizing cost-effective, low-precision 3D maps (e.g., open-source OpenStreetMap (OSM) data), inherent topological errors—such as over-smoothed surfaces, displaced building boundaries, or missing fine structures—severely compromise the RT pathfinding process, which is strongly constrained by the geometric propagation mechanisms implemented by the solver [21]. These errors are not limited to small perturbations in path loss. They can change whether a path is visible, move the reflection or diffraction point, alter the propagation distance and interaction angle, or change the blockage relation between a transmitter (Tx) and a receiver (Rx). As a result, the low-fidelity solver may omit a valid path, introduce a path that is absent from the detailed scene, or produce a multipath component (MPC) with substantially different delay and power. The resulting low- and high-fidelity MPC sets can therefore differ in cardinality, topology, and delay-power distribution, even for the same Tx–Rx locations and radio settings. These differences propagate to several channel statistics: changes in reflection and blockage affect total received power, while changes in delayed energy affect root-mean-square (RMS) delay spread, mean excess delay, and the complete power-delay profile (PDP). This geometric degradation inevitably leads to the misalignment of multipath trajectories or even the complete loss of valid physical paths, motivating a channel-level cross-fidelity calibration method rather than a path-by-path correction.

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has developed rapidly, demonstrating formidable capabilities in solving complex, high-dimensional non-linear mapping problems. Naturally, researchers have begun exploring the integration of AI with RT to address its inherent limitations. Current literature on AI-assisted RT can be broadly categorized into two paradigms. The first category focuses on constructing “Surrogate Models” [22, 23, 24, 25]. These studies utilize deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or generative models, to learn the mapping from environment maps to channel characteristics (e.g., RadioUNet), thereby significantly accelerating the RT computational process [26, 27, 28, 29]. While these approaches effectively reduce computational overhead, the fundamental nature of surrogate models dictates a critical limitation: the “student” (the AI model) inherits the limitations of the “teacher” (the RT supervision target). Because these models are supervised entirely by the deterministic outputs of RT, they inherit all the inherent physical and geometric errors of the baseline simulator, offering speed at the expense of true physical fidelity.

Because these models are supervised entirely by the deterministic outputs of RT, they inherit all the inherent physical and geometric errors of the baseline simulator, offering speed at the expense of true physical fidelity.

The second category leverages the backpropagation characteristics of modern AI frameworks to perform end-to-end calibration of the electromagnetic parameters involved in RT calculations. A prominent representative of this approach is Nvidia’s Sionna RT, a differentiable RT platform [30]. Differentiable RT allows gradients to flow through geometric propagation paths, enabling the reverse optimization of material properties (such as relative permittivity and conductivity) using gradient descent by comparing the simulated channel impulse response (CIR) with real-world measurements [31]. However, material-parameter calibration can modify the response of paths already generated by the solver, but it cannot by itself restore a propagation path that is absent from the topology induced by the input geometry. If an MPC is entirely lost during the ray-finding phase due to missing topological details (e.g., an over-smoothed edge in a low-precision 3D model), fine-tuning material parameters cannot recover this missing physical path. Existing AI-assisted studies have considered RT acceleration, radio-map estimation, and channel super-resolution [32], but the compensation of geometry-induced changes in the MPC topology and delay-power statistics remains comparatively underexplored.

papers.title: Wake 5: A Python Framework for Solidity Testing, Fuzzing, and Static Analysis
papers.abstract: Smart-contract fuzzers differ by an order of magnitude in throughput and by design in how they construct inputs, yet published comparisons rarely separate the two. We present Wake 5, an open-source Python framework for Solidity testing, fuzzing and static analysis, and use it to locate the binding constraint of stateful smart-contract fuzzing. Wake 5 replaces the JSON-RPC connection to an external node with an in-process EVM (revm) and exposes its static analysis to language-model agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. On the Daedaluzz maze benchmark (153 reachable assertions, guard constants below 2^32), Wake 5 executes 29,931 transactions per second, on par with Foundry (30,186) and 11.5x faster than Echidna (2,600). In eight-hour campaigns, however, the three tools plateau at medians of 75, 71 and 70 assertions, and their union reaches 93. We show that Wake's integer generator places 51% of its probability mass below 2^32 and that, once shallow assertions are exhausted, the generator prior rather than throughput bounds every tool. A harness written by a language-model agent, which derives inputs with a constraint solver, reached all 153 assertions in each of five campaigns executed by Wake, in 33 to 79 minutes. A complementary ablation in an agentic audit of a production Go codebase found that static-analysis tools improved recall for none of three models, raised precision for all three, and increased language-model cost by up to 12.7%. We discuss correlated oracles and non-deterministic completion, and argue that the fuzzer's role is shifting from search to execution.

papers.intro:
Smart contracts on the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) [51] are immutable once deployed and directly custody value, which makes pre-deployment testing unusually consequential. A companion dataset of 135 decentralised-finance (DeFi) incidents from the first half of 2026 found that, among the 68 incidents with identified pre-incident audit history, 94% of reported losses came from attack paths outside every identified pre-incident audit scope [26]. Fuzzing is the dominant dynamic technique for finding such paths before an attacker does: Echidna [27], Foundry [23], Medusa [47], Harvey [54] and ItyFuzz [43] all generate transaction sequences and check assertions or invariants, and Daedaluzz [16, 53] was introduced to compare them on a common footing.

Two questions about these tools remain poorly separated in the literature. The first is architectural: does the execution engine matter? Python-based frameworks such as Brownie [20] and Ape [9] drive an external node over JSON-RPC, while Foundry and Echidna execute in-process; a study of eleven contract fuzzers found throughput and seed quality pivotal and a standalone EVM the main throughput lever, but left property-based tools such as Echidna and Foundry outside its scope [52]. The second is methodological: once a fuzzer is fast, what limits the bugs it finds? Coverage-guided greybox fuzzing [12] answers this for C programs, but stateful contracts with arithmetic guards over multi-transaction state behave differently, and a third participant has entered the workflow: language-model agents that write the harness [57, 55].

This paper describes Wake 5 and uses it to measure both questions. Wake is an open-source framework in which tests, fuzz harnesses and static analyses are written in Python against types generated from the Solidity compiler’s output [1]. The framework has been used in commercial security reviews since 2023 and its fuzz tests are credited with critical and high-severity findings in several public audit reports [2, 3, 5]. Wake 5 is the first release whose default execution engine is an EVM embedded in the Python process rather than an external node reached over a socket.

papers.title: SAFTAC: Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning of Open-Source LLMs for Analog Circuit Design
papers.abstract: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.

papers.intro:
Analog integrated circuits (IC), such as amplifiers, oscillators, and voltage regulators, are used to process electrical signals that are continuous in both time and amplitude. A typical process of circuit design for analog ICs first defines the circuit topological structure, then selects concrete device and component values, and finally uses SPICE Nagel and Pederson (1973) simulation to verify whether the circuit satisfies the performance specifications. This is a fundamentally difficult task because circuit topology, component value assignments, and circuit performance are tightly coupled, and analog circuit design must navigate trade-offs among often competing specifications. This contrasts with circuit design for digital ICs Blocklove et al. (2023); Chang et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023), where voltages can often be abstracted as binary values and correctness can be checked through discrete functional equivalence. Consequently, off-the-shelf general-purpose large language models (LLMs) struggle to reliably satisfy stringent specifications in analog circuit design tasks, as they are not trained to reason jointly over circuit topology design, device and component value assignment, and simulation-grounded performance constraints.

To address these challenges, we develop a simulation-grounded data curation and LLM fine-tuning pipeline for analog circuit design. We first construct a large-scale analog circuit design-task dataset through an automated data curation pipeline that transforms raw circuit sources into complete design tasks. Each task includes a textual description, target specifications, labeled I/O ports, a testbench, circuit load, and a reference netlist. The resulting dataset contains 8,626 design tasks across 10 common analog circuit types. Building on this dataset, we propose SAFTAC (Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Analog Circuit design), which combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT). The SFT stages progressively teach circuit-domain knowledge, component-level understanding, and simulation feedback-guided correction. The RFT stage further optimizes the model using rewards from a full circuit validation pipeline, including circuit topology check, Bayesian Optimization (BO)-based component sizing, and SPICE simulation. In addition to the standard netlist generation task, we include a simulation feedback-guided correction task, where the model revises failed netlists using rich diagnostic feedback from the validation pipeline. This enables the model to generate initial circuit designs and repair failed designs toward functional, specification-satisfying analog circuits.

papers.title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
papers.abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.

They provide an interaction-centered cue for downstream robot learning without requiring paired robot actions. Extraction is difficult because fingertips are small or occluded, background corners produce competing responses, and multiple hands and objects create association ambiguity. Changes in hand color and appearance, viewpoint, illumination, background, and camera setup further challenge transfer from limited point annotations.

papers.title: Provable State Estimation with Recurrent Models
papers.abstract: Estimating the state of a dynamical system from observations is a crucial task in robotics and control. Despite their empirical success, recurrent models often lack formal guarantees on convergence and robustness. We bridge this gap by analyzing these architectures from the perspective of nonlinear observer theory. By framing RNNs as a time-discretization of continuous latent dynamical systems (Neural ODEs), we demonstrate that enforcing a contraction condition on the latent flow guarantees the existence of a smooth, injective map of the true physical state into the latent space. We prove that this architecture acts as a tunable observer: by increasing a single scalar gain that scales the latent vector field, the estimation error can be driven to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of zero at an exponentially fast rate. We further establish quantitative bounds on the MLP complexity required to decode this latent state, and extend our formal guarantees to the discrete-time residual RNN implementation. We validate the theory on a real mobile robotic task, where a provably contracting model outperforms a vanilla GRU with substantially more stable training. We also report that unconstrained GRUs converge to contracting dynamics on this task, suggesting that contraction is an emergent property of well-trained sequence models.

papers.title: SafeOrchestrate: Runtime Checked Intent-Driven Orchestration for Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: Modern cyber physical systems (CPS) integrate heterogeneous sensors, actuators, controllers, and services, composed at runtime rather than at design time. Orchestrating such systems through natural language (NL) is attractive, but unconstrained large language model (LLM) tool use is risky because actions must respect device capabilities, runtime state, and safety constraints. We present Safe Orchestrate, a reference architecture for runtime checked, intent driven CPS orchestration. Given an NL intent, it derives atomic goals, generates a runtime checkable specification for each, grounds the specifications to device affordances, and verifies every candidate action against runtime state and safety constraints before execution. In a Web of Things (WoT) instantiation, the architecture produces Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) style specifications from the NL intent, grounds them to Thing Description (TD) affordances exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and checks candidate actions against satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) backed guardrails. We evaluate this instantiation on simulated smart home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks against a direct LLM to MCP baseline. Safe Orchestrate maintains 100% required action accuracy on every task and 100% MCP Execution Similarity (MCP ES) on all but one, where MCP ES is 92%. By contrast, the baseline degrades on multi device, event triggered, and ordered tasks, with MCP ES falling to 13%. These results suggest that combining LLM based specification generation with role aware grounding and runtime constraint checking improves reliability for open CPS orchestration without enriched TD annotations or planning domain expertise.

papers.intro:
Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are increasingly assembled from independently developed constituent systems (CSs), including sensors, actuators, controllers, and cloud services. When composed at runtime, these CSs can exhibit systems-of-systems (SoS) behavior that no individual CS provides [17, 3]. For example, a smart building can coordinate lighting, ventilation, and occupancy sensing; an agricultural setup can jointly react to temperature, humidity, and soil moisture; and an industrial cell can coordinate perception, manipulation, and material handling. Historically, such coordination was fixed at design time: developers hard-coded device pairings and rules, assuming that goals, participating devices, and failure modes were known in advance. Open SoS deployments break this assumption because new goals emerge and the set of available devices changes over time [21]. Composition must therefore be derived at runtime from the current deployment, available devices, and operator intent.

papers.title: Sensed but Not Told: Hidden Physiological Adaptation Shapes LLM Persuasion
papers.abstract: Wearable sensors, including those embedded in VR headsets, can provide LLM-based chatbots with physiological signals that users do not explicitly communicate. We tested whether such hidden input changes persuasion. In a $2\times2$ within-subjects study ($N=24$), a chatbot argued against participants' self-selected opinions with or without turn-level heart-rate and pupil-diameter features; sensing was disclosed halfway through the study. Before disclosure, sensing increased perceived persuasiveness by 1.42 points. Across the study, sensing was associated with a 0.57-point greater shift toward the chatbot's position and 3.20 times the odds of any movement toward it. Persuasiveness ratings were lower after disclosure, although disclosure was confounded with session order. Dialogue logs suggested a more declarative interaction style when sensing was on: chatbot replies contained question marks less often, and conversations contained fewer turns. These findings motivate making biosignal-driven adaptation inspectable and providing a genuinely non-sensed mode.

papers.title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
papers.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.

papers.intro:
Long-context language models now support context windows of hundreds of thousands of tokens (Achiam et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Whether these models actually use the information in such windows, however, remains an open question. Models often attend to the beginning and end of the input while neglecting the middle, a phenomenon known as “lost-in-the-middle” (Liu et al., 2024). Benchmarks designed to probe context utilization (Modarressi et al., 2025; Hsieh et al., 2024a) show that accuracy drops sharply as context grows, especially when the relevant evidence shares little surface overlap with the query. This paper therefore aims to improve how models use the information already in the context window, rather than to extend the window further.

Part of this utilization gap may stem from rotary position embedding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), the position encoding adopted by most modern LLMs. RoPE represents position as rotations in many two-dimensional planes, each with a distinct frequency. Over a long distance, the fast-rotating planes complete many full turns and no longer carry a consistent distance signal. Evidence far from the query is thus matched through fewer planes than nearby text. This long-range decay depends on the positional distance between tokens. Assigning relevant evidence a position closer to the query can therefore mitigate the decay without changing the input text.

Existing methods that target lost-in-the-middle fall short of intervening on RoPE in a query-aware manner. Input compression methods (Jiang et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023) delete low-importance tokens and thus discard graded relevance information. Attention reweighting methods (Zhang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024b; Guardieiro et al., 2025) strengthen attention to selected tokens, but only after RoPE has weakened the positional signal between distant tokens. RoPE-level methods (Zhang et al., 2024c; Jin et al., 2024; An et al., 2025) modify position encoding directly, yet apply the same remapping regardless of the query. A separate line of work shows that a few attention heads already attend to query-relevant spans in long inputs (Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). Such attention signals have been used to select KV cache entries (Li et al., 2024), filter input tokens (Shi et al., 2026), or re-rank documents (Zhang et al., 2025a), but always by deleting or reordering content. In short, no existing method uses the model’s own query relevance to reshape RoPE positions while keeping every token in place.

papers.title: Thermalization of coarse-grained variables in the Toda lattice: a numerical study
papers.abstract: We present here a numerical study of the Toda lattice Hamiltonian dynamics showing how, despite model integrability, it is possible to find many macroscopic observables which display standard equilibrium behavior. In particular, we study numerically the energy time correlation of certain coarse-grained variables, showing that it decays with either exponential or stretched exponential behaviour, thus indicating good thermalization properties. The spirit of our observation is complementary to that of standard Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou-like numerical experiments, in which the breaking of integrability is regarded as the key ingredient for relaxation to thermal equilibrium. The present communication corroborates, on the contrary, the view that integrability is not an obstacle to thermalization, provided that a sufficiently weak definition of the latter is accepted. In the Toda lattice we have introduced several kinds of coarse-grained variables, constructed with the purpose to maintain a thermodynamic relevance also for large system sizes, which all show good thermalization properties.

papers.title: Slow structures, fast degrees of freedom, and the morphology of chess openings
papers.abstract: Chess openings naturally separate into slow and fast degrees of freedom: pawns evolve through irreversible moves, whereas pieces can be rapidly reorganized within the resulting structure. We exploit this separation to construct a quantitative morphology of opening space. From a catalogue of 3810 named variations, 1749 reach a common depth of $N=10$ plies, corresponding to 619 distinct positions and only 435 joint pawn structures. We characterize these positions through observables measuring pawn commitment and spatial organization, blockade and tension, and piece activity and centralization. Their partial independence reveals a multidimensional opening space and in order to explore its structural organization, we construct a network whose nodes are distinct White pawn structures, connected when a single pawn move or capture transforms one into another. Remarkably, 139 of the 149 observed structures belong to a single connected component containing $98\%$ of all positions. This network exhibits a statistically significant modular organization, with eight communities whose representative structures correspond to familiar pawn formations. Rather than forming isolated categories, these formations emerge as distinct regions of a connected structural landscape. Our approach thus complements the traditional opening taxonomy by revealing similarities between differently named openings and providing a quantitative basis for comparing the positions they produce.

A central problem in statistical physics and complex-systems science is to identify effective variables that describe a system at a useful scale without retaining all of its microscopic information [29, 16, 1]. Such a reduction is particularly interesting in sequential systems, where present states retain traces of previous decisions and where different degrees of freedom evolve on different persistence timescales.

Chess provides a formidable setting for a quantitative study of complex sequential systems [17, 27], because its rules are fixed, the state space is large but precisely defined, and extensive databases make both trajectories and positions directly observable. One advantage is that, unlike several empirical complex systems, no hidden variables or measurement errors are required to define the microscopic configuration. Interestingly, the chess rules suggest a natural organizing principle, because pawn motion is irreversible: pawns move forward but cannot retreat. Every pawn advance therefore records a structural decision and progressively modifies the geometry available to the other pieces. This persistence of pawn structure has long been central to positional chess theory, from Steinitz’s emphasis on lasting pawn weaknesses and structural advantages [31] to modern classifications of recurring pawn formations [30, 13]. Knights, bishops, rooks, and queens can, by contrast, be rerouted and redeployed much more rapidly. This suggests a natural separation between a slow, history-bearing sector, defined primarily by the pawns, and a fast, rearrangeable sector, associated with piece organization. The separation is both dynamical and structural: the pawns form a slowly evolving background on which the faster piece degrees of freedom reorganize.

We first analyze these two sectors separately. For the pawns, we measure how much irreversible advancement has occurred, where it is located, and how the black and white pawn structures interact. We then examine the geometry of the set of realized pawn skeletons itself. For the pieces, we measure total activity and where that activity is directed. papers.title: An Empirical Study on Clustering-based Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for Regression Test Case Selection
papers.abstract:
Regression testing assesses whether software components that have already been developed and tested continue to work correctly after modifications. Ideally, regression testing re-executes the entire test suite after each modification, but this is infeasible in real-world scenarios because of the computational burden; therefore, optimized approaches, such as Test Case Selection, have been developed. The state of the art in regression testing optimization includes both classical approaches, such as Additional Greedy and DIV-GA, and quantum approaches, such as SelectQA, BootQA, and IGDec-QAOA. However, while the former incur high computational costs, the latter are constrained by the physical limitations of currently available quantum machines.
  This paper extends the evaluation of QAOA-TCS, our quantum approach for the test case selection problem. We thoroughly evaluate its performance, compare it with state-of-the-art classical and quantum approaches, and assess its robustness to quantum noise.
  The results show that QAOA-TCS outperforms state-of-the-art multi-objective approaches in most cases and maintains stable performance even under high noise levels. In the single-objective formulation, QAOA-based methods perform comparably. In terms of efficiency, our previous method based on quantum annealing, namely SelectQA, is the most efficient for large problems in the multi-objective formulation, whereas QAOA-TCS offers the best trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency in the single-objective formulation when run on realistic noisy simulators. However, such analysis is constrained by the different computational environments used to run the algorithms.

papers.intro:
In modern software development, software systems undergo continuous modifications and enhancements, particularly since the advent of Agile methodologies (Annosi et al., 2024; Meier and Kock, 2023). In this landscape, each modification could interfere with the proper behavior of already developed system components; hence, there is a strong need to continuously monitor software quality. To address this problem, regression testing (Yoo and Harman, 2012) verifies, after each developer modification, whether previously implemented and tested components still function as expected, and plays a key role. The ideal regression testing approach, also called retest-all, re-executes the entire regression test suite after each software modification; however, in real-world scenarios, it quickly becomes impractical (Rothermel and Harrold, 1998; Perrouin et al., 2012). Therefore, many Regression Test Suite Optimization (RTSO) methods have been proposed to drastically reduce the costs of regression testing, without losing its effectiveness in finding defects, either by reducing the size of the starting test suite according to specific strategies, or by finding an optimal execution order following some prioritization criteria (Yoo and Harman, 2007; Yoo and Harman, 2010; Yoo et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013; Panichella et al., 2014; Arrieta et al., 2019; Xue and Li, 2020). Above all, Test Case Selection (TCS) (Engström et al., 2010; Yoo and Harman, 2012) is one of the most adopted approaches, focusing on identifying a minimal subset of the initial regression suite to minimize overall regression testing cost while preserving effectiveness, as often measured by fault and statement coverage.

Although state-of-the-art classical strategies, such as Additional Greedy (Yoo and Harman, 2007) and DIV-GA (Panichella et al., 2014), have proven effective for solving TCS, their practical use is limited by their computational burden. Therefore, research has focused on alternatives that leverage the potential of quantum computing, such as superposition and entanglement (Hoare and Milner, 2005; Knight, 2018), to overcome the limitations of classical strategies in execution costs without sacrificing solution quality. Currently, such proposed strategies are: SelectQA (Trovato et al., 2024), BootQA (Wang et al., 2024b), and IGDec-QAOA (Wang et al., 2024a). The major limitation of the aforementioned approaches lies in their decomposition strategy; BootQA totally commits to random sampling to produce the sub-suites to optimize, resulting in unstable results; IGDec-QAOA relies on an impact-guided strategy, which does not take into account dependencies among the test cases; finally, SelectQA does not rely on a tailored decomposition strategy at all, thus worsening its efficiency.

papers.title: pESTO: Iterative p-greedy kernel regression with risk-driven Early STOpping
papers.abstract: Kernel-based greedy algorithms select suitable approximation nodes by minimizing point-wise error indicators, such as the power function; in this context, they are usually referred to as p-greedy approaches. In the presence of noisy data, deterministic criteria may fail, as the discrepancy between the true solution and its estimate is influenced by both approximation error and noise amplification, and the balance between the two is unknown. This study explicitly separates these two contributions, which are governed by the power function and a Lebesgue-type term, respectively. These bounds motivate the use of the Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE) as a proxy of the mean squared error, which in turn provides a principled and computable stopping criterion for the number of nodes to select in the p-greedy procedure. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively balances deterministic accuracy and statistical noise contributions.
papers.intro:
Given a set of measurements sampled at multivariate scattered points, a kernel-based greedy scheme partitions the data into a training set and a validation set. The training set is used to construct an initial coarse interpolant, which is then progressively refined by iteratively adding the most informative samples selected from the validation set according to a prescribed rule. Such selection rules may rely on residuals or on deterministic error indicators, such as the power function, that exclusively depends on the kernel and on the node locations. In the interpolation setting, the latter, namely the pp-greedy scheme, provides a reliable and well-established criterion for a priori node selection. However, when observations are affected by noise, relying solely on the power function may lead to suboptimal performances.

Kernel regression in the presence of noise has been extensively studied (see, e.g., (1, Chapter 15)). Likewise, greedy techniques for the corresponding problem have been considered [2]. However, to the best of our knowledge, a stopping rule for the respective greedy algorithms is still missing. Of course, the availability of a stopping criterion is of interest not only from a theoretical perspective, but also for computational efficiency. Typical stopping rules for kernel methods in the absence of noise can be based on the analysis of errors or residuals [3]. In the general case of iterative methods with noisy data, one can also consider the discrepancy principle introduced by Morozov [4], Generalized Cross Validation (GCV) [5], and risk-based criteria [6]. Among these methods, the Stein’s unbiased risk estimator (SURE) [7] has been employed as a data-driven criterion for parameter selection [8]. In the present work, we propose to employ such an estimator to identify the optimal iteration of greedy methods applied to kernel interpolation in the presence of noise. This is of interest, for instance, in combination with inverse problems for the purpose of image reconstruction [9].

The goal of the present work is to study error estimates for noisy data that can be used as the target quantity of iterative greedy methods. In particular, we show that a statistically equivalent derivation of the power-function error bound in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHSs) needs to account for the trade-off between approximation accuracy and noise amplification. These non-sharp bounds, involving the power function, a Lebesgue-type term, and a noise contribution, are not computable in practice. Indeed, they require the knowledge of the norm of exact function, while only noisy observations are available. This motivates the use of SURE in this context as a proxy for the Mean Squared Error (MSE). Building upon this characterization, the ppESTO algorithm, proposed in this paper, provides a principled stopping rule for the iterative greedy selection by balancing approximation error and statistical noise effects.

papers.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data
papers.abstract: In permutation tests with discrete data, especially in small samples, different permutations often yield the same test statistic. The resulting ties can make the test conservative and reduce power. This conservatism can be particularly pronounced for maximum statistics: permutations may have the same maximum but differ at other endpoints, so the remaining endpoint statistics are discarded. We develop two power improvements for closed permutation maxT tests by refining the treatment of ties. The first method uses a single uniform random variable shared across all local tests in the closed testing procedure. This shared-uniform construction maximizes the rejection probability of every elementary hypothesis among all ways of coordinating the same randomized local tests. It also preserves an exact linear step-down shortcut. The second method is the deterministic two-endpoint augmentation (tea) test, which uses the second-largest endpoint statistic to resolve ties in the maximum. This additional information can favour rejection under alternatives while preserving null validity, without auxiliary randomization. Its full closure admits an exact quadratic shortcut. More generally, augmentation using any fixed number of endpoint statistics admits an exact polynomial shortcut. Both procedures retain every rejection made by classical closed maxT procedures and provide strong finite-sample control of the family-wise error rate under intersection-null permutation invariance. In simulations with sparse binary outcomes, both methods improve power over classical closed maxT testing. When many endpoints are tested, the tea test also often outperforms shared-uniform randomization.

Conservatism can be particularly pronounced: permutations may share the same maximum while differing at other endpoints, so information in the remaining endpoint statistics is discarded.

One approach to reducing conservatism is the mid-pp method, which counts half the probability of a tie (Lancaster, 1961). However, it need not control the type I error at the nominal level (Agresti, 2013), so it does not generally provide the local validity required by closure. Randomization instead counts a uniformly random fraction of the tie probability and removes local conservatism while preserving validity (Tocher, 1950; Lehmann & Romano, 2005). Although randomized marginal pp-values have been studied in multiple testing (Habiger & Peña, 2011; Habiger, 2015), the coordination of auxiliary randomization across the local tests of closed permutation maxT procedures has not, to the best of our knowledge, been investigated.

papers.title: A Fast and Accurate Algorithm for the $p \to q$ Norm of Sparse Non-Negative Matrices
papers.abstract:
We present an algorithm that computes the $p \to q$ norm of a non-negative matrix with $s$ nonzero entries to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in time $\widetilde{O}(s^{3/2} \log (1/\varepsilon))$, for any $p \ge q \ge 1$. The fastest algorithm previously designed for this problem has running time $\widetilde{O}(s / \varepsilon)$ (Objois and Vladu, 2026), which is slower when high accuracy solutions are desired.
  Our algorithm employs a surprising application of Laplacian solvers inside an Interior Point Method (IPM). We formulate the problem as a linear optimization problem over a product of power cones, and show that the Newton updates of the IPM can be computed by solving a Laplacian system in a Schur complement after subtracting a rank-2 matrix.
  We also discuss an implementation of our algorithm, showing that it is practical and it outperforms optimized solvers such as MOSEK by factors of up to $20\times$ on a variety of tasks.

papers.title: Verification of Security Properties of Cryptographic Protocols
papers.abstract: Developing cryptographic protocols that are free from vulnerabilities is very challenging, as evidenced by numerous design flaws and implementation bugs in widely used protocols. Recent work has leveraged model checking to generate negative test cases, that is test cases that include the behavior of Dolev-Yao attacker. In this paper, we address the problem of analyzing execution traces produced by testing protocol implementations with such negative test cases. We propose a method for detecting violations of security properties by model-checking execution traces. Our approach employs a model checker based on DLTL, a Linear Temporal Logic with freeze operators, and supports automation of the testing process through pre- and post-processing steps. These steps, respectively, bridge the gap between different levels of abstraction and synthesize the results produced by the model checker.We present experimental results as a proof of concept for the feasibility of the proposed method.

papers.intro:
Developing cryptographic protocols free from vulnerabilities is very challenging. Many protocols have been repeatedly found to contain design flaws and implementation bugs [15]. Symbolic techniques have been successfully applied primarily to the verification of cryptographic protocols in their early stages enabling the identification of vulnerabilities exploitable by Dolev-Yao attacks [5], where the attacker has full control over the network. The main drawback of tools supporting symbolic analysis is their limited scalability [5], which can make the verification of real-world case studies extremely time-consuming.

Symbolic techniques have been successfully applied primarily to the verification of cryptographic protocols in their early stages enabling the identification of vulnerabilities exploitable by Dolev-Yao attacks [5], where the attacker has full control over the network. The main drawback of tools supporting symbolic analysis is their limited scalability [5], which can make the verification of real-world case studies extremely time-consuming.

At later stages of development, recent works have leveraged model checking to generate test cases for protocol implementations [11, 16]. In particular, in [11] a method is proposed for generating negative test cases, i.e., test cases that incorporate the Dolev-Yao intruder. A negative test case is automatically derived from counterexamples generated by model checking protocol specifications against security goals, such as secrecy and authentication.

At later stages of development, recent works have leveraged model checking to generate test cases for protocol implementations [11, 16]. In particular, in [11] a method is proposed for generating negative test cases, i.e., test cases that incorporate the Dolev-Yao intruder. A negative test case is automatically derived from counterexamples generated by model checking protocol specifications against security goals, such as secrecy and authentication.

In this paper, we build on [11] and take a step further by addressing the problem of analyzing execution traces produced by testing protocol implementations with such negative test cases. Specifically, we propose a method to determine whether the implementation pass or not a test case by verifying the execution traces against a security goal defined in the original protocol specification. This technique can serve as an alternative when symbolic techniques are impractical, for instance due to time constraints.

Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) is a formalism used to specify and reason about the behavior of systems over time, where properties are expressed along a single trace (a linear sequence of states or events). It introduces temporal operators such as X (neXt), F (Eventually), G (Globally), and U (Until) to describe how propositions evolve across future points in the trace [12].

Alur and Henzinger introduced Timed Propositional Temporal Logic (TPTL) [1], which augments LTL with freeze quantifiers, a mechanism that allows one to bind a variable to a state and subsequently compare these frozen state values with later states, within a temporal formula. This makes TPTL capable of expressing data-dependent temporal constraints, whereas standard LTL only reasons about Boolean propositions without memory of specific values. Thus, TPTL with freeze operators is strictly more expressive than classical LTL. DLTL logic [9] adopts the same perspective as TPTL, but adapting it to the case of finite traces, and also adding past operators.

papers.title: Talanov dynamics and chirp-controlled rogue-wave formation for the vector nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation
papers.abstract: We study the focusing vector nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, or Manakov system, for a pair of coupled initial conditions with compactly supported, concave parabolic density profiles and phases depending quadratically on the spatial coordinate. We focus on the natural class of self-similar solutions generated by such profiles, whose dispersionless evolution we refer to as Talanov dynamics. We extend the criterion for blow-up in finite time, first established for a single field, to the Manakov case. For arbitrary initial chirps in the two fields, we provide closed-form expressions for their evolution, and an explicit expression for the time of the gradient catastrophe, if it occurs, and we classify the effect of the coupling on the catastrophe. Depending on the initial chirps, the two fields may catastrophise, or relax, as each would if decoupled. However, coupling can also force the catastrophe in fields that would otherwise relax if decoupled. For identical initial supports, and in the presence of dispersion, we numerically show that the same dispersionless criterion determines, in the semiclassical regime, whether the fully dispersive solution relaxes or develops a rogue wave in each field, whose onset time is accurately predicted by the corresponding dispersionless catastrophe time, in direct analogy with the scalar case. As chirp and amplitude are relatively easy to control experimentally, we expect these results to be relevant to experiments in nonlinear optics and Bose-Einstein condensates, extending to coupled systems observations made for the scalar equation.

The vector NLS equation was introduced by Manakov [1] in the context of the self-focusing of electromagnetic waves of arbitrary polarisation, where it was shown to be integrable via the inverse scattering transform and its soliton solutions were constructed. Zakharov and Schulman [2] subsequently established that, up to rescaling, only three choices of the relative sign between the self- and cross-focusing coefficients preserve integrability, namely the defocusing, the mixed, and the focusing regime considered in this paper. Further families of exact soliton solutions, including the energy-redistributing collisions peculiar to the vector case, were obtained within the same inverse scattering framework [3, 4, 5]. In this paper we refer to system (1.1) as the vector NLS equation, but in the literature it is also commonly referred to as the Manakov system or the coupled NLS system.

Similarly to the scalar case, the vector NLS system is also deemed a universal model, as it emerges via multiscale reduction from a broad range of different, generically non-integrable, physical contexts. It was derived, prior to the proof of its integrability, as the natural envelope equation for two circularly polarised waves in an isotropic Kerr medium [7]. It arises as the effective envelope system of the physically realistic, non-integrable propagation equations of a birefringent optical fibre [8, 9], and it emerges from the coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations of a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate with matched scattering lengths [10]. More recently, a coupled-NLS-type system has been derived from a fluid-Maxwell model for two electromagnetic wavepackets of opposite circular polarisation co-propagating in a magnetised plasma [11]. Beyond these derivations, the vector NLS system finds direct application across a wide variety of further contexts: crossing sea states in fluid dynamics [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17], multi-component Bose-Einstein condensates [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23], polarisation dynamics in birefringent nonlinear optical fibres [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29], and the nonlinear coupling of electrostatic wavepackets in plasma physics [30, 31, 32, 33]. The magnetised, birefringent ionospheric plasma supports two co-propagating modes governed by a coupled NLS system [7, 11], and the initial data (1.2) may accordingly be regarded as describing a pair of parabolic radio beams interacting with the medium and with each other.
