The magnetised, birefringent ionospheric plasma supports two co-propagating modes governed by a coupled NLS system [7, 11], and the initial data (1.2) may accordingly be regarded as describing a pair of parabolic radio beams interacting with the medium and with each other.

papers.title: Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling
papers.abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. More importantly, DISCO yields a more faithful representation of the underlying data distribution and---crucially---enables accurate sampling from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers. This capability opens the door to principled and flexible probabilistic reasoning with score-based models.

Diffusion models currently define the state of the art in generative modeling, with remarkable success in image synthesis, molecular design, and protein structure generation [33, 41]. At their core, they arise from classical score matching [13] and its denoising variant [39], which learn the score function rather than the density itself. Classical score matching learns the score mainly near the data manifold, leaving low-density regions unconstrained, so that sampling trajectories are easily led astray. Diffusion-based models [30, 33] mitigate this by progressively broadening the region where the score is learned and sampling then iteratively denoises from high to low noise.

However, the diffusion mechanism requires learning an entire family of score vector fields, one for each noise level. This design choice has important consequences for principled probabilistic inference—the hallmark of probability theory as a rigorous framework for reasoning under uncertainty [14, 27], which ultimately reduces to two fundamental operations: marginalization and conditioning [9]. In the context of score-based generative models this translates into the question whether faithful samples can be drawn from the model’s marginals and conditionals. While drawing from marginals is trivial—simply discard variables from joint samples—drawing from conditionals requires conditioning the entire diffusion process, which is generally intractable. Existing approaches rely on ad-hoc heuristics [33, 12, 17] or on particle-based methods [42], which are asymptotically exact but can be difficult to tune in practice. As demonstrated in Figure 1, conditional samples of these methods are often substantially biased—even on elementary toy problems like GMMs—revealing the brittleness of diffusion-based probabilistic reasoning.

papers.title: Plus Constructions and Canonical Induction for Green Categories
papers.abstract: We develop canonical induction for Green categories associated with Mackey systems. We establish a change-of-rings framework in which the lower-plus and upper-plus constructions are realized by induction and coinduction of modules. The two plus adjunctions yield the mark morphism, and, when the relevant group orders are invertible in the coefficient ring, M\"obius inversion gives an explicit inverse. Using the resulting linearization and tom Dieck maps, we construct a canonical induction map, give an explicit formula for it, and characterize when it is a right inverse of linearization. In the classical setting of Mackey functors, our construction and splitting criterion recover Boltje's results.
papers.intro:
Brauer’s induction theorem states that every complex character of a finite group can be expressed as an integral linear combination of characters induced from linear characters of elementary subgroups. Boltje [Bol98] developed canonical induction in the general setting of Mackey functors. In this framework, a Mackey functor MM plays the role of the character ring, while the restriction functor AA plays the role of the linear characters. Unlike MM, the functor AA is equipped with restriction maps but not induction maps. The lower-plus construction produces a Mackey functor A+A_{+} from AA, together with an induction morphism A+→MA_{+}\to M. Canonical induction seeks a restriction-compatible section to this morphism, and Boltje established criteria for when such a splitting exists. The upper-plus construction provides a complementary construction A+A^{+}, related to A+A_{+} by the mark morphism A+→A+A_{+}\to A^{+}. This relationship plays a central role in constructing canonical induction formulas.

papers.title: Robust Deep Prototype Classifiers via Lipschitz Training
papers.abstract: Robustness and interpretability are interrelated and desirable properties of machine learning models. A model that changes its prediction under imperceptible perturbations behaves inconsistently with human-recognizable features and, hence, is not interpretable. Prototype-based classifiers such as Generalized Learning Vector Quantization address both at once. They are interpretable by construction because they make the decision by comparing the input to the prototypical example; and their hypothesis margin yields a closed form robustness certificate. However, on high-dimensional data, these shallow models need deep embedding networks to achieve high accuracy, and this voids the robustness certificate. The margin is a statement about distances in the embedding space, and an unconstrained network can map an arbitrarily small input perturbation to arbitrarily large attacks in the embedding space. We close this gap with a theorem: if the embedding network is locally L-Lipschitz around a point, and the classifier is {\epsilon}-robust around its embedding, then the full model is {\epsilon}/L-robust in the input space. Based on this, we propose a Lipschitz training scheme to achieve L-Lipschitz properties for embedding networks. We evaluate three classification heads (linear, linear Support Vector Machine, and GLVQ) crossed with two embedding networks (standard and Lipschitz-constrained) on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenette-160, under FGS, PGD and C\&W attacks. The evaluation results show that combining a prototype-based head with a Lipschitz-constrained embedding provides the strongest robustness. This suggests that the Lipschitz constraint provides an additional robustness benefit in addition to the advantage provided by the prototype-based head. Since the Lipschitz constraint is enforced by sampling rather than by construction, the reported robustness is empirical rather than certified.

papers.intro:
Machine learning systems have achieved remarkable breakthroughs in recent years, enabling applications across a wide range of domains, including medical imaging, computer vision, autonomous driving, and security monitoring. In these safety-critical applications, erroneous predictions or decisions can have potentially catastrophic consequences [59]. Therefore, such applications demand not only accurate predictions but robustness and interpretability [4, 18]; robust in the sense that decisions should remain stable under small changes in the input that a human would consider insignificant [45, 16, 52]; and interpretable in the sense that users should be able to understand why a particular decision was made [19, 51, 2], to assess the system before deployment and to diagnose potential failures afterwards. High accuracy on a test set alone does not guarantee either of these properties.

In these safety-critical applications, erroneous predictions or decisions can have potentially catastrophic consequences [59]. Therefore, such applications demand not only accurate predictions but robustness and interpretability [4, 18]; robust in the sense that decisions should remain stable under small changes in the input that a human would consider insignificant [45, 16, 52]; and interpretable in the sense that users should be able to understand why a particular decision was made [19, 51, 2], to assess the system before deployment and to diagnose potential failures afterwards. High accuracy on a test set alone does not guarantee either of these properties.

Szegedy et al. [45] were among the first to demonstrate this gap. They showed that small, often imperceptible changes to the input can completely change a network’s prediction, and that such changes often transfer between independently trained models. Over the past decade, researchers have confirmed that even models with excellent accuracy on clean data can be reduced to near-zero accuracy under white-box attacks [16, 31, 5]. Vulnerability to adversarial attacks can also indicate a lack of interpretability, as the model may rely on features that are not meaningful or recognizable to humans. Therefore, robustness and interpretability are closely connected rather than being distinct goals. Both assess whether the model makes decisions based on features that humans can understand and recognize. This connection is the main focus of this paper.

Two main defense approaches (adversarial training and Lipschitz-based methods) have been proposed in the literature, each with its own strengths and drawbacks. Adversarial training adds adversarial examples into the training data and remains the most effective empirical defense [31, 57]. However, this approach requires an inner optimization at every training step, trades clean accuracy for robustness [46, 57], and provides no formal guarantees: robustness is only certified against the attacks that were actually tested. Lipschitz-based methods, on the other hand, bound how much the model can amplify input differences, providing an attack-independent guarantee [13, 48, 22]. Yet a Lipschitz bound alone is not a defense. In fact, the most Lipschitz-stable model is the constant function, which is useless for prediction [60]. Therefore, we propose to combine a Lipschitz constraint for a deep embedding network with the robustness guarantees of shallow classification models.

Prototype-based classifiers are such intrinsically robust classification models—and they additionally offer interpretability as a bonus. A nearest prototype classifier assigns an input to the class of its closest prototype. Thus, its decisions are interpretable as long as the prototypes themselves are interpretable [2, 11]. Since the decision depends solely on distances to a fixed set of prototypes, the distance to the decision boundary can be calculated in closed form. This distance, known as the hypothesis margin [8], was originally introduced to derive generalization bounds for Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ)—a specific family of prototype-based classifiers [8, 20]. Saralajew et al. [39] later showed that it also yields an adversarial robustness guarantee. Subsequent work has tightened these bounds further and has shown that prototype classifiers can be competitive with certified neural networks [49], while empirical studies report that GLVQ models are robust even before any explicit certification [38].

The challenge, however, is that LVQ operates on distances in the input space, where the Euclidean distance is not meaningful for image data [25]. The common solution is a hybrid approach: train a deep network ϕ\phi that embeds inputs nonlinearly, and then use prototype-based decisions in this embedding space [7, 30, 44]. While this approach improves accuracy, it implicitly compromises the formal robustness guarantee. The certificate of a nearest prototype classifier is only valid in the space where the prototypes live. However, an unconstrained embedding network can map an arbitrarily small input change to an arbitrarily large change in the embedding space [26]. Therefore, a certified radius in the embedding space does not provide information regarding robustness in the original input space—unless we have a guarantee that distances in the embedding space are bounded by distances in the input space, which is precisely what a Lipschitz constraint does. As illustrated in Figure 1 (compare the top-left and top-right panels), without a Lipschitz constraint, small changes in the input space can result in large changes in the embedding space, invalidating the robustness guarantee.

In more detail, our main contributions are: • A composition theorem (Theorem 1) that transfers local ϵ\epsilon-robustness guarantees in the embedding space to the input space using LL-Lipschitz continuity of the deep embedding network, yielding a radius of ϵ/L\epsilon/L around each correctly classified point. • A Lipschitz loss and corresponding training scheme which enhances the Lipschitz continuity of deep embedding networks by sampling Gaussian noise around the training data during training and punishes violations of the desired Lipschitz constant LL. Because sampling Gaussian noise is cheap, this is substantially cheaper than adversarial training [31] and less restrictive than a global Lipschitz bound. • An evaluation on three data sets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenette-160) using three classifiers (linear, linear SVM, and GLVQ) and two embedding networks (standard and Lipschitz-constrained) under three adversarial attacks (FGSM, PGD, and C&W)

papers.title: The exceptional set of Goldbach numbers among polynomial values
papers.abstract: Let $\phi$ be a fixed polynomial with integer coefficients, positive leading coefficient and degree $k\geq2$. We prove that the values $2\phi(n)$, $1\leq n\leq N$, can be written as the sum of two primes, apart from at most $N^{\alpha_k+o(1)}$ exceptional indices, where $\alpha_k<1$. For quadratic polynomials the exponent is $1/2$, for cubic polynomials $5/8$, for quartic polynomials $3/4$, and for $k>4$ it is $1-1/(k+1)$. The proof combines a fourth-moment estimate over primes with mean-value estimates over arbitrary subsets of polynomial sequences.

papers.title: A tractable transition function for the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection via gamma duality
papers.abstract: The transition function of the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection is a fundamental object for non-neutral evolutionary modelling and likelihood-based inference, but, unlike in the neutral case, existing representations are impractical or inefficient. Spectral approaches rely on truncation levels that grow with selection strength and the number of alleles, thus leading to rapidly increasing computational costs, while existing duality-based expansions lead to multi-type dual processes whose transition probabilities involve intractable normalising constants. In this paper we obtain a new transition-function representation for the multi-allelic Wright-Fisher diffusion with parent-independent mutation and genic selection that makes transition-law evaluation and simulation practically feasible in regimes where existing methods are costly or unavailable. The key tool is a new gamma duality, obtained by augmenting classical polynomial duality by an exponential tilting and yields a multivariate birth-death dual with fully explicit infinitesimal rates and an entrance-boundary construction. This is used to express the Wright-Fisher transition law as an explicit mixture of standard Dirichlet components, with mixing weights obtained from the dual started from its entrance boundary. We characterise the dual stationary distribution and its small-time behaviour, and develop practical and efficient sampling procedures for both transition and stationary laws, including a fast approximate stationary sampler with explicit error control. Numerical experiments illustrate substantial runtime gains over specialised methods in regimes where they apply, while our approach remains applicable for arbitrary numbers of alleles and selection coefficients.

papers.intro:
The Wright–Fisher (WF) diffusion arises as a scaling limit of finite-population Markov chains, including the WF and Moran models and, more generally, Cannings-type models. It provides a canonical model for the evolution of allele frequencies in a population under random genetic drift, mutation, and selection (Ethier and Kurtz, 1986, Ch. 10), and also appears in a range of other applied fields, including econometrics and mathematical finance (Gourieroux and Jasiak, 2006; Larsen and Sørensen, 2007; Ackerer et al., 2018; Arrouy et al., 2022), game theory (Chen, 2018), topic modelling (Perrone et al., 2017), Bayesian nonparametric statistics (Mena and Ruggiero, 2016), opinion formation (Chen et al., 2016; Furioli et al., 2017), and models of neuronal activity (D’Onofrio et al., 2024). See also Pal (2013); Costantini et al. (2017); Garcia-Pareja et al. (2021); González Casanova and Spanò (2018); Cordero et al. (2025) for recent work extending the classical WF diffusion.

See also Pal (2013); Costantini et al. (2017); Garcia-Pareja et al. (2021); González Casanova and Spanò (2018); Cordero et al. (2025) for recent work extending the classical WF diffusion.

The primary domain of application is in population genetics, where the relative importance of drift, mutation, and selection in driving evolution has long been a central question (Ewens, 2004). This focus naturally leads to inferring evolutionary forces from discretely observed allele-frequency time series, for which the WF diffusion has become a standard workhorse (Bollback et al., 2008; Steinrücken et al., 2014; Schraiber et al., 2016; He et al., 2020; Tataru et al., 2017; Buzbas and Joyce, 2009). Parameter estimation in such settings requires the repeated evaluation of, or sampling from, transition laws across multiple time points and parameter values, both within likelihood-based inference (including diffusion-driven hidden Markov models), as well as in simulation-based approaches such as exact data augmentation schemes and particle filters. Therefore, the absence of a tractable transition function representation (and consequently of an efficient sampler with controlled error) constitutes a key computational bottleneck in this regard.

For the neutral WF diffusion (i.e., in the absence of selection), the identification of the transition function dates back to Kimura’s classical spectral expansions, summarized in Kimura (1964), which express the transition density in terms of an orthogonal polynomial family of eigenfunctions, with Griffiths (1979) extending these results to incorporate recurrent mutation. Later, a probabilistic series expansion was derived, expressing the transition density as an infinite mixture of Dirichlet distributions (Griffiths, 1980; Griffiths and Li, 1983; Tavaré, 1984). See also Feng et al. (2011); Griffiths et al. (2025) for analogous representations in closely related infinite-dimensional settings. The spectral and probabilistic representations are equivalent (Griffiths and Spanò, 2010), but the Dirichlet-mixture form is particularly appealing computationally, as it enables exact simulation routines for neutral WF paths and bridges (Griffiths and Li, 1983; Jenkins and Spanò, 2017; Sant et al., 2023; Sant et al., 2025), thereby enabling likelihood-based inference for discretely observed diffusions and diffusion-driven hidden Markov models.

See also Feng et al. (2011); Griffiths et al. (2025) for analogous representations in closely related infinite-dimensional settings. The spectral and probabilistic representations are equivalent (Griffiths and Spanò, 2010), but the Dirichlet-mixture form is particularly appealing computationally, as it enables exact simulation routines for neutral WF paths and bridges (Griffiths and Li, 1983; Jenkins and Spanò, 2017; Sant et al., 2023; Sant et al., 2025), thereby enabling likelihood-based inference for discretely observed diffusions and diffusion-driven hidden Markov models.

By contrast, obtaining a workable transition-function representation for the non-neutral WF diffusion is substantially more challenging. Classical spectral approaches lead to eigenfunctions which are typically available only through special function representations instead of multivariate polynomials (Kimura, 1955). Probabilistic arguments still yield an exact mixture expansion in terms of exponentially tilted Dirichlet components (Barbour et al., 2000), but the associated multi-type birth-death dual has state-dependent rates involving intractable normalising constants, a difficulty that propagates to likelihood evaluation and reduces its practical applicability (Donnelly et al., 2001; Buzbas and Joyce, 2009). Alternatively, one can suitably truncate the spectral representation obtained by considering an exponentially tilted version of the neutral basis eigenfunctions (Song and Steinrücken, 2012; Steinrücken et al., 2013), which enables likelihood methods (Steinrücken et al., 2014) to be used (including the diploid selection case). However, the computational cost grows rapidly with the number of alleles and especially with the selection strength, as the truncation level required for accuracy increases accordingly. Exact transition-law simulation via retrospective rejection sampling provides a viable alternative (Schraiber et al., 2013; Jenkins and Spanò, 2017), but acceptance rates deteriorate as either the magnitude of selection or the time horizon increases, with current implementations being available only in the one-dimensional setting (Sant et al., 2023).

The key tool enabling this representation is a new gamma duality for the WF diffusion with selection. Duality (Jansen and Kurt, 2014) is pervasive in WF-type models and links allele-frequency diffusions to genealogical or particle systems, yielding moment identities and sampling representations (Ethier and Kurtz, 1986; Möhle, 1999; Etheridge and Griffiths, 2009; Etheridge et al., 2010; Carinci et al., 2015; González Casanova and Spanò, 2018) and lending itself to inference for certain hidden Markov models (Papaspiliopoulos and Ruggiero, 2014; Ascolani et al., 2023; Kon Kam King et al., 2024; Dalla Pria et al., 2026). In particular, Barbour et al. (2000) exploit a polynomial moment duality to derive a transition-function expansion in the non-neutral case, but the resulting dual dynamics involve ratios of normalising constants that are not tractable to evaluate or simulate from. Since the dual dynamics are straightforward to simulate, this removes the normalising-constant bottleneck and allows us to build practical and efficient samplers for both transition and stationary laws.

papers.title: Levenshtein-type bounds for $(a,b)$-avoiding spherical codes
papers.abstract: We develop a Levenshtein-type linear programming framework (for maximal $s$-codes and for minimal energy) for $(a,b)$-avoiding spherical codes, that is, codes whose inner products between distinct points avoid $(a,b)$. We introduce and investigate signed measures that are positive definite up to an appropriate degree and yield stationary auxiliary linear programming polynomials and exact quadrature formulas. We give explicit conditions for positivity of the quadrature weights and sufficient Krein-type conditions for nonnegative Gegenbauer coefficients (positive definiteness of the candidate optimal linear programming polynomials). Under these hypotheses and suitable node-location assumptions, the resulting cardinality bounds are optimal within the corresponding degree restriction and unique under natural nondegeneracy conditions. Under proper conditions on the quadrature nodes, we obtain universal lower energy bounds by utilizing Hermite interpolants as polynomial solutions of the respective linear program. Common test functions characterize optimality in the full polynomial linear programs under mild additional assumptions.

papers.intro:
Bounds for the cardinality and energy of finite point sets on spheres are closely related problems in discrete geometry. The linear programming method of Delsarte, Goethals, and Seidel [24] (see also [6, Chapter 5], [21, Chapter 9], [25, Chapter 2], [29]) converts restrictions on pairwise inner products into inequalities for Gegenbauer expansions. Levenshtein’s bounds [33] (see also [34, 35, 36]) organize this method into families of auxiliary polynomials associated with orthogonal polynomials and positive quadrature formulas. These quadratures explain both the quality of the bounds (cf. [36, Theorem 5.39]) and their optimality among auxiliary polynomials of specified degrees (cf. [8, Theorem 3.1], [36, Theorem 5.47]).

papers.title: Finite-sample Calibration Guarantees for Binary Segmentation
papers.abstract: Machine learning based segmentation models are frequently miscalibrated, producing for each pixel a label prediction whose associated confidence does not accurately reflect the true underlying probability. This limitation is particularly critical in high-stakes applications such as medical image segmentation. Although several calibration methods have been proposed, only a small subset of them provides theoretical guarantees on the calibration error, i.e., they do not typically ensure that, with high probability, the model exhibits a low calibration error. In this work, we develop a post-hoc calibration method for which formal calibration guarantees can be established. To achieve this, we derive from standard concentration inequalities an improved theoretical bound that explicitly accounts for the spatial dependence inherent in binary segmentation outputs. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed calibrator satisfies the derived guarantee and outperforms existing post-hoc calibration approaches.

papers.intro:
The calibration of a segmentation model is a fundamental task in machine learning that needs to be addressed in order to align the predicted confidence of a model with the true reliability of its prediction. It is essential to obtain reliable models for real-world applications. In the context of deep learning, the confidence of a model refers to the probability it assigns to its predicted output. Ideally, this confidence should faithfully reflect the true likelihood of correctness. However, modern neural networks tend to be overconfident, which means that their predicted confidence scores are poorly aligned with the actual accuracy (Guo et al., 2017; Ovadia et al., 2019). This misalignment becomes particularly crucial in critical-domain applications such as medical image segmentation, where erroneous predictions can have severe consequences. In such settings, a miscalibrated model may assign high confidence to incorrect segmentations, leading practitioners to place unwarranted trust in flawed outputs. In contrast, a well-calibrated model ensures that a predicted confidence of, say, 90% corresponds in the long run to a true correctness rate of approximately 90% (Dawid, 1982).

In contrast, a well-calibrated model ensures that a predicted confidence of, say, 90% corresponds in the long run to a true correctness rate of approximately 90% (Dawid, 1982).

The calibration problem has been extensively studied, and existing approaches can broadly be categorized into three groups (Wang et al., 2023). Post-hoc calibration methods operate after training, adjusting the model’s output probabilities without modifying its parameters. Classical techniques include Platt scaling (Platt and others, 1999), Temperature Scaling (Guo et al., 2017), Dirichlet calibration (Kull et al., 2019), Histogram Binning (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2001), Meta-cal (Ma and Blaschko, 2021), and Isotonic Regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002). Although originally introduced for classification, these methods can be applied to segmentation by treating each pixel independently. Moreover, there are also spatially aware extensions, such as (Ding et al., 2021; Rousseau et al., 2025; Küppers et al., 2022). The second group, Train-time calibration, has also been widely explored. Mixup (Zhang et al., 2018), CutMix (Yun et al., 2019), and label smoothing (Szegedy et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2019) regularize confidence by exposing the model to soft or interpolated targets. This group also includes methods that modify the training loss to penalize miscalibration: representative examples in the classification setting include Focal Loss (Lin et al., 2017), FLSD (Mukhoti et al., 2020), MMCE (Kumar et al., 2018), and DECE (Bohdal et al., 2023), all of which encourage the model to reduce overconfidence while preserving discriminative performance. Several approaches have also been developed specifically for segmentation tasks, such as MDCA (Hebbalaguppe et al., 2022), as well as methods tailored to the medical imaging domain (Barfoot et al., 2024; Barfoot et al., 2026; Murugesan et al., 2025; Murugesan et al., 2023). The third group of calibration approaches are uncertainty estimation methods, which includes Monte Carlo dropout techniques (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016; Kendall and Gal, 2017) and Deep Ensemble Networks (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Mehrtash et al., 2020). However, these methods, rather than recalibrating the model, primarily identify and highlight regions of high uncertainty.

papers.title: Ensemble Individual Mode Frequency Modeling of Kepler Giants - Extending the IACgrid towards the red-giant branch
papers.abstract: Precise stellar parameters, in particular ages, are vital for understanding the formation and history of the Milky Way. Usually, this is achieved by fitting stellar evolution models to observational constraints such as spectroscopic and astrometric parameters. Adding global asteroseismic properties to the classical parameters (global seismic modeling) breaks some degeneracies and improves the results. However, this approach has its limitations, with red-giant random age uncertainties usually $\sim$ 20-50%, and often lacking proper quantification of the systematics. We aim to extend seismic modeling to include individual mode frequencies for red-giant branch stars, increasing the number of evolved solar-like oscillators with precise stellar parameters (ages, masses, and radii), and allowing us to quantify the systematics in global seismic modeling. We developed a grid of stellar evolutionary models and computed the individual oscillation frequencies, including a figure of merit to find the best-fitting model. We validate our methodology on a sample of red giants with individual frequency modeling from the literature, finding our masses, radii, and ages in close agreement. We then apply our method to around 100 Kepler red-giant branch stars of near-solar mass and metallicity, which previously have only been modeled with global seismic parameters. We obtain random average uncertainties of 3.4%, 1.3%, and 13.2%, for stellar masses, radii, and ages, respectively. We find that ages from individual mode frequency modeling are significantly, 14% on average, larger than those from global seismic mass-constrained modeling. The modeled luminosities agree within 1.0% with those derived from Gaia parallaxes. We conclude that modeling individual mode frequencies improves age precision by a factor of two for red-giant branch stars, providing stronger constraints for galactic archaeology.

papers.intro:
Unlocking the evolutionary history and origins of our Galaxy fundamentally depends on deriving precise stellar properties, in particular stellar ages (Freeman and Bland-Hawthorn 2002; Gallart et al. 2019, e.g.). However, stellar ages are only inferable from modeling age-dependent observables (Soderblom 2010). Isochrone fitting long served as a standard approach for estimating stellar ages across evolutionary stages; however, with varying precision. While for sub-giant stars close to the main-sequence turnoff, it provides reasonable precision (Godoy-Rivera et al. 2021), it fails to deliver that for main-sequence (MS) and red-giant branch (RGB) stars, where typical relative age uncertainties with this approach are typically 30-50 % (Casagrande et al. 2016). Recently, space missions such as the NASA Kepler mission (Borucki et al. 2010) and the NASA Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (Ricker et al. 2014, TESS;), have provided photometric data that allowed us to obtain precise asteroseismic parameters from observables for ∼\sim10510^{5} stars on the MS and RGB presenting solar-like oscillations (Yu et al. 2018; Mackereth et al. 2021; Mathur et al. 2022; Hatt et al. 2024; Lund et al. 2024; Hon et al. 2024; Nielsen et al. 2025; Hookway et al. 2025; Grusnis et al. 2025, e.g.,). These precise asteroseismic datasets, combined with advancements in stellar evolutionary modeling, enable a further, more precise method for age determination of MS and RGB stars: asteroseismic modeling. Ages derived from asteroseismic modeling have already proven advantageous for Galactic studies (Miglio et al. 2021, e.g.,).

Generally, asteroseismic modeling combines spectroscopic and seismic observables to determine stellar masses, radii, and ages. Two distinct approaches are used: fitting global seismic parameters (e.g., the large frequency separation, Δ​ν\Delta\nu, and the frequency of maximum oscillation νmax\nu_{\rm max}), or fitting individual mode frequencies. The global seismic modeling approach has been applied successfully to several thousand MS and RGB stars, in particular thanks to projects such as the third iteration of the Apache Point Observatory Kepler Asteroseismic Science Consortium collaboration (Pinsonneault et al. 2025, APOKASC-3;). It is especially powerful when combined with constraints from binary systems (Murphy et al. 2021; Grossmann et al. 2025; Schimak et al. 2026), globular clusters (Moser et al. 2023; Howell et al. 2024, e.g.) or open clusters (Brogaard et al. 2023). However, when applied to single field stars without further constraints available, it is usually limited to a precision of ≈5%\approx 5\,\% in mass and ≈20%\approx 20\,\% in age. Furthermore, global asteroseismic age estimations are known to have systematic biases (Tayar and Joyce 2025, e.g.), in particular in certain parameter ranges, such as in the low metallicity regime (Epstein et al. 2014) or in binary systems due to mass loss (Mazzi et al. 2025).

papers.title: The small ball problem for the Brownian sheet: sharp bounds via entropy numbers in $L_\infty$
papers.abstract: We settle the uniform small deviation conjecture for the Brownian sheet in every dimension $d\ge2$, namely, that the logarithmic exponent is $2d-1$. Our proof proceeds through sharp entropy and Kolmogorov estimates for the associated anchored mixed Sobolev embedding in the uniform norm. Their connection to small deviations is known from the Kuelbs--Li theorem. To establish the entropy estimates, the key is a probabilistic small ball inequality for smooth tensor product atoms whose exceptional set has Gaussian measure exponentially small in the number of atoms. Its proof combines a count of dyadic rectangles with tools from probability, in particular Ehrhard's Gaussian Brunn--Minkowski inequality. This also yields sharp entropy and Kolmogorov number estimates for embeddings of periodic mixed Sobolev, Besov and Nikol'skii classes with smoothness $r>1/2$ in $L_\infty$. Finally, we extend our results to fractional and integrated Brownian sheets.

papers.title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
papers.abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.
papers.intro:
Contract review systems read documents authored by an adversarial counterparty. Unlike the chat setting that prompt guards were built for, the untrusted text is the task input: the legal contract authored by a counterparty. It is long, and it is dense with legitimate directive language that may be aimed at human parties or at AI reviewers that have grown in popularity. Recent and concurrent work evaluates prompt injection guards on domains with unique structure, such as résumés (Zhang et al., 2026; Augey et al., 2026) and agentic workflows (Liu, 2026). No published false positive rate exists for prompt injection guards on legal contracts, which leaves open the question: how well do guards defend against contract-borne injections?

We make the following contributions: 1. A taxonomy of legal-specific indirect prompt injections (§3). We characterize a taxonomy of statements that may influence automated legal review, some of which differ from traditional prompt injections. 2. A new challenge setting for prompt guards (§4). We show a specialized use case for which eleven leading prompt guards have unusably high false positive rates or low recall. We release a taxonomy-structured benchmark of contract-borne injection and matched benign control strings that are hand-written, factorially generated, and model-generated with independent audit, along with insertion manifests that constructed injected documents from publicly available legal contracts. 3. Analysis of general and model-specific failure modes (§5). We find that detection tracks the instruction’s register, not its function, and a telltale addressee cue runs backwards in more than half of the guards. We also show that some models’ flagging is keyed on narrow phrasing or even input length. 4. A cost-efficient cascaded LLM detector (§6). A prompted frontier LLM is near the ceiling on the threat model that guards are formulated for, and makes appreciable progress defending against a threat that prompt guards cannot see. A mid-tier model also outperforms all guards, and the two can be combined in a cascade (Fig. 1) that achieves near-frontier performance at less than a sixth of the cost.

papers.title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recommendation systems often enter a new serving window before enough outcomes are available to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. At this scale, existing fine-tuning and meta-learning methods still estimate target-specific updates from extremely sparse feedback, leaving the update direction weakly identified. SAGE-PAIR instead transfers a source-supported residual correction space and only calibrates this space using target outcomes. We introduce SAGE-PAIR, a staged adapter that pretrains a low-dimensional global residual on an adjacent source period and adds a soft router over residual experts conditioned on source user profiles. Target feedback then calibrates this residual state rather than relearning the recommender. On a locked test split of KuaiSAR-v2, SAGE-PAIR (Full) achieves a 1.77% relative improvement in NDCG@10, while a core-protocol comparison shows a further 0.25% gain from routed experts beyond source-pretrained PAIR. Matched source-pretrained LoRA and Adapter-Tuning baselines remain near the source model, supporting the need for a different adaptation space. Thus, SAGE-PAIR improves ranking quality with millisecond-scale adaptation and inference costs. Sparse-feedback adaptation is fundamentally governed by the identifiability of the update space rather than by label count alone. Source pretraining supplies estimable correction directions for scarce labels, while user-conditioned routing contributes a consistent, differentiated cross-user correction on top of the global correction. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SAGE-PAIR-610E/.

papers.intro:
Recommendation systems are frequently updated on a rolling schedule, but the evidence needed for a reliable update arrives more slowly than the serving schedule Koren (2009); Wang et al. (2019). In particular, the shift from an adjacent source window (e.g., May 27) to a target window (e.g., May 28) can change user activity and item responses before enough outcomes are observed for retraining. This temporal drift can arise from daily changes in user activity, freshness- or event-driven item popularity, and delayed feedback that makes observed outcomes lag behind exposures Wang et al. (2019); Yang et al. (2021). We study this time-distribution-shift setting with an available source recommender, a fixed target exposure pool, and only a tiny fraction of target outcomes acquired before the next ranking update. The goal is to improve future user-grouped top-kk ranking while leaving the deployed backbone unchanged.

Achieving this goal requires estimating a deployable correction from far fewer target outcomes than the degrees of freedom of a recommender. Conventional adaptation procedures are mismatched to this constraint because they use the scarce labels to estimate updates in high-dimensional, target-specific parameter spaces. Full target fine-tuning updates user, item, and interaction parameters from the small target label set, so its update is weakly identified and can overwrite useful source structure. Parameter constraints such as L2-SP reduce this drift, but still optimize in the full backbone parameterization Xuhong et al. (2018). Adapter- and LoRA-style parameter-efficient tuning reduce the number of updated parameters by learning inserted or low-rank transformations Houlsby et al. (2019); Hu et al. (2021); under our budget, however, they still estimate target-specific transformations across representation layers and leave the update directions weakly identified. MAML-style adaptation likewise relies on noisy task gradients in that high-dimensional space Finn et al. (2017). Cross-domain and cold-start methods transfer user representations or learn fast adaptation initializations Bharadhwaj (2019); Wang et al. (2021); Zhu et al. (2022); Li et al. (2023); Wu and Zhou (2023); their objectives are complementary, but they do not directly address a fixed temporal exposure pool in which the deployable change is a very small residual around a frozen ranker.

A global residual is a robust answer because a few labels can estimate a small number of item-side directions. Following this principle, we develop SAGE-PAIR as a modular framework for adaptation under temporal distribution shift. Its first module is a frozen-backbone residual adapter: a compact global correction uses source behavior statistics to define an update space while the deployed recommender remains unchanged. Its second module is staged source-to-target calibration: the residual is pretrained on the immediately preceding source window, then warm-started and calibrated with the sparse target outcomes, so the target labels estimate a small set of source-supported directions rather than a new recommender. Its third module is user-conditioned expert routing: a soft router maps stable source profiles and activity features to a mixture of residual experts, allowing the same global direction to receive differentiated corrections across user groups. These modules are optimized through the staged protocol and can be carried across successive target windows, providing a compact update path for continual serving.

papers.title: Primordial non-Gaussianity as a large-scale cosmic-web bias
papers.abstract: Primordial non-Gaussianity is a unique probe of the physics of inflation, but its large-scale-structure signature is difficult to measure because it appears on the largest, most cosmic-variance-limited modes. The standard view of local-type primordial non-Gaussianity is isotropic: it induces a scale-dependent correction to tracer bias, $\Delta b(k)\propto f_{\rm NL}k^{-2}$, on large scales. Here we show that the same large-scale response can be reformulated as an anisotropic, nonlocal environmental-bias effect. Motivated by the spectral cosmic-web hierarchy of Kitaura and Sinigaglia, we define a Hessian field $\mathcal{H}_{ij}(\bf{x})\equiv\partial_i\partial_j\nabla^{-4}\delta(\bf{x})$, whose trace obeys $\mathrm{Tr}\mathcal{H}=\nabla^{-2}\delta$ and therefore carries the same $k^{-2}$ enhancement that appears in the Dalal et al. scale-dependent-bias term. Diagonalizing $\mathcal{H}_{ij}$ defines four large-scale web environments, analogous to knots, filaments, sheets, and voids, although operating on scales much larger than the conventional nonlinear cosmic web. We assign one weight to each environment and test the construction with the AbacusPNG suite of local-PNG $N$-body simulations, using $f_{\rm NL}=\{-100,-30,30,100\}$. We show that these four weights reproduce the large-scale $k^{-2}$ rise of the tracer bias. We further show that existing halo catalogs without PNG can be post-processed to imprint an effective $f_{\rm NL}$ signature. Beyond mock generation, the resulting cosmic-web response motivates an observational statistic based on changes in tracer occupation of large-scale environments relative to a matched Gaussian reference, complementary to the conventional low-$k$ power spectrum.

papers.title: Fejer-Riesz factorization for free products
papers.abstract: We establish an operator-valued Fejer-Riesz factorization theorem for the algebraic free product A of C[F], the group algebra on the free group F on finitely many generators, with finitely many finite dimensional C-star algebras. With respect to a natural reduced-word length, called extent, we show that every linear combination F of elements of A with coefficients from the algebra of operators on a Hilbert space of extent at most 2d that is positive under all finite-dimensional unital *-representations of A admits a factorization F=B^*B with B of extent at most d. This sharp half-extent bound holds without strict positivity. The proof combines a new finite-dimensional realization theorem for positive truncated kernels with operator-system methods. We also establish factorization results for tensor products with group algebras of arbitrary discrete groups under strict positivity in the maximal C-star-tensor product; for amenable groups, strict positivity in the minimal tensor product suffices.

papers.title: AnomSep: Bridging Optimization-Based Separation and Deep Neural Refinement for Anomaly Detection with Listenable Explanations
papers.abstract: We propose AnomSep, which combines optimiza-tion-based separation with deep neural refinement to achieve accurate anomaly detection with listenable explanations. Anomaly detection requires no predefined anomalous categories, and understanding the basis for each detection helps security personnel assess the validity of each detection. End-to-end anomaly detectors can achieve high detection accuracy but output only scalar scores, and existing anomalous sound separation methods provide listenable explanations with limited detection accuracy. AnomSep first obtains preliminary normal-sound and anomalous-sound estimates through optimization-based separation using a dictionary learned from normal sounds in the target environment. Deep neural refinement then improves the preliminary estimates in a pretrained audio latent space. The separated anomalous sound serves as the listenable explanation, and its energy determines the anomaly score. Experiments on synthetic mixtures and real mixtures show improved separation quality over baseline separators. AnomSep achieves detection performance competitive with the end-to-end baseline and provides listenable explanations directly linked to each detection decision.
papers.intro:
Security monitoring aims to detect events that deviate from everyday conditions and may require the attention of security personnel. Camera-based monitoring is widely used in security applications [4]. Acoustic sensing is also useful as a complement to camera-based monitoring because sound can reveal events outside a camera’s field of view, behind obstacles, or under poor lighting conditions [2, 23]. A monitoring system that screens long audio streams for anomalous events that differ from normal sounds can therefore provide information unavailable from visual sensing alone.

Security monitoring aims to detect events that deviate from everyday conditions and may require the attention of security personnel. Camera-based monitoring is widely used in security applications [4]. Acoustic sensing is also useful as a complement to camera-based monitoring because sound can reveal events outside a camera’s field of view, behind obstacles, or under poor lighting conditions [2, 23]. A monitoring system that screens long audio streams for anomalous events that differ from normal sounds can therefore provide information unavailable from visual sensing alone.

A key practical challenge is that deviations from everyday conditions are rare and diverse, making it difficult to explicitly define every category of anomaly. For example, classifying sounds with a zero-shot model [6] requires predefined text prompts that serve as class labels for normal and anomalous sounds. Such closed-set classification may miss anomalies outside the predefined taxonomy. An alternative is to learn the normal sound distribution in a target environment and detect deviations from that distribution [29]. In this study, an anomalous sound is a sound that deviates from the normal sound distribution in the target environment.

Because false detections are difficult to eliminate completely from monitoring systems, security personnel need to identify which sound triggered each detection to assess the validity of the detection. Presenting an anomalous sound separated from the input mixture as a waveform would allow security personnel to hear what was detected. We adopt the term listenable explanations from prior work [12] to describe the estimated anomalous-sound waveforms presented to explain individual detections.

papers.title: Absolute Calibration of a Broadband Transmission Grating Spectrometer from 5 to 400 nm with Uncertainty Estimates
papers.abstract: We present the absolute calibration of a transmission grating spectrometer (TGS) with uncertainty estimates in the 5--400 nm range using synchrotron radiation at the BEAR beamline at Elettra light source in Trieste, Italy. Firstly, the spectral responsivity of a Si photodiode in the spectrometer was absolutely calibrated with respect to the absolutely-calibrated beamline photodiode. Subsequently, this photodiode was used to calibrate the transmittance of Zr and Al thin-film filters, along with bulk MgF$_2$ and UV-grade fused silica windows at their operating positions in the spectrometer to minimize mounting-induced uncertainties. Next, the quantum efficiency of the spectrometer's CCD camera was calibrated over the 5--400 nm range. Lastly, three gratings with line densities of 10000, 3000, and 1000 lines/mm were calibrated for spectroscopy in the ranges extending from soft X-ray to extreme-, vacuum- and deep-ultraviolet (DUV) wavelengths, respectively. The combination of various filters and gratings enables absolutely calibrated spectroscopy with high versatility across a broad wavelength range from soft X-rays to DUV.

papers.intro:
Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is the leading technology for modern semiconductor manufacturing, using laser-produced tin (Sn) plasma as the light source[1, 46]. The light originating from multiply charged Sn10+–Sn15+ ions is mainly centered around 13.5 nm[9, 7, 8, 29, 40, 5, 41, 39]. The produced light is transmitted to a Si wafer through a series of optical components, the most critical of which are multilayer Mo/Si mirrors whose reflectance passband is precisely tuned to match the plasma emission around 13.5 nm[25, 20]. In addition to the dominant 13.5 nm emission, the plasma also emits in a broad wavelength range from soft X-rays to vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) and deep-ultraviolet (DUV)[13, 12, 38, 4]. In particular, radiation in the 30–90 nm wavelength range is strongly absorbed by the hydrogen buffer gas in lithography scanners. Photoionization of hydrogen generates a secondary plasma that must be precisely controlled to prevent damage to the scanner components[45]. Furthermore, portions of the VUV and DUV radiation may be transported through the multilayer mirrors and reach the wafer surface. Given the broad wavelength range, the cumulative dose can be absorbed by the photoresist, causing parasitic exposure and lowering the contrast and quality of the image [44, 43]. Therefore, accurate characterization of the plasma emission spectrum in this broad wavelength range from soft X-rays to DUV is important for a better understanding of the EUV emission mechanisms and developing potential improvement strategies for the lithography process.

In recent years, spectrometers with free-standing transmission gratings have been used to measure plasma spectra over this broad wavelength range[4]. Standard Si microfabrication techniques combined with nano-imprint or electron-beam lithography, enable patterning high line densities up to 10 00010\,000 lines/mm, allowing sufficient spectral dispersion for soft X-ray and EUV wavelengths in a compact geometry[10, 11, 35, 47, 24, 37, 16, 22, 48]. Furthermore, combining gratings with different line densities on the same Si chip enables covering longer wavelengths using gratings with lower line densities, e.g. 10001000 lines/mm, hence allowing to cover the soft x-rays to DUV range in a compact spectrometer design[14, 2, 4]. However, the efficiency of individual components of a transmission grating spectrometer (TGS), such as filters, gratings, and detectors, exhibits significant variations in the broad wavelength range covered. Previous intensity calibration efforts revealed that there are large variations, up to a factor of two in certain wavelength regions, among the reported efficiency curves of the CCD camera used in the spectrometer[4]. Furthermore, rigorous uncertainty quantification is not available, which limits both the accuracy of the absolute calibration capability and the reliability of the interpretation of the measured spectra.

papers.title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
papers.abstract:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory.
  In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation.
  Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.

papers.intro:
A central objective in computing foundations is to understand how computational power scales with access to additional resources. The classical hierarchy theorems from computational complexity theory establish that increased time or space yields strictly greater computational capability. The two most fundamental results in this regard are the Time Hierarchy Theorem and the Space Hierarchy Theorem. Intuitively, the Time Hierarchy Theorem states that if t⁡(n)≥nt(n)\geq n is a sufficiently nice complexity-bounding function (i.e., time-constructible function), then there are problems solvable in time slightly more than t⁡(n)t(n) that cannot be solved in time t⁡(n)t(n). In particular, the most well-known version of this principle states that TIME​(t1​(n))⊊TIME​(t2​(n))\mbox{\rm TIME}(t_{1}(n))\subsetneq\mbox{\rm TIME}(t_{2}(n)) if t1​(n)​log⁡t1​(n)=o⁡(t2​(n))t_{1}(n)\log t_{1}(n)=o(t_{2}(n)) [11]. Here TIME​(t​(n))\mbox{\rm TIME}(t(n)) is the class of languages that are decidable in time O⁡(t⁡(n))O(t(n)) on inputs of length nn using a multi-tape Turing machine. Hierarchy theorems formalize a basic structural principle: bounded resources induce strict stratifications of computational power. Even though hierarchy theorems are intuitive, it is far from trivial to establish such quantitative results. Without such results, we cannot rule out the possibility of universal thresholds on resources that are required to solve any decidable problem.

Modern AI architectures, particularly transformer architectures, have introduced new models of computation that are both practically powerful and theoretically intriguing. Transformers, built on mechanisms such as self-attention and layered representations, have achieved remarkable success across domains including natural language processing, vision, and scientific computing. The success of transformer architectures led to a new line of research to understand their computational power. Recent research formulated this question by modeling transformers as a computation device, thus enabling rigorous study of the power and limitations of this new model.

Modern AI architectures, particularly transformer architectures, have introduced new models of computation that are both practically powerful and theoretically intriguing. Transformers, built on mechanisms such as self-attention and layered representations, have achieved remarkable success across domains including natural language processing, vision, and scientific computing. The success of transformer architectures led to a new line of research to understand their computational power. Recent research formulated this question by modeling transformers as a computation device, thus enabling rigorous study of the power and limitations of this new model.

A growing body of work has identified fundamental limitations of standard transformer architectures [9, 3, 13, 10, 14, 15, 16]. In particular, under realistic assumptions, constant-depth transformers are less powerful than finite state machines, arguably the simplest computational model. A recent survey [21] gives an excellent account of the expressive power of transformers as a computational device. The intuitive reason is that constant-depth transformers operate in a largely feedforward manner and lack the ability to perform the iterative computation required for multi-step reasoning. As a result, even tasks that are conceptually simple but require sequential composition of intermediate steps fall outside their effective computational capabilities [17, 6, 23].

A classical technique underlying hierarchy theorems is diagonalization. In the setting of Turing machines, diagonalization constructs a language that disagrees with every Turing machine running within a given resource bound, by simulating each such machine on carefully chosen inputs and flipping its output. This approach relies on two key properties: (i) machines can be effectively enumerated, and (ii) there exists a universal machine that can take the description of another machine as input and simulate its execution with controlled overhead. These properties make it possible in the Turing machine model to carry out self-referential constructions in a clean and uniform way.

papers.title: Anisotropic three-point statistics of the peculiar velocity and galaxy density fields: modelling in Fourier and configuration space
papers.abstract: By the equivalence principle, large-scale peculiar velocities provide a kinematical probe of the matter distribution independent of the biased galaxy distribution. Their three-point correlation with galaxies assesses the nonlinear coupling between cosmic flows and the surrounding density field. We develop a tree-level model of the anisotropic correlation between one line-of-sight peculiar velocity and two galaxy densities in redshift space, including quadratic and tidal galaxy bias. Starting from the corresponding velocity-divergence bispectrum, we derive predictions in both Fourier and configuration space through a spherical-harmonic expansion. We test the Fourier-space calculation against a closed-form expression and assess the numerical convergence of the configuration-space predictions. For a fiducial model, the signal is dominated by a dipolar dependence on triangle orientation relative to the line of sight, while subdominant multipoles distinguish the responses to growth and galaxy bias. In configuration space, the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) feature depends on which triangle side crosses the acoustic scale and on the velocity projection. We also relate the model to the density-weighted statistic measured by peculiar-velocity catalogues and formulate estimators for its observable multipoles. This framework supports future measurements and covariance analyses needed to establish the additional cosmological information carried by velocity-density three-point correlations.

Galaxy redshift surveys trace the large-scale distribution of galaxies, providing measurements of the expansion history and growth of cosmic structure. Most constraints have come from two-point statistics, with baryon acoustic oscillations providing a standard ruler and redshift-space distortions constraining the growth rate [30, 2]. Nonlinear gravitational evolution generates non-Gaussianity whose leading signature in the correlation statistics is the connected three-point correlation function, or its Fourier counterpart, the bispectrum [18, 3]. Its dependence on triangle shape and orientation helps distinguish gravitational evolution from galaxy bias and provides information beyond two-point correlations [17, 55, 52].

Joint two- and three-point analyses have consequently become an important part of spectroscopic-survey cosmology [56, 19, 20, 40, 22], supported by advances in perturbative modelling and efficient estimators in both Fourier and configuration space [48, 49, 53, 23, 11]. In DESI DR1, joint analyses tighten the constraint on the amplitude of fluctuations by approximately 20%20\% with respect to the power spectrum alone [40, 41, 16, 21, 8]. In configuration space, these estimators have led to measurements of the galaxy three-point correaltion function (3PCF) in several spectroscopic samples [38, 58, 57], to the detection of the baryonic acustic oscillations (BAO) feature in the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) [47, 39] and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) DR1 [31], and to constraints on massive neutrinos [33]. The two representations are complementary, since Fourier space offers a compact model and nearly diagonal covariances, whereas configuration space confines the baryon acoustic oscillation feature to a narrow range of separations and simplifies the treatment of the survey window. All these measurements, however, concern the galaxy density alone. Extending three-point analyses to peculiar velocities and their correlations with galaxy density is the natural next step.

papers.title: Overview of the ImageCLEFmedical 2026 GANs task: Exploring fingerprint detection, privacy leakage, and synthetic medical image generation
papers.abstract: The 2026 ImageCLEFmedical GANs Task Exploring Fingerprint Detection, Privacy Leakage, and Synthetic Medical Image Generation continues to investigate privacy and security concerns around using patient data to generate synthetic medical images, now in its fourth edition. This edition introduces three complementary subtasks: the first extends prior editions by asking participants to detect which real images were used in training a Generative Adversarial Network to produce given synthetic outputs; the second is a novel subtask requiring participants to identify which latent vector produced each synthetic image, probing the faithfulness and reversibility of the latent-to-image mapping; the third asks participants to generate privacy-preserving CT slices, quantifying the trade-off between image fidelity and patient privacy. Ground-truth annotations and benchmark datasets of real and GAN-generated lung CT slices are provided for all subtasks. Evaluation is based on Cohen's Kappa for Subtask 1, matching accuracy for Subtask 2, and a combination of FID and Privacy Preservation Score (PPS) for Subtask 3. Overall, 37 teams registered for the task, with 10 teams submitting runs across subtasks and 6 teams submitting working notes papers. This paper presents an overview of the task setup, datasets, evaluation metrics, and summarises the approaches and results of participating teams.

papers.intro:
AI and computer-aided diagnosis systems for medical tasks such as prediction, detection, and classification depend on access to large and diverse datasets for effective training. High-quality data enable these models to learn complex patterns, improving both accuracy and reliability. However, obtaining real medical data is difficult due to strict privacy regulations and ethical concerns. Patients typically consent to the use of their medical information for their own clinical care, but not for broad research purposes. As a result, collecting sufficiently large datasets for training AI models remains a significant challenge and slows progress in developing advanced healthcare tools.

However, obtaining real medical data is difficult due to strict privacy regulations and ethical concerns. Patients typically consent to the use of their medical information for their own clinical care, but not for broad research purposes. As a result, collecting sufficiently large datasets for training AI models remains a significant challenge and slows progress in developing advanced healthcare tools.

Synthetic medical data has emerged as a promising solution Frid-Adar et al. (2018). Generative models such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) Goodfellow et al. (2014) can produce realistic-looking images that resemble true medical data without being directly tied to any specific patient, potentially easing data-access barriers and enabling greater diversity and scalability. However, the privacy guarantees of synthetic data are not unconditional. Generative models are trained on real patient images, and may inadvertently retain hidden traces or “fingerprints” of their training data in the images they produce. If synthetic images can be linked back to specific patients or reveal patient-specific anatomical details, the privacy benefit of using synthetic data is fundamentally undermined. Ensuring that generative models do not memorise or propagate identifiable patterns from their training data is therefore a critical open problem, and one that must be rigorously studied before synthetic medical images can be safely deployed in research and clinical AI development.

papers.title: Interplay of Ni Order and Local Moments in Intercalated NixNbS2
papers.abstract: Magnetic ions intercalated into the van der Waals gaps of layered transition metal dichalcogenides provide a system where local moments interact strongly with a metallic host. How the order of the intercalant sublattice affects their magnetism is important but rarely addressed, although disorder is hard to avoid, in particular in thin films and heterostructures. Here this question is examined in single crystals of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ with $0.10 \leq x \leq 0.57$, whose composition and Ni order were determined by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy and synchrotron x-ray diffraction. Anisotropic magnetic susceptibility measurements reveal three regimes. Long-range antiferromagnetic order appears only for $0.25 \leq x \leq 0.33$, where the Ni ions form the $2 \times 2$ and $\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}$ R$30^\circ$ superstructures, and $T_\mathrm{N}$ reaches 96 K at $x = 1/3$. In this range the effective moment, $\approx 2.5 \mu_\mathrm{B}$ per Ni, agrees with DFT+$U$ calculations, in which the Ni spin is partly delocalized onto the surrounding S ligands. For $x \leq 0.18$ the dilute, randomly distributed Ni ions remain paramagnetic down to 2 K with a reduced moment. For $x \geq 0.37$, where Ni-Ni contacts are unavoidable, long-range order gives way to a short-range ordered state below 10-15 K with a further reduced moment. As calculations for ordered Ni arrangements find the Ni state nearly independent of $x$, even at $x = 1/2$, the reduction of the moment is attributed to a disorder-enabled reduction of the charge transfer from Ni to the NbS$_2$ layers. The magnetism of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ is thus governed by the (dis)order of the Ni sublattice rather than by the Ni concentration alone.

papers.title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence
papers.abstract: Digital traces may complement population surveys in the measurement of well-being, but the two sources do not necessarily capture identical constructs. We compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (HFGI) with World Values Survey and European Social Survey measures across three domains using structural equation models. The results show strong within-source coherence and construct-specific cross-source correspondence. Cross-source convergence varies across domains; the observed pattern is consistent with stronger correspondence where the underlying indicators are more closely aligned conceptually. Near-perfect agreement would be unexpected, since surveys elicit standardized self-reports, whereas HFGI captures naturally occurring public expressions. HFGI should therefore be viewed as a distinct but empirically connected measurement system that complements survey-based evidence on well-being.

papers.intro:
National well-being has become a central component of the assessment of social progress and an increasingly important complement to conventional economic indicators. GDP and related measures remain indispensable for describing production and material resources, but they do not directly capture how people evaluate their lives, experience positive or negative emotions, or perceive their capacity to act and influence their circumstances (Diener et al., 2009). This has motivated the broader “Beyond GDP” agenda and the development of national statistical frameworks in which subjective well-being is treated as a relevant dimension of economic and social performance (Stiglitz et al., 2009; OECD, 2013; OECD, 2025; Helliwell et al., 2025). Well-being research has consequently relied heavily on population surveys measuring constructs such as happiness, life satisfaction, and perceived control. These measures remain essential for comparing how people assess their lives across countries and over time, although the distinction between evaluative and affective well-being must be preserved (Diener, 1984; Deaton and Stone, 2013).

Survey-based measurement nevertheless has important practical limitations. Cross-national surveys are costly and are generally conducted in periodic waves, while national estimates may refer to different years and require complex harmonisation procedures. They therefore offer relatively sparse observations of a phenomenon that may change in response to economic, political, and social shocks. The increasing availability of digital traces offers a potentially valuable complement. Social-media data contain large volumes of geographically referenced language produced continuously and at relatively low marginal cost, making it possible to study social processes at a temporal and spatial resolution that traditional surveys rarely provide (Salganik, 2017; Iacus and Porro, 2021). At the same time, the ready-made character of digital trace data does not remove the need for sampling, validation, and measurement design: the advantages of scale and timeliness coexist with problems of selection, platform dependence, changing data-generating processes, and the risk that large datasets create a misleading appearance of representativeness (Lazer et al., 2014; Olteanu et al., 2019; Hargittai, 2020).

These initial studies showed, in brief, that HFGI can document county-level differences between evaluative and affective well-being, identify rural–urban variation in job-satisfaction expressions, and provide a fine-grained geographic and temporal resource for well-being research (Iacus and Porro, 2026b; Iacus and Porro, 2026a; Iacus et al., 2026c). Establishing this relationship is therefore an empirical question rather than an assumption. The present study extends the empirical scope of HFGI beyond its initial U.S.-focused applications by examining its cross-national correspondence with two external survey sources, the World Values Survey (WVS) and the European Social Survey (ESS).

The issue matters for both the interpretation and the practical use of digital well-being measures. If online and survey indicators recover similar cross-national structure, digital traces may provide complementary evidence alongside conventional surveys. Where correspondence is weaker, the two sources may instead capture different dimensions of a broader construct. We therefore examine three domains for which meaningful cross-source comparisons can be constructed: mental and subjective well-being, spiritual and religious expression, and physical well-being. Rather than assuming that similarly labelled indicators are equivalent, we ask whether each source forms a coherent measurement system and the extent to which the resulting latent constructs correspond across countries.

Comparing online and survey-based well-being measures raises a measurement problem that cannot be resolved simply by correlating indicators with similar labels. The same construct may be observed through different measurement systems, while the same measurement system may capture several related but distinct aspects of well-being. The relevant question is therefore not whether HFGI and survey indicators use comparable terminology, but whether they represent the same cross-national variation in an underlying well-being construct.

papers.title: PoseRieFlow: Riemannian Flow Matching for Whole-Body Text-to-Pose Generation
papers.abstract: We present PoseRieFlow, a compact flow-matching framework for text-conditioned generation of whole-body 3D human poses. Prior text-to-pose methods either neglect articulated hands or model rotations in Euclidean space despite their non-Euclidean geometry. PoseRieFlow instead formulates generation directly on the product manifold of SMPL-H joint rotations, learning a text-conditioned vector field that transports samples from an isotropic $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ Gaussian prior to the data distribution along Riemannian geodesics. A part-tokenized Diffusion Transformer aggregates the 52 joints into eight body-part tokens, allocating a dedicated token and nonlinear projector to each hand, and restores per-joint resolution through part-specific decoders, shortening the sequence while improving kinematic fidelity over per-joint tokenization. With only 21.6M trainable parameters, PoseRieFlow supports expressive SMPL-H generation with detailed hand articulation at a fraction of the scale of recent LLM-based generators. On PoseScript, it attains the lowest whole-body kinematic error among all hand-producing methods, with consistent kinematic gains from the Riemannian formulation over its Euclidean counterpart at every practical inference budget, while distributional and retrieval metrics remain comparable between them.

papers.intro:
Generating 3D human poses from natural language is a fundamental problem spanning vision, graphics, and embodied AI. Recent progress in text-conditioned generative modeling has advanced text-to-motion synthesis through diffusion and flow-based approaches [37, 16, 36]. In contrast, text-to-pose generation [8, 15, 23] remains comparatively underexplored despite posing a distinct challenge: unlike motion generation, which benefits from strong temporal continuity priors, single-frame pose generation must model a highly multimodal distribution over articulated 3D configurations from language alone. This challenge becomes harder when extending from coarse body posture to whole-body articulation with expressive hand poses.

This challenge becomes harder when extending from coarse body posture to whole-body articulation with expressive hand poses.

Current text-to-pose methods exhibit two limitations. First, most approaches model joint rotations in Euclidean parameterizations such as axis-angle or continuous 6D rotations [53], and optimize Euclidean regression objectives. However, articulated pose lies on a product manifold of rotation groups rather than a flat vector space. As a result, linear interpolation and Euclidean velocity regression produce optimization targets that are not aligned with the geodesic structure of rotations, particularly for large joint rotations and high-dimensional whole-body configurations. Recent work on geometry-aware articulated modeling [18, 30] suggests that respecting manifold structure can improve generative learning, but these ideas have not yet been explored in text-conditioned single-frame pose generation.
