papers.title: Electoral Intelligence: A Neural Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Model for Forecasting Swedish Municipal Elections
papers.abstract: Forecasting local elections is difficult because electoral competition is geographically heterogeneous, highly overdispersed, and characterized by many party-municipality combinations with little or no electoral activity. This article develops a bounded neural zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model for forecasting party-level vote counts in Swedish municipal elections. The model combines a count component for expected votes, a zero-inflation component for structural electoral absence, municipality-specific dispersion, and learned embeddings capturing latent party, municipality, and party-municipality structure. Model training relies on data from the 2014, 2018, and 2022 Swedish municipal elections and performance is evaluated on a held-out set of municipalities. Testing results show strong predictive accuracy in both vote counts and vote shares. Explanatory diagnostics indicate that latent party structure, local party-municipality relationships, electoral persistence, organizational capacity, and candidate-electorate representational similarity are among the most important determinants of predictive performance. Following model evaluation and diagnostics, the selected specification is refit on all historical data and applied to generate forecasts for the 2026 municipal elections. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach for studying local electoral competition in multiparty systems characterized by heterogeneous party presence and substantial geographic variation.

papers.intro:
Election forecasting occupies a central position in empirical political science because it provides both a practical tool for anticipating electoral outcomes and a means of evaluating theories of political behavior. A long tradition of forecasting research has demonstrated that election results can often be predicted well in advance using political and economic fundamentals, historical voting patterns, opinion polls, or combinations thereof. Beyond prediction itself, successful forecasts can reveal the underlying structure of electoral competition and improve our understanding of how voters respond to political, economic, and institutional conditions (Lewis-Beck and Tien, 2016; Lewis-Beck et al., 2025).

A long tradition of forecasting research has demonstrated that election results can often be predicted well in advance using political and economic fundamentals, historical voting patterns, opinion polls, or combinations thereof. Beyond prediction itself, successful forecasts can reveal the underlying structure of electoral competition and improve our understanding of how voters respond to political, economic, and institutional conditions (Lewis-Beck and Tien, 2016; Lewis-Beck et al., 2025).

Despite considerable methodological progress, most election forecasting models have been developed for national elections and often focus on two-party systems (such as the US election). Forecasting in multiparty settings presents additional challenges because party support is inherently compositional and electoral competition is distributed across multiple parties simultaneously. Recognizing these difficulties, recent work has extended forecasting methods to multiparty systems, primarily through Bayesian approaches that combine polling data with structural fundamentals (Stoetzer et al., 2019). However, much of this literature remains oriented toward national elections and relies heavily on polling information, which are typically unavailable or sparse in local elections.

Swedish municipal elections provide a particularly demanding forecasting environment. Electoral competition involves multiple national parties, hundreds of local parties, and substantial geographic heterogeneity. These characteristics lead to a large number of party–municipality combinations in which parties receive either very few votes or no votes at all. The resulting data exhibit two features that challenge conventional forecasting models. First, party support contains many excess zeros arising from limited local party presence. Second, electoral support varies considerably across municipalities, producing substantial over-dispersion relative to standard count models. Traditional linear forecasting models are not well suited to accommodate these characteristics simultaneously.

At the same time, local elections contain rich sources of information that are often ignored in conventional electoral forecasting. Historical electoral performance, local candidate-list characteristics, municipality-specific voter composition, and the similarity between candidates and electorates may all contribute to electoral success. Furthermore, local electoral competition is shaped by persistent party identities and municipality-specific political contexts that are difficult to represent using standard fixed-effect approaches. These features suggest the need for forecasting models that are flexible enough to capture nonlinear relationships while remaining interpretable and capable of quantifying uncertainty.

papers.title: TwinLight: A Multi-Timescale Physical-Layer-Aware T-API-Compliant Optical Domain Controller Digital Twin
papers.abstract: We demonstrate TwinLight, an open-source optical-network digital twin acting as an optical domain controller. Its T-API REST and telemetry streaming interfaces expose a physical-layer engine that combines a GNPy steady-state baseline with four analytical transients.

papers.title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
papers.abstract: Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

Bilateral trade is a fundamental model of economic exchange under private information. A seller holds an item that a buyer may wish to purchase, and an intermediary facilitates the transaction by offering a purchase price to the seller and a sale price to the buyer. Classical mechanism design studies how private valuations constrain the efficiency of such exchanges [24]. More recently, starting with the seminal work of [11], considerable attention has been devoted to learning bilateral-trade mechanisms when the distribution of agents’ valuations is unknown [10, 2, 5, 22, 12].

papers.title: The Re-Foundation of Radar Meteorology
papers.abstract: Since the early development of radar meteorology in the 1940s, rainfall retrieval has traditionally relied on empirical scaling relationships between radar variables and rainfall rate. Here, we revisit the premise that horizontal and differential reflectivity sufficiently constrain the rainfall rate despite the variability of the underlying drop size distribution. Motivated by evidences that this variability requires at least three degrees of freedom, we develop a nonparametric statistical retrieval algorithm that considers different combinations of drop count and distribution shape compatible with the same radar observations. The method separates the contributions of drop count and distribution shape. It then empirically estimates how the shape factors for rainfall rate and horizontal reflectivity, as well as differential reflectivity, vary with the mean and skewness of the drop diameter distribution. These relationships identify compatible combinations of drop count and shape, from which rainfall rates are calculated and their median returned as the estimate. Neither a prescribed analytical drop size distribution nor a scaling rainfall estimator or explicit classification of precipitation regimes is required. We evaluate the method using a worldwide database (149 disdrometer datasets from 76 locations), with radar observables calculated from measured drop spectra. In cross-dataset validation, the method achieves lower median dispersion of relative retrieval errors across all 16 combinations of training and validation instrument types with respect two benchmark methods consisting of the traditional scaling law relationship, and a direct nonparametric fit. These findings motivate a reassessment of the foundations of radar rainfall retrieval by incorporating the range of rainfall rates compatible with radar observation.

papers.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Annealing for Protein Side-Chain Optimization: A Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical annealing solvers are moving from research laboratories toward industrial use, but their advantage over classical optimization appears to be confined to a narrow class of problems. A recent systematic benchmark of the D-Wave hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers, across several classes of optimization problems, found it to be most competitive on binary quadratic programs, while noting that few industrial problems take this form. Therefore, identifying real-world industrial problems that can be modeled with this structure is a key challenge. We propose protein side-chain optimization, a core step of computational protein design, as one of these problems: it is natively a binary quadratic program, and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. In this feasibility study, we test whether the competitiveness of the hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers extends to this problem. On 40 instances derived from 20 experimentally determined protein structures with up to about 200 amino acids and 2000 binary variables, we compare the results achieved with a hybrid solver, run for 5 seconds, against those of the commercial solver Gurobi, run for 10 seconds, 1000 seconds, and 4 hours. The hybrid solver reaches the certified optimum whenever one is available, matches Gurobi's performance on smaller instances, and outperforms it on larger instances, finding lower-energy solutions. These results show that the competitiveness of the hybrid solver on binary quadratic programs, so far observed only on a synthetic benchmark, extends to a real-world problem. This motivates comparisons with classical heuristics specific to protein side-chain optimization.

papers.intro:
Quantum annealing is an analog computing paradigm in which an optimization problem is encoded into the physical Hamiltonian of the processor. Current annealers implement only a restricted class of Hamiltonians, so they are not universal quantum computers; however, they have the advantage of being more mature than general-purpose gate-based quantum devices: D-Wave processors have grown from 512 qubits in 2013 to more than 4,400 qubits in the current Advantage2 systems [1]. In addition, hybrid quantum-classical solvers combine both types of computation: they are built on classical algorithms and call the Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) only when it is useful. Since the quantum component is added on top of a classical solver, these systems are already approaching practical maturity and are moving from research to industrial applications [2].

Since the quantum component is added on top of a classical solver, these systems are already approaching practical maturity and are moving from research to industrial applications [2].

Their practical computational advantage, however, appears to be limited to a narrow class of problems. A systematic comparison with commercial classical solvers on linear, quadratic, and mixed-integer formulations [2] found the D-Wave hybrid solvers to be most competitive on Binary Quadratic Programs (BQPs), i.e., problems that are natively quadratic in binary variables, while noting that only a limited number of industrial optimization problems are pure BQPs. Identifying practically relevant problems with this structure is therefore a prerequisite for the effective application of hybrid annealing.

PSCO is a core step of computational protein design, and is solved routinely in industrial and academic design pipelines within Rosetta, one of the most widely used software suites for molecular modeling, through a simulated annealing algorithm [3]. With the energy functions used in practice, its objective is exactly quadratic in binary selection variables, and its only constraints are one-hot constraints on groups of these variables: PSCO is then natively a BQP. In addition, protein design requires pools of many low-energy candidates rather than a single optimum, which matches the ability of annealers to return samples of low-energy solutions.

With the energy functions used in practice, its objective is exactly quadratic in binary selection variables, and its only constraints are one-hot constraints on groups of these variables: PSCO is then natively a BQP. In addition, protein design requires pools of many low-energy candidates rather than a single optimum, which matches the ability of annealers to return samples of low-energy solutions.

Quantum approaches to PSCO have been explored with several quantum technologies. The first study based on quantum annealing [4] analyzed how the time to solution scales with problem size on design problems small enough to be solved directly on the D-Wave 2000Q processor, with up to about 60 binary variables, and compared it with the Rosetta packer and the exact solver toulbar2; under pessimistic assumptions on future connectivity and noise, the authors estimated that annealers about 400 and 10,000 times larger would be needed to compete with toulbar2 and with the Rosetta packer, respectively. The scaling comparison therefore concerned the quantum processor alone. The hybrid algorithm qbsolv was used only on larger instances to assess solution quality without a scaling analysis. Recent work has applied photonic entropy-computing hardware to PSCO instances involving 493 to 943 variables [5], while a separate study explored the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on gate-based quantum computers for the same problem up to 54 qubits [6]. Quantum annealing, either directly on the QPU or through D-Wave hybrid solvers, has also been applied to other problems in protein modeling, including folding, design, and conformational sampling [10, 9, 8, 7, 11, 12]. Two of these studies compare a D-Wave hybrid solver with Gurobi, finding Gurobi to perform better [7] or comparably [8]. A systematic comparison between current hybrid solvers and classical solvers on PSCO instances of increasing, realistic size, which would show whether the competitiveness found in [2] also holds for this problem, is still missing.

In this paper, we address this question as a feasibility study, to assess whether this direction is worth a more detailed investigation. Our contributions are the following: • We propose PSCO as a real-world industrial problem suited to hybrid annealing, since it is natively a BQP with only one-hot constraints and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. • We formulate PSCO, with energies computed by Rosetta on experimentally determined protein structures, as a constrained quadratic model that the hybrid solver receives with explicit one-hot constraints. • We benchmark the D-Wave hybrid solver, run for 5 s, against Gurobi, run for 10 s and 1000 s, on 40 instances with up to 1970 binary variables, using as reference 4 h Gurobi runs that certify optimality on the smallest instances. • We show how the quality gap between the two solvers evolves with instance size, and discuss what this result does and does not imply with respect to classical heuristics specific to PSCO.

papers.title: The variational formulation of the follow-the-leader model
papers.abstract: We provide a variational formulation of a finite-dimensional Follow-the-Leader system through a minimizing-movement scheme based on a discrete transport distance with nonlinear mobility. Despite the degeneracy of the kinetic action at maximal density, we prove finiteness of the distance, $C^1$ regularity of geodesics, and suitable Euler--Lagrange relations. For a decreasing external potential, we show that the JKO scheme yields an approximate implicit Euler discretization of the Follow-the-Leader dynamics. Consequently, as $\tau\to0^+$, the piecewise affine interpolations converge, up to a subsequence, to a $C^1$ solution of the continuous Follow-the-Leader system. This complements the many-particle convergence theory for the discrete nonlinear-mobility transport distance by establishing the continuous-time limit at fixed number of particles.

The relation between scalar conservation laws, FTL systems and gradient-flow structures has already been observed from a discrete particle viewpoint. In [13], scalar conservation laws are discussed from the perspective of gradient flows and the FTL system is interpreted as a gradient flow on a non-flat metric at the discrete level. Related deterministic particle schemes have also been used to construct solutions of transport and aggregation–diffusion equations with nonlinear mobility; see, for example, [17, 6]. These works highlight that the geometry perceived by a particle is naturally modified by the local discrete density and suggest that nonlinear-mobility transport metrics are well suited to the Lagrangian description of such systems.

papers.title: From Shape to Species: The Use of Persistent Homology in Restructuring the Taxonomy of \textit{Acropora} corals
papers.abstract: Traditional coral taxonomy is increasingly challenged by recent advances in molecular evidence. Quantitative methods previously used to identify morphological descriptors have not been successful at detecting significant differences at the macroscale. It is of great interest to optimise methods for effectively delimiting species within the complex genus \textit{Acropora} to ensure sustainable, long-term management of these vital ecosystems. Topological Data Analysis (TDA) is designed to study the shape of data and can detect features that familiar methods overlook. This novel approach makes TDA and persistent homology a logical choice for studying coral morphology in a taxonomic context. The results show that valid topological information can be extracted from in-situ coral images and that there is great potential in further refining this method. This study is a first exploration into the potential of persistent homology in supporting the delimitation of the reef-building scleractinian corals \textit{Acropora}.

papers.intro:
Robust taxonomy that accurately reflects the diversity and evolutionary history of a clade underpins virtually all aspects of biological, ecological, and conservation science and management (Thomson et al., 2018; Sandall et al., 2023). For over two centuries since the formalization of the binomial system of classification by Linnaeus (1758), species identities and systematic relationships were inferred almost exclusively through comparative analysis of morphological traits. However, the advent of molecular phylogenetics in the 1970s provided a new tool to examine evolutionary relationships and has fundamentally altered our understanding of the systematics and evolution of many groups across the Tree of Life. Specifically, molecular phylogenies regularly illuminate the fact that morphological characters traditionally used to delineate species or higher taxonomic groups are homoplasies and not indicative of close evolutionary affinities (Moore and Willmer, 1997; Mahler et al., 2013). Consequently, robust delineation of lineages that reflects evolutionary history requires the identification of morphological characters that are phylogenetically informative; that is, that they are diagnostic of a particular clade.

Hard corals are the dominant ecosystem engineers of tropical reefs, the most diverse marine ecosystems on Earth. However, the abundance of corals on reefs is declining rapidly due to climate change and other anthropogenic activities (Hughes et al., 2017). Despite their ecological importance and well-documented declines in abundance, we still lack the capacity to accurately identify coral species. Consequently, little information is available on key questions such as species abundances, geographic ranges, population trajectories, or extinction risk. This knowledge gap is driven primarily by the fact that some coral species exhibit extensive plasticity at the macromorphological level (Todd, 2008), while others can appear very similar despite deeply divergent evolutionary histories (Fukami et al., 2004); in other words, in some cases a single species can vary extensively in morphology, while in others two distantly related species can appear very similar.

For most of their taxonomic history, corals have been classified based on morphological traits of their aragonite skeletons. In most cases, the authors of the taxonomic monographs of the 19th century that described coral species and placed them into their respective higher-level taxonomic groupings were based in museums in Europe or North America, and few had ever seen corals in the field. Even those that did participate in scientific expeditions were still limited by the technology of the day, and corals could only be collected either from very shallow reef flats at low tide or by destructive means such as dredging. The advent of SCUBA diving in the 1970s as the primary method for studying corals enabled researchers to access a much wider range of coral reef habitats and observe corals in situ, and popularized the idea that much of the variation observed between species was actually intraspecific variation within a single species depending on the environment (Veron and Pichon, 1976). The influential series of monographs ‘Scleractinia of Eastern Australia’ (Veron and Pichon, 1976; Veron and Pichon, 1980; Veron and Pichon, 1982; Veron and Wallace, 1984; Veron et al., 1977) were the first taxonomic revisions based on extensive collections of corals collected on SCUBA. The idea that morphological variation between species was due to environmental plasticity, combined with the idea that most coral species had wide geographic ranges spanning much of the Indo-Pacific (Stehli and Wells, 1971; Veron, 2000), led to the synonymy of many nominal species on the basis that they represented intraspecific variation within morphologically variable and geographically widespread species.

These results indicate that many clades do indeed possess phylogenetically informative traits, but identifying them requires examining which traits are conserved within clades delineated by molecular phylogenies.

papers.title: On Differentially Private Mechanisms for Linear Regression
papers.abstract:
We study the classic least-squares linear regression problem under differential privacy (DP) in the batch and the continual observation setting. In the latter setting, the mechanism receives a stream of $n$ data points $(x_i,y_i)$ ($x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$) and must output an estimate of the optimal parameters at each time step $i$. Although differentially private linear regression has been extensively studied in the batch setting, the problem remains underexplored for the continual setting, with prior work being restricted to constrained linear regression and update time polynomial in $n$.
  In this work, we introduce ContinualAdaSSP, the first mechanism for unconstrained linear regression under continual differential privacy. Our mechanism's suboptimality gap is proportional to $\sqrt{d}\operatorname{polylog}(n)$. It requires $O(d^2\log{n})$ space and $O(d^2\log{n}+d^{\omega})$ update time, where $d$ is the dimension of the input space.
  We also study fundamental limits of differentially private linear regression by showing the first lower bounds for the box-constrained least-squares linear regression problem. Our lower bounds are proportional to $\min(n,\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\log^{1.5}d})$ for $(1,O(\frac{1}{n}))$-DP, and $\min(n,\frac{d}{\epsilon})$ for $\epsilon$-DP, and are derived using a reduction from a fingerprinting code problem from [Peter et al., 2024], providing new insights into the inherent hardness of this canonical task.
  Our experimental evaluation on real-world datasets shows that the accuracy of our continual observation mechanism clearly outperforms any other known differentially private mechanism for this problem such as rerunning the batch algorithm at each time step.

papers.title: Improved Approximation and Hardness Bounds for $\beta$-TSP
papers.abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) asks for a minimum-length Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. Its approximability depends on the edge lengths: unrestricted instances admit no constant-factor approximation unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, metric instances admit Christofides' $3/2$-approximation, and fixed-dimensional Euclidean instances admit a PTAS. We study $\beta$-TSP, where the edge lengths satisfy $ \ell_{uw}\leq\beta(\ell_{uv}+\ell_{vw}) \qquad \forall\,u,v,w\in V\ \text{pairwise distinct}, \quad \beta\in\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]. $ The condition arises naturally in various settings, for example, when metric travel times are combined with positive service times at the vertices. The previous best approximation algorithm, due to B\"ockenhauer et al., ranges from $1$ at $\beta=1/2$ to $3/2$ as $\beta$ approaches $1$. We obtain a strictly better guarantee for every $1/2<\beta<1$ by combining two simple constructions whose guarantees counterbalance each other. We also improve the best known approximation hardness bound for every $1/2<\beta<1$.

The approximability of TSP changes substantially as additional structure is imposed on the edge lengths. With unrestricted lengths, no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation exists unless P=NP\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}. papers.title: Absence of Excited Bound States for All Fibers of the Fr\"ohlich Polaron at Weak Coupling
papers.abstract: We study the discrete spectrum of the three-dimensional Fr\"ohlich polaron at weak coupling and fixed total momentum. We prove that, for sufficiently small coupling and every total momentum $0<|\xi|\le 1/4$, the ground-state eigenvalue is the only eigenvalue below the essential spectrum. Our proof builds on the analogous zero-momentum result of Seiringer (2023). Combined with that result and the work of Dahlbaek (2017), this implies that, at sufficiently weak coupling, no fiber Hamiltonian has a discrete excited eigenvalue.

papers.title: Multiscale Closing Index (MCI) for measuring structural similarity between 2D point sets
papers.abstract: We introduce Multi-scale Closing Index (MCI), a new dissimilarity measure for evaluating the alignment of two 2D point sets. MCI is bounded between 0 and 1 and is based on multiscale mathematical morphology operations, with smaller values indicating greater structural agreement. The measure was motivated by the need to assess the quality of registration between point sets representing cell populations in biological images. To evaluate its behaviour under controlled conditions, we generated synthetic point clouds from Perlin-noise-based spatial structures, following established approaches for simulating biologically plausible spatial organization. We assessed MCI between those point clouds and different transformed versions, obtained by local perturbation, point removal, translation, rotation and addition of impulsive noise. Across these experiments, the dissimilarity MCI increased gradually and consistently with perturbation severity, while showing a clear discontinuity between clouds originating from the same underlying spatial structure and point clouds generated from different structures. We further compared MCI with commonly used point-set distances, including Hausdorff-based measures and Sliced Wasserstein distance. These experiments show the ability of MCI to capture structural agreement and quantify deviations between point sets, highlighting its potential as a complementary metric for evaluating two-dimensional point-set registration.

Point-set registration aims to align two or more point sets by estimating correspondences and a spatial transformation that brings them into agreement [30, 14, 19]. It is widely used in computer vision, robotics, medical imaging, and spatial data analysis, but remains challenging in the presence of noise, outliers, missing points, partial overlap, and heterogeneous sampling.

It is widely used in computer vision, robotics, medical imaging, and spatial data analysis, but remains challenging in the presence of noise, outliers, missing points, partial overlap, and heterogeneous sampling.

Evaluating the quality of an alignment is itself nontrivial because different measures capture different notions of disagreement. Nearest-neighbour distances quantify local geometric error, whereas distributional distances characterize the displacement of the point sets more globally. More elaborate kernel, probabilistic, graph-based, or correspondence-based criteria also exist, but many are designed as components of the registration procedure itself rather than as simple post-registration similarity measures. Here, we focus on three complementary references for already aligned 2D point sets.

papers.title: Rigid continua containing an arbitrary Peano continuum
papers.abstract:
Bani\v c and Kac, and later \v Crepnjak and Kac, constructed an uncountable family of continua with different types of rigidity. For every continuum $X$ with the mentioned property, the inverse limit $\varprojlim\{X,f_n\}$ is homeomorphic to $X$ for an arbitrary sequence of continuous surjective functions $f_n: X \to X$.
  We extend these results by proving that for any Peano continuum $X$ there exists an uncountable family ${\cal F}$ of rigid, for each positive integer $m$, $\frac{1}{m}$-rigid, and $0$-rigid continua such that each $Y \in {\cal F}$ contains a homeomorphic copy of $X$ and for each $Y \in {\cal F}$ it holds that the inverse limit $\varprojlim\{Y,f_n\}$ is homeomorphic to $Y$ for arbitrarily sequence of continuous surjective functions $f_n: Y \to Y$.

papers.title: Adaptive Data Analysis and Adversarial Robustness on Insertion-Deletion Streams
papers.abstract: Classical streaming algorithms and statistical mechanisms frequently fail when future inputs or queries depend adaptively on prior outputs. In this work, we resolve central open questions in both adaptive data analysis (ADA) and adversarially robust turnstile streaming by introducing a unified hierarchical estimator-corrector-learner framework. For adaptive data analysis over an unrestricted domain, we design a randomized mechanism that answers $k$ adaptively chosen statistical queries to within additive error $\alpha$ using $\tilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\alpha^2})$ samples, nearly matching the lower bounds of Hardt and Ullman [FOCS 2014] and Steinke and Ullman [COLT 2015] while improving upon the classic $\tilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha^2})$ bound of Dwork et al. [STOC 2015] and Bassily et al. [STOC 2016]. For known finite domains $U$, we combine our mechanism with private multiplicative weights to improve the sample complexity to $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^2}+ \min\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha}, \frac{\sqrt{\log |U|}}{\alpha^2}\right)\right)$. Building on our ADA mechanism, we construct a fixed linear sketch with a stateful decoder that answers $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ adaptive $F_2$ moment estimation queries to within a $(1\pm\epsilon)$-multiplicative factor using $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ bits of space. Finally, by embedding this sketch into a binary-tree recursion, we obtain the first nearly space-optimal adversarially robust algorithm for $F_2$ estimation on insertion-deletion streams. Our algorithm uses $\tilde O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ bits of space, improving upon the $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^4})$ bound of Gribelyuk et al. [STOC 2026] and matching the insertion-only bound of Woodruff and Zhou [FOCS 2021]. This demonstrates that no asymptotic space overhead in $\epsilon$ is required to achieve adversarial robustness in the turnstile model.

papers.intro:
Over the past three decades, the streaming model has emerged as a central paradigm for studying algorithms which process massive amounts of data. Specifically, updates to an underlying dataset arrive sequentially, and the task of the algorithm is to maintain a compact summary (or a sketch) which supports dynamic updates and allows the user to recover various statistics about the dataset. Typically, the algorithm is only given a single pass over the data stream and must use space which is sublinear in both the universe size nn and stream length mm. As the streaming model effectively captures data-processing pipelines in practical systems, there have been numerous works aimed at achieving optimal space streaming algorithms for a variety of problems.

It is a core assumption in the design and analysis of randomized algorithms that the input sequence is fixed in advance and independent of the internal parameters of the algorithm. However, in many applications, the intermediate responses of the algorithm may influence the distribution of future inputs to the system. For example, optimization procedures update intermediate iterates based on prior estimates, future queries to a database often depend on previous query outputs, and investors respond to changes in financial markets, which in turn shape future transactions. A special case of this paradigm is studied in adaptive data analysis, where a randomized mechanism is given a sample of i.i.d. points from an unknown distribution before the query sequence arrives, and the task of the algorithm is to return an accurate estimate for the population mean of each query ftf_{t} on the underlying distribution, where queries may depend adaptively on prior estimates. While a common technique in the non-adaptive setting would be to return the empirical average of the sample points, an adaptive analyst can select queries which overfit to the sample, causing a significant deviation from the population mean. Likewise, the correctness analyses of classical streaming algorithms are completely invalidated when the update sequence may depend on the internal random bits (or sample points) used by the algorithm, necessitating the development of new approaches to reason about and ensure correctness. To this end, our work focuses on both settings simultaneously, developing techniques which are broadly applicable to both adaptive data analysis and adversarial streaming. Next, we describe each problem setting and motivation separately, beginning with the adversarially robust streaming model.

papers.title: Marginal-Nonuniform Multiclass Learning
papers.abstract: We study the problem of multiclass classification within the framework of marginal-nonuniform learning, where the constants in the learning rate may depend on the unknown marginal distribution generating the unlabeled data, but not on the target concept. This notion naturally lies between classical PAC learning, where the constants are independent of both the marginal distribution and the target concept, and more recent universal learning, where the constants may depend on both. We give a complete characterization of the optimal marginal-nonuniform learning rates, establishing a fundamental trichotomy: exponential, linear, and arbitrarily slow rates. This characterization is witnessed by a new combinatorial dimension, termed the uncentered DS-eluder dimension. A key ingredient in the upper-bound proofs is a set of new distributional exhaustion lemmas that exploit the sequential nature of this dimension and may be of independent interest.

papers.intro:
A fundamental question in statistical learning theory is to determine when finite samples suffice for reliable prediction on unseen data. The classical PAC (probably approximately correct) model (Valiant, 1984; Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971) provides a foundational formalization of this question. In the binary setting, the VC dimension gives an exact combinatorial characterization of learnability. In its standard form, the PAC guarantee is uniform: the same learning rate must hold simultaneously for all target concepts in a concept class and all marginal distributions over the domain. This uniform perspective yields a clean worst-case theory of learnability, but does not distinguish between marginal distributions that may be easy or hard for a given class.

A fundamental question in statistical learning theory is to determine when finite samples suffice for reliable prediction on unseen data. The classical PAC (probably approximately correct) model (Valiant, 1984; Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971) provides a foundational formalization of this question. In the binary setting, the VC dimension gives an exact combinatorial characterization of learnability. In its standard form, the PAC guarantee is uniform: the same learning rate must hold simultaneously for all target concepts in a concept class and all marginal distributions over the domain. This uniform perspective yields a clean worst-case theory of learnability, but does not distinguish between marginal distributions that may be easy or hard for a given class.

In this work, we study such a distribution-dependent framework in the context of multiclass PAC learning, called marginal-nonuniform learning (Ben-David et al., 1995; Hanneke et al., 2025a). This notion lies between classical uniform PAC learning and the more recent framework of universal learning (Bousquet et al., 2021). In universal learning, the constants in the error rate may depend on both the marginal distribution and the target concept. In marginal-nonuniform learning, by contrast, the rate may depend on the marginal distribution generating the data, but once this marginal is fixed, the guarantee must hold uniformly over all target concepts in the class.

In marginal-nonuniform learning, by contrast, the rate may depend on the marginal distribution generating the data, but once this marginal is fixed, the guarantee must hold uniformly over all target concepts in the class.

One natural setting where such guarantees arise is when data are collected before the prediction task is fully specified. For example, a medical center may gather a large repository of radiology images, while the eventual task may later be chosen as detecting an abnormality, identifying its location, or classifying the subtype or severity of a disease. The question is then how many labeled examples suffice to ensure accurate learning once the target labeling rule is specified.11 1 Note that this setting is distinct from semi-supervised learning, as we study solely labeled sample complexity under a fixed marginal distribution. Uniform PAC guarantees may be overly pessimistic when the marginal distribution has benign structure, such as concentration near a low-dimensional manifold. Fully universal guarantees, on the other hand, may be too fine-grained for deciding in advance how much data is needed, since they can depend on the eventual target concept. Marginal-nonuniform guarantees capture a natural middle ground: the sample complexity may depend on the data distribution, but not on the target concept.

(1995), who studied learnability under all four choices of uniform versus nonuniform dependence on concepts and marginal distributions (see Definition 1). The complementary notion of concept-nonuniform learning, where the rate may depend on the target concept while remaining uniform over all marginals, goes back to Benedek and Itai (1988). Recently, the possible error rates in the marginal-nonuniform regime were characterized in the binary case (Hanneke et al., 2025a), which we extend to multiclass in this work.

papers.title: PhoPunct: A Large-Scale Benchmark of Transformer Architectures for Vietnamese Punctuation Restoration
papers.abstract: Vietnamese punctuation restoration is often evaluated on relatively small benchmarks, limiting conclusions about how architectural choices scale with data volume. We present a controlled benchmark on News and Novels corpora containing 22.1 million labeled tokens (19.9M News and 2.2M Novels). We evaluate 17 architectures formed from four pretrained Transformer backbones and optional bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) and conditional random field (CRF) layers, together with a PhoBERT-large-Bi-LSTM-CRF model, PhoPunct. Every model is trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and without architecture-specific tuning. Under this fixed budget, adding Bi-LSTM and CRF layers does not reliably improve macro F1: in seven of eight matched domain-backbone comparisons, a plain Transformer classifier matches or outperforms its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart. PhoPunct obtains the best News result (61.35), whereas XLM-R with a CRF obtains the best Novels result (50.18), exceeding PhoPunct (48.97). These results show that the value of recurrent and structured-prediction heads depends on their optimization regime and motivate explicit separation between architectural improvements and improvements due to architecture-specific tuning. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/aisia-research-lab/PhoPunct

papers.intro:
Punctuation restoration recovers punctuation marks from unpunctuated text. It is an important post-processing step for automatic speech recognition (ASR), where output is commonly produced without reliable punctuation, and it also supports readability, text normalization, and downstream language processing. The task is typically formulated as word-level sequence labeling: given a sequence of lexical tokens, a model predicts the punctuation mark that follows each token or predicts that no mark is present.

Recent systems use contextual representations from pretrained Transformers and may add recurrent or structured-prediction layers. For Vietnamese, Tran et al. (2021) evaluated multilingual BERT, XLM-R, and Vietnamese-specific pretrained encoders on News and Novels data. Related Vietnamese work has also examined an earlier CRF-based approach (Pham et al., 2019), deep neural punctuation prediction (Pham et al., 2020), and joint capitalization and punctuation recovery (Uyen et al., 2022). These studies establish the effectiveness of pretrained encoders, but the effect of adding a Bi-LSTM or CRF on top of such encoders remains unclear, especially when architectures are compared under the same optimization budget.

(2021), excluding synthetic augmentation. We evaluate 17 architectures under an identical eight-epoch schedule and a single learning rate for all parameters. Second, it evaluates four pretrained backbones with Plain, Bi-LSTM, CRF, and Bi-LSTM–CRF prediction heads, together with PhoPunct, a PhoBERT-large–Bi-LSTM–CRF model. Third, it identifies a practically important negative result: under the shared budget, recurrent and structured-prediction layers do not consistently improve macro F1. This finding makes the optimization of newly initialized components a central experimental variable rather than an implementation detail.

papers.title: The Sparse-Complement Conjecture for Two Distinct Eigenvalues
papers.abstract: For a graph $G$, let $q(G)$ be the minimum number of distinct eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix whose off-diagonal zero--nonzero pattern is $G$. We prove that $q(G)=2$ whenever the complement $H=\overline G$ of a graph of order $n\ge3$ has at most $n-3$ edges, resolving the sparse-complement conjecture of Fallat and Mojallal. If $H$ contains a cycle, the proof constructs a nontrivial orthogonal projector with the strong spectral property and rank at most $|E(F)|-|V(F)|+4$, where $F$ is the union of the cyclic components of $H$. The construction combines faithful stress-free Gram representations, a one-coordinate lift for each excess core edge, exact orthogonal-frame completion, and a Stiefel-manifold pendant-extension argument.

papers.title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
papers.abstract: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

papers.intro:
As AI-generated content has become increasingly widespread within contemporary information ecologies, there has been a simultaneous proliferation of AI detection practices, both formal and informal. Discourses and practices of AI identification have become an everyday part of how people interact with texts: from tools to help teachers determine the authorship of an essay to Redditors helping someone figure out if their aunt’s new online boyfriend is true love or a romance scam. Despite the fact that detection studies in controlled environments show that untrained human raters typically perform near chance in distinguishing AI-generated from human-generated text (Clark et al., 2021; Jakesch et al., 2023; Ippolito et al., 2020; Dugan et al., 2023; Fleckenstein et al., 2024; Porter and Machery, 2024; Russell et al., 2025), folk theories, practices, and discourses of AI identification flourish, both online and off, and there seems to be a widespread sense that there exists a recognizable, describable AI ‘‘voice’’ or ‘‘accent’’: a way of writing that is distinctly ‘‘AI-esque’’ or ‘‘AI-y’’, on account of being full of ‘‘AI-isms’’ and ‘‘AI stuff’’11 1 All of these descriptors are direct quotations from our study participants..

Associations, accurate or not, between form and context are not unique to AI. Research in linguistic anthropology and sociolinguistics has long demonstrated how people make inferences about speakers based on the formal features of their speech and these indexical inferences, regardless of accuracy, can in turn spur evaluations of the trustworthiness and value of both the speaker and the utterance itself (Agha, 1998; Eckert, 2000; Irvine, 2002; Johnstone and Kiesling, 2008; Mendoza-Denton, 2002; Bourhis and Giles, 1976). Thus, to understand communication–when, and why, it succeeds or breaks down–in this contemporary moment, it is imperative to take these folk discourses seriously and further our understanding of how, when, and why people flag writing as AI-generated in real-world encounters.

We find that the cited motivations for AI identifications are diverse, but also often contradictory. Types of evidence range from discrete textual features, judgments about content, inferences about the author, and circular appeals to an “AI-like” quality; and the two communities contradict each other in ways that reflect their own sociolinguistic norms (e.g., students read neutrality and lack of emotion as AI, while Wikipedia editors read enthusiasm and promotional tone as AI) (RQ1). The justifications editors use to flag something as AI are shortening over time, and a growing share of editors in later months only cite an external community noticeboard rather than naming any feature of the text at all (RQ2). Finally, some students interpreted the statement “this feels very chatgpt” as a dismissal or chastisement of an interlocutor’s stance or behavior, rather than an observation about the text itself (EA1).

papers.title: KnowEvo: Knowledge Evolution for Protein Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in scientific discovery, yet systematically accumulating and refining reusable scientific knowledge remains challenging. Existing approaches primarily improve LLM-based problem solving through parameter optimization or feedback-driven refinement of prompts, programs, and solution trajectories, leaving acquired expertise either embedded in model weights or scattered across iterative problem-solving processes. As a result,knowledge is difficult to systematically inspect, evaluate, and refine. We propose KnowEvo, a framework that treats externalized knowledge itself as the optimization target. Our key insight is that scientific knowledge is inherently modular: multiple interacting mechanisms jointly determine the design outcomes. This makes knowledge evolution fundamentally challenging, as improvements cannot be attributed to individual components in isolation. To address this, KnowEvo represents knowledge as executable expertise blocks and organizes their refinements into strategy mutation trees, enabling structured exploration over a combinatorial knowledge space. The framework combines a Thompson-style forward allocation strategy that adaptively distributes evaluation budgets across strategy variants with a backward revision process, in which a code agent operates in an isolated sandbox to translate rollout evidence into localized program updates. This design enables persistent accumulation, evaluation, and refinement of mechanistic expertise across iterative experimentation. We evaluate KnowEvo on protein optimization tasks including stability and solubility. Results show that knowledge evolution consistently improves over initial strategy blocks and outperforms monolithic program evolution and prior LLM-guided evolution baselines across metrics such as pass@k, MRR, MAP,and NDCG@5. Code is available at https://github.com/recynie/KnowEvo.

Scientific discovery is inherently iterative. In domains such as protein engineering, progress depends not only on generating candidate solutions, but also on accumulating, revising, and reusing knowledge across repeated rounds of experimentation. Human experts rarely solve such tasks through isolated reasoning alone; instead, they progressively refine mechanistic heuristics from experimental feedback and reuse them in future design decisions.

papers.title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
papers.abstract: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

papers.title: Reconciling European Electricity Data with Diffusion Priors Learned from Observations Alone
papers.abstract: The ENTSO-E Transparency Platform publishes generation, load, and cross-border power flows for European bidding zones. The values carry undocumented errors and violate energy conservation, and data reconciliation consists in correcting them to satisfy that balance. In this work, we formulate data reconciliation as Bayesian inference. Classical methods implicitly take a uniform prior, which we replace with a diffusion model estimated from the observations alone by empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. The resulting posterior is sampled with a guided process whose projection step makes every sample satisfy the balance exactly. On synthetic systems of six to thirty-five bidding zones, built from ENTSO-E resource-adequacy data, the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation, increasingly so as the system grows. Its credible intervals are calibrated or conservative, and it remains the most accurate under a misspecified noise covariance. Finally, when the generation of entire zones goes unreported, the classical methods fail while the learned prior recovers it from cross-zone structure.

papers.intro:
Monitoring, planning, and operating electricity systems requires accurate data on generation, load, and cross-border power flows, a need the European Union answered by requiring their publication through the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform, established in 2015 under Regulation (EU) No 543/2013 [1]. The platform reports for every bidding zone the generation by fuel type, the electrical load, and the physical flow on each border. The values are communicated by the transmission system operators (TSOs), who meter large units and interconnections, while the load is derived from generation and exchanges [1]. The quality of the values varies across TSOs and reported quantities [2, 3, 4], and no TSO documents the uncertainty of the submitted data. In practice, we observe that, at any hour, the reported generation and imports of a zone do not balance its reported load and exports, with residuals sometimes reaching thousands of megawatts. We call these reported values observations. The state is the same quantities free of reporting errors and satisfying energy conservation.

papers.title: Future-Informed Actor-Critic
papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods optimize a parametrized policy using a critic to estimate their policy gradient. Recent work has shown that conditioning the critic on features of future states, actions, or rewards can improve sample efficiency and even final return. However, existing methods are restricted to exogenous features (independent of actions), overlooking endogenous features (dependent on actions) that may be crucial for credit assignment. We introduce the future-informed value function, which can be conditioned on both exogenous and endogenous features of future states, actions, and rewards. Then, we express the policy gradient using this value function, yielding the future-informed policy gradient. Building on that, we propose the future-informed actor-critic algorithm. Empirical results show that this algorithm leveraging endogenous features of the future outperforms standard actor-critic algorithms in environments with noisy and sparse rewards.

papers.intro:
A central component of actor-critic (AC) methods is the critic, a function approximator of a value function that allows reducing the variance of policy-gradient (PG) estimates at the price of an estimation bias. Since the critic is only used during training, it can be conditioned on privileged information available during training, a method known as asymmetric actor-critic. Under partial observability, this privileged information is usually the state of the environment (Pinto et al., 2018; Baisero and Amato, 2022; Ebi et al., 2025). This method has contributed to several recent successes of RL, such as tokamak plasma control (Degrave et al., 2022), drone racing (Kaufmann et al., 2023), car racing (Vasco et al., 2024), and table tennis (Dürr et al., 2026). Alternatively, Mesnard et al. (2021) and Sinclair et al. (2023) condition a critic on features of future states and rewards. They empirically demonstrate improvements in return or sample efficiency in some environments. To ensure unbiased policy gradients, these methods restrict the privileged information to exogenous features (independent of actions). Instead of conditioning a critic on future information, hindsight credit assignment methods (Harutyunyan et al., 2019; Meulemans et al., 2023; Ramesh et al., 2026) reweight rewards by a ratio measuring the dependence of a future state or the return on the action taken. Their empirical results show that endogenous information (dependent on actions) is valuable for credit assignment. To our knowledge, no existing method uses a critic conditioned on endogenous features to estimate the policy gradient. The closest work is from Guez et al. (2020), who learn an uninformed critic that takes only the history as input and an informed critic that takes the history and a window of future states. Both are trained by minimizing a multi-step TD loss. An auxiliary loss trains the uninformed critic to generate the same features from the history as the informed critic. Only the uninformed critic is used in the PG estimate.

papers.title: Spin to Orbital Angular Momentum Conversion in the Neutron Nucleus Weak Interaction
papers.abstract: The neutron nucleus weak interaction generates a small parity non conserving rotation of the neutron spin as the neutron moves through matter. This parity-odd neutron rotary power can reach up to 2.2e-3 rad * cm-1 for slow neutrons in 139La, which possesses a p-wave resonance at 0.7 eV where the parity-odd asymmetry is greatly amplified. This spin rotation must conserve total angular momentum. Here we show that this conservation occurs through neutron orbital angular momentum generation. We experimentally demonstrate that a neutron prepared initially in a longitudinal spin-orbit state experiences no change in total angular momentum.

papers.title: On a Problem of Gordon and Hughes: The 11-adic Properties of Meromorphic Modular Functions on $\mathrm{X}_0(22)$
papers.abstract: Congruence families occur throughout the theory of modular forms. These families superficially resemble one another, though they can vary substantially in their overall difficulty. One major complication resides in the topology of the modular curve associated with a given congruence family. All previously studied families are associated with curves of genus 0 or 1. The existence of a family associated with a curve of genus 2 (and the associated difficulties of a proof thereof) was first speculated upon by Gordon and Hughes. We give the first explicit congruence family associated with $\mathrm{X}_0(22)$, a modular curve of genus 2, and prove it. We also propose two families of conjectures associated with the same modular curve.

papers.title: Regime change in a model for political opinion dynamics
papers.abstract: Political crises involving a series of violent events are the rule rather than the exception in history. Here, we use a minimal opinion dynamics model to describe regime change as a contested transition between dominant shared ideas in a society. New opinions spread with a cumulative advantage, and agents do not return to opinions they held before, resulting in recurrent boom-and-bust dynamics without tuned parameters. During a transition, opinion changes grow approximately exponentially and then saturate in the finite system, declining approximately linearly as spreading is limited by the shrinking interfaces between opinion groups. We compare qualitative features of these transitions with historical data of political violence, used as an empirical proxy for contested transitions. A permutation test shows that violent events cluster in time in the dense Chinese and US records. Around their peaks, violent events rise in an accelerating way and then decline; in the Chinese data, the decline is consistent with the approximately linear decline in the model. We also use a fragmentation measure that serves as an early warning signal for transitions in the model. Overall, the patterns in the empirical data and the dynamical behavior of the model could contribute to a better understanding of long-term historical processes.

By regime change we mean the replacement of a dominant shared idea in a society, such as a ruling elite, a dynasty or a political order, by a new one. Such transitions are typically contested: competing ideas confront each other until one prevails. Political violence is one observable proxy for this contest, but not the same thing: regimes have changed without large-scale violence, and violence has occurred without a change of regime. Mathematically, one can model this common idea as an opinion. In this article, we will use an opinion dynamics approach to modeling the patterns of shifts in shared ideas and phases of societal discord, and subsequently relate the model dynamics to the observed patterns of political violence in the empirical data. Note that there is a difference between the opinion of an individual and the shared ideas in a society as a whole. Groups act as an important structural layer, which can compete in non-violent exchange of views and ideas. However, competition can also occur violently as shown in the empirical data of group-level conflicts within a state in Fig 1. These are the mechanisms that we aim to represent in an agent-based mathematical model of opinion dynamics.

What spreads in the model can be interpreted in terms of elites, which is motivated in the following. The important role of elites in a society dates back to classical elite theory [12, 13, 14] and is supported empirically [15, 16, 17]. Turchin and colleagues argue that intra-elite conflict is an essential factor for major political transitions and violent conflict [5, 6]. During stable periods, a large support for a specific elite group dominates the political landscape, and a common idea is shared among society. During unstable periods, different elite groups are in conflict with each other, challenging older ideas with potentially violent uprising. A political opinion in this sense is much more dividing than, for example, the preference for one of several democratic parties, and the relevant timescales are inter-generational rather than electoral. Opinion spreading can therefore be read as elites being replaced by new elites. Mathematically, it is the same in the model whether an agent changes its opinion or is replaced by a new agent holding that opinion, and replacement may well be the dominant process on long inter-generational time scales: fundamental political views develop in the early years of an individual and are mostly not altered afterwards in their professional life, known as the impressionable years hypothesis [18, 19].

papers.title: Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.

An ideal method would turn more compute into better results steadily. We study tasks where a verifier can score every attempt and only the best solution matters. Many tasks for coding agents have this form (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025) because a scorer can check each attempt automatically and only the fastest kernel or the finished proof matters. The first is best-of-NN sampling, one of the strongest methods when a verifier is available (Chen et al., 2021; Cobbe et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2024). It runs NN independent agents and keeps the one with the highest score. Yet best-of-NN over individual agents saturates quickly. In our experiments, 50 agents already reach 81% to 100% of the gain that 100 agents reach.

We introduce parallel agent teams, which combine the two by applying best-of-NN to independent small teams of collaborating agents (Figure 1a). A simple statistical model of best-of-NN explains why parallel small teams win. The expected best of several samples is the mean score of one sample plus a gain from variance, which grows with the number of samples the budget buys. Parallel agents collect the largest gain from variance because they draw the most samples, but each agent has a low mean. One big team has a high mean, but it is a single sample and wastes the gain from variance, and a larger team does not guarantee a higher mean. Parallel small teams balance the two. Each team has a much higher mean than an agent, and several teams still collect most of the gain from variance. They also keep improving as the budget grows. At a given budget they draw fewer samples than parallel agents because each team costs several agents, so their best-of-NN curve is still on its steep early part, where each additional sample raises the best result the most.

papers.title: PhotoFinish: Portable Timerless Probing of Microarchitectural Latencies
papers.abstract: Timing measurements are a fundamental building block of microarchitectural attacks, enabling software to convert otherwise invisible latency differences into architectural observations. Thus, restricting high-resolution timers is a common defense, especially in constrained environments such as web browsers. Timerless probing primitives provide an alternative approach. Instead of reading or constructing a timer, they observe architectural events that correlate with the microarchitectural state. However, such primitives typically rely on platform-specific behavior, and none generalizes across the wider computing landscape. In this paper, we present PhotoFinish, a portable timerless probing primitive that converts latency differences directly into an architectural value. PhotoFinish races an operation under test against a fixed reference in two parallel threads that then write unique values to the same shared location, resulting in a latency-dependent architectural value. PhotoFinish only requires parallel execution and shared memory, without constructing or reading a clock. We evaluate PhotoFinish on 38 CPUs spanning four ISAs and demonstrate reliable cache state classification across widely different microarchitectures, with comparable fidelity when compiled to WebAssembly and executed inside a browser. We further use PhotoFinish in AES T-table and Evict+Reload attacks, show that it applies beyond caches to TLB and execution-engine latencies, and demonstrate sufficient precision to identify the LLC slice of an address. Our results demonstrate shared-memory races as a generic and precise replacement for explicit timing, showing that restricting timers alone does not prevent software from observing fine-grained microarchitectural latency differences.

papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
papers.intro:
In nature, manipulation draws on general intelligence. Animals can recruit their memory, reasoning, and problem-solving faculties when interacting with objects, with cognitive processes continuing to shape action as it unfolds [1, 2, 3]. In robotics, much recent work has focused on models specialized for robot control, including vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), trained or fine-tuned on robot demonstrations [4, 5].

In nature, manipulation draws on general intelligence. Animals can recruit their memory, reasoning, and problem-solving faculties when interacting with objects, with cognitive processes continuing to shape action as it unfolds [1, 2, 3]. In robotics, much recent work has focused on models specialized for robot control, including vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), trained or fine-tuned on robot demonstrations [4, 5].

Generalist AI models have also been applied to manipulation, often through skill orchestration or offline program synthesis. In the first setting (skill orchestration), the model selects and sequences low-level skills such as grasping and placing [6, 7, 8]. It can revise the plan as new observations arrive, but the available skills limit the generalist model’s control authority and the granularity at which it can command the manipulator. Since the generalist model’s interactions with the world are mediated by the provided skills, it is constrained by the skills’ limitations. In the second setting (offline program synthesis, sometimes known as ‘code-as-policies’), the model writes a control program before execution [9, 10, 11, 12]. The program can incorporate perception and feedback, but the generalist model is not in the loop and cannot reconsider the overall control strategy as the task unfolds.

However, spatial cognition has been advancing [14, 15], with recent models demonstrating convincing spatial planning, sensorimotor coordination, and embodied fluid intelligence [16, 17]. These advances make a third approach increasingly viable: the generalist model remains in the control loop and commands the manipulator directly, revising its actions as the task unfolds [18, 19, 20, 21]. We refer to this category as Agentic Manipulation Policies (AMPs).

We document emergent behaviors that arise as the agent brings its broader cognitive faculties to bear on manipulation. When a book lies flat on a table and cannot be grasped as is, the agent pushes it to the table edge to expose a graspable surface. When a target object is hidden, the agent moves occluding objects out of the way to find it. When a large fruit is too wide to grasp, the agent pins it against a heavier object, slides the gripper underneath, and lifts it like a forklift. Failed actions can themselves supply information: the agent infers an unseen shelf from a blocked motion and changes its grasp and approach. On the real robot, the agent diagnoses camera calibration errors from discrepancies between commanded and observed motion, then compensates for them in subsequent actions. None of these behaviors are specified in the prompt or supplied as skills in the harness. The generalist model develops them within each episode by reasoning about geometry, contact, and the consequences of its own actions.

We also investigate few-shot and continual learning from the agent’s own experience. We equip AMP1 with a persistent memory, allowing the agent to record useful observations, strategies, and code after reflecting on its successes and failures. Experience accumulates in this memory bank, while the model’s weights remain fixed. No expert demonstrations or gradient updates are required. We evaluate this approach on the 42 bimanual manipulation tasks of RoboDojo [25]. Practicing individual tasks raises the success rate on unseen layouts from 26.4% to 84.1%, above all entries on the benchmark’s leaderboard. We also test whether the agent can accumulate knowledge across tasks via continual learning. In this setting, the agent attempts each task once, in sequence, and updates its memory representation in the course of this continual deployment. A single pass through the tasks more than doubles the success rate, to 57.6%. Learning transfers to tasks not yet attempted without erasing gains on tasks already encountered. Experience improves efficiency as well: an agent with memory uses about 35% fewer model calls in comparison to zero-shot deployment.

We conduct controlled experiments to isolate the effects of the model, its reasoning effort, and the harness’s perception and motion interfaces. The choice of model has the largest effect. For example, AMP1’s success rate on RoboLab-120 is 82.8% with Opus 5.5, 51.6% with Haiku 5.5, and 35.2% with Opus 4.5. More reasoning helps all evaluated models. The value of additional harness support depends on the model. Weaker models are helped by assistive grasping and placing routines, while stronger models perform best without these routines. Stronger models also cope better with missing sensory information. With the AMP1 harness, Opus 5.5 achieves a success rate of 82.8% with full sensory input, 81.1% without direct depth input, and 75.8% without depth or camera calibration. While the overall success rate does not suffer much, sensory impairment takes a toll on efficiency. The agent routes around limited sensory input by reconstructing 3D points via triangulation across views and, when needed, estimates camera calibration from images taken at known gripper poses. The mean number of model calls per episode rises from 34.8 with full sensory input to 46.3 without direct depth input and 53.5 without depth or camera calibration. A weaker model cannot compensate for impoverished perception: the success rate of AMP1 with Haiku 5.5 on RoboLab-120 collapses from 51.6% with full sensory input to 10.7% without depth or camera calibration. Our experiments also indicate that replacing visual input with textual descriptions has a sharply detrimental effect, for example cutting the success rate of AMP1 with Opus 5.5 from 82.8% to 36.8%; this contrasts with prior work, which recommended replacing visual input with textual descriptions [18].

papers.title: Permutation order governs basin entropy in critical one-input Boolean networks
papers.abstract: Basin entropy measures uncertainty about a network's long-term behavior. For every critical one-input synchronous Boolean network with $m$ relevant nodes, we show that the permutation structure induced by its feedback loops determines basin entropy, up to a universal error. Although the loops oscillate independently, their relative phases can be offset, producing a deviation from additivity that can grow linearly in $m$. Yet at the ensemble level, a previously derived additive prediction is preserved through the first subleading term, with the discrepancy appearing at order $\ln m\ln\ln m$.

papers.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
