papers.intro:
Many multimodal tasks require more than direct visual recognition. Visual mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and expert-level multimodal exams often require a VLM to inspect visual details, combine them with textual context, and perform multi-step inference [15, 27, 41, 39]. Reasoning traces have therefore become an important mechanism for improving model accuracy on complex inputs. Chain-of-thought and related reasoning methods have shown strong gains in language models [29, 28, 38, 7, 11], and recent VLMs extend this idea by training models to produce explicit intermediate reasoning before answering visual problems [32, 37, 6, 40, 25, 36].

Many multimodal tasks require more than direct visual recognition. However, always using slow reasoning is inefficient. Many practical VLM inputs can be answered by direct recognition, short visual grounding, or simple text-image matching. The key observation of this work is that offline adaptive thinking is not merely a problem of controlling response length, but a dual-reference optimization problem. Fast direct answers and slow reasoning traces are often generated by distinct behavior policies: concise answers may come from an instruct or no-think policy, while reasoning traces may come from a thinking or chain-of-thought policy. This matters for offline reward optimization. BOLT decouples response generation from optimization and projects a prompt-normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution through weighted next-token training [23]. We propose DR-BOLT, an offline optimization framework for adaptive VLM thinking. Instead of treating direct answers and reasoning traces as two styles sampled from one policy, our method models them as samples from two behavior policies and optimizes under a fast/slow mixture reference. papers.title: Isomorphisms and representations of noncommutative function algebras
papers.abstract: Let $V$ be a noncommutative (NC) variety in a NC operator ball. We study the dual operator algebra $H^\infty(V)$ of bounded NC functions on $V$, and the operator algebra $A(V)$ obtained as the closure of NC polynomials in $H^\infty(V)$. We identify the space of weak-$*$ continuous finite-dimensional representations of $H^\infty(V)$ as the similarity envelope $\widetilde{V}$ of $V$, and equip $\widetilde{V}$ with a metric which turns $\widetilde{V}$ into a complete invariant for $H^\infty(V)$, in the sense that $H^\infty(V)$ is weak-$*$ continuously isomorphic to $H^\infty(W)$ if and only if $\widetilde{V}$ and $\widetilde{W}$ are NC biholomorphic via a bi-Lipschitz map. Similar results are obtained in the completely bounded category as well as for the algebras $A(V)$ when $V$ is assumed homogeneous. In the case of homogeneous varieties $V$ and $W$, we obtain a sharper classification result, by which $H^\infty(V)$ is (completely) boundedly isomorphic to $H^\infty(W)$ if and only if there is a linear map which gives a bi-Lipschitz bijection between $\widetilde{W}$ and $\widetilde{V}$. The reduction to the linear case in the generality we work in depends on showing that the existence of maps implies the existence of origin-fixing maps, which we show using a novel ``two-circle trick" of independent interest. In the important case where the varieties are the full NC operator balls we find a striking rigidity phenomenon: if $A(B_E)$ and $A(B_F)$ are completely boundedly isomorphic then $E$ and $F$ are completely isometric. We also present a variety of examples illustrating the results and their sharpness, showing how several results from the literature fail to generalize to the setting studied here.

papers.intro:
A pervasive theme in operator algebra since the early development of the field has been the construction of operator algebras that encode a particular mathematical object, and the subsequent study of the relationship between the algebra and the underlying structure. Examples include the von Neumann algebra of a group or of a measurable action on a space, full and reduced group C*-algebras, and graph C*-algebras. The quintessential example is the algebra C⁡(X)C(X) of continuous functions on a compact Hausdorff space. By Gelfand theory, we know that C⁡(X)C(X) and C⁡(Y)C(Y) are isomorphic as algebras if and only if XX is homeomorphic to YY. In fact, the isomorphisms C⁡(X)→C⁡(Y)C(X)\to C(Y) are precisely the maps f↦f∘hf\mapsto f\circ h induced by homeomorphisms h:Y→Xh:Y\to X. This, in itself, is a beautiful example of a categorical equivalence, but combined with Gelfand’s characterization of commutative C*-algebras, it hints at something deeper: every operator algebra can be viewed as an algebra of “functions” on some “space”. This opens the door to the paradigms of noncommutative analysis and noncommutative geometry.

Our research fits in this tradition of studying operator algebras through an underlying geometric structure. The classes of algebras that we study in this paper consist of bounded noncommutative functions on subvarieties of operator balls. The underlying geometric structures are, interestingly, not the subvarieties themselves, but rather their similarity envelopes, endowed with NC holomorphic structure and a certain metric. Concretely, the main goal of this paper is to classify algebras of bounded NC functions on NC subvarieties of operator balls via their spaces of finite-dimensional representations, which are concretely identified as certain NC varieties.

The study of the isomorphism problem for algebras of NC functions is a worthwhile pursuit for several reasons. First, it enriches the theory of operator algebras by establishing an intimate familiarity with a large class of nonselfadjoint operator algebras with tractable invariants allowing to compare and distinguish between pairs. Recently, we have observed that these algebras provide concrete representations of universal operator algebras generated by an operator space and its quotients [42, 43], and this suggests deep interactions between operator space theory and NC analytic function theory.

papers.title: GuardrailAgent: An Agentic Framework for Jailbreak Defense
papers.abstract: Despite undergoing safety training to align with human values, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that circumvent built-in safeguards and elicit malicious behaviors given by the adversary. Existing defenses are mostly static and fail to adapt to new or unknown attack strategies, providing limited resilience. To address these, we propose a multi-agent defense framework, GuardrailAgent, that offers adaptive, end-to-end protection. The system autonomously gathers and summarizes attack characteristics into a continuously updated knowledge base that supports both input- and output-side detection. A feedback module integrates misclassified cases for iterative improvement at minimal cost. Tested on over ten representative jailbreaks, the framework achieved a 93.1% input-side detection rate, 93.9% overall detection, and a 95.8% F1 score, while rapidly adapting to unseen attacks. These results demonstrate GuardrailAgent's outstanding capability to maintain LLM safety in the face of evolving jailbreak tactics.

papers.intro:
Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving, with new variants emerging almost daily [32, 11, 12, 54, 9, 10, 63]. In contrast, current defenses, whether they involve extensive safety fine-tuning [7, 6]) or external safeguards [3, 17, 31, 21, 16], remain largely static and non-adaptive. They are typically optimized against previously known prompts or attack strategies, but struggle to generalize to unseen jailbreaks in a timely manner.

In contrast, current defenses, whether they involve extensive safety fine-tuning [7, 6]) or external safeguards [3, 17, 31, 21, 16], remain largely static and non-adaptive. They are typically optimized against previously known prompts or attack strategies, but struggle to generalize to unseen jailbreaks in a timely manner.

This mismatch severely limits practical utility. More fundamentally, existing defenses fail to evolve in step with adversaries: their detection logic is typically tied to fixed rules, datasets, or training distributions, such as [3, 16, 42], which quickly become outdated as new jailbreak variants emerge [52, 30]. As a result, even defenses that are effective against known attacks often struggle to maintain robustness as jailbreak behaviors continue to evolve over time. These limitations highlight the urgent need for a defense framework that can continuously and autonomously adapt to a rapidly shifting jailbreak landscape.

To this end, we propose GuardrailAgent, a framework that provides comprehensive and self-evolving protection against unseen and emerging jailbreak attacks. Unlike existing defenses that primarily rely on static patterns, GuardrailAgent is designed to continuously evolve through automated updates from both external resources and internal feedback. This self-evolving capability enables the framework to adapt over time, allowing it to remain effective as jailbreak attacks continue to change. As illustrated in Figure 1, GuardrailAgent adopts a multi-agent architecture composed of two specialized agents: InputAgent and OutputAgent. These agents conduct analysis via a knowledge-driven system, which is built upon three specialized knowledge bases (KBs) and their corresponding analysis tools: the Prompt KB and Material KB for input-side detection, and the Response KB for response monitoring. Externally, the framework autonomously crawls the latest in-the-wild prompts and extracts and summarizes new attack strategies from relevant research papers and write-ups to regularly update its KBs. Internally, it includes a crucial feedback loop: whenever an attack bypasses input detection but is successfully caught at the output side, the missed instance is promoted into the Prompt KB for future detection. This mechanism ensures that the framework can autonomously learn from its past failures in a timely manner, thereby improving its overall generalization.

papers.title: Lea: An Agent Backbone for Mathematician-Controlled Formalization in Lean
papers.abstract: Agentic systems now formalize research-level mathematics in Lean, but they are built for autonomy: the mathematician states a target and inspects a result. The alternative, a general-purpose coding harness, is domain-neutral and must be assembled into a formalization workspace before any mathematics begins. Mathematicians, however, report wanting to keep high-level control over how an argument is decomposed and established. We present $\textbf{Lea}$, a Lean-specific agent backbone for mathematician-facing software rather than a single interface. Lea exposes runs, sessions, and typed events through one application-neutral API, and ships with Lean tooling (blueprints, LSP, Loogle, SafeVerify) already wired. We report two applications built on it: $\textbf{LeaChat}$, a web client for interactive proof authoring, and $\textbf{LeaOverleaf}$, which formalizes theorems annotated directly in an Overleaf document; a session begun in either continues in the other. Lea and both applications are released as open source so that further mathematician-facing tools can be built on the same backbone.

papers.title: Microscopic theory of exciton polarons in transition metal dichalcogenides
papers.abstract: Polarons are composite quasiparticles formed when charge carriers strongly couple to lattice vibrations, manifesting as carriers dressed by a surrounding cloud of phonons. Although this dressing fundamentally renormalizes the effective mass and mobility of carriers, its impact on electrically neutral exciton polarons in 2D semiconductors has received limited attention. In particular, despite the growing interest in polaronic effects in atomically thin semiconductors, only a few theoretical studies have addressed spectral signatures and renormalized properties of exciton polarons in these materials. Here, we develop a microscopic model to describe exciton polarons in transition metal dichalcogenides. Applying this model to $1s$ acoustic polarons in an MoSe$_2$ monolayer, we reveal a distinct kink in the polaron dispersion, accompanied by a pronounced broadening of its spectral function. These spectral signatures mark a critical transition from a regime of well-defined bound exciton polarons, characterized by a renormalized energy, reduced group velocity, and enhanced effective mass, to a regime dominated by exciton-phonon scattering. Furthermore, by incorporating intervalley exciton-phonon interaction, we demonstrate that the energetic position of momentum-dark excitons strongly modifies the exciton-polaron lifetime. Overall, our work provides a microscopic framework for determining renormalized properties of exciton polarons and establishes experimentally accessible polaron signatures in 2D semiconductors.

papers.intro:
Semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers host excitons, which are tightly bound electron-hole pairs [1, 2]. The low dimensionality of TMD monolayers results in a reduced dielectric screening and strong geometrical confinement, which substantially enhance the Coulomb interaction between electrons and holes. Consequently, excitons in TMD monolayers exhibit exceptionally large binding energies and oscillator strengths [3, 4], enabling the formation of excitons that remain stable even at room temperature. Owing to these properties, excitons dominate the optical and optoelectronic response of TMD monolayers, governing their absorption and photoluminescence [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Beyond their central role in optical spectroscopy, excitons in TMD monolayers have shown the potential to form a variety of many-body quasiparticle complexes, including exciton-polaritons [13, 14, 15, 16], charged excitons (trions or Fermi polarons) [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22], and biexcitons [23, 24, 25]. In this context, and among the many-body interactions determining exciton dynamics, coupling to phonons is particularly important, as it influences the relaxation process [26, 27, 28], coherence lifetime [29, 30, 31], and transport [32, 33, 10] of excitons. When this coupling is sufficiently strong, excitons can be dressed by lattice distortions, forming exciton polarons.

Polarons have been extensively studied in the context of charge carriers in semiconductors [35, 36, 6, 38]. These quasiparticles arise when an electron traveling through the semiconductor induces a local distortion within the crystal lattice, thus displacing the constituent ions from their respective equilibrium positions. This distortion produces a local polarization in the lattice that acts as a potential well, effectively binding the electron to the induced lattice deformation. This process can be conceptually described as the electron being dressed by the surrounding cloud of phonons that accompany its motion through the crystal. As a consequence of this dressing, the properties of the electron are modified, resulting in an energy redshift, a reduced group velocity, and an enhanced effective mass of polarons compared to that of free electrons with the same momentum [38].

Polaron effects have been widely observed across a variety of material systems, including organic semiconductors [39], halide perovskites [40], and 2D materials [41, 42, 43]. Recent theoretical advancements have enabled first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations of exciton polarons [46]. However, these approaches are computationally demanding for excitonic systems. Consequently, an accessible yet robust theoretical framework capable of microscopically capturing the renormalized quasiparticle properties and spectral signatures of exciton polarons in TMDs is still pending.

In this work, we develop a microscopic theoretical framework based on the Matsubara Green’s function formalism [1, 2, 3] that is capable of describing exciton-polaron quasiparticles in TMD monolayers. This feature serves as a signature of the presence of exciton polarons in TMD monolayers and highlights the crossover between a regime of bound exciton polarons and a regime dominated by exciton-phonon scattering, as schematically shown in Fig. 1. Below Qc{Q_{\text{c}}}, well-defined bound polarons are formed, characterized by an energy redshift, a reduced group velocity, and a mass enhancement compared to that of 1​s1s excitons with the same center-of-mass momentum. papers.title: The AIDA-TNG project: Galactic bar pattern speeds in self-interacting dark matter
papers.abstract: Cosmological simulations within the standard cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm systematically predict higher values of the dimensionless bar-speed parameter, $\boldsymbol{R} \equiv R_{\mathrm{cr}}/R_{\mathrm{bar}}$ (where $R_{\mathrm{cr}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{bar}}$ denote the corotation radius and the bar radius, respectively), than those inferred from observations of local galaxies, a discrepancy known as the fast-bar tension. Since bar slowdown is primarily driven by dynamical friction with the dark matter halo, bar dynamics is inherently sensitive to the properties of dark matter particles. We aim to determine whether dark matter self-interactions alleviate or exacerbate the fast-bar tension, and to identify the physical mechanism behind the differences in bar dynamics between CDM and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models. We use the $51.7\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ box of the AIDA-TNG cosmological simulations, run with three different dark matter models: standard CDM, and two SIMD models one with a constant cross-section model (SIDM1), and the other with a velocity-dependent model (vSIDM). We identify barred disk galaxies with stellar mass $M_* > 10^{10}\,M_{\odot}$ at redshifts $z=0.2,\,1.0,\,1.5,$ and $2.0$, and measure the bar fraction, bar strength, bar length, pattern speed $\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}$, and the ratio $\boldsymbol{R}=R_{\mathrm{cr}}/R_{\mathrm{bar}}$. The pattern speeds in the SIDM1 and vSIDM models are generally lower than in CDM at nearly all redshifts probed in this study. The subsequent slowdown proceeds with nearly 10\% more effective in the SIDM models likely due to velocity-anisotropy. Consequently, at low redshift the mean value of $\boldsymbol{R}$ is significantly higher in the SIDM models, indicating that the fas-bar tension is further exacerbated in these scenarios.

papers.intro:
Stellar bars are among the most common morphological features of disk galaxies, being present in roughly half to two-thirds of the disk galaxy population in the local Universe (Erwin 2018). Far from being passive structures, bars are principal drivers of the secular evolution of their hosts: they redistribute angular momentum within the disk–halo system, channel gas inflows toward galactic centers, and influence the growth of bulges and supermassive black holes (Gadotti 2009; Frosst et al. 2025). The bar pattern speed, Ωp\Omega_{\rm p}, which quantifies the angular velocity of the bar, is a fundamental parameter governing these processes: it sets the location of the resonances through which the bar couples to the other galactic components and regulates the exchange of angular momentum between the bar and the dark matter halo (Athanassoula 1992; Athanassoula et al. 2013; Sellwood 2014). Because this coupling depends directly on the properties of the surrounding halo, the pattern speeds of galactic bars provide a sensitive dynamical probe of the distribution, and potentially the fundamental nature, of dark matter.

The corotation radius is related to the pattern speed Ωp\Omega_{\rm p} by the equation Ω⁡(Rcr)=Ωp\Omega(R_{\rm cr})=\Omega_{\rm p}, where Ω\Omega represents the angular velocity derived from the circular velocity of the stars, given by vcir=R​Ω​(R)v_{\rm cir}=R\,\Omega(R). Bars with ℛ<1.4\mathcal{R}<1.4 are conventionally classified as “fast”, while those with ℛ>1.4\mathcal{R}>1.4 are “slow”. Cosmological simulations such as EAGLE (Schaye et al. 2015) and IllustrisTNG (Pillepich et al. 2018b; Springel et al. 2018; Nelson et al. 2018; Naiman et al. 2018; Marinacci et al. 2018; Nelson et al. 2019a; Nelson et al. 2019b; Pillepich et al. 2019), where the dynamics and properties of stellar bars have been widely studied (Izquierdo-Villalba et al. 2022; Rosas-Guevara et al. 2024; Rosas-Guevara et al. 2025; Gonçalves et al. 2025; Gonçalves et al. 2026; Chim-Ramirez et al. 2026, e.g.,), predict that most bars are slow, whereas observations of local galaxies indicate that a considerable fraction of bars are fast (Aguerri et al. 2015; Algorry et al. 2017; Cuomo et al. 2020; Roshan et al. 2021). For instance Géron et al. (2023) measured the pattern speed of 225 barred galaxies11 1 While Géron et al. (2023) report pattern speed measurements for 225 barred galaxies, it is likely that only a subset of these have high-accuracy determinations of Ωp\Omega_{\rm p}. Notably, among the 50 randomly selected galaxies presented in their Table 3, more than 40% of the measured pattern speeds exhibit relative errors exceeding 30%.. This study benefits from a larger sample of galaxies than previous studies. They found that about 62% of the bars in their sample are slow. However, the mean value of ℛ\mathcal{R} is approximately 1.7, which remains significantly different from the TNG50 value of about 3.1 (Roshan et al. 2021). This discrepancy is referred to as the “fast-bar tension”. The only plausible resolution of this tension proposed to date is that of Frankel et al. (2022), who attribute the large values of ℛ\mathcal{R} in TNG50 to the short-bar problem, that is, the absence of sufficiently long bars in the simulation, rather than to the pattern speed itself. They further argue that the short-bar problem may partly reflect inconsistencies in the comparison between simulations and observational data.

The physical origin of slow bars in simulations is well understood. A rotating bar embedded in a live dark matter halo loses angular momentum to the halo through resonant interactions, a process usually described as dynamical friction (Tremaine and Weinberg 1984; Weinberg 1985; Debattista and Sellwood 2000; Athanassoula 2003). As a result, bars in NN-body simulations robustly decelerate with cosmic time, and their corotation radii migrate outward, driving ℛ\mathcal{R} into the slow regime. The apparent reduction of the effect of this mechanism in observed galaxies therefore raises critical questions about the angular momentum exchange between bars and their surrounding halos, as well as the influence of baryonic processes on bar dynamics (Debattista and Sellwood 2000; Fragkoudi et al. 2021). One class of proposed solutions invokes baryonic physics: in simulations with high baryon dominance in the inner regions, dynamical friction is weakened and bars remain fast (Fragkoudi et al. 2021). An alternative possibility is that the discrepancy reflects the nature of dark matter itself, since the efficiency of dynamical friction depends on the microphysics of the dark matter. A notable example is ultralight (fuzzy) dark matter, for which the frictional drag can be substantially suppressed compared to the classical Chandrasekhar expectation (Hui et al. 2017; Lancaster et al. 2020). Different dark matter models therefore predict different frictional couplings between bars and halos, and hence potentially distinguishable distributions of bar pattern speeds.

papers.title: Hecke Algebras for Minimal Equicontinuous Cantor Actions
papers.abstract: In this work we extend the concept of Hecke algebras to a pair of a separable infinite profinite group and a closed core-free subgroup. Motivated by applications to minimal equicontinuous Cantor actions, which are characterized by such pairs, we characterize isometric *-algebra isomorphisms between such Hecke algebras by showing that they always arise as Koopman operators of homeomorphisms between the double coset spaces combined with the multiplication by some character. We then prove that two minimal equicontinuous Cantor actions with isometric isomorphic Hecke algebras have the same Steinitz order. We provide examples including the infinite dihedral group and the Grigorchuk group.

papers.title: Spontaneous Formation of Lateral Defect-Density Gradient in CVD-Grown MoS2 Monolayers
papers.abstract: Defect engineering in two-dimensional materials is a powerful strategy for tuning electronic, optical, and catalytic properties. While pristine molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) has been thoroughly studied, defective MoS2 remains poorly understood due to the complexity and inconsistency of controlled defect creation. Here, we report a defect-density gradient that forms spontaneously in MoS2 flakes during chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth. Photoluminescence and Raman spectroscopy mapping reveal the lateral arrangement of this gradient across a single flake. Deconvolution of the excitonic photoluminescence emission identifies electron doping as the key factor governing the spatial variation in optical response. This doping likely originates from sulfur vacancies formed during CVD growth, as further supported by the observed Raman mode shifts. We propose that this gradient arises from precursor depletion near the nucleation center during growth, resulting in a gradual variation in defect density. This lateral defect structure provides a convenient platform for systematically characterizing defective MoS2 across a continuous range of defect densities within a single sample. The sulfur-vacancy-driven surface activation identified here can also be important for future catalytic applications.

papers.title: Breathers across the Focusing-to-Defocusing Transition: From Diffraction-Like Dynamics to Talbot Carpets
papers.abstract: We experimentally investigate fundamental unstable breather wave groups propagating across the transition from focusing to defocusing regimes. In hydrodynamics, this transition is realized through a rapid reduction in water depth over a short spatial interval. We demonstrate that the time-periodic Akhmediev breather develops a Talbot-like recurrence pattern in the defocusing regime, although only its initial stages are experimentally accessible. In contrast, the Peregrine breather exhibits qualitatively different behavior, characterized by oscillatory envelope dynamics. These oscillations can be understood as a purely linear phenomenon arising within the nonlinear Schr\"odinger framework when dispersion dominates over nonlinearity, as further confirmed by numerical simulations over extended propagation distances. The experimental observations agree closely with finite-depth nonlinear Schr\"odinger predictions across regimes with substantially different relative strengths of dispersion and nonlinearity. Our findings reveal a temporal analogue of diffraction and provide a foundation for exploring focusing-to-defocusing transitions in other nonlinear dispersive media.

Here, we report an experimental study analyzing the propagation of modulationally unstable wave groups in the form of ABs and PBs over a rapid depth variation in a large-scale water wave facility, which implies a transition from the focusing to the defocusing regime, i.e., a sign change of the nonlinearity in the hydrodynamic NLSE Mei et al. (2005); Chabchoub et al. (2015). Our data allow us to explore the long-term behavior of these two types of fundamental wave groups before and after the transition. The experiments show that ABs exhibit the initial stages of Talbot-like pattern formation upon transitioning into a nearly linear regime, while PBs transform into an oscillating pattern that spreads while propagating. This can be interpreted as a time-analogue of diffraction, since linear effects dominate over nonlinear ones. This latter phenomenon is sensitive to the phase of the wave packet at the point where nonlinearity ceases to be effective. These findings are expected to stimulate further experimental, numerical, and theoretical work, not only in water waves, but also in optics, plasma, transmission lines, and Bose-Einstein condensates, to elucidate which linear and nonlinear effects are triggered by rapid dispersion and nonlinearity variations in the medium.

papers.title: Optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming: Complexity and Implementations
papers.abstract: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) extends Answer Set Programming with the possibility of representing uncertain data. Among the possible available semantics, we focus here on the credal semantics. In this setting, prior work has focused exclusively on plain ASP programs, i.e., programs without optimization constructs. However, many real world tasks define optimality criteria over the possible solutions, which cannot be conveniently modeled with existing probabilistic ASP frameworks. In this paper, we close this gap and propose optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming, which extends PASP by also allowing weak constraints, which are the standard optimization construct of ASP. We define the semantics of such programs, study the computational complexity of the inference and most probable explanation tasks, and propose practical implementations based on Algebraic Model Counting and Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers. An empirical evaluation of the proposed approach on three real world tasks confirms the applicability of our framework.

papers.title: A Structured-Surrogate Double-Model Approach to Regularization Parameter Selection
papers.abstract: Double-model methods select a regularization parameter by matching the discrepancy between two reconstructions of the same data to a prescribed target. The Structured-Surrogate Double-Model (SSDM) framework is developed around a computationally inexpensive structured surrogate of the forward operator and a spectrally explicit perturbation, with the selected parameter subsequently applied to the original inverse problem. Given a prescribed target, parameter selection requires neither prior knowledge of the noise level nor training data. For a class of Tikhonov regularization problems, the squared discrepancy is shown to attain a strict maximum at zero regularization, decay as $\lambda^{-2}$, and decrease strictly beyond an explicit phase-aware threshold. A complementary, data-dependent certificate is established to guarantee strict monotonicity on finite intervals, enabling unique and reliable target matching even when the global threshold is overly conservative. The discrepancy is further connected to directional roughness in image deblurring, providing a geometric interpretation of the selection principle. Experiments on synthetic images and on synthetically blurred natural photographs illustrate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical applicability of certified parameter selection.

This is the idea behind the operator-approximation framework introduced in [5], which chooses the parameter λ\lambda using an approximate operator and then transfers it to the original problem.

The second idea is to reconstruct the same data twice using two deliberately different models and measure how much the reconstructions disagree [17, 11, 21]. This idea is explored in the dual-grid method presented in [11], where the second model is the first model applied on a grid shifted by half a pixel. When λ\lambda is small, both reconstructions are dominated by amplified noise and by detail that depends on the precise model, and they disagree. As λ\lambda grows, both reconstructions are smoothed, and they come to agree. Selecting the λ\lambda at which the disagreement reaches a prescribed level τ\tau gives a parameter choice that needs neither a noise level nor training data. In the context of tomography, the results in [21] show that a proportional feedback controller can drive the disagreement to τ\tau. Related feedback principles appear in the controlled-sparsity approaches of [19, 18, 15].

We propose a double-model rule that combines both ideas. For each λ\lambda, it computes two Tikhonov reconstructions from two different surrogate models and measures how much they disagree. The rule selects the λ\lambda at which this disagreement equals an acceptable level, the target τ\tau. The target is taken as prescribed: it could be supplied by the application, calibrated using representative data, learned, or set based on user experience. The rule is well-defined only if matching the target determines a parameter, which requires that the discrepancy between the two reconstructions decrease as λ\lambda grows. Earlier double-model work assumes this or observes it numerically when using an image-similarity (SSIM) measure to define the disagreement, leaving uniqueness and formal conditions as open research questions [11, 21]. For the classical discrepancy principle, the corresponding property is automatic, because the residual of the Tikhonov solution is monotone in λ\lambda [6]. For the double-model discrepancy, it is not. Even in one dimension, a perturbation that merely rescales the model makes the discrepancy dip to zero, rise, and then decay, crossing the target several times (Section A.1). We therefore ask when a target has a unique solution, and how to compute it.

Its defining choice is that the second model A~​S\widetilde{A}S is obtained from the surrogate by a perturbation SS that is diagonal in the surrogate’s own basis. Both reconstructions are then filtered mode-wise, and the squared disagreement becomes a weighted sum of explicit one-mode functions whose weights are the data energies. This makes the disagreement analyzable, and the analysis takes place at two levels (Figure 1).

At the data-independent level, for a surrogate, its perturbation, and a regularization operator that are simultaneously unitarily diagonalizable, and a perturbation that amplifies no mode, the disagreement has a clean global shape. It is largest at zero regularization, decays like λ−1\lambda^{-1}, and decreases strictly beyond a threshold computed from the spectra alone. Tracking the relative phase between the two models sharpens this threshold optimally: under a mild sign-change condition, no argument that ignores the data can establish a decrease below it. This motivates the data-dependent level. In our half-pixel deblurring example, the threshold lies between about 1.61.6 and 33, whereas the parameters selected experimentally lie between 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} and 0.120.12. In the practical range, monotonicity is a property of the data. We give a finite certificate: on the cells of a partition, it bounds the derivative of the disagreement from above, using one cubic polynomial per mode. Where the certificate holds, every target in range is met at exactly one parameter, and a bracketing solver finds it in about a dozen evaluations.

papers.title: Multilingual Artificial Datasets for AI-Driven Cardiology: the CliTe and ParaCliTe corpora
papers.abstract: Background and Aims. Comparable, multilingual, validated cardiology corpora are critical to advance trustworthy natural language processing (NLP) models for cardiology but such resources are scarce due to privacy concerns. This study aimed to cover this gap by presenting suitable artificial corpus creation guidelines and by releasing 3 multilanguage corpora. Methods. Following purpose-specific publicly-available corpus construction guidelines, cardiologists from 7 European hospitals generated artificial clinical records in Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, Spanish and Swedish, ensuring clinical diversity and sex balance, resulting in the CliTe corpus. A CliTe subset underwent a multi-stage manual translation into the other 6 languages, resulting in the parallel ParaCliTe corpus, while the remaining reports were automatically translated, constituting ParaCliTe Silver. Results. CliTe is a collection of 699 artificial cardiology reports, mostly outpatient notes (340 documents), discharge reports (263), and inpatient notes (89), describing fictional patients with ischaemic heart disease (199 patients), heart failure (188), and valvular disease (79), among others. ParaCliTe contains reports from 94 fictitious patients, each available in seven languages with sentence-level alignment, resulting in 658 documents. The corpus mainly comprises discharge reports (322 documents), and outpatient (196) and inpatient (140) notes, describing patients with heart failure (399 documents), ischaemic heart disease (287), and valvular disease (238). Empirical results illustrate the utility of ParaCliTe and highlight the limitations of state-of-the-art NLP models adapted to the cardiology domain. Conclusions. The creation of multilingual, equitable and realistic corpora of artificial patients capable of strengthening NLP performance for cardiology is feasible when supported by detailed guidelines.

papers.title: Driving Atomic Spins through Their Substrate Electrons
papers.abstract: Coherent control of single spins on surfaces has relied on decoupling them from the substrate with insulating films, which protects the spin but also removes any electronic means of addressing it. Here we show that a local electric potential can drive an adatom spin through the substrate electrons themselves. An exact reciprocity relation fixes the torque, which equals the change of the local electron density when the moment rotates; the drive map is thus a ground-state property that can be measured independently. The relation also implies sharp selection rules, since point-contact spins, spin-$1/2$ and the central transition of half-integer spins remain dark. On a normal metal the hybridization responsible for the drive also destroys coherence, but on a superconductor the drive survives while substrate damping is confined to subgap transitions. For atomically sharp tips we find Rabi frequencies of several MHz at RF amplitudes of tens of mV, with substrate-limited linewidths below $0.1$~MHz, so that strong hybridization, usually the enemy of spin coherence, becomes an asset.

papers.title: Exciton design via topological spin textures
papers.abstract: Excitons carry energy and information through a semiconductor without carrying charge. This makes them attractive for optoelectronics, but also hard to guide. Magnetic skyrmions, on the other hand, are moved by small electrical currents. Here we develop a theory of excitons interacting with a skyrmion in which the electron and the hole are treated as distinct constituents, each with its own spin--orbit coupling. We find that the topology of the skyrmion is transferred to the exciton only when the exchange coupling exceeds the relevant spin--orbit splitting. The exciton then experiences a full flux quantum, with opposite signs in the two valleys. The quantum metric of the spin texture creates a ring-shaped barrier that traps excitons, whereas the topological charge fixes the angular momentum of the trapped states and hence their optical selection rules. Because the trap moves with the skyrmion, excitons can be transported by current pulses, and small skyrmions accommodate a single exciton, which opens the door for potential hybrid applications in future information technology intertwining topological magnetic bits with optical excitations.

papers.title: Definitions, Label Names, or Demonstrations? Auditing What Governs LLM Annotation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate social-science texts, but high accuracy does not establish that they apply researcher-supplied category definitions: predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations. We introduce a counterfactual audit that reassigns definitions among output labels, distinguishing adherence to supplied definitions from preservation of a dataset's original mapping. Across three political-text datasets, models rarely follow reassigned definitions, and standard fine-tuning strengthens the original mapping without reliably increasing definition adherence. We then study retrieval-augmented annotation. Retrieving the nearest training examples generally outperforms retrieving examples separately within each category despite using fewer demonstrations. On the two tasks with substantial gains, direct \(k\)-nearest-neighbor classification recovers 74--93\% of the improvement, indicating that neighborhood labels provide much of the predictive signal. Relabeling fixed demonstrations redirects predictions, whereas aligning demonstrations with reassigned definitions substantially increases adherence to the new mapping. Thus, accuracy-improving interventions need not increase codebook adherence; definitions, category labels, demonstrations, retrieval, and training data should be aligned and validated jointly.

papers.title: Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization
papers.abstract: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.

papers.title: Analytic information encoded in the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of genus-one plane branches
papers.abstract: We give an explicit formula recovering the Zariski invariant of a plane branch with one Puiseux pair from its Bernstein-Sato polynomial. Thus the Bernstein-Sato stratification refines the Zariski-invariant stratification. We determine the generic roots in each stratum from the value semigroup and the Zariski invariant, refining Yano's description for a fixed topological class. We also compute the maximal spectral-exponent discrepancy and relate it to the dimension of the generic Bernstein-Sato locus and the minimum Tjurina number.

papers.title: pfoqcompiler: Efficient Compilation of Quantum Control in Recursive First-Order Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: Recursive quantum control allows for simple and concise descriptions of algorithms. However, a naive circuit compilation sequentializes the different branches of the quantum if-statement and results in an exponential increase in circuit depth. Existing techniques can parallelize these branches, but do so at the cost of an exponential number of ancillary qubits. We present pfoqcompiler, a compiler targeting Qiskit for the first-order quantum programming language FOQ that exploits program structure to merge compatible recursive procedure calls across quantum branches. We introduce weaker syntactically-checkable conditions for well-foundedness, recursive halving, and uniformity, while preserving previously demonstrated complexity characterizations. For weakly well-founded bounded-width programs, the compiler produces polynomial-size circuits; weakly recursively halving programs additionally yield polylogarithmic depth, while weak uniformity removes the asymptotic overhead of branch sequentialization.

papers.title: Differentiation of tepui groupoids and the holonomy groupoid of singular foliations
papers.abstract: Tepui groupoids are a generalization of Lie groupoids which allow the arrow space to be singular, as is the case for holonomy groupoids of singular foliations. We construct a Lie differentiation functor for a large class of tepui groupoids. When restricted to effective and source-connected tepui groupoids, this differentiation recovers the correspondence between holonomy groupoids and their underlying singular foliations.

papers.title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
papers.abstract: Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.

papers.title: SAS: Scene-Annotated AudioSet Strong for Joint Scene-Event Analysis
papers.abstract: Context is central to human auditory perception, as listeners interpret sounds within their acoustic environment to resolve ambiguity. However, large-scale datasets that jointly capture sound events and acoustic scenes remain limited. We address this by augmenting AudioSet Strong with clip-level scene annotations under two taxonomies for joint sceneevent modeling. A corpus-scale analysis shows that scene identity is better captured by events distinctive to a scene than by those that merely occur frequently. Reweighting event co-occurrences toward scene-specific associations produces representations that better align with human-derived taxonomies, while also exposing scenes where the acoustic and semantic views diverge. This geometric divergence predicts classification errors, while supervised validation confirms that the proposed scene annotations provide meaningful complementary information for developing scalable context-aware machine listening systems.

authors.name: Romain Serizel
authors.institution: Laboratoire Lorrain de Recherche en Informatique et ses Applications

papers.title: Ontology-Driven Control of Conversational Agents with a Use-Case for Job Interview Practice
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used as conversational agents in both domain-specific and open-domain situations. In domain-specific context, it is often necessary to adapt those LLMs to obtain conversations with desired characteristics, whether those apply at the level of each response (e.g. for tone or style) or more globally (i.e. at the level of a conversational strategy). Such adaptations are, however, generally realized in an ad hoc way, through specific, non-reusable, and non-transparent developments. In this paper, we propose an ontology-based approach to design conversational strategies that rely on the desired and measured characteristics of textual utterances in the conversation. Through a use case related to job interview practice, we show how this approach can be used to control LLMs to follow the strategy defined in the ontology. To this end, we automatically fine-tune the LLM to improve its compliance with ontologically-defined conversation characteristics. Our results show that training the LLM from formally defined concepts effectively enhances alignment with the requested characteristics. Hence, this work demonstrates how ontology-guided conversation control can be achieved while taking into account multiple, concurrent conversation aspects that are formally and transparently defined.

papers.title: Regularity of planar Griffith minimizers with connected cracks through a monotonicity formula
papers.abstract: We prove a new monotonicity formula for the two-dimensional Neumann elasticity equation with connected boundary. From this we deduce a regularity result for two-dimensional minimizers of the Griffith energy with connected crack set: the crack may be partitioned into regular points, triple junctions, and cracktips. We give a classification of the global minimizers of the Griffith energy with connected crack set. Finally, we discuss some consequences of the monotonicity formula on the evolution of the stress intensity factors along a crack, which may present independent interest.

papers.title: Shortest Synchronizing Words on Product Automata
papers.abstract: We consider some operations on finite automata graphs, in particular various product, union and merge operations, and investigate how they relate to the parameter~$\mathrm{rt}$, the \emph{length of a shortest synchronizing word}. We derive some lower and upper bounds for the operations that we study. We also examine several classes of automata (for instance, partially ordered, commutative or idempotent automata) that are preserved under these operations and show in which way the parameter $\mathrm{rt}$ behaves in these automata classes. Also, we consider automata classes that can be constructed by combining automata from better known classes; in particular, these new classes of automata will also satisfy the bound of the famous \v{C}ern\'y conjecture. This also motivates us to study even more closure properties. In particular, we show that certain automata classes related to synchronization form pseudo-varieties. We also commence a similar study concerning the length of shortest homing sequences of Mealy automata.

papers.title: Backward--forward interacting systems with probability-valued strategies and common noise
papers.abstract: We study a system of interacting agents in which a backward stochastic equation is coupled to the forward evolution of a probability-valued strategy distribution. The agents interact through their empirical state--strategy law and are exposed to a common Brownian noise. Under Lipschitz, mass-conservation, and positivity assumptions, we establish well-posedness of the finite-agent system on a sufficiently short time interval. We then identify its large-population limit as a conditional mean-field backward--forward system and prove conditional propagation of chaos. When agent characteristics take finitely many values, we obtain order $N^{-1}$ bounds for the expected squared particle--copy error and the expected squared Wasserstein distance of order one between the empirical law and the conditional limiting law. An adaptive-strategy model with replicator dynamics illustrates the theory, accompanied by a numerical comparison of the two errors.

papers.title: SQUALO II: Probing Accretion Through CO Molecular Outflows in Massive Star-forming Clumps
papers.abstract: Molecular outflows probe protostellar accretion and mass transfer from clump scales to forming stars. We present an ALMA study of CO (J=2-1) outflows toward 13 massive clumps from the SQUALO sample, spanning a broad evolutionary range and exhibiting clump-scale infall. We identify 51 high-velocity CO lobes associated with 31 outflow systems and derive their physical and dynamical properties assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium. Outflow inferred accretion rates are typically 10^{-5}-10^{-3} Msun/yr, consistent with active massive star formation. The maximum outflow velocity shows little dependence on candidate driving-core mass, indicating that it is not a reliable tracer of protostellar mass in clustered environments. Outflow momentum flux correlates positively with clump surface density, whereas accretion rate shows a tentative, statistically nonsignificant decrease with increasing virial parameter. Total outflow inferred accretion rate shows a tentative positive relation with clump-scale infall rate but remains systematically lower, suggesting that the detected outflows represent only part of the large-scale mass flux. The clump L/M ratio moderately anticorrelates with projected outflow length, although projection, observational limitations, and the embedded source population prevent a unique evolutionary interpretation. Together with the continuum derived fragmentation properties, our results show that compact cores embedded within infalling clumps drive the outflows. The tentative relation between clump-scale infall and protostellar accretion suggests a possible connection across these scales, although our observations do not directly trace mass transfer from filaments to individual protostars.

papers.title: Fast and Actionable Classification of HPC I/O Time Series
papers.abstract: Input/output (I/O) is a major bottleneck for highperformance computing (HPC) performance. One of the challenges is the contention between jobs when sharing the parallel file system. However, tackling this issue depends on knowing the temporal behavior of jobs. In this paper, we propose a clusteringbased approach to characterize jobs' temporal I/O behavior. We propose SAGE, a lightweight method that cuts I/O traces into short windows and learns an alphabet from them. The trace then becomes a sequence of symbols, which we call ''genome'', and we use clustering to separate them into classes. We evaluate SAGE and its two-stage variant SAGE-2 on 819,771 real traces from 2 HPC systems. We compare them against other techniques from the state of the art on three metrics, including one we propose. Compared to K-shape, the best baseline available, SAGE-2 lowers the median intra-cluster metrics by 9.1% on average, and achieves this in 2 minutes of clustering time versus 3.8 hours, a 109x speedup. More importantly, clusters created by SAGE and SAGE-2 carry enough information to act on: we evaluate the use of the cluster centroids for I/O scheduling, and show that our approach can decrease I/O stretch by up to 24% compared to the state of the art (round-robin placement).

papers.title: Bridging Spiking and Continuous Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks: A Muscle-Inspired Model
papers.abstract: Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks. In biological systems, a similar transformation occurs when muscles integrate neural spikes to produce smooth, coordinated movements. Inspired by this mechanism, we introduce a muscle-response model, a biologically motivated dynamical layer that converts spike trains into continuous representations. Our approach uses second-order dynamics to model the temporal integration of spiking activity. We investigate how the number of spiking neurons and temporal resolution affect the quality of the generated signals in a text-to-speech task, showing that increasing representational capacity has a greater impact than increasing temporal resolution under the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned dynamics reveals that, without explicit constraints on the response type, most neurons converge toward non-oscillatory behavior. These results demonstrate the potential of biologically inspired dynamical decoders for bridging spiking neural computation and continuous signal generation.

papers.title: Expert Spindles in the Wild: Enriched Supervision for a Dense Detector
papers.abstract: Sleep spindles are a hallmark of healthy NREM sleep whose frequency, amplitude, density, duration and topography vary with brain maturation, age and disease. Their manual annotation is impractical and variable between scorers, yet the public references used to train automatic detectors cover these characteristics only partially: stage N2 only, a single central derivation, or short pre-selected segments. Measuring duration and density requires dense detectors that learn event boundaries from annotated onsets and offsets, and therefore inherit the protocol under which those boundaries were scored. We introduce Expert Spindles in the Wild (ESW), a stage-agnostic expert spindle annotation set covering 19 complete MASS-SS2 recordings ($\approx$150 h of continuous EEG, 29,819 events). A sleep neurophysiologist annotated the recordings using the full EEG montage, blinded to sleep-stage labels and prior spindle annotations. On the 15 nights shared with historical scorers, ESW recovers 92.7% of E1 and 73.7% of E2 events, while recovering 81.6% of the MODA expert-consensus events on the common excerpts. Despite stage-blind annotation, 99.0% of ESW events occur in N2/N3. Used to train a fixed dense detector on a frozen SleepFM encoder, ESW reaches an event-level $F_1$ of 0.680 on 166 unseen MODA subjects, compared with 0.635 for E2 ($\Delta F_1$ = +0.045, paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.024, 0.065]). ESW is thus useful supervision for cross-dataset detection, and closer annotation-level agreement with the MODA consensus did not translate into better transfer performance in this experiment. The annotations are released under the MASS data-use terms (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23894975).

papers.title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
papers.abstract: We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.

papers.title: Vertex Deletion on $H$-Induced-Minor-Free Graphs: Subexponential FPT Algorithms and Approximation Schemes
papers.abstract: We study vertex-deletion problems on string graphs and, more generally, on graphs excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor. For every fixed graph $H$, fixed nonnegative integer $t$, and fixed monadic second-order formula $\phi$, we consider the problem of finding a minimum-cardinality set $S$ such that $G-S$ has treewidth at most $t$ and satisfies $\phi$. This captures classic problems such as Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and deletion to graphs of any fixed bounded treewidth. We give an algorithm with running time $2^{k^{2/3} \log^{O(1)} k}n^{O(1)}$ on $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, where $k$ is the optimum deletion-set size. This resolves in the affirmative the open problem highlighted by Bonnet and Rz\k{a}\.{z}ewski [Algorithmica 2019] and Berthe, Bougeret, Gon\c{c}alves, and Raymond [ICALP 2025] regarding the existence of a subexponential parameterized algorithm for Feedback Vertex Set on string graphs. Our algorithm significantly improves over existing parameterized algorithms for more restricted classes of problems on more restricted classes of graphs. When the property defined by $\phi$ is hereditary, we also obtain a quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme, namely an algorithm that produces a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate solution in quasi-polynomial time. Both the sub-exponential algorithm and the quasi-polynomial time approximation scheme build on the same new structural and algorithmic insights.

papers.title: Green500: Adventure in Qualifying a Cluster
papers.abstract: Energy effciency has become a key metric for evaluating High Performance Computing (HPC) systems, as reflected by the Green500 ranking. However, energy effciency alone does not capture the full environmental impact of an HPC cluster. Using the Kuma cluster at EPFL, we report on two Green500 measurement campaigns at Level 2 and Level 3, and extend this analysis to a full carbon footprint assessment using the MITSI life-cycle based methodology. GPU power capping experiments show that energy effciency peaks at 450 W, achieving an 11% performance loss offset by a 20% reduction in energy consumption. When embodied emissions are accounted for, the optimal power cap for carbon effciency shifts to 500 W under Switzerland's low-carbon electrical grid, revealing a tension between minimizing usage and embodied contributions. We discuss the challenges of generalizing this approach into a broader carbon-based HPC ranking, and argue that moving beyond energy effciency is both necessary and feasible.

papers.title: Momentum-space engineering in van der Waals heterostructures
papers.abstract: Twenty years of graphene research have established Dirac fermions as a versatile platform for exploring quantum topological phenomena. Yet control over graphene's low-energy spectrum mostly follows the route of miniband engineering using real-space superlattices. Here we introduce a complementary approach based on momentum-space 'Umklapp' band engineering. This is realised by matching reciprocal space positions of band edges of two adjacent highly incommensurate 2D crystals to coincide upon a boost from their Bragg vectors, creating resonant interlayer hybridisation that qualitatively reconstructs their spectra. To demonstrate this approach experimentally, we use monolayer graphene on MoS$_2$, twisted such that MoS$_2$ Q-valley states are brought by Umklapp into energy-momentum resonance with graphene's Dirac cones. The ensuing hybridization results in the formation of a clear additional Dirac-like spectral feature, identified by a distinct Landau-level fan and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations characteristic to Berry phase $\pi$ electrons. These new topological spectral features create a spin-valley locked Ising system which is robust against small twist-angle variations that can be further tuned by an external displacement field. More broadly, Umklapp band engineering offers a practical strategy for tailoring the electronic structure in van der Waals heterostructures, expanding the design space of quantum materials beyond moir\'e superlattices and weak proximity effects.

papers.title: Unique ergodicity of systems of finite order and the density finite sums theorem in arbitrary abelian groups
papers.abstract: Let $\Gamma$ be a countable abelian group and $k\geq 1$. We establish that every minimal topological $\Gamma$-system of order $k$ is uniquely ergodic. This result, which was previously only known for finitely generated groups for arbitrary $k$, answers a question of Glasner, Gutman, and Ye and yields the answer to multiple questions by Candela, Gonz\'alez-S\'anchez, and Szegedy. As applications of our dynamical results, we obtain the following combinatorial theorems. Let $A\subseteq \Gamma$ be a set of positive upper Banach density. Then there are infinite sets $B_1,\ldots, B_k\subseteq \Gamma$ such that $B_1+\dots+B_k\subseteq A$. If $\Gamma$ satisfies a necessary divisibility assumption, then there are also $t\in \Gamma$ and an infinite set $B\subseteq \Gamma$ such that $A-t$ contains the set of all sums of $m$ pairwise distinct elements of $B$ for all $m\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. For arbitrary $k$, these density finite sums theorems were only known in the integers previously.

papers.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
papers.abstract: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.

papers.title: Mosaic:montage-agnostic self-distilled graph learning for subject-independent ieeg seizure detection
papers.abstract: Intracranial EEG provides high signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution for detecting epileptic activity, but patient-specific electrode placement leads to substantial variation in channel count and montage across subjects. This heterogeneity limits the generalization of existing detectors under subject-independent evaluation. We propose MOSAIC (MOntage-agnostic Self-distilled Adaptive Inter-channel Connectivity learning), a lightweight graph-learning framework for subject-independent iEEG seizure detection. MOSAIC pairs a shared convolutional channel encoder with a patient-agnostic channel-attention module that infers a weighted inter-channel adjacency matrix from the encoded features, requiring no fixed montage graph. An exponential moving average self-distillation objective regularizes each prediction toward a slowly updated per-patient teacher. Across four public iEEG corpora (SWEC-ETHZ long- and short-term, Mayo, FNUSA), MOSAIC outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in F2 and Cohen's $\kappa$ while learning more stable inter-channel adjacencies, demonstrating that self-distilled connectivity learning transfers across unseen implantations.

papers.title: Mode interaction in inclined-layer convection: a physical interpretation
papers.abstract: We carry out a numerical investigation of the Oberbeck--Boussinesq equations in a fluid layer inclined against gravity. Equilibria containing different numbers of co-rotating rolls are computed. Mixed-mode branches connect branches containing states with four and six identical co-rotating rolls. These branches display two contrasting routes to reducing (or increasing) the number of rolls, one in which rolls disappear (or appear) and another route in which rolls merge (or split). These results are interpreted in light of the $(2,3)$ mode interaction scenario.

papers.title: AR-Edit: Training-Free Autoregressive Video Editing without Inversion
papers.abstract: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.

papers.title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
papers.abstract: Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.

papers.title: Constructing Casimirs for the quantum reflection equation
papers.abstract: We explore the quantum reflection equation in the case of a full-dimensional $n\times n$ matrix $\mathbb A$. Using the technique of $q$-determinants, we find closed expressions for the quantum Pfaffian (in the case of even $n$) and for new quantum Casimirs that are ratios of special quantum (Sklyanin) minors of $\mathbb A$. Special attention is paid to the self-adjointness property of the newly constructed Casimirs. We put forward a conjecture that, adopting a natural ansatz for a quantum deformation of a Casimir of a classical algebra, self-adjointness implies commutativity. We also explore the relationship to networks of quantum cluster variables.

papers.title: Positivity of metric entropy of the standard map at large parameters
papers.abstract: We prove that the standard map $f_k(x,y)=(x+y+k\sin2\pi x,\,y+k\sin2\pi x)$ of the two-torus satisfies $\log(2\pi k+4)-2^{430}\le h_m(f_k)\le\log(2\pi k+4)$ for every $k\ge\exp(2^{50000})$, where $h_m$ is the metric entropy with respect to area. Thus $h_m(f_k)=\log k+O(1)$, the order of growth observed numerically since Chirikov; in particular $h_m(f_k)>0$ for all large $k$ and $h_m(f_k)\to\infty$, as conjectured by Sinai. Moreover, for each fixed $c<1$ the points whose top Lyapunov exponent is below $c\log k$ fill an area $O(1/\log k)$. Positivity of $h_m(f_k)$ for all sufficiently large $k$, with a threshold that is not effective, was obtained in a recent preprint by OpenAI. We keep some of its architecture and follow it closely in about a third of the results. New here are an explicit covering argument for cancellations and a balance across scales at a fixed parameter, an inequality between mean shortfalls that replaces the compactness argument over limits of rescaled orbit geometries; together they yield the explicit constants and the entropy bound.

papers.title: Discrete total variation under the multinomial, Part 4: variance under a general distribution
papers.abstract: We study the variance of the reference-centered discrete total variation $d_{\mathbf p}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|X_{j+1}-X_j-N(p_{j+1}-p_j)|$ of $X\sim\mathrm{Mult}(N;\mathbf p)$ for fixed $n\ge3$ and fixed $\mathbf p$ with all $p_i>0$, as $N\to\infty$. We prove $\mathrm{Var}(d_{\mathbf p})=N\,v(\mathbf p)+O(1)$, where $v(\mathbf p)$, the variance of the sum of absolute values of the limiting Gaussian edge vector, is expressed through the exact multinomial edge variances and correlations and Nabeya's covariance formula for folded bivariate normal variables. Unlike in the uniform case, non-adjacent edge pairs generally contribute to $v(\mathbf p)$. The $O(1)$ remainder is controlled by a lattice Edgeworth expansion and Poisson summation; it oscillates with the lattice phases $\{N(p_{j+1}-p_j)\}$, and for $n=3,4$, where a pair of edges exhausts the bins, the summation runs over a sublattice coset. The formula reduces to the known uniform result (the classical Hoel--Kamat variance), gives a closed form when the reference law is a symmetric comb, and has a shape-independent large-bin limit for positive $C^1$ profiles. For the statistic $d_{\mathbf r}$ centered at a reference law $\mathbf r\ne\mathbf p$ the absolute values linearize: when every edge is mismatched the variance is that of a linear form in the counts up to an exponentially small error, and in mixed (triangular-array) regimes it is given to $o(N)$ by bivariate folded-normal covariances. The two-bin formulas are recorded from the companion preprints, and exact finite-$N$ reductions for $n\le4$ are used for validation.

papers.title: PH-Symb : Sparse symbolic identification of nonlinear port-Hamiltoniansystems using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks
papers.abstract: The paper introduces PH-Symb, a novel symbolic structure-preserving identification method, that combines Kolmogorov Arnold networks and sparse regression to build explicit port-Hamiltonian (pH) models from data. Unlike other Machine Learning or neural pH approaches, PH-Symb recovers physically interpretable and explicit-symbolic components and enforces pH structure by construction. It also introduces a new normalization method that preserves the pH structure. It allows handling both identification from input-state-output (ISO) data and input-output (IO) data, and applications show it delivers interpretable models and lower errors than neural baselines on synthetic and real-world systems.
