papers.title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
papers.abstract: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.

papers.title: InstaGen: Group-Shared Importance Sampling for Fast Video Generation
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).

papers.title: Path Isolation and Reachability in Surface-Embedded Graphs with Restricted Cycle and Cut Structure
papers.abstract:
We study the reachability problem in directed surface-embedded graphs under two structural restrictions, using isolating weight assignments.
  First, we consider graphs whose underlying undirected embeddings contain at most polynomially many simple surface non-separating cycles. We develop a polynomially bounded, logspace-computable skew-symmetric edge-weight assignment with nonzero circulation around every simple cycle. This yields an unambiguous logspace (UL) upper bound for directed reachability. The construction also gives an SPL upper bound for bipartite perfect matching in the corresponding undirected graph class.
  Second, for $g$-genus directed graphs admitting a balanced hierarchical genus decomposition with $O(\log n)$ crossing edges at every partition, we obtain an unambiguous $O(\log g \cdot \log n)$-space bound for reachability. Our approach combines path-isolating weights for lower-genus subgraphs using polynomially bounded FKS hashing refinements at successive merging levels.

papers.title: Different exact-law formulations to calculate the energy cascade rate in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence with and without mean magnetic fields
papers.abstract: At scales much larger than the ion inertial length and ion-gyroscale, space-plasma turbulence is often described within the framework of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). Using high-resolution direct numerical simulations with $1024^3$ grid points, we perform the first systematic numerical comparison of three exact-law formulations for the total energy cascade in homogeneous, but not necessarily isotropic, MHD turbulence: the Yaglom-Monin (YM), Banerjee-Galtier (BG), and two-point correlator formulations. Despite directional variations, the angle-averaged energy transfer rates for all three formulations show excellent agreement for zero, moderate, and strong background magnetic fields. These results clearly suggest the usefulness of alternative BG and correlator formulations for estimating the energy cascade rates in turbulent space plasmas when the required spatial derivatives are accessible through multi-spacecraft measurements. We also argue that the isotropic Politano-Pouquet (PP) formulation does not provide a true directional transfer rate and therefore its application as a single-direction energy transfer rate estimator leads to inaccurate values, especially under anisotropic conditions. Decomposing the exact formulations into RMHD and non-RMHD contributions, we also show that the RMHD cascade rates cannot be obtained merely by increasing the strength of the mean magnetic field in incompressible magnetohydrodynamic turbulence. Finally, a term-by-term analysis of different formulations reveals how different nonlinear interaction channels coexist and collaborate with each other to maintain the same energy cascade rate across the inertial scales.

papers.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
papers.abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.

papers.title: Local cohomology over Steenrod algebras
papers.abstract: Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field with $q = p^s$ elements. Let $S = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} S_n$ be a non-negatively graded commutative, Noetherian $\mathbb{F}_q$-algebra. Assume $S$ has a structure of an unstable Steenrod algebra. Let $M$ be a finitely generated graded unstable $S$-module. Let $I$ be a homogeneous ideal in $S$. We prove that for $i \geq 0$ the local cohomology modules $H^i_I(M)$ has a structure of a Cartan $S$-module. As application we give a direct and considerably simpler proof of D. Bourguiba and S. Zarati's generalization of Landweber-Stong conjecture. We also give a necessary and sufficient condition for $S$ to have $S_r$-property of Serre in terms of Dickson polynomials.

papers.title: Immobilisation and remobilisation of surfactant-covered drop interfaces in electric fields: Simulations
papers.abstract: Fluid--fluid interfaces are seldom clean due to the presence of surfactants, which can strongly modify their dynamics. Interfacial flow redistributes surfactant, creating concentration gradients whose Marangoni stresses can immobilise the interface. By contrast, surface diffusion or exchange with the bulk can reduce these gradients and restore interfacial motion. We study this competition using a two-dimensional model of a surfactant-covered leaky-dielectric drop in a uniform electric field. Electric stresses drive the classical Taylor circulation, in which the drop remains non-rotating. At stronger fields, convection of interfacial charge can destabilise this state and produce the Quincke regime, characterised by spontaneous mean rotation. Using a fully nonlinear model on a fixed circular interface, we show that weak surfactant diffusion allows Marangoni stresses to suppress the Taylor circulation almost completely. Quincke rotation remobilises this nearly arrested interface and restores a substantial straining circulation, whose orientation varies with the applied field. Surfactant also shifts the critical field for rotation and can change the onset from subcritical to supercritical. Surface diffusion and exchange with a well-mixed bulk reservoir can produce similar flow responses and rotation thresholds despite different surfactant distributions. The spatial variation of surfactant concentration therefore provides additional information for distinguishing the two transport mechanisms.

papers.title: Electrohydrodynamic interactions of two Quincke rotors: asymptotic theory and boundary element simulations
papers.abstract: Weakly conducting spheres suspended in a leaky dielectric fluid can undergo spontaneous Quincke rotation when the applied electric field exceeds a critical value. We investigate how electric and hydrodynamic interactions modify this instability and the subsequent rotation of two spheres at fixed separation and orientation. Starting from electric dipole and hydrodynamic rotlet interactions, we develop a systematic far-field asymptotic theory. Away from onset, slow drift of the rotation axes makes a regular expansion fail at long times. A multiple-scale expansion gives slow phase equations that select the axes according to pair orientation and field strength. Near onset, weak interactions produce corrections comparable to the isolated rotation magnitude. A detuned multiple-scale expansion gives coupled equations for the transverse dipole amplitudes. Their linearization identifies four collective rotation modes, whose critical fields and steady branches with one active mode are determined together with their stability. At leading order near onset, electric interaction shifts all four modal thresholds equally, whereas hydrodynamic interaction makes counter-rotation appear first for pair angles below $\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\simeq54.7^\circ$ and co-rotation above it. Away from onset, the angle separating stable counter-rotation from stable co-rotation increases with field strength. Boundary element method (BEM) simulations place onset within a field interval for each configuration and resolve the growth and relaxation of rotation. Steady-speed comparisons show how pair orientation changes the balance between electric and hydrodynamic effects. We compare the unexpanded dipole-rotlet model of Das and Saintillan [Phys. Rev. E 87, 043014 (2013)] with our asymptotic theory and BEM simulations.

papers.title: Safety-Focused Reinforcement Learning Using Risk-Sensitive Coupled Control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the coupled control problem within safety-focused reinforcement learning, addressing the essential challenge of achieving optimal performance while ensuring safety in systems operating within complex environments. We define safety as the requirement to prevent the system from reaching undesirable or hazardous states. We propose a coupled control approach that prioritizes safety by employing effective methods to prevent the system from entering unsafe states while optimizing the performance metric, defined as the average cost. We propose a novel problem transformation that reformulates it into a risk-sensitive problem combined with an average reward criterion. We present a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm where in the faster timescale, the algorithm solves a risk-sensitive control problem to ensure safety, while on a slower timescale, the algorithm focuses on average cost control. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of our algorithms, establishing their significance in ensuring safe, optimal control in dynamic environments. We validated the performance of our approach using GridWorld and CarGoal task in Safety Gymnasium.

papers.title: Sharp isoperimetry in groups of polynomial growth
papers.abstract: We study weighted edge boundary and outer vertex boundary on Cayley graphs of polynomial growth of degree $Q>1$. For every finite symmetric generating set, we prove that each exact isoperimetric profile satisfies $I(n)=c n^{(Q-1)/Q}+O(n^{(Q-1)/Q-\beta})$, where $\beta=1/(8Q^2)$. We identify the leading constant with the isoperimetric constant of a horizontal perimeter on the limiting Carnot group, after accounting for the counting density. Its integrand is a norm with polyhedral unit ball, determined by a convex minimization with one real variable for each coset of a torsion-free nilpotent subgroup. For every asymptotically minimizing sequence, we translate its vertex sets so that the characteristic functions of the associated rescaled regions are precompact in $L^1$. The limiting regions minimize continuum perimeter at fixed volume. The exact-cardinality estimate requires no regularity assumption on these regions. For virtually abelian groups, we prove a quantitative stability estimate using a discrete approximation to the Euclidean Wulff body. The relative symmetric difference from a translate is bounded by the square root of the sum of the relative boundary deficit and a cardinality error. We also characterize when bounded additive changes of Cayley metric preserve the leading vertex constant. Failure occurs already in rank two; we construct pairs with the same measured asymptotic cone whose leading constants have an unbounded ratio as the rank grows.

papers.title: Forecasting Fundamental-Plane Tests of Intermediate-mass Black Holes in Radio-selected Dwarf Galaxies
papers.abstract: A radio/X-ray Fundamental Plane (FP) test of an intermediate-mass black hole is informative only when the compact radio emission, hard X-rays, accretion state, and host association refer to the same accretor. We used published VLA, VLBA, \textit{Chandra}, and \textit{HST} observations of a radio-selected dwarf-galaxy sample to determine when present nondetections are constraining and what observations are required for a stronger test. The VLBA follow-up reveals that compactness alone does not establish association with the target dwarf, while for the best nuclear candidates the radio component relevant to the FP has not yet been isolated on the intermediate physical scales between the VLA and VLBA measurements. We therefore recast the FP as a forward question: for an assumed black-hole mass, how likely is a given radio observation to detect the compact core? The calculation includes intrinsic FP scatter, X-ray uncertainties, the radio spectral index, the accretion state, and source size relative to the beam. The existing VLBA nondetections have low completeness across the adopted intermediate-mass range and do not provide useful black-hole mass upper limits. Meaningful tests require deeper resolution-matched radio imaging, recovery of intermediate-scale structure, and contemporaneous measurements of the intrinsic hard-X-ray component. Because the calculation returns a mass-dependent detection function for each source, the same framework can be applied to larger dwarf-galaxy samples to quantify survey completeness and build selection functions for population studies of low-mass black holes.

papers.title: Rethinking Data Selection as Distribution Matching on Semantic Manifolds
papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

authors.name: Peng Sun
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory on Integrated Optoelectronics

authors.name: Yao Zhu
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: On PMU Adequacy for Wideband Dynamics Tracking Beyond Attenuation Assumptions
papers.abstract: Recent work highlights the inadequacy of standard synchrophasors in capturing high-frequency grid dynamics, including data center oscillations, primarily due to filtering and windowing attenuation during phasor estimation. This letter shows how synchrophasor ambient data spectrum itself contains information on attenuation, which provides a way to identify critically impacted measurements and potentially estimate and undo the effect. Results are shown for synthetic data as well as actual synchrophasor estimates from digital fault recorders (DFRs) within the Dominion Energy system.

papers.title: Composition Theorem for Randomized Query Complexity
papers.abstract: For bounded-error randomized query complexity, we resolve the composition conjecture up to logarithmic factors. The general upper bound $R(f\circ g) = O\!\left(R(f)R(g)\log(R(f)+1)\right)$ was already known. Although Meiburg recently disproved constant-factor multiplicative composition for total Boolean functions, the conjecture allowing polylogarithmic losses remained open. We settle this question by proving that, for all (possibly partial) Boolean functions $f$ and $g$, \[ R(f\circ g) = \Omega\!\left(\frac{R(f)R(g)}{\log(n+1)}\right), \] where $n$ is the input size for $f$.

papers.title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
papers.abstract: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.

authors.name: Yize Zhao
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: FORGE'd In The Early Universe II: Constraining The Pop III Initial Mass Function
papers.abstract: We present a cosmological radiation-magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) zoom-in simulation of $56$ Population III stars using FORGE'd in FIRE. Our simulation combines a cosmological initial condition centered on an isolated ultra-faint galaxy ($M_{\mathrm{halo}} \sim 10^9 M_\odot$ at $z=0$) with individual-star formation and feedback physics, reaching a maximum mass resolution of $\sim 10^{-2} M_\odot$ and spatial resolution of $\sim 10^{-3} \mathrm{pc}$. We follow continued star formation for just over $500$ Myr, from $z \sim 16$ to $z \sim 7$, substantially longer than what has been achieved before, and track star formation across five distinct minihalos. From our stellar population, we self-consistently resolve an emergent stellar initial mass function (IMF) and find $\alpha = 1.9$ for $dN/dM \propto M^{-\alpha}$ at $M_{\star} \gtrsim 2.2 M_{\odot}$. Additionally, we form both single and multiple stellar systems, including binaries and higher-order multiples, as well as stars with masses below $1 M_{\odot}$. At early times, the stellar mass distribution is more top-heavy, with a high-mass slope of $\alpha\sim1.4-1.5$, similar to previous Pop. III simulations, and steepens as star formation continues. This suggests that differences between our final IMF and previous studies may partly reflect the much longer evolution followed here, approximately five orders of magnitude longer than in several previous Pop. III sink-particle simulations. The first star-forming minihalo, which hosts the most massive stars in our simulation, has a shallower IMF slope of $\alpha\approx 1$, while later-forming minihalos produce lower maximum stellar masses in lower-density parent clouds.

papers.title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
papers.abstract: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

papers.title: A Poincare-Einstein Liouville Theorem and the Yamabe Invariant of Lens Spaces
papers.abstract:
Schoen conjectured that the Yamabe invariant of every lens space is achieved by the round metric. A proof of this conjecture is presented for all lens spaces, together with rigidity: equality is only achieved for the round class. The key step is to show that every $\mathbb Z_p$-invariant Yamabe-positive conformal class on $S^3$ admits a $\mathbb Z_p$-equivariant Poincar\'e-Einstein filling. The distance function from a fixed point of the filling then gives an invariant test function with Yamabe quotient at most $\sigma(S^3)$, which descends to the lens space.
  The proof of the main theorem was generated by AI (ChatGPT Astra, September 2026); this is mainly a learning note of the AI generated proof.

authors.name: Xin Zhou
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Through Ups and Downs: the Transient Lensing Behaviour of SIDM halos undergoing Core Collapse
papers.abstract: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes can become extremely dense following gravothermal core collapse, motivating their use as explanations for unusually concentrated gravitational lenses. Using an emulator calibrated on gravothermal fluid calculations, we investigate whether increasing central density necessarily strengthens lensing. We follow initially Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) haloes through core formation and collapse deep into the short-mean-free-path regime, and compute finite-source magnifications, critical curves, and source-plane lensing cross sections for isolated spherical haloes with elastic, velocity-independent self-interactions, including external shear in selected calculations. Lensing strength evolves non-monotonically: it initially decreases during core formation, rises during early collapse, and generally declines at later stages despite continued growth of the central density. This decline accompanies the emergence of a dense inner core whose mass and radius decrease within a more extended, lower-density core. Time-averaged enhancement relative to NFW haloes depends on the lensing statistic, halo concentration, and interaction cross section. Generalized NFW haloes with central cusps $\rho \propto r^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma \geq 2$ always have larger lensing efficacies than core-collapsed SIDM haloes of equal mass and are therefore poor proxies, including in terms of the demographics (size and radial thickness) of arcs and Einstein rings. The core collapse stage at which SIDM haloes are optimal lenses coincides with the epoch at which the characteristic core surface density is close to critical, which typically occurs during the early stages of core collapse. These results demonstrate that central density alone is insufficient to characterize SIDM lensing and that its evolving mass distribution must be modelled explicitly.

papers.title: Experimental Evaluation of High-Throughput Structure Predictions
papers.abstract: High throughput computational databases such as Materials Project, the Open Quantum Materials Database, and Alexandria now each list on the order of 10^5 predicted stable compounds. However, the overall reliability of these predictions in terms of actual experimental synthesizability remains poorly understood. In this work we attempt to synthesize, via arc melting, 34 different predicted ternary compounds. The majority of these materials did not form in the predicted structure, instead resulting in disordered variants or multiphase mixtures. Four formed ordered structures not reported before, one of them at a composition reported earlier without a structure. We discuss both the failures and the successes, and identify simple filtering criteria that can help researchers avoid hypothetical materials that are unlikely to form.

papers.title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers
papers.abstract: Probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers need to represent both uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence to support grid operations. This paper develops an open, grid-oriented benchmark using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster. Forecasts are evaluated through four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation, and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Following a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves only 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, while online regime-conditioned calibration increases coverage to 87.3%. Even with well-calibrated marginal forecasts, independent sampling produces unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence from historical forecast errors reduces the discrepancy in ramp statistics and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4-10.6% across three forecasting tasks. These findings show that marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions and motivate joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure, and decision outcomes.

authors.name: Jianhui Wang
authors.institution: Changchun University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Energy- and momentum-resolved Cooper-pair emission from a cuprate superconductor
papers.abstract: Superconductivity arises from Cooper pairing, but conventional photoemission probes electrons individually rather than as pairs. Here we report the observation of Cooper-pair emission from an optimally doped cuprate superconductor using two-electron angle-resolved photoemission (2e-ARPES). Below the superconducting transition, we observe a distinct two-electron emission peak at zero pair binding energy and zero pair momentum that disappears in the normal state, revealing the characteristic fingerprint of a Cooper pair. Unexpectedly, the joint energy distribution broadens markedly along the relative-energy axis as temperature decreases, while the total energy width remains nearly unchanged. This anomalous behavior cannot be explained by instrumental resolution, static disorder or thermal broadening, and instead points to scattering processes involving collective excitations of the superconductor. Our results establish 2e-ARPES as a probe of both Cooper-pair emission and the many-body dynamics of the superconducting state.

papers.title: GRAC: Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning for Surgical Scene Description
papers.abstract:
Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge.
  Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation.
  Results: On the EndoVis-18 benchmark, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.88, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest conventional Transformer baseline. Exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy reached 52.6%, compared with 32.7% for SGT and 26.2% for the strongest conventional baseline. These results demonstrate improvements in language quality and factual agreement. On TORS, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.06, compared with 3.80 for the strongest baseline.
  Conclusion: GRAC demonstrates that combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves surgical scene captioning and produces more contextually meaningful descriptions.

papers.title: Stability of large dynamical systems using Gershgorin Disc Theorem
papers.abstract: Understanding the stability of large nonlinear dynamical systems is a fundamental problem in many fields, including biological, technological, and social networks. Traditional stability methods often rely on explicit eigenvalue calculations or the construction of Lyapunov functions, which become computationally difficult for large interconnected systems. In this work, we introduce a stability classifier that provides a computationally efficient way to determine the stability of complex systems without performing full spectral analysis. Our approach combines the Dynamical Jacobian Ensemble framework, which uses the network structure and the underlying dynamics to construct a Jacobian, with the Gershgorin disc theorem, which provides bounds on the eigenvalues of the system's Jacobian matrix. Using this combination, we derive an analytical classifier that predicts whether a dynamical system is asymptotically stable, unstable, or sensitively stable based on a small set of dynamical and network parameters. The analysis reveals that the stability of large dynamical systems is strongly influenced by highly connected hub nodes. This observation allows the stability condition to be simplified by focusing on the contribution of the hub-associated Gershgorin disc. Extensive numerical simulations on large ensembles of Jacobian matrices confirm that the proposed classifier accurately separates stable, unstable, and sensitively stable regimes across a wide range of dynamical parameters and network structures. The resulting framework provides a simple and scalable tool for predicting the stability of large dynamical networks while capturing the interplay between network topology and interaction dynamics.

papers.title: TriNetra: Thermal-Reliability-Guided RGB-Thermal Fusion and Tracking for Surveillance
papers.abstract: Visible cameras fail at night and thermal sensors fail under saturation, blur or loss of contrast, yet most RGB-thermal (RGB-T) detectors mix the two streams with fixed weights and cannot tell when one modality has become unreliable. TriNetra is a reliability-aware surveillance framework built around this problem. The proposed solution computes a frame-level Thermal Reliability Coefficient (TRC) from five label-free image cues, uses it to gate the thermal features of a dual-branch YOLOv8m detector whose visible branch, neck and head are frozen and COCO-pretrained, and passes the same score to a ByteTrack-based tracker that feeds a rule-based behaviour analyser. On the M3FD benchmark (2,940/630/630 split) the detector reaches 87.6% precision, 79.4% recall, 70.0% mAP@50 and 47.8% mAP@50:95 on the test split, with 17.0 M of its 42.9 M parameters trained. TRC stays near 0.78 on clean frames (standard deviation 0.012), decreases with the severity of thermal saturation and blur, reaching 0.53 and 0.69 at full severity, and is insensitive to RGB-thermal misalignment. With identical weights, the adaptive gate matches a fixed gate on clean data (70.0% versus 69.8% mAP@50) but keeps 43.6% mAP@50 when the thermal stream is corrupted, against 38.4%, 29.2% and 25.0% for a fixed gate, full thermal admission and a closed gate; the 5.1-point gain over the fixed gate has a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of +3.6 to +6.5 points. In tracking, the TRC-gated association performs on par with ByteTrack on a synthetic benchmark with exact ground truth and on 14 M3FD clips, and is slightly less stable under thermal saturation, so its measured benefit is confined to the detector. The limitations of the current evaluation are reported together with the results.

papers.title: PhyCAD: Physics-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Language-driven computer-aided design (CAD) generation enables the creation of editable parametric models from text, yet geometric correctness alone does not ensure physical feasibility. We present PhyCAD, a framework for physics-aware Text-to-CAD generation that trains language models to produce executable CadQuery programs under geometric and physical constraints. To support this setting, we construct a Text-to-CAD dataset that links parametric CAD models with geometric specifications, loading conditions, and physical constraints. We further develop an automated CAD--CAE verifier that combines program execution, geometric checks, and finite element analysis to provide feedback for model training. A key learning challenge is to prioritize joint satisfaction of geometric and physical constraints while retaining informative feedback on partial progress. A flat aggregation of heterogeneous rewards can obscure this priority, allowing improvements in individual criteria to compensate for unmet design requirements. We therefore introduce a Hierarchical Balanced Advantage for Group Relative Policy Optimization, grouping candidates into levels according to their verification status and combining between-level progress with objective-wise peer ranking within each level. This formulation preserves cross-level priority in the training signal while providing fine-grained feedback for satisfying constraints and improving feasible designs. Experiments across multiple language models show that PhyCAD consistently improves joint geometric and physical constraint satisfaction. These results demonstrate the value of verifiable engineering feedback for advancing language-driven CAD generation beyond geometric reconstruction toward physics-aware design.

authors.name: Zhengyang Li
authors.institution: Tianjin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: CRTrack-Cap: A New Benchmark for Cross-View Dense Video Object Captioning
papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.

papers.title: Spectral Rigidity of Stochastic Operators with Heavy Tailed Perturbations
papers.abstract: In this paper, we provide a new set of tools for establishing the number rigidity of point processes which are particularly well suited for the spectral processes of stochastic operators. These tools allow one to prove the number rigidity of a wide class of stochastic operators that had been previously inaccessible to the standard methods in the area, such as the variance of linear statistics, which require being able to precisely analyze correlations between individual points. We propose an alternative mechanism which uses a pathwise comparison between the growth rate of the unperturbed eigenvalues and the cumulative random noise which allows one to convert the probabilistic problem into a more tractable perturbation theory problem. This new approach allows us to prove the rigidity of previously inaccessible operators including those with heavy tailed perturbations or complex correlation structures. As a demonstration, we use these tools to prove the number rigidity of new classes of stochastic Schr\"odinger and Sturm-Liouville Operators which are resistant to analysis using the standard rigidity toolkit.

papers.title: Fortuitous Cancellation of Competing Effects in the Free Energy of Water Autoionization: Long-Range Electrostatics, System Size, and Nuclear Quantum Effects
papers.abstract: Few molecular processes are more fundamental to chemistry than the autoionization of water, whose equilibrium constant, $K_w \approx 10^{-14}$, underlies acid-base equilibria and the chemistry of life. Yet the molecular origins of the free energy cost of forming and separating ions remain incompletely understood. Efforts to explain it have been limited by the difficulty of modeling water reactivity in sufficient detail. Here we combine machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with spectral adaptive biasing force enhanced sampling to connect proton transfer and water wire configurations to the underlying free energy landscape. We identify competing influences of long-range electrostatics, system size, temperature, and nuclear quantum motion on the predicted ionization thermodynamics. The free energy surface extends from neutral water to ions separated beyond the solvent-separated ion pair (SSIP). It reveals a transition state in which a proton is shared between the second and third molecules of a three-membered water wire. The contact ion pair is unstable and the SSIP only weakly metastable, so determining pK$_w$ requires sampling longer wires. Long-range electrostatics raise the free energy at ion separations beyond $3\,\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$. Models with comparable force errors give substantially different free energy profiles in this region. Increasing system size lowers the calculated pK$_w$, while nuclear quantum effects bring it closer to experiment and reproduce the higher pK$_w$ of D$_2$O relative to H$_2$O. These results establish a baseline for interpreting thermodynamic results from MLIP simulations in which charged and polar groups react and diffuse in finite cells. Our analysis also explains how cancellation among competing effects can yield ionization constants close to experiment even when simulations omit several physical contributions.

papers.title: Stable probabilistic emulation of partially observed dynamical systems
papers.abstract: Predicting the long-term behavior of partially observed dynamical systems such as the coupled atmosphere-ocean system is central to societal decision-making. Motivated by the success of deep learning emulators in weather forecasting, data-driven climate models represent a promising approach. However, climate emulation poses distinct challenges: models must account for unresolved fast variables introduced by unavoidable coarse-graining, reproduce long-term statistics, and remain stable over arbitrarily long rollouts and under external perturbations. These requirements motivate stochastic data-driven emulators, but modern generative models lack stability guarantees. We introduce forced-dissipative stochastic interpolants, a generative framework for learning stochastic reduced dynamics. Its architecture uses structural constraints inspired by turbulent dynamics, which provide stability by design while retaining the flexibility of stochastic interpolants to represent complex probabilistic dynamics. Building on the theory of Markov-chain stability, we establish a Foster--Lyapunov drift condition and prove geometric ergodicity for our emulator, together with stability under steady external forcing. We evaluate the framework on the two-timescale Lorenz-96 system, a prototype of partially observed multiscale turbulence. The resulting emulator remains stable over long integrations and under finite-amplitude forcing, with accurate prediction of forced responses of both the mean and variance.

papers.title: The Multiscale Single-Index Model: An MSE Analysis of Online SGD Dynamics
papers.abstract: We consider the Multiscale Single-Index Model (MSIM), first introduced by Oymak and Soltanolkotabi (2021), as a stylized model for hierarchical feature learning with scale separation. Each layer extracts a shared single-index feature at one physical scale and passes it to the next, giving a tractable setting in which to study how deep architectures learn local multiscale representations. Under non-degeneracy and delocalization assumptions on the link function and planted features respectively, for the two hidden-layer case ($K=2$), we analyze joint online spherical SGD under MSE loss, which is a canonical regression objective, in discrete time and show that it achieves weak recovery from random initialization in $O(d\log^2 d)$ samples, followed by strong recovery to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in $O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))$ additional samples. The main technical challenge arises from the non-Gaussian learned features observed by the second layer. We address this challenge through a quantitative Gaussian comparison using delocalization, combined with sharp trajectory-level control of the coupled SGD dynamics. This work is a companion to Bruna (2026, arXiv:2607.03347), which studies recovery under a correlation objective for general $K$.

papers.title: AISHELL8-FISHEYE: A Fisheye Audio-Visual Dataset for Target Speaker Extraction with Distortion-Aware Baselines
papers.abstract: Fisheye cameras offer wide visual coverage but distort facial and lip geometry, challenging audio-visual target speaker extraction. We introduce AISHELL8-FISHEYE, a 47.03-hour corpus of 94 Mandarin speakers with synchronized audio and paired fisheye and normal-camera videos. Speaker-disjoint splits and synthetic two-speaker mixtures support reproducible evaluation under matched acoustic conditions. We also establish a baseline that combines a lip-reading encoder with a frozen distortion-aware branch transferred from fisheye head pose estimation. On fisheye video, adding this branch to an adapted lip encoder improves scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio improvement from 10.47 to 11.84 dB. The branch does not improve performance with a frozen lip encoder, highlighting the importance of visual adaptation. A substantial gap to paired normal-camera inputs remains. The corpus and baseline resources support further research on speech extraction from distorted visual cues.

papers.title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
papers.abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.

papers.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
papers.abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.

papers.title: FoleyForge: Free-form, Controllable, Rectified-flow Editing of Sound Effects
papers.abstract: We present FoleyForge, a generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects. Given an input clip and a free-form instruction describing the desired change, it applies the edit while preserving the input's identity. A single model handles semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like changes. We introduce a data pipeline that guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits, thus addressing the lack of publicly available audio editing data. Such data is then used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generation model, which we extend to expose attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance, yielding a more expressive editing model. FoleyForge achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.

papers.title: Structuring Survey Histories for LLM Digital Twins: A Controlled Study of Background, Decision Procedure, and Evaluation Profiles
papers.abstract: LLM-based digital twins aim to predict how individuals would respond in new settings from representations of their prior responses. Existing evidence that compression of survey histories need not reduce predictive accuracy suggests that representation structure, rather than information volume alone, may be an important design choice. We study BDE, a fixed representation that organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. We evaluate it on Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025) by predicting each respondent's held-out answers on 17 tasks. In a paired evaluation with 100 respondents, a fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over the raw survey transcript by 1.27 percentage points (pp) on gpt-5.4-nano (p < 0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p < 0.001). Three analyses then examine the schema, extraction depth, and component composition. Against a length-matched free-form profile written from the same transcript by the same extractor, BDE improves pricing accuracy on both simulators (2.15 pp on nano, p < 0.01; 1.38 pp on mini, p < 0.05), while its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p < 0.05). Allowing deeper inference during extraction yields no statistically significant gain on either simulator. By contrast, adding Evaluation to a Background--Decision procedure profile improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano (p < 0.001) and 1.22 pp on mini (p < 0.001). These results indicate that the advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone, and attribute it primarily to profile composition rather than deeper extraction.

papers.title: MEDALLION: Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON
papers.abstract: Dimensionality reduction is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data and guide scientific discovery, yet interpreting which original features contribute to low-dimensional representations remains challenging, particularly for black-box methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. We introduce \textbf{MEDALLION} (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON), a novel framework for interpreting low-dimensional embeddings through knowledge distillation and neural feature attribution. MEDALLION distills any given embedding with a neural encoder which we explain via a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods. Through experiments on MNIST and applications in single-cell transcriptomics, we show MEDALLION provides informative feature attributions that cast additional insights into the underlying embedding and compare its performance with existing interpretability approaches.

authors.name: Genevera I. Allen
authors.institution: Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute

papers.title: AircraftWitness: How Often Aircraft Can Locate Recordings
papers.abstract: Aircraft overhead can reveal where an outdoor recording was made. Propellers and rotors leave Doppler curves in audio, and public ADS-B archives log equipped aircraft. We measure how often, blind and against chance. Our main test was registered and timestamped before any audio, and its two amendments came before any answer was read. It covers 24 new places, with the recorders' own clocks, a 300 s slack and a 20 km square. The best of three locators places clear-pass clips within 1 km at 4 places, where a uniform guess predicts 0.57 (p = 0.0065 after correcting for the pick). With the wrong time or swapped audio it places none. The other two hit 1 and 2. On 360 clips from 7 places of a GPS-timed network, two locators place 6% and 8% within 1 km. By place, a unit chosen after that run, they hit 4 and 5 of 7 where a uniform guess predicts 2.3. On 1,600 random public recordings, picked and cut without the truth in a time-bounded run, the three locators answer at most 20 times and place at most 2. We release AircraftWitness, a benchmark, and pass labels for 11.7 million recordings.

papers.title: Impact of color in computer and human-based object recognition under occlusion
papers.abstract: Partial occlusions challenge object recognition in both human and computer vision (CV), but the impact is largely dependent on the occlusion and model design. Properties relating to color are particularly important in biological recognition and frequently leveraged for camouflage, however there are still open questions about what makes them effective and how they translate to CV. This work studies partial occlusions that create camouflage, including those that blend in with target objects or with scenes, which alter object representations in distinct ways. Experiments evaluate recognition performance on both human participants and models ranging from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to transformers, and additional analysis is performed on models to uncover trends in processing and object representations under multiple occlusion types. Novel metrics offer explainability of model behavior under occlusion: non-occlusion precision (NOP) and non-occlusion recall (NOR) measure alignment of model activations with and without occlusion, and activation in occlusion (AIO) measures the percentage of activations that occur in occluded regions. Findings show that human recognition, and most transformers, are negatively impacted by generated camouflaging occluders, with scene-based camouflage performing worse than object-based. Classical CNNs show a strong opposite trend, performing the worst on neutral-colored occlusions, suggesting that contextually-related colors, particularly scene-based, benefit object recognition rather than disrupting shape or boundary cues. Additionally, generated camouflaging occluders for training augmentation improves robustness to unseen camouflage for selected CNN model, and occlusion metrics suggest trends about learned mechanisms. Findings have interesting implications for alignment in human and computer vision, model vulnerabilities, and explainability.

papers.title: Ordered Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.

papers.title: Polynomial complexity, random graphs, and strict ergodicity
papers.abstract:
We construct infinite words $w$ whose complexity functions are quadratically bounded, but whose discrete derivatives are not linearly bounded, resolving a question of Cassaigne.
  Moreover, we construct infinite words of polynomially bounded complexity, and subshifts of quasi-linear complexity, whose discrete derivatives do not decay compared to their complexity functions, thus exhibiting a typical exponentially-growing behavior. As an application, we give the first examples of subshifts of polynomial complexity whose Rauzy graphs do not have Benjamini-Schramm limits.
  Finally, we realize (up to an inevitable linear error factor) every function satisfying the necessary conditions, as the complexity function of a minimal, uniquely ergodic, cube-free subshift, strengthening previous realization results in this direction, and derive consequences for the growth of simple algebras and just-infinite semigroups satisfying nontrivial laws.

authors.name: Efim Zelmanov
authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Rethinking Latent Reasoning for Generative Recommendation: Beyond Teacher-Generated CoT and Recurrent Hidden-State Feedback
papers.abstract: Latent reasoning in generative recommendation faces two practical barriers: constructing teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is costly, and recurrent hidden-state feedback requires a specialized execution loop. We revisit both the supervision source and the computation interface. A step-level diagnosis measures how recommendation CoT supports next-item prediction and trace coherence. In the analyzed traces, history analysis is the only step with positive mean contributions on both dimensions, while later preference and intent steps have negative mean answer contributions. Guided by this finding, we propose PHiT (Prefilled, History-Informed Thought Tokens), which learns intermediate states from semantic targets extracted directly from observed item histories. PHiT aggregates cached sparse item encodings to construct these targets and supervises the contextual states of distinct vocabulary thought tokens. All thought tokens are supplied together as ordinary input IDs during a single causal prefill, removing the need for recurrent final-state feedback. With supervised fine-tuning alone, PHiT outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. Controlled ablations support the value of input-matched semantic supervision, while cost measurements show fast target construction with training time comparable to the recommendation-only thought-token baseline.

papers.title: Asymptotic stability of high-index saddle dynamics
papers.abstract: High-index saddle dynamics (HiSD) has been extensively adopted to compute saddle points of arbitrary index, with various applications such as constructing solution landscapes of complex systems. In this work, we prove the asymptotic stability of various HiSD methods, including the idealized, perturbed, and coupled HiSD methods, as well as their momentum-accelerated variants. The analysis is Jacobian-free and thus compensates for the linear stability analysis in the literature. The results not only provide specific characterizations for the convergence rate and the basin of attraction, but also reveal intrinsic correlations among dynamics in the coupled HiSD. Theoretical results are substantiated by numerical experiments.

papers.title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.

papers.title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.

papers.title: Exploring the Regular and Singular Loci of Group Representation Varieties
papers.abstract: Let $B$ be the Borel Subgroup of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$, and let $G_m=\langle x,y,z\mid x^2y^3=z^{2m+1}\rangle$, $m\geq2$. The $G_m$ are parafree of rank two and deviation one. We compute the integral homology of the regular and singular loci of $X_m=\mathrm{Hom}(G_m,B)$. Each $X_m$ is a four-dimensional irreducible affine variety with the homotopy type of a two-dimensional torus. Its singular locus is a disjoint union of $16m$ affine lines. The regular locus has Betti numbers $b_0=1$, $b_1=2$, $b_2=16m+1$, and $b_3=b_5=16m$, with all other Betti numbers zero. Thus, although each $X_m$ has the homotopy type of a torus and its singular locus is a disjoint union of contractible lines, removing the singular locus creates $16m$ additional independent homology classes in each of degrees $2$, $3$, and $5$, arising from the transverse link $S^2\times S^3$. We also establish that the regular loci are not affine.

papers.title: Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation
papers.abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.

papers.title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.

authors.institution: Changchun University of Science and Technology

papers.title: On the Effectiveness and Limitations of Open-Weight LLMs for Low-Resource Offensive Language Detection in Danish
papers.abstract: We study the effectiveness and robustness of open-weight large language models (LLMs) for Danish offensive language detection, an underexplored low-resource task. We evaluate four model families (Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen) across eleven prompting strategies spanning five design categories, cross-prompt generalization, Danish orthographic variation, and robustness under balanced and naturally imbalanced class distributions. We compare against three BERT-family baselines with distinct pre-training strategies, evaluated via both masked language model prompting and supervised fine-tuning. Even without task-specific fine-tuning, LLMs can surpass all three fine-tuned BERT baselines, and lightweight finetuning yields substantial further gains. No single model or prompt category dominates, underscoring that prompt design interacts with model pre-training in ways that cannot be predicted a priori. Semantically grounded prompts transfer more robustly, while format-constrained patterns consistently fail to generalize. ASCII transliteration of Danish-specific characters ({\ae}, {\o}, {\aa}) generally degrades performance, indicating these characters encode meaningful signal. At the same time, the gap between a balanced test set (best F1 of 0.84) and the corpus's natural class skew (0.62 trained on skewed data, 0.70 trained on balanced data) -- relative drops of 26.2\% and 16.7\% -- shows that class imbalance remains a critical open challenge. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/PASHAADC/Danish-LLM-HateSpeech.

papers.title: Borel rigidity for higher rank lattices
papers.abstract: In this paper we focus on rigidity in descriptive set theory. Building on cocycle superrigidity results of Popa, Furman and Ioana, we prove rigidity in the purely Borel context for the orbit equivalence relations arising from the shift actions and translation actions of lattices in semisimple Lie groups with higher rank. Our results sharpen work of Adams and Kechris.

authors.name: Filippo Calderoni
authors.institution: Center for Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science

papers.title: Classical control of quantum-state relaxation in confined molecular hydrogen
papers.abstract: Quantum-state conversion between the ortho and para nuclear-spin states of H$_2$ is forbidden in the isolated molecule but these states can become connected through interactions with a surrounding environment. How that same environment governs the dynamics of the newly connected states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this problem using H$_2$ confined in crystalline molecular solids, where the host environment selectively enables conversion between a pair of otherwise disconnected ortho-H$_2$ and para-H$_2$ states. Rotationally resolved infrared spectroscopy directly determines the state-specific conversion dynamics in crystalline CO$_2$ and N$_2$O at 10 K, revealing that increasing H$_2$ concentration suppresses nuclear-spin conversion by nearly an order of magnitude, reaching complete suppression by 20% H$_2$ loading. Molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations identify two complementary origins of this concentration dependence: changes in the thermally populated phonon modes available to mediate relaxation, and strain-driven H$_2$ clustering that progressively removes molecules from the host crystal field responsible for enabling conversion. The resulting picture connects a classical collective response of the host to microscopic quantum-state dynamics: H$_2$ loading generates strain that reorganizes the local molecular environment, thereby modifying both the phonon bath and the molecular coupling to that bath. These results establish a multiscale mechanism by which condensed-phase environments can govern the connectivity and dynamics of an effective two-level system.
