papers.title: Conley index theory for asymptotically autonomous systems and UV-to-IR connections
papers.abstract: Many non-equilibrium systems, such as expanding plasmas, evolve by equations that depend explicitly on time and interpolate between autonomous early-time (UV) and late-time (IR) limits. After time is compactified, fixed points lie on invariant boundary fibers, where the Conley index is one-sided and blind to the UV. For time dependence that admits a $C^1$ compactification, we reflect the extended phase space across these fibers. Both sheets of the double run from the UV to the IR, and the UV index reappears, suspended by one degree. Extending one sheet slightly beyond both fibers gives an explicit UV-to-IR transport map between the Conley indices of the limit systems, and its non-vanishing forces connecting solutions. If one block with a fixed strict entrance/exit decomposition serves every frozen system, this map is an isomorphism at every admissible rate. If the block also has nonzero relative homology, the isolated invariant sets of the two limits are connected at every rate. In the Gubser flow of Israel-Stewart theory, the separatrix between two classes of initial data is a transversal connection at every finite relaxation scale $c$, with splitting $\Delta(c)\propto1/c$. In the Bjorken flow at the lowest moment truncation, we prove existence and uniqueness of the attractor solution without regularization. For the three-dimensional Gubser system we construct the global Morse decomposition. In the one-loop flow of the $(4+\epsilon)$-dimensional $O(N)$ model with cubic anisotropy, a shift of $N$ through $N=4$ has vanishing transport map, but a driven connection and a nonzero connecting homomorphism detect it at every rate.

papers.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
papers.abstract: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.

papers.title: Attaining Optimal Values under Sure Constraints
papers.abstract: A game may have, for each target below its value, a finite controller meeting that target, yet no finite controller attaining the value itself. We study finite stochastic games with a hard specification that must hold on every supported execution, including paths of probability zero. Max uses a pure finite controller; Min may use any pure public-history strategy. We distinguish three numerical questions: can a supplied target be met, can the unspecified optimum be attained, and what is one exact value? For explicit hard and Boolean soft Streett conditions, the strict and non-strict supplied-threshold problems are coNP-complete, attainment of the unsupplied supremum is $\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete, and one exact reduced fraction is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete under polynomial metric reductions. The proofs preserve both the value and its finite attainability when fixing a single opponent, and encode adaptive queries without computing unknown subgame values. The same construction yields matching value-comparison and exact-output lower bounds for ordinary stochastic Streett games with unrestricted randomized history strategies. We also bound the memory needed for optimal finite implementations for arbitrary Muller hard conditions and rational rewards in $[0,1]$ determined by infinitely recurring states. One controller is sure from the entire original sure region and attains at every finitely attained start, with no attainment premise on the other states. For $n$ states in that region it uses $2^{O(n\log(n+1))}Q(1+\log R)$ modes, where $Q$ is the product of the least common denominators of full original chance rows sourced in that sure region and $R$ clears all reward values. Its joint dependence on $Q$ and $R$ is worst-case sharp at each fixed $n\ge6$ when $Q,R\ge2$. Optimal dependence on arena size and efficient general synthesis are not resolved here.

papers.title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
papers.abstract: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM and used it for the matching. Our question is whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Improving its accuracy required fusion with a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single shift per ground track, then per observation. For most tracks, the shifts nearly matched those from the airborne LiDAR DTM, likely because DTM errors canceled out across many observations. Per-observation corrections, however, did not match. At a single observation, the error does not cancel out and is too large for the correction. This error likely originates mainly from the input DTM. Therefore, even without a 1 m-resolution DTM, a roughly 10 m-resolution DTM, fused with a global DTM and super-resolved to 1 m, should yield track-wise corrections nearly matching those from a 1 m-resolution DTM.

papers.title: Language, Not Code Abstraction: Natural-language Training Shapes Brain-aligned Geometry
papers.abstract: Code-trained language models produce positive brain scores, which raises the question of whether abstract structure learned from programming languages can substitute for natural-language training. We trained 25 GPT-2-small models on TinyStories, Python, C functions, x86-64 assembly, and the corresponding machine code, and scored them using a shared tokenizer and encoding procedure against matched random-weight models. On Pereira-243 and Tuckute2024, TinyStories exceeds the mean of the four code models by $\Delta r = 0.053$ and $0.059$ (Holm-corrected $p<0.001$), while code training leaves alignment near the random-weight level. The language advantage is benchmark-specific: Blank2014 shows no corrected language-code difference, and Fedorenko2016 shows no language benefit. Geometry tracks the encoding result on Pereira-243: TinyStories seeds converge on the most similar representations, and its fit-free correspondence with neural dissimilarity peaks at $\rho = 0.14$, twice the code and random-weight levels. Binary-trained models have about three effective dimensions, so seed agreement alone does not imply neural correspondence. Updating only the embedding matrix on English improves mean-over-depth alignment for every code model more than an equal update on its own corpus. Within this architecture and training setup, natural-language training produces a distinct representational geometry with closer neural correspondence on Pereira-243

papers.title: The GPU Needs an Operating System
papers.abstract: AI chips sit mostly idle while serving models, because replies must be fast and each step waits on memory. On two large open models, the math units were busy only about 6-11% of the time. We argue the GPU needs an operating system that keeps urgent work on schedule and fills idle capacity with other useful work. A feature that ships today recovers a quarter of a GPU with work designed to share, and a tenth with real jobs, at 5% slower decode. Our research system does better: one resident kernel runs a whole model faster than vLLM's best for a single request, and shares the GPU at under 2% slowdown. Scaling beyond one hand-built model needs compilers and a few new chip features, which we specify.

papers.title: Fujita's Very Ampleness Conjecture for $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$-Bundles over Curves
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a vector bundle of rank $n\geq 2$ over a smooth projective curve $C$ over $\mathbb{C}$. We prove that $K_{\mathbb{P}_C(\mathcal{E})}+\mathcal{L}_1+\dots+\mathcal{L}_k$ is very ample for arbitrary ample line bundles $\mathcal{L}_i$ when $k\geq n+2$.

papers.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
papers.abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

papers.title: Structure and Lineage Evidence for Vietnamese Statutory Article Retrieval on DRiLL
papers.abstract: We study Vietnamese statutory Article retrieval on DRiLL using features for provision identity and local form, same-law support, and citation and lineage evidence. Across five random seeds, selectors sharing candidates, listwise Qwen evidence, and learner settings improve official $F_2$ from 71.77% to 72.91%, with the largest descriptive gain on two-Article questions. Added features account for 18.20% of the proposed selector's total decision-tree split gain, measured as training-objective reduction, mainly from same-law and citation evidence. Cases reveal base provisions and amendments, companion recovery, distractor removal, and failures. These findings motivate research on other datasets, representations, and learners without establishing individual feature effects or requiring LightGBM, hand-crafted scores, or explicit graphs.

authors.name: Duc-Vu Nguyen
authors.institution: Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City

authors.name: Ngan Luu-Thuy Nguyen
authors.institution: Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City

papers.title: Tailoring resonator geometry for astigmatism compensation with structured light in birefringent optical cavities
papers.abstract: In this work, we experimentally investigate the astigmatism induced by a birefringent crystal inside an optical cavity and demonstrate a geometric compensation strategy for structured modes carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). We show that the astigmatism observed in the semimonolithic configuration can be fully compensated by introducing a third mirror to fold the cavity, thereby exploiting the geometric astigmatism arising from oblique incidence on the curved mirror. By performing a study of the resonator geometry, both theoretical and experimental results confirm that this approach enables the preservation of OAM between the pump beam and the converted signal and idler modes, providing an effective design strategy for birefringent optical cavities.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic Natal Kicks and Formation of Black Hole Binaries
papers.abstract: The observation of over 300 Gravitational Wave (GW) events by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, has yielded information of the merger of compact object binaries, such as their individual masses and spins. However, the effective spin parameter obtained from the GW signal provides important information that could be used to discern the binary's formation channel. Overall, binaries formed from dynamic interactions in dense stellar environments are expected to have a random distribution of effective spins between -1 and 1. Meanwhile, binaries formed from the evolution of isolated stellar binaries are expected to have positive effective spins unless there is a large enough natal kick during the compact object formation that could significantly alter the orientation of the individual spins with respect to the binary's angular momentum. We study the viability of obtaining large natal kicks during the formation of massive Black Holes by studying the asymmetric mild explosion of $13\text{M}_{\odot}$, $21\text{M}_{\odot}$, $28\text{M}_{\odot}$ and $34\text{M}_{\odot}$ pre-supernova stellar models, by means of 3D Smooth Particle Hydrodynamics simulations. Our results show that, even kicks in the order of $\sim$ 1000 km/s, which are among the highest values observed for natal kicks, can't consistently change the orientation of the orbit. Physical setups where the orientation of the orbit changes require the kick to be directed correctly, and they would also require for the supernova explosion energy to be quite high.

papers.title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
papers.abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

papers.title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
papers.abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.

papers.title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
papers.abstract:
Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts.
  Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance.
  Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation.
  Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold.
  Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

papers.title: Dynamic signatures of collective knowledge through navigation in a network with semantic structure
papers.abstract: What distinguishes how humans navigate an information network like Wikipedia from what the underlying graph structure and language statistics alone predict? To study human collective navigation, we analyze 70,770 human trajectories through Wikispeedia, an online game where players navigate between articles to reach a target. To compare groups of trajectories rather than individual ones, we merge all trajectories leaving or entering a given article into a Flow Tree. Flow Trees compress collections of trajectories into hierarchies of group splits. We build forward and reverse Flow Trees for 815 of the most commonly traversed articles, representing divergence and convergence, respectively. We compare humans against four random-walker null models, either unweighted or weighted by graph structure, word frequency, or semantic similarity to target. Human Flow Trees are deeper with longer trunks and later splits, indicating players stay together longer than random walkers, whose Flow Trees tend to fan out immediately. An article's degree predicts 51.3-70.9% of the variation in Flow Tree branching factor for random walkers, but only 24.1-36.2% for humans. Taking what graph structure fails to predict as a two-dimensional coordinate system, we define four article types (beacons, funnels, forks, and corridors), distinguished by how humans enter and exit them. These human-defined types are not explained by out-degree or title-word frequency are, and are not recovered by any random walker. A fifth null model, built from first-order human click preferences, partially reproduces human Flow Tree shape but differs significantly in how much of that shape degree explains. We consider collective knowledge to be the structure shared by players who never communicate, beyond what graph structure imposes. It comprises first-order click preferences and a significant component that extends across clicks.

papers.title: TopoSHAP: Shapley for Explainable and Efficient Topological Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Topological deep learning (TDL) extends learning on graphs, such as molecules or social networks, to higher-order structures, such as rings in a molecule or groups in a social network. Explaining which of these structures drive a model's predictions, and which architectural components matter most for its performance, remains challenging. We introduce TopoSHAP, an efficient and general explanation framework that addresses both questions across topological domains and model architectures. TopoSHAP-cell assigns Shapley values to topological data cells and extracts compact explanations. These explanations match or outperform graph-based counterparts on GraphXAI benchmark data while running up to 112$\times$ faster. They also reveal advantageous topological feature design, leading to measured improvements in explanation recovery and predictive accuracy. On the architecture side, TopoSHAP-neighbor explains how neighborhoods contribute to model performance, and turns these evaluations into a backward-elimination search that identifies smaller, competitive architectures early in training. This is up to $11.3\times$ cheaper than traditional TDL training sweeps.

papers.title: MotionBench-XAI: Benchmarking What Shapes Shapley Explanations in Spatiotemporal Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Predicting outcomes from spatiotemporal data, such as assessing Parkinson's severity from human motion, often requires explainability in addition to accuracy. Practitioners need to know what drove the prediction, whether it be spatial (a body joint), temporal (a specific window), or both. Shapley values are attributions computed by treating input features as players in a cooperative game and measuring how the model output changes as coalitions of players are removed. Computing them involves choosing what counts as players, how absent players are imputed, and how the game is evaluated. How these choices affect explanation quality is poorly understood for spatiotemporal data, and real data carries no ground-truth attributions to check against. We present MotionBench-XAI, a benchmark built on i) five synthetic spatiotemporal datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, ii) three real datasets across clinical gait, electrocardiogram, and audio, iii) ten attribution methods across three player sets, and iv) three trained architectures. We show that grouping features into players, across time, space, or both, matters more than the choice of imputer. Generative imputers improve explanations only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics select contradictory best methods. We distill these findings into practical insights and provide an open-source pipeline.

papers.title: On nonlocal geometric rigidity estimates in bounded uniform domains
papers.abstract: We prove fractional geometric rigidity estimates and fractional Korn's first inequalities with general singular weights in bounded uniform domains in $\mathbb R^n.$ The classical choice of the energy well $SO(n)$ for the geometric rigidity estimate fails due to the lack of a notion of orientation for Lebesgue fields. The remedy is to choose $O(n)$ as the energy well. Due to the recently developed theory of local-to-nonlocal passage of rigidity estimates developed by the first author, both estimates reduce to the analogous local estimates on the cube, which we prove in several steps by compactness and linearization arguments.

papers.title: Nonstandard Dark Matter at Nonlinear Scales
papers.abstract: We investigate how two extensions of the standard $\Lambda$CDM scenario affect the evolution of the matter density and velocity divergence fields, from the linear regime to deeply nonlinear scales, using $N$-body simulations. We consider two well-motivated scenarios in which the canonical properties of dark matter (DM) are modified. In the first scenario, DM interacts with dark energy (DM--DE interaction). In the second scenario, we allow the DM equation-of-state parameter to deviate from the canonical pressureless limit, $w_{\rm DM}=0$. For the coupled DM--DE scenario, we find significant and scale-dependent deviations from $\Lambda$CDM of order $50$--$100\%$ in the matter power spectrum, persisting throughout the nonlinear regime, with the velocity divergence spectra providing complementary and partially independent sensitivity. For the $w_{\rm DM} \neq 0$ scenario, we find systematic but remarkably small deviations confined within $5\%$ across all scales probed. Our results identify which scales carry the greatest discriminatory power between these nonstandard scenarios and $\Lambda$CDM. We show that testing these models with current and forthcoming LSS surveys, through the analysis of density and/or velocity fields, will require a deeper theoretical understanding and accurate nonlinear modelling before robust constraints can be derived from observational data.

papers.title: Can a Language Model Write the Weights? An Empirical Study of LLM-Written Scoring Networks for Column Generation and MILP Branching, with a Bus-Driver Scheduling Application
papers.abstract: This paper was generated by an AI model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) under the author's direction; all results come from computations run on the author's machine, and every reference was checked. Weight-space programming (WSP) is the idea that a large language model (LLM) can write the weights of a small neural network directly, guided only by reading forward-pass outputs, with no gradient training. We test whether WSP can improve exact operations research algorithms where they rely on cheap scoring rules. In four studies, an LLM wrote small multilayer perceptrons that (i) select arcs, labels and ng-neighbourhoods inside column generation for the vehicle routing problem with time windows, and (ii) choose branching variables in SCIP's branch-and-bound. The algorithms stay exact whatever the weights; a bad network only costs time. In column generation, no lever gave a material gain. In branching on synthetic classes, a hand-written network solved independent-set instances in 0.37x the time of SCIP's default rule (18 paired instances, Wilcoxon $p<10^{-5}$) and matched or beat networks trained by imitation of strong branching, but on 39 MIPLIB 2017 instances it solved 19 versus 24. In an application built from the real GTFS feed of Atlanta's transit agency (MARTA), a crew scheduling set-partitioning model solved by a native C plugin with SCIP's factory settings, the LLM-written rules took 0.63x the default's time on 32 held-out instances ($p<10^{-4}$), but SCIP's plain pseudocost rule did exactly as well (ratio 0.99, $p=0.19$). In these settings, the gains came from being cheap, not from what the LLM wrote. All code, logs and the numbers behind every figure are released.

papers.title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
papers.abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

papers.title: Experimental realization of twofold topological phase transition induced by long-range hoppings in one-dimensional chains
papers.abstract: Long-range hoppings offer a powerful mechanism to engineer exotic topological phases beyond conventional tight-binding models. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a twofold topological phase transition driven by third-nearest-neighbor couplings in a one-dimensional phononic chain that emulates cis-polyacetylene. Tunable hopping parameters in highly structured aluminum plates allow us to observe the emergence of Dirac points, a valley pseudospin structure, and topological edge states. The experimental results are supported by non-equilibrium Green's function transport calculations. Our findings confirm the predicted long-range phase diagram and establish phononic metamaterials as a versatile platform for exploring topological phenomena beyond the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger paradigm.

papers.title: An Overview of Classical Scattering by a Lennard-Jones Potential
papers.abstract: We present a numerical and conceptual overview of classical scattering under a Lennard-Jones potential. All results were obtained by direct integration of particle trajectories in the two-dimensional plane for varying impact parameters and energies. From these trajectories, we compute deflection functions, identify critical values associated with unstable circular orbits, and visualize non-monotonic behavior in the angular deflection. We construct color maps representing the deflection angle and interaction delay time as functions of energy and impact parameter, and determine the differential cross section from the deflection function, accounting for multi-valued contributions. These results are displayed both as individual plots and as a full color map in the energy-angle plane, providing a detailed picture of the scattering behavior in this central potential.

papers.title: Analytical mean-field model for electrochemical metallization memristors with a nanoporous matrix: application to Ag/anodic alumina/Al
papers.abstract: Memristors based on electrochemical metallization with many filaments are usually modeled by microscopic simulations with many parameters or by phenomenological laws whose parameters are hard to relate to physical quantities. We present an analytical mean-field model for a population of Ag filaments confined in the pores of a nanoporous matrix, built on Ohm's law, Faraday's law and a power-based rupture criterion. The filaments have a truncated normal distribution of cross-sections and rupture leaving lognormally distributed gaps whose median grows with the dissipated power. Gap closing shifts the distribution of squared gaps rigidly, and the model therefore admits closed-form expressions for the switching voltage, the read current, the rupture branch and the high-voltage current. We apply it to Ag/nanoporous anodic alumina/Al structures fabricated from industrial-grade aluminum, with a 2.4$\mu$m alumina layer, and measured under ambient conditions. The parameters were fitted to the bipolar sweeps, with the gap dispersion taken from the temporal shape of the read after a pulse. They reproduce the bipolar response, including voltage-controlled negative differential resistance, and predict without refitting the unipolar sweeps and the amplitude of the pulse response, where state memory appears. A second sample, with a larger contact deposited chemically, is described by the same model. In vacuum the devices neither switch nor show negative differential resistance, as expected if adsorbed water supplies the counter reaction; the residual high-voltage current follows ionic hopping conduction.

papers.title: Hostages
papers.abstract:
Our house has been taken over. It is not completely destroyed, but many of its essential functions and facilities no longer work as they used to. Essentially, they are out of our control. Artificial intelligence, through its large language models (LLMs), has taken it. And we, the inhabitants of the house, without really noticing what was happening, and surprised by the effectiveness of LLMs, have handed over our most sacred belongings: the capacity to think about a problem, the joy of having an idea that solves it, the beautiful effort needed to consolidate an idea in our common language. And there is no turning back.
  We are mathematicians, and our whole world is in check. We wonder: is it checkmate? Can we take back control of our house, which will undoubtedly not work in the same way?
  Paradoxically, the weapons that attacked us are built on some of our own ideas. Of course, it is not entirely our work. The computer science knowledge needed to develop these large models evolved in both its theoretical and its material aspects. As technology evolved (infinitely small processors, infinitely large computing centers), turning quantity into quality, computer scientists encoded into software the ideas needed to produce these tools (let us not call them weapons).
  These notes look into the past and the future of the mathematical profession. What will inevitably happen? What will remain and what will disappear? And, in consequence, what is our line of action? To organize the ideas, after some introductory historical comments, we try to answer the questions: (1) Is mathematics necessary for the development of our society? (2) Will mathematicians be necessary in the near future? (3) How the profession will change, through a list of exercises: open questions and possible actions.

authors.name: Ernesto Mordecki
authors.institution: Universidad de la República de Uruguay

papers.title: Fractional Fefferman--Stein inequalities on infinite rooted $k$-ary trees
papers.abstract:
We study weighted endpoint estimates for the centered fractional maximal operator on the infinite rooted $k$-ary tree, $T$. Our first result is a Fefferman--Stein type estimate \[ w\bigl(\{M_\alpha f>\lambda\}\bigr) \lesssim_{\alpha,s} \frac1\lambda\sum_{x\in T}|f(x)|M_{\alpha,s}w(x), \qquad s>1, \] with a constant independent of the branching parameter $k$. Although the proof is inspired by the non-fractional argument of Ombrosi, Rivera-R\'ios and Safe in \cite{ORRS}, the fractional normalization introduces a genuinely new scale interaction. At radius $r$, one must renormalize the function by $k^{r\alpha}$ while keeping the dyadic cutoff at $k^r$; this leads to a new summation mechanism involving simultaneously $k^{r\alpha}$ and $k^{r(1-\alpha)}$.
  We then study sharpness and the geometry of admissible weights. We construct counterexamples showing that the estimate cannot in general be reduced to $s=1$ for any $0<\alpha<1$. In the subcritical range $0<\alpha<1/2$, we characterize power-type radial weights satisfying the natural fractional $A_1$ condition and prove that the failure persists after any fixed finite number of iterations of $M_\alpha$. We also prove that $M_\alpha w\lesssim w$ is necessary for the corresponding weighted weak type estimate but is not sufficient in the subcritical range. Finally, we identify a phase transition: for $1/2\le\alpha<1$ no nonzero global weight can satisfy $M_\alpha w\lesssim w$.

authors.name: Jorgelina Recchi
authors.institution: Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas

papers.title: Proof of the Cordero-Torregrosa Conjecture and an Improved Order Bound for Paired Jacobian Evaluations
papers.abstract:
In solving systems of nonlinear equations, one of the main objectives is to construct iterative methods that attain high orders of convergence using as few evaluations as possible. However, the information a method obtains during each iteration imposes limitations on the order it can guarantee. The Cordero--Torregrosa conjecture proposes a bound on this order in terms of the number of evaluations of the function and its Jacobian.
  In this work, we prove this bound for the universal local order of one iteration, without requiring the number of Jacobian evaluations to be less than or equal to the number of function evaluations. In particular, our result also covers the case in which more evaluations of the Jacobian than of the function are performed. The proof encompasses deterministic, causal, memoryless methods whose rules may be arbitrary, without imposing rationality, continuity, or computability conditions.
  Moreover, we prove that when each Jacobian evaluation is performed at a point where the value of the function is already known, a more restrictive bound on the order of convergence can be obtained. Finally, we propose a new conjecture that establishes a refined bound through a product of factors determined by the distribution of evaluations, under additional dimensional conditions. These results provide a better understanding of the limitations imposed by the available information and raise new possibilities for studying high-order iterative methods.

papers.title: Global Two-Sided Estimates for Time-Fractional Diffusion Kernels on Hyperbolic Space
papers.abstract: We study time-fractional diffusion on real hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$, $n\ge2$, with Caputo order $0<\alpha<1$. We establish global two-sided pointwise estimates for the homogeneous fundamental kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$ and the inhomogeneous (Duhamel) kernel $Y_{\mathbb H}(t,r)$, uniformly over all $t>0$ and positive geodesic distances $r$. By combining inverse-stable subordination with global bounds for the hyperbolic heat kernel, we distinguish a short-time local regime, a large-time interior region, and an exterior region governed by a saddle-point problem with parameter $r/t$. Both kernels have the same exterior exponential rate, while their amplitudes are related by an explicit saddle-point factor. The estimates are uniformly comparable on the interfaces between regimes, recover the Euclidean time-fractional singularities at small scales, and identify the influence of hyperbolic geometry on large-scale decay. The kernel $Z_{\mathbb H}$ also describes the one-time marginal density of hyperbolic Brownian motion under an independent inverse stable clock. This representation yields a radial limit law, moment and quantile asymptotics, and a change in the mean square displacement from order $t^\alpha$ at small times to order $t^{2\alpha}$ at large times.

papers.title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. We argue, through an information view of the feedback, that an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies. We propose Breakpoint Debugging (BPD), which returns the failed program annotated inline with its variables' runtime values. We take the tasks that iterative repair failed to fix with five repair attempts and compare two ways of spending five further generations on them: BPD, and resampling. On BigCodeBench, BPD repairs 26.7% of these tasks against 22.4%, and its advantage grows with model size. On HumanEval, BPD outperforms resampling but only slightly, and on LiveCodeBench, fresh sampling repairs more (6.5% against 4.9%). Furthermore, BPD reduces unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench. Using only the first failing test's trace, it outperforms tracing all failing tests while using fewer tokens than both all-trace BPD and plain iterative repair. On LiveCodeBench, BPD gives no gain even on the public tests, so a visible failing input is not enough for a trace to help. These results match the information view: a trace helps only when the test exposes a failing input, and the fault is an implementation slip; otherwise, a repair loop should resample rather than trace.

papers.title: Special line bundles on tetragonal curves
papers.abstract: One can associate a pair of vector bundles $(E, F)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ to every tetragonal curve: $E$ is the Tschirnhausen bundle and $F$ records numerical data of the ideal for the curve under its relative canonical embedding. In this note, we show that a Hurwitz--Brill--Noether general tetragonal curve must have balanced $E$, $F$ bundles, and provide counterexamples for the converse when $g = 8$ or $g \geq 10$.

papers.title: The quaternionic reflection groups with imprimitive complexifications and the finite subgroups of GL(2,C)
papers.abstract: We give a transparent development of the quaternionic reflection groups which have imprimitive complexifications, including a description of their reflections and the corresponding normal reflection subgroups. They are seen to be of rank one or rank two, and are obtained from minimal complex reflection groups by the addition of one quaternionic reflection and a complex scalar matrix of finite order. In the case of the rank two groups, we use our techniques to consider the broader question of what are the minimal irreducible subgroups of GL(2,C) with a given collineation group. This leads to a complete classification of the finite irreducible subgroups of GL(2,C) in terms of the minimal groups, with the groups giving rise to quaternionic reflection groups located within it.

papers.title: Price-Volume Correlations Are Always Zero
papers.abstract: We argue that the use of the empirical time series of values, volumes, and prices of consecutive trades made during the averaging interval to calculate the price-volume correlation in a way that follows the definition of correlation always gives zero correlation. We show that the usual expression for the empirical calculation of the correlation misleads the researchers and doesn't fulfill the definition of price-volume correlation. The mistake has its origin in the dependence of volume weighted average price on the mean values and volumes of trades during the averaging interval but not on time series of prices only. The true sense of the declared positive or negative results of the empirical calculations of price-volume correlations made by numerous researchers in reality is determined by the difference between the volume weighted average price and its limiting expression of average price, which is correct only when all volumes of consecutive trades are constant, and multiplication of this difference by the mean trade volume. To empirically determine the statistical dependence between time series of prices and trade volumes, one should calculate the correlations between prices and squares of trade volumes or correlations between squares of prices and squares of volumes. We derive the expressions for empirical calculations of these correlations.

papers.title: Predicting next-week VIIRS fire detections in Bolivia: a reproducible benchmark with temporal and geographic evaluation
papers.abstract: Weekly detection forecasts could help prioritize fire monitoring across Bolivia. We estimate the probability of at least one fire detection by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite in each 0.05-degree cell during the following 7 days. Primary models were fixed before test scoring. Calibrated LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision-tree model, reaches 2023-2025 temporal-test average precision (AP) of 0.323 (95% block-bootstrap interval 0.222-0.383), compared with 0.167 for climatology and 0.143 for persistence. Its paired AP gain over climatology is 0.1567 (0.0998-0.2179). A separately selected geographic model reaches AP 0.384 versus 0.181 for persistence in regions excluded from fitting. In the temporal-test population, reviewing the highest-ranked 5% and 10% of eligible area would have covered 38.4% and 55.8% of cell-weeks with detections. Probabilities still overestimate detection frequency in the highest-probability group. Retrospective rainfall provides no clear AP improvement; the primary validation comparisons for vegetation, land cover and their combination are inconclusive. Positive secondary or exploratory intervals do not change those decisions. Evaluation requires complete target and recent-history observations and measures satellite detections, not individual fires, causes or burned area. Prospective evaluation should archive inputs at each weekly issue and measure ranking, calibration and the usefulness of selected cells for monitoring decisions.

In the Chiquitano dry forest, chaqueo uses fire to prepare land for agriculture and pasture (Maillard et al., 2024), within a broader lowland land-conversion context involving mechanized agriculture, cattle ranching and small-scale farming (Müller et al., 2012). Fundación Amigos de la Naturaleza (2019) reported a preliminary national burned area of 5,358,4925,358,492 ha as of 25 September 2019. August and September were the peak fire months in the Chiquitania hotspot record (Devisscher et al., 2016). This seasonal concentration motivates short-horizon forecasts to prioritize monitoring, while satellite detections alone reveal neither a fire’s cause nor its legality.

papers.title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
papers.abstract:
This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology.
  Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.

papers.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
papers.abstract:
LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge.
  We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query.
  Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
papers.intro:
LLM agents are increasingly deployed beyond question-answering: writing code, managing infrastructure, orchestrating multi-step workflows. Yet they are memoryless learners: every session begins from the same blank state. Every correction must be repeated. Every hard-won behavioral insight is lost.

LLM agents are increasingly deployed beyond question-answering: writing code, managing infrastructure, orchestrating multi-step workflows. Yet they are memoryless learners: every session begins from the same blank state. Every correction must be repeated. Every hard-won behavioral insight is lost.

Consider a security analyst correcting an agent over many sessions: “always check Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies before network configurations,” “use --recursive when scanning S3 buckets,” “that API returns paginated results, so loop.” Within each session the agent improves as corrections accumulate in context. But the next day every correction must be re-issued, in the same order, with the agent making the same mistakes with the same confidence.

The problem has two dimensions. First is the loss of human corrections: explicit feedback transferring domain expertise about metrics, parameters, and strategies. Second is the loss of self-generated patterns: signals from the agent’s own execution such as tool retries that eventually succeed, errors that force strategy changes, and outputs the user silently regenerates. Existing prompt-engineering practice is fundamentally lossy (most corrections never propagate to system prompts), situational (most judgments are conditional), and ignores self-generated signals entirely. What is needed is a system that captures situational judgments as they occur and surfaces the right judgment at the right moment.

The agent memory landscape has grown rapidly [5, 6]. Many systems emphasize facts, such as a meeting on Tuesday, a Python version, or a preference for dark mode. Other systems extend memory beyond factual recall by learning user preferences from edits [7] and reusable procedures from interaction traces [8, 9, 10]. We study how a tool-using agent can turn explicit corrections and implicit execution signals into actor-scoped guidance, determine when that guidance applies, and deliver it at the decision point where it can change behavior. Storing the correction “use QRR for enterprise revenue” is trivial; knowing when, how, and whether to apply it is the hard problem.

What the agent has is the session itself: an explicit human correction, or an implicit cue in its own execution, such as a tool call that fails and then succeeds on retry, or an output the user silently regenerates.

This paper makes three contributions: 1. DC-Bench. A benchmark of 71 scenarios across 9 behavioral dimensions and two agent domains, built from real traces captured by running agents in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. Each scenario seeds corrections on one subject and tests on another, so it measures whether a correction is applied, not whether it is recalled. 2. Forge Decision Context (forge_dc). A system that learns from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures without a reward signal, compiles both into scoped, actor-attributed rule directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. It reaches 95% compliance on DC-Bench, against 12–15% for factual-memory systems and 34–49% for procedural-memory baselines. 3. Empirical findings from a five-stage system progression. The progression reveals an advantage for directive-form memory, a retrieval gap between formatting and content rules, the failure of implicit signals without explicit extraction, and sensitivity to the injection channel (Section 7).

papers.title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
papers.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.
papers.intro:
To a model, weights are both meaning and behaviour. Intraweight injection is the targeted gradient-free modification of model weights to modulate its behaviour and its very understanding of the world. It is the art, as we shall see, of convincing a model that the word ‘saffron’ denotes, in fact, a six-sided solid of eight vertices (the object more commonly known to the rest of us as a cube), purely by way of gradient-free weight edits, and doing so in a manner that preserves other capabilities.

Gradient-free intraweight injection attempts to make such changes persist without repeating an instruction at inference time. Established methods, including ROME, MEMIT and MEND, provide ways to edit particular factual associations [1, 2, 3]. Recent work on weight-space programming asks whether a language model can read and modify a neural network’s weights directly [5]. Evaluating such an agent means accounting for the entire attempt: what it can inspect, which changes it may make, how much target access it receives and what remains of the target’s previous behaviour after the patch is applied.

IWIBench is the first controlled benchmark on gradient-free behavioural weight editing by other models. It targets ten exemplary weight editing task families. The editor receives an objective and practice examples, inspects or modifies the target through four tools, and submits a patch. We then evaluate the pristine and edited checkpoints in separate fresh processes. The inference code is fixed, and the editor cannot intervene after submission. Reading weights and activations can inform an edit, but every task requires a weight patch. The IWIBench repository contains the implementation, task definitions and results.

papers.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
papers.abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.
papers.intro:
Long-lived language model systems now maintain state across conversations and tasks. Personal and agent memory systems retain preferences, project facts, files, summaries, tool outputs, and prior decisions, allowing future inference to start from accumulated context rather than an empty prompt [10, 11, 12]. Open-weight frontier models are also increasingly optimized for agentic tool use and long-context work [14]. These trends make memory a runtime control problem: the model does not merely retrieve information; it is shaped by what the system allows to become cognitively available. The motivating case is emergent memory, in which useful context forms through repeated work, reinforcement, forgetting, and revision rather than being stored by hand [1]; the controller proposed here applies to persistent memory in general.

Mechanistic interpretability and model-editing work shows that causal interventions on model internals can localize or alter behavior [8, 9]. Influence functions trace training examples to predictions [7]. These literatures supply useful tools, but a persistent organizational memory system needs a distinct runtime question: Which memory intervention should be permitted to affect this model now, what effect is expected, and what should happen if the effect is wrong?

papers.title: Generative Search and Recommendation at Shopify
papers.abstract: Search and recommendation at Shopify require retrieving relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of products under strict latency constraints. We present SID-LLM, which casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens representing products. We jointly pre-train SID-LLM on catalog and behavioral data, giving search and recommendation a shared representation and training objective. We show that reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance. Furthermore, distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation quality over joint supervised fine-tuning without a statistically detected loss in search quality. Finally, for efficient serving, we pair multi-token prediction with a lightweight ranker, improving retrieval quality over our autoregressive baseline while reducing latency. We evaluate SID-LLM both as a standalone retriever and as a component of Shopify's production search and recommendation systems. As a standalone search system, SID-LLM achieves quality comparable to Shopify's existing multi-model search stack while meeting production latency requirements. Integrating SID-LLM into the search and recommendation stacks provides significant gains in both offline evaluations and online A/B tests. Together, these results demonstrate the practical value of semantic-ID generation as a unified approach to product discovery at scale.

Search and recommendation connect buyers with relevant products across Shopify’s large and diverse catalog across millions of merchants on their web storefront, Shopify-built Shop App, and Shopify’s Catalog API designed for conversational commerce and AI agents. Both require understanding products and their relevance to a particular buyer at the scale of billions of products with very low latency.

There is no explicit query expressing the buyer’s current need, so the model must infer it from this context. The task is to identify products the buyer is likely to engage with next.

Industrial recommendation systems commonly separate candidate retrieval from ranking (Covington et al., 2016). A two-tower retriever (Yi et al., 2019) encodes the buyer and each product separately and scores their compatibility with an inner product. This supports efficient nearest-neighbour retrieval, but compresses the buyer’s history into a fixed vector before scoring candidates. Multi-interest methods (Li et al., 2019) use several buyer vectors, each still computed independently of the candidate.

Sequential generative recommenders learn to predict the next item from the interaction sequence (Zhai et al., 2024). Representing products as atomic IDs gives each product its own learned embedding, with no content-based relationship between identifiers. Semantic-ID generation (Rajput et al., 2023) instead shares tokens across related products. In SID-LLM, the history remains part of the prompt throughout generation, and a pretrained language backbone provides an initial representation of product language. We evaluate the resulting generator both on its own candidates and on the purchases it adds to the combined candidate pool (Section 9.2.1).

Lexical retrieval matches query terms to product text through an inverted index, using a scoring function such as BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009). It is useful for exact terms such as brands and model numbers, but encounters a vocabulary mismatch when buyers and merchants use different words for the same thing (Furnas et al., 1987). Dense semantic retrieval addresses this mismatch by encoding queries and products into a shared vector space (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Nigam et al., 2019) and searching an approximate nearest-neighbour index (Jégou et al., 2011; Malkov and Yashunin, 2020). Like two-tower recommendation, it scores separately computed representations.

papers.title: Joint Approximation and the Mixed-Prime Character Group
papers.abstract: For the integer metric defined by the square denominators of two distinct primes, we prove simultaneous approximation to zero in one prime metric and to any prescribed integer in the other. A normalized convolution argument gives a uniform central spectral bound. Random relative translations of smooth weights produce an exact positive cas cade; Fourier positivity places every normalized finer convolution below its value at zero. A far-field recursion, the growth of merged square powers, and a two-term logarithmic-form estimate give summable fac tor bounds. Consequently, for every fixed pair of distinct primes p,q, the mixed continuous character group is Z[1/(pq)]/Z: no irrational pa rameter is continuous. The mixed completion is the product of the one-prime completions. For each fixed pair this also gives a compati ble rational join and a strictly finer compatible join of the associated real TVG topologies, with the same prescribed real character group. Exact witness search terminates at every strict precision and integer target. We retain the structural, density, divisibility, sequence and finite-certificate results leading to this proof. The existence argument does not give practical witness-size or runtime bounds, and it does not assume independence or equidistribution of the two digit systems. Se lected abstract components have been checked using Lean and Mathlib; the complete analytic argument has not been formalized. The corre sponding problem for three or more primes remains separate.

papers.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd's syndicates
papers.abstract: A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd's syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820's 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.

papers.intro:
Suppose an insurer with £500m of gross claims reserves wants to use the market’s worst reserve movements as stress scenarios. One candidate is Syndicate 5820’s 2016 year. During that year the estimated gross claims on its older underwriting years rose by an amount equal to 0.67 of the £57m of claims reserves it held at the start. Should the £500m book stress itself by 0.67 of its reserves? Across the market, small books’ movements are more dispersed than large books’. The transfer of this paper assumes that a movement is comparable between books once it is standardised by each book’s fitted scale. Under that assumption and the size law fitted here, 0.67 on the £57m book corresponds to about 0.34 on the £500m one. That is the model’s transfer, not an observed effect of the same event on a larger book, and not a demonstrated capital requirement. So a movement observed on one portfolio needs re-expressing on the target’s basis, under a stated assumption, before it is compared with the target’s own assumptions or reused as a scenario. This paper estimates one way to do that, and tests where it works.

The question matters for capital. Under Solvency II, retained in the United Kingdom as Solvency UK (Prudential Regulation Authority, 2024), the solvency capital requirement is calibrated to the 99.5% one-year value-at-risk (VaR) of basic own funds (European Parliament and Council, 2009). For reserves, one-year development compares the opening best estimate with claims paid during the year plus the closing best estimate of outstanding claims; it measures change over one year, not uncertainty over the full run-off (Merz and Wüthrich, 2008; Szatkowski and Delong, 2021; Munroe et al., 2018). A firm’s own history is short in the adverse tail, so calibration leans on pooled market data and tail extrapolation (CEIOPS, 2010; International Association of Insurance Supervisors, 2024). In its guidance for new syndicates, Lloyd’s Standard Model uses net volatilities calibrated to an average market portfolio; Lloyd’s notes that these may not suit an unusual book (Lloyd’s of London, 2024).

papers.title: The Drawing You Watch Is the Portrait You Keep: A Replayable Machine Portrait Studio
papers.abstract: Ask an image model for your portrait and a finished picture arrives: no first line, no second thoughts, no record of how it got there, and a different picture if you ask again. I built a portrait studio that works the other way. A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, each written with a city, a medium and a tempo of its own, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a drawing of themselves appear over 44 seconds. One still is sent after consent, a hosted image model returns a private study the sitter never sees, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document. The live drawing, the saved sheet, the vector export and the film all read that document, and a replay makes no model call, so the drawing you watch is the portrait you keep. I describe the compiler in enough detail to rebuild it and say plainly what it is: an authored reconstruction at a compressed speed, not a recorded hand. On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills and nearly all shorter than one video frame, and recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. The paper also traces a bug that matters more than any of that. The earlier compiler estimated the paper colour tile by tile, read dark skin as paper, and in all eight hands kept less of a deep-complexioned face than a fair one (13 to 48 percent against 41 to 56). On 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent), so the fairness question has moved upstream, to the study and the hosted model. The two test sitters are generated and differ in more than complexion, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet. The studio is live at https://everyfaceproject.com.

papers.title: Same Facts, Different Remedy: Linguistic Profiling and Arbitrariness in LLM and System One Decisions
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and the way complainants write varies with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES). We audit three remedy-decision systems using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that are instructed to preserve every fact: two generative LLMs that return a single label (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini) and a probabilistic "System One" model that returns a distribution over remedies (Jev). Using pre-registered hypotheses tested once on held-out complaints, we separate two phenomena that single-label audits conflate. At the group scale, older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies; these effects replicate but are small, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual scale, two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. In a variance-component analysis of the probabilistic model, persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation. The persona gaps are associated mainly with delivery (vocabulary, grammar, politeness) rather than content. Positive controls show that all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87% while retaining fact sensitivity, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent LLM auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites, and instability persisted among unflagged rewrites. Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in consequential administrative decisions, including the triage and resolution of consumer complaints. Complainants differ in how they write, and these differences are not random: vocabulary, grammar, formality and politeness vary with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES).

A system that responds to how a complaint is written rather than what it says can disadvantage particular groups without ever observing a demographic attribute. Sociolinguists have studied such linguistic profiling since the matched-guise experiments of Lambert et al. [14]. Recent work shows that LLMs exhibit covert dialect prejudice that standard alignment does not remove [9], and that LLM underwriting recommendations can differ across otherwise-identical applicants [1].

Most audits of such systems compare a single predicted label across demographic groups. This approach overlooks two issues. First, when a single label is sensitive to wording, option order or sampling noise, it produces disagreements that resemble disparities but are better described as arbitrariness. It is well established that prediction variance can be large enough to make individual decisions effectively arbitrary, and that it confounds fairness measurement [5, 15]. Arbitrariness carries its own normative weight [6]. An audit that does not separate arbitrariness from profiling cannot determine which problem it has identified. Second, audits rarely ask whether a statistically detectable disparity is material, or through which channel it operates. Both questions bear directly on whether, and how, to intervene.

papers.title: Quantitative group testing with a fixed shore: sharp asymptotics and exact formulas
papers.abstract: We study adaptive quantitative group testing with one defective item in each of two disjoint sets. When one set has fixed size, we determine the leading term of the difference between the binary bound and the largest searchable opposite set size. The result extends to fixed unions of complete bipartite graphs and to positive weighted sums of the opposite set sizes. We determine exact eventual formulas when the fixed set has six, seven or eight items. The eight-item formula has a period-three correction. papers.title: Slim Polygons, Hyperbolicity, and a new Quasi-Isometric Invariant
papers.abstract:
We introduce the slimness function, $\mathrm{Slim}_X(n)$, of a geodesic metric space, which records the maximal slimness of its geodesic polygons as a function of the number of sides. We study the large-scale behaviour of this function and its relation to hyperbolicity, growth function, and quasi-isometries.
  We first establish that the slimness function is a natural quasi-isometric invariant in the hyperbolic setting. We then obtain quantitative estimates for geodesic polygons in hyperbolic spaces and bounded-valency graphs. In particular, we show that sufficiently slow growth of the slimness function forces tree-like geometry. We also prove a decomposition result for hyperbolic groups admitting a finite graph of hyperbolic groups decomposition.
  Finally, we investigate the interaction between polygonal slimness and the growth of connected bounded-valency graphs. Combining the resulting estimates with large-scale dimension theory, we obtain criteria implying that an unbounded graph has asymptotic dimension one.

The geometry of metric spaces, particularly in the realm of geometric group theory, is deeply intertwined with large-scale invariants that capture coarse geometric structures. Classical notions such as Gromov hyperbolicity rely heavily on the concept of δ\delta-slim triangles (and polygons). In this paper, we systematically investigate the quantitative aspects of slimness for polygonal structures across various geodesic metric spaces.

papers.title: A Taxonomy-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Retrieval Effectiveness and Fairness Evaluation in Hiring
papers.abstract: While machine learning hiring tools are ubiquitous, the need for privacy regulations and commercial sensitivity makes public benchmarking legally complex. We address this challenge by introducing a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark to simultaneously evaluate retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles, our multilingual corpus features candidate profiles, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins. Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models reveals performance divergence from general MTEB scores, alongside fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages. This demonstrates that general benchmarks are insufficient for HR, requiring tailored evaluations to identify Pareto-optimal models that balance semantic accuracy and fairness.
papers.intro:
Human resources (HR) increasingly relies on machine learning for candidate evaluation and job matching (Geyik et al., 2019), yet the methods used to validate these tools for bias are rarely fully transparent (Raghavan et al., 2020). Furthermore, evaluating these models in real-world scenarios is often complicated by the commercial sensitivity and personally identifiable information (PII) inherent in professional data.

Furthermore, evaluating these models in real-world scenarios is often complicated by the commercial sensitivity and personally identifiable information (PII) inherent in professional data.

To bridge this evaluation gap, we present a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark designed to simultaneously measure retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Leveraging an empirical foundation of over 660K real freelancer profiles, we constructed a diverse, multilingual corpus of candidate records, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins, yielding 1.6M scored interactions.

To bridge this evaluation gap, we present a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark designed to simultaneously measure retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Leveraging an empirical foundation of over 660K real freelancer profiles, we constructed a diverse, multilingual corpus of candidate records, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins, yielding 1.6M scored interactions.

Auditing state-of-the-art text embedding models with this benchmark reveals several domain-specific insights. We find that model performance does not strictly correlate with parameter count or inference time. Furthermore, domain-specific evaluation matters: for instance, Arctic Embed (v2, l) outperforms instruction-tuned models on project briefs by 0.07 NDCG@10 despite scoring 6–7 points lower on general MTEB multilingual benchmarks (Muennighoff et al., 2023). When evaluating grammatically gendered languages, we observe no systematic relationship between model scale and fairness: models of similar size can differ markedly in their robustness to gender perturbations. This work highlights that fairness and retrieval effectiveness are not necessarily conflicting objectives, and that tailored evaluations can identify Pareto-optimal models that balance both.
