papers.title: RoleWalk: training-free structural embeddings for directed graphs that transfer across graphs
papers.abstract: Structural role embeddings describe a node by its position in a graph - hub, bridge, periphery, member of a dense core - rather than by who its neighbours are. Existing methods either learn coordinates specific to one graph (struc2vec, Role2Vec, RESD) or read scales and normalisations from the whole graph (GraphWave, Digraphwave), so the same neighbourhood can receive different coordinates in two graphs; few read edge directions. We present RoleWalk, a training-free embedding that follows a short lazy random walk from each node and records, at each step, two distributions: that of the transition probabilities, through its characteristic function at a fixed grid of frequencies, and that of the walker's distance to its starting node. On directed graphs, walks that go forward then backward add who shares a node's targets or sources. The embedding depends only on a node's neighbourhood within a fixed radius, so its coordinates mean the same thing in every graph. We show that, without curvature, it is the kernel mean embedding of the walk's footprint, that it separates graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot, and that pruning small probabilities comes with a per-node error certificate. Empirically, RoleWalk is competitive with the best role embeddings on five classification benchmarks at a fraction of their cost, has the highest scores on real directed roles in Wikipedia adminship, exceeds the published accuracy of Digraphwave at every noise level of its own Enron network-alignment benchmark, transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than existing inductive embeddings, hand-made features and a trained GIN, and embeds a million nodes in 20 s to 3 min on one CPU core. The code is open source (BSD license): https://github.com/kerighan/rolewalk
papers.intro:
Two airports can play the same role — a regional hub feeding a national one — without sharing a single route. Structural embeddings capture this kind of similarity: nodes are close when their neighbourhoods look alike, wherever they are in the graph [9, 19, 4]. Three properties matter in these uses, and current methods rarely combine them. Transfer: for alignment, or for a model trained on one graph and applied to another, a coordinate must mean the same thing in every graph. Methods that fit a skip-gram model or an autoencoder per graph [19, 1, 27] produce coordinates that are only defined up to that fit; GraphWave [4] averages over all nn nodes and picks its diffusion scale from each graph’s spectrum, so identical neighbourhoods in graphs of different sizes get different coordinates. Directions: in a vote, a citation or an email, who points to whom is part of the role, yet most role embeddings drop directions. Cost: in our benchmarks, learned and diffusion methods take seconds to minutes on graphs of a thousand nodes, and most do not run at a hundred thousand within an hour or 16 GB.

RoleWalk starts from a simple observation. After ww steps of a random walk from node uu, two things characterise uu’s position: how concentrated the walk is (a hub spreads its mass thinly, a leaf keeps most of it) and how far it has gone (a node in a triangle-rich region keeps returning near its start). papers.title: The Woo-Yong conjecture
papers.abstract: We prove the Woo-Yong conjecture: the non-Gorenstein locus of a type A Schubert variety is the union of its generically non-Gorenstein maximal singular components. More strongly, at every scheme point, local Weil divisor classes are detected at the generic points of the maximal singular components containing that point. For arbitrary finite crystallographic type, the analogous localization map is injective on the torsion subgroup of the source local class group. This determines Cartier indices of locally $\mathbb{Q}$-Cartier divisors and gives the Woo-Yong criterion on the $\mathbb{Q}$-Gorenstein locus. A type D family shows the necessity of this hypothesis: the ambient variety is generically Gorenstein along its singular locus but not $\mathbb{Q}$-Gorenstein along a deeper nonempty locus. The type A proof and the counterexamples are geometric; the general torsion proof also uses bounded finite inputs with explicit certificates and reproducible reconstruction programs.

papers.title: A splitting theorem for Einstein manifolds with symmetries
papers.abstract: We prove that every negative-Einstein manifold with cocompact symmetries splits isometrically as a Riemannian product $H \times K$ with $H$ homogeneous and $K$ compact. This confirms a conjecture due to B\"ohm and Lafuente. As a consequence, we obtain a new proof of the 1975 Alekseevskii conjecture.

papers.title: The End-of-Day Reversal After 2019: A Pre-Registered Test on S&P 500 Stocks Excluding Heavily Traded Names
papers.abstract: Baltussen, Da and Soebhag (2025) document an end-of-day reversal in U.S. stocks through December 2019: intraday losers outperform intraday winners over the last half hour of trading. We test it on later data, on point-in-time S&P 500 members excluding about 80 heavily traded stocks we had examined in earlier, unpublished work. Under a private pre-registration, the 2016-2019 data had to reproduce the published sign before any statistic linking the sort to the outcome was computed on later primary-sample data. Measured to the last trade before the closing auction, the dollar-volume-weighted reversal is 3.13 bps per day (t = 7.5) in 2016-2019 and 3.05 bps (t = 3.0) in 2023-2026, with a one-sided 95% bound on the decline of 61%. The result depends on the window: the reversal is indistinguishable from zero in 2020-2022, 2023 carries much of the later estimate, and from 2020 onward it is 1.69 bps (t = 2.3), with a bound of 91%. A proxy sample, added after the run, gives 2.81 and 3.86 bps. On the full index the reversal falls from 3.40 to 0.74 bps (t of the change -1.83, short of the registered bar of -3); descriptive comparisons concentrate this weakness in the very largest stocks. No pre-registered mechanism test passes.

papers.title: Orthogonal Norm Growth in Two-Tower Retrieval: A Popularity Mechanism for Unified Discovery
papers.abstract: Unified search and recommendation systems may update the same item vectors from both interaction streams. We study how repeated updates can increase an item vector's norm and affect retrieval under an unnormalized dot product. A cosine-only loss makes the output gradient perpendicular to the current item vector - tangent to its constant-norm sphere. Training changes encoder parameters, however, so the realized item-vector movement need not remain tangent. We derive sufficient conditions under which it does; every nonzero update then increases squared norm by its squared length. When the tasks share an item encoder, sequential updates from both can accumulate in the same norm, which raw-inner-product serving can expose for either task. This conditional result is not a theorem about joint SGD. Controlled ablations test these conditions. On MovieLens 32M and Amazon Books, accumulated tangent movement accompanies frequency-norm association and additional head-item exposure under raw-dot rather than normalized-item ranking. In a nonlinear tower combining a per-item ID vector with a shared content encoding, active item movement remains near-tangent. We separate its norm change into the ID-update contribution and other output changes, then use a matched training intervention that removes immediate norm growth caused by the ID-row update. The intervention reduces norm-related exposure but also recommendation utility, so it is diagnostic rather than a proposed mitigation. Our logs are recommendation-only: the formulation supplies a shared-representation audit, while prevalence in joint traffic remains open.
papers.intro:
Search and recommendation are complementary routes to a shared catalog: search starts from an explicit query, whereas recommendation infers an information need from a user and context. Unified systems connect their behavior sequences, supervision, model parameters, or item representations (Yao et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). At candidate-generation scale, both tasks commonly use bi-encoder or two-tower retrieval: a request-side encoder produces a query or user vector, an item-side encoder produces a catalog vector, and a simple similarity enables precomputation and approximate nearest-neighbor search (Huang et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2024). Sharing the item tower is efficient, but it also lets training on one surface change the representation served on the other. Consider an item that receives repeated search-side updates. Under the conditions derived below, those updates add to the squared norm of the same catalog vector later used by recommendation. If recommendation retrieves with raw inner products, this search-derived magnitude enters its scores even if its request tower is unchanged; normalizing item vectors before serving removes this particular channel. This cross-surface dependency motivates measuring norm growth separately by task.

papers.title: One complex metric and geometric adelic nefness
papers.abstract: We prove that an arithmetic adelic line bundle on a smooth quasi-projective variety over a number field has nef geometric part if its prescribed continuous metric at one complex embedding has semipositive first Chern current. The proof constructs semiample approximations to every positive rational ample perturbation by boundary extension, multiplier ideals, and Nadel vanishing, followed by specialization and Galois descent. This gives geometric nefness of Gao--Zhang's canonical Gross--Schoen adelic line bundle.

papers.title: Against All Likelihood
papers.abstract: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth. Unlikely events happen every day, and frequently repeated statements can be false. Drawing on a philosophical tradition that ties objectivity to invariance rather than probability (from Nozick's account of objective facts and Wigner's principles of invariance to the structural realism of Poincar\'e and Cassirer), we argue that the truth of a statement should be judged not by its probability under a single distribution, but by its invariance across relevant transformations of the environment. We connect this view to machine learning literature on out-of-distribution generalization and invariant learning, sketch how invariance could be tested at inference time with language models, and discuss implications for continual learning.
papers.intro:
What are the statistical footprints of truth? By scaling transformer architectures with maximum likelihood estimation, we have built systems that mimic vast textual corpora, producing fluent text often indistinguishable from human writing. Yet, while these models are good at reproducing the form of knowledge, they can miss the truth behind it: they hallucinate facts with high confidence (Kalai et al., 2026), fail to extrapolate simple algorithmic rules to longer sequences (Ahuja and Mansouri, 2024), and degrade outside the distribution of their training data (Yuan et al., 2023).11 1 Throughout this article, the terms “truth” and “objective fact” are used interchangeably.

Yet, while these models are good at reproducing the form of knowledge, they can miss the truth behind it: they hallucinate facts with high confidence (Kalai et al., 2026), fail to extrapolate simple algorithmic rules to longer sequences (Ahuja and Mansouri, 2024), and degrade outside the distribution of their training data (Yuan et al., 2023).11 1 Throughout this article, the terms “truth” and “objective fact” are used interchangeably.

We argue that the reliance on likelihood as the primary proxy for truth is a category error. Machines trained via maximum likelihood produce probable tokens: x^t+1∼P^D(xt+1∣x1:t),\hat{x}_{t+1}\sim\hat{P}_{D}(x_{t+1}\mid x_{1:t}), where P^D\hat{P}_{D} is the model’s estimate of the next-token distribution of the training data DD. Likelihood is therefore a historical metric, rooted in the conditional correlations of the training data, and not in the structural reality of what is true.

On the one hand, likelihood is not necessary for truth. In fact, low-probability events happen all the time. On a daily basis, someone wins the lottery, someone else is diagnosed with a rare disease, and yet another person stumbles upon an old acquaintance on their commute to work. A model optimized solely for likelihood will discount such rare events, favoring generic continuations over sharp, improbable truths.

A model optimized solely for likelihood will discount such rare events, favoring generic continuations over sharp, improbable truths.

On the other hand, likelihood is not sufficient for truth. A lie repeated a million times in the training corpus becomes highly probable, yet it remains false. Hallucinations are a related symptom: outputs that are likely under surface statistics but unsupported by fact. The probability of a statement under a model reflects not its truth, but simply how often similar statements appear in the training corpus. For this reason, Bottou and Schölkopf (2025) argue that maximum likelihood estimation yields fiction machines, that is, models that latch onto the narrative necessities of their training data and inference context.

For this reason, Bottou and Schölkopf (2025) argue that maximum likelihood estimation yields fiction machines, that is, models that latch onto the narrative necessities of their training data and inference context.

Truth, by contrast, is associated with stability. In Invariances, Nozick (2001) argues that objective facts are invariant across admissible transformations. They remain constant when perspectives shift, environments change, and the subjective conditions of the observer are stripped away. Similarly, Stephen Gaukroger argues that objectivity “involves the ability to shift perspective,” making judgments “free of prejudice and bias” and providing us with “accurate representations” of the world (Gaukroger, 2012). The limit of this ideal, according to Thomas Nagel, is the “view from nowhere,” a perspective that transcends the limitations of any particular subject or location: To acquire a more objective understanding of some aspect of life or the world, we step back from our initial view of it and form a new conception which has that view and its relation to the world as its object. In other words, we place ourselves in the world that is to be understood. The old view then comes to be regarded as an appearance, more subjective than the new view, and correctable or confirmable by reference to it. The process can be repeated, yielding a still more objective conception. The wider the range of subjective types to which a form of understanding is accessible—the less it depends on specific subjective capacities—the more objective it is. […] We may think of reality as a set of concentric spheres, progressively revealed as we detach gradually from the contingencies of the self. (Nagel, 1986, pp. 4–5)

On the invariance account, the pursuit of truth consists in identifying what resists variation across distributional shifts; more i.i.d. data may only reinforce bias. Rather than seeking precise predictions about a single setting (depth), the invariance approach advocates simple models for a complex world to generalize across environments (breadth). Consider a bicycle: most riders cannot draw an accurate sketch of one (Lawson, 2006), yet they reliably predict its behavior across changes in speed, weight, maintenance conditions, and weather. In fact, Nozick argues that greater accuracy can hinder predictive power across a wide array of circumstances:

An accurate representation is not the same as a true one, and “more accurate” does not necessarily mean better. The greater accuracy might make the representation too confusing or too difficult to work with, as does a map with too many details. What is wanted is something accurate enough for the purposes. […] We can distinguish the breadth of a general characterization, the range of possible worlds in which it applies, from the depth of a characterization, how much it tells us, and explains, about the actual things of that kind. Max Born considered the capacity to look past surface statistics and grasp invariant features to be “the most impressive fact of our mental structure.” For Born (1953), invariance was the central epistemological tool driving scientific progress:

The main advances in the conceptual structure of physics consist in the discovery that some quantity which was regarded as the property of a thing is in fact only the property of a projection. […] The transformations of classical mechanics, often called Galilean transformations, kept space and time apart. The experiences condensed in the theory of relativity showed that this does not agree with facts. One has to use a wider group, called Lorentz transformations, in order to introduce an intimate connection between space co-ordinates and time. Naturally, quantities regarded by the older theory as invariants, like distances in rigid systems, time intervals shown by clocks in different positions, masses of bodies, are now found to be projections, components of invariant quantities not directly accessible. […] The feature which suggests reality is always some kind of invariance of a structure independent of the aspect, the projection. (Born, 1953, p. 144)

papers.title: Trace and Regularized Index of Callias Operators on Hyperbolic Space
papers.abstract: Let $d \geq 3$ be odd. On hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^d$, we consider Callias-type operators, i.e. Dirac-Schr\"odinger operators of the form $D = ic \nabla + A$, where $c \nabla$ is the Dirac operator and $A$ a function with values in the self-adjoint operators, and provide an explicit formula for the iterated trace $\text{tr}_{L^2(\mathbb{H}^d,H)} \text{tr}_{S}( e^{-tD^*D} - e^{-tDD^*})$, $t>0$, that appears in the formulation of the Witten index. Thereby, the operator $D$ is not assumed to be Fredholm.

papers.title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
papers.abstract: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

The full-batch k-means algorithm, also referred to as the Lloyd algorithm, starts from an initial set of centroids. At each iteration, Lloyd performs full-dataset assignment to the centroids and then updates each centroid as a mean of its assigned points. The optimization is guaranteed to converge to a local minimum in a finite number of iterations (Lloyd, 1982). In practice, the number of iterations (or epochs) is capped.

At each iteration, Lloyd performs full-dataset assignment to the centroids and then updates each centroid as a mean of its assigned points. The optimization is guaranteed to converge to a local minimum in a finite number of iterations (Lloyd, 1982). In practice, the number of iterations (or epochs) is capped.

Another line of work, known as mini-batch k-means, updates the centroids from mini-batches rather than from the whole dataset. It has proven itself a low-latency alternative to full-batch Lloyd for web-scale clustering (MacQueen, 1967; Sculley, 2010). It is also used in streaming settings, where the incoming data may undergo concept drift (Apache Spark, 2014; Bidaurrazaga et al., 2021), codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs being an example (van den Oord et al., 2017).

Where mini-batch kk-means has been compared to Lloyd, it typically has a higher approximation error, though with faster convergence. For static fixed datasets, Lloyd remains the default in the literature, reaching the lowest MSE when run with enough iterations or combined with initialization schemes (Hartigan and Wong, 1979; Fränti and Sieranoja, 2019; Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007; Béjar, 2013). Sculley (2010)’s mini-batch kk-means and MacQueen (1967)’s sequential formulation are the most influential mini-batch implementations with a gradient descent update rule. In both, a centroid is the running mean of the points assigned to it throughout the training (Bottou and Bengio, 1994).

Our approach, e-means, applies a specialized optimization procedure based on exponential moving average (EMA) updates (van den Oord et al., 2017) with mini-batches. Where VQ-VAEs use EMA to track a shifting embedding distribution, we apply several modifications to retarget it at the canonical kk-means problem, i.e. minimizing MSE on a fixed dataset. papers.title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting
papers.abstract:
Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken.
  In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found.
  We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $\Delta$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 \Delta$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.

papers.title: Deformation of Associative Submanifolds joining Minimal Surfaces in Hyperbolic Geometry
papers.abstract: Donaldson and Thomas proposed a Floer-type theory on a Calabi-Yau threefold $M$, generated by the complex curves, and whose boundary operator is given by counting appropriate associative submanifolds in $M\times \mathbb{R}$. We consider a similar setting, in which the Calabi-Yau manifold is replaced by the twistor space $Z$ of an oriented hyperbolic 4-manifold $X$ and the $J$-holomorphic curves in $Z$ project to minimal surfaces in $X$. We give a formula for the virtual dimension of (a subset of) the moduli space of associatives asymptotic to a pair of $J$-holomorphic curves in $Z$, proving it equals the difference of the Morse indices of the corresponding minimal surfaces in $X$.

papers.title: How far does a hash-only sender go? A pre-registered map of sender memory versus bits for short text messages
papers.abstract: Can a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain? We answer with one pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver 100% of the messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.
papers.intro:
Some links charge dearly per bit or per frame: LoRa, LoRaWAN at low data rates, APRS, satellite short-burst data. We use these links only to price bits and frames; we do not claim a market for free text on them. Language models compress text well, but a compressor that codes with a model’s predictions needs the same model at the decoder, and in practice at both ends [14, 4]. (For LLMZip this is our inference from the scheme, not a statement of its abstract.) We ask the opposite question: can the sender stay modest, computing only hashes at run time, while a receiver with a language model reconstructs the message?

papers.title: Directed systems of A-spaces and weak cores
papers.abstract: We prove that for any regular CW-complex $X$ there exists a quotient map $X\to Y$ that is a weak homotopy equivalence and which is minimal with that property, meaning that any quotient $Y\to Z$ that is a weak equivalence, must be a homeomorphism. The space $Y$ we obtain is an Alexandroff space: a space in which arbitrary intersections of open sets are open. The weak core $Y$ of $X$ is not unique in general. We study homotopy invariants preserved by filtered colimits of Alexandroff spaces. This can be seen as an analogous to Stong's theory of cores of finite topological spaces.

An Alexandroff space (or A-space) is a topological space in which arbitrary intersections of open sets are open. In 1937, Alexandroff [1] showed that A-spaces are the same as preordered sets. More specifically, there is an isomorphism between the category 𝖠𝖳𝗈𝗉\mathsf{ATop} of A-spaces with continuous functions, and the category of preordered sets with order-preserving maps, which is the identity on the underlying sets and the corresponding maps. Moreover, this functor restricts to an isomorphism between T0T_{0} A-spaces and posets.
